questions.question: As pilot-in-command of a Part 91 helicopter, what is your responsibility regarding the airworthiness of the aircraft before flight?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.7, the PIC is directly responsible for, and the final authority as to, the safe operation of the aircraft. The PIC must not begin a flight if the helicopter is known to be in an unairworthy condition. Additionally, 14 CFR 91.7(b) states the PIC must discontinue a flight when an unairworthy condition becomes apparent. The FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8 reinforces that the PIC is responsible for ensuring the helicopter is in an airworthy condition before each flight. This includes verifying required inspections are current, all required documents are aboard, and no unresolved maintenance discrepancies exist that would make the aircraft unairworthy.

questions.question: During preflight you discover a discrepancy — a non-essential light is inoperative. Walk me through the two methods under Part 91 you could legally use to defer that item, and what documentation is required for each.
questions.answer: Under Part 91, two methods exist for deferring inoperative equipment: (1) 14 CFR 91.213(d) — the 'no MEL' deferral provision. You must determine the equipment is not required by the VFR day equipment list (91.205), not required by an AD, not required by the RFM/POH, and is not part of the type design required for the certificate. If all criteria are met, the item must be deactivated (if it could be a hazard), placarded INOPERATIVE, and a logbook entry made describing the inoperative item. If deactivation requires maintenance (including removal), a certificated mechanic must perform it. (2) FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List (MEL) — the FAA considers an approved MEL to be an STC for that specific aircraft. The MEL lists specific items that may be deferred with defined conditions and procedures. The PIC determines airworthiness per the MEL conditions. Both methods require the inoperative item to be placarded and a maintenance record entry made.

questions.question: Your helicopter has just come out of a 100-hour inspection but hasn't had its annual inspection in 13 months. Can you legally fly it under Part 91, and what inspections would be overdue?
questions.answer: No, you cannot legally fly it under Part 91 for general operations. Under 14 CFR 91.409(a), aircraft operated under Part 91 must undergo an annual inspection every 12 calendar months. If the annual has not been completed within the past 12 calendar months, the aircraft is not airworthy for general Part 91 operations. The 100-hour inspection (required under 91.409(b) only when the aircraft is used for hire or flight instruction for hire) does not substitute for the annual. At 13 months, the annual is overdue. The only legal flight permitted without a current annual would be a ferry flight under a Special Flight Permit issued per 14 CFR 21.197, which authorizes flight to a location where maintenance can be performed. The owner or operator bears responsibility for ensuring required inspections are current per 14 CFR 91.409.

questions.question: What is a Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (SAIB), and how does it differ from an Airworthiness Directive? Does a pilot have to comply with an SAIB?
questions.answer: A Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (SAIB) is a communication tool issued by the FAA to alert owners, operators, and manufacturers of design concerns or unsafe trends that do not yet meet the legal threshold requiring an AD. SAIBs are informational and advisory in nature — they are NOT regulatory and compliance is NOT mandatory. They typically recommend actions such as increased inspection intervals, awareness of a trend, or voluntary maintenance practices. An Airworthiness Directive, by contrast, is issued under 14 CFR Part 39 when an unsafe condition is found to exist and is legally enforceable — compliance is mandatory. A pilot reviewing maintenance records should confirm AD compliance is documented but may simply note an SAIB as a recommendation. The FAA may later upgrade an SAIB to an AD if the unsafe condition becomes confirmed.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 39; FAA Advisory Circular AC 39-7D

questions.question: Your helicopter has a major structural repair that was completed and signed off in the maintenance logbook, but the 337 Form was never submitted to the FAA. Is the aircraft airworthy, and what are the implications for you as PIC if you fly it?
questions.answer: This is a serious airworthiness concern. Under 14 CFR 43.9, all maintenance must be recorded in the aircraft maintenance records. Under 14 CFR 43.7, only authorized persons may approve an aircraft for return to service after a major repair or alteration. However, major repairs and major alterations also require FAA Form 337 to be submitted to the FAA Aircraft Registry and a copy retained in the aircraft records per 14 CFR 43.9(b). If the 337 was never submitted, the major repair documentation is incomplete and the aircraft may not have been legally returned to service. As PIC, under 14 CFR 91.7 you are responsible for determining airworthiness before flight. Flying an aircraft with an unresolved major repair documentation deficiency could expose you to a certificate action under 14 CFR 91.7 and potentially 14 CFR 91.409. You should ground the aircraft until the mechanic or repair station that performed the work submits the 337 and the records are complete.
questions.follow_up: What if the mechanic tells you they submitted the 337 verbally to the FSDO but never mailed the form — is that acceptable, and who has ultimate enforcement exposure?
questions.follow_up_answer: No, verbal notification is not acceptable. 14 CFR 43.9(b) requires a completed FAA Form 337 to be submitted in duplicate to the FAA, with a copy retained in the aircraft records. There is no provision for verbal or informal submission. The certificated mechanic or repair station that performed and signed off the work bears primary responsibility for submitting the 337, as they are the ones approving the aircraft for return to service. However, as PIC, you still bear responsibility under 91.7 for not flying an aircraft you know has incomplete airworthiness documentation. Both the mechanic and the PIC could face certificate action. The owner/operator is also responsible under 14 CFR 91.409 for ensuring required maintenance records are complete.

questions.question: A new AD is issued with an immediate compliance requirement, but your helicopter is grounded 50 miles away at a remote field with no maintenance available. What legal options do you have to get the helicopter to a maintenance facility?
questions.answer: When an AD prohibits flight and maintenance is unavailable at the current location, the pilot may apply for a Special Flight Permit (also called a ferry permit) under 14 CFR 21.197 and 21.199. A Special Flight Permit authorizes a flight to a location where maintenance can be performed, for the purpose of making required repairs or alterations, even if the aircraft does not currently meet applicable airworthiness requirements. The application is made to the FAA FSDO responsible for the area where the aircraft is located. The applicant must provide: the purpose of the flight, the itinerary, the crew required, any limitations needed for safe operation, and any other information requested by the FAA. The FAA may impose conditions on the permit. The permit is issued for a specific flight or series of flights and does not make the aircraft airworthy — it only authorizes the specific transit flight. The owner, operator, and PIC share responsibility for complying with all conditions stated in the permit.
questions.follow_up: Can you carry passengers on a Special Flight Permit ferry flight, and can you fly the helicopter at night under such a permit?
questions.follow_up_answer: Generally, no passengers should be carried unless specifically authorized by the Special Flight Permit. The permit is issued to allow safe transit to a maintenance facility, and the FAA typically restricts or prohibits passenger carriage because the aircraft is not in an airworthy condition. Night flight would also be subject to the specific conditions and limitations stated in the permit — the FAA may restrict the flight to daytime VFR only, depending on the nature of the unairworthy condition. Any limitations imposed by the permit are legally binding on the PIC. The PIC must carefully read and comply with all conditions in the Special Flight Permit, and if the conditions do not address a specific scenario (such as night flight), it would be safest to request clarification from the issuing FSDO before attempting that operation.

questions.question: Under what regulation is a certificated pilot allowed to perform preventive maintenance on an aircraft they own or operate?
questions.answer: 14 CFR 43.3(g) allows a certificated pilot (private, recreational, or sport pilot certificate or higher) to perform preventive maintenance on any aircraft owned or operated by that pilot, provided the aircraft is not used under Part 121, 129, or 135 operations. The specific list of allowable preventive maintenance tasks is found in 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A(c).

questions.question: Give me three specific examples of preventive maintenance tasks a private pilot is legally authorized to perform on their helicopter.
questions.answer: Per 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A(c), examples of pilot-performed preventive maintenance include: (1) changing engine oil and filter, (2) replacing safety wiring or cotter pins, (3) replenishing hydraulic fluid, (4) replacing prefabricated fuel lines, (5) servicing landing gear wheel bearings, and (6) replacing bulbs, reflectors, and lenses of position and landing lights. The full list is specified in Appendix A(c) and is exhaustive — tasks not listed are not authorized.

questions.question: After completing a preventive maintenance task on your helicopter, what record-keeping is required before returning the aircraft to service?
questions.answer: Per 14 CFR 43.9, the pilot must make an entry in the aircraft maintenance records that includes: (1) a description of the work performed, (2) the date the work was completed, (3) the name of the person performing the work, (4) the pilot certificate type and number, and (5) the signature of the person who performed the work. The entry must also include the statement that the aircraft was returned to airworthy condition. Failure to make this entry means the maintenance is not complete and the aircraft is not legally airworthy.

questions.question: You operate your personal R44 under Part 91. During preflight you notice the landing light bulb is burned out. You happen to have a replacement bulb in your flight bag. Walk me through whether you can legally replace that bulb yourself and what you must do before departing.
questions.answer: Yes, this is legal. Replacing bulbs, reflectors, and lenses of position and landing lights is specifically listed as allowable preventive maintenance in 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A(c). As the certificated pilot owner/operator flying under Part 91, you may perform this task yourself. After replacing the bulb, you must make a proper maintenance record entry per 14 CFR 43.9 that includes: a description of the work, the date, your name, certificate type and number, and your signature. You should verify the replacement bulb is an approved part per the aircraft's Type Certificate Data Sheet or RFM documentation. Only then is the helicopter legally returned to airworthy condition.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A(c); 14 CFR 43.9; 14 CFR 43.3(g)

questions.question: A student pilot you're flying with asks if they can top off the helicopter's engine oil during your preflight. Are student pilots authorized to perform preventive maintenance? What about private pilots who are flying under a Part 135 charter operation?
questions.answer: Student pilots are NOT authorized to perform preventive maintenance. 14 CFR 43.3(g) specifically requires a private, recreational, or sport pilot certificate at minimum — student pilot certificates do not qualify. Regarding Part 135 operations: 14 CFR 43.3(g) explicitly excludes aircraft used in Part 135 operations from pilot-performed preventive maintenance. Even if the pilot holds a private or higher certificate, preventive maintenance on an aircraft being operated under Part 135 must be performed by a certificated mechanic (A&P). The restriction is on the operation type, not just the aircraft category.

questions.question: You've just changed the engine oil on your Robinson R66 under the preventive maintenance provisions. A week later, during the annual inspection, the A&P mechanic notices the oil cap was not properly secured after your oil change and there is evidence of oil leakage. Who bears responsibility here, and what are the potential consequences for you as the pilot?
questions.answer: As the person who performed the preventive maintenance, you bear direct responsibility for the quality and correctness of the work performed. Under 14 CFR 43.13, any person performing maintenance must use methods, techniques, and practices acceptable to the FAA and must complete the work so the aircraft is at least equal to its original condition. Improperly performed maintenance that results in an unsafe condition could expose you to FAA certificate action under 14 CFR 61.15 and 91.7, and potentially civil liability. Additionally, if the aircraft was flown in that condition, you may have violated 14 CFR 91.7 (operating an unairworthy aircraft). The PIC is ultimately responsible for airworthiness before each flight per 14 CFR 91.7.

questions.question: During preflight on your privately owned helicopter, you notice a fuel line appears cracked and you want to replace it yourself under preventive maintenance provisions. What specific criteria must that replacement fuel line meet, and what would happen to your ability to perform this task if you discovered the line was attached using a B-nut fitting that required a specialized torque specification from the maintenance manual?
questions.answer: 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A(c) permits replacement of 'prefabricated fuel lines' as preventive maintenance. The critical word is 'prefabricated' — the replacement line must be a manufactured, ready-to-install part, not fabricated by the pilot on-site. The replacement part must conform to the aircraft's Type Certificate and be an approved part per the TC Data Sheet or an approved parts manual. Regarding the torque specification scenario: if the installation of the fuel line requires a specific torque value from the aircraft maintenance manual, this elevates the task beyond simple preventive maintenance into a procedure that requires reference to and compliance with aircraft maintenance data. At this point, depending on the complexity of the task and whether it requires maintenance manual data to complete correctly, a reasonable interpretation is that this exceeds pilot-performed preventive maintenance and requires a certificated A&P mechanic. The prefabricated fuel line provision is intended for straightforward, drop-in replacements — not jobs requiring aircraft maintenance manual data and precision tooling.
questions.follow_up: After you replace the prefabricated fuel line yourself and make the logbook entry, you ask your A&P to double-check your work. The A&P finds the installation is correct and serviceable. Does the A&P need to make any additional logbook entry, or does your entry as the pilot suffice?
questions.follow_up_answer: Your logbook entry as the performing pilot is the required entry per 14 CFR 43.9, and the A&P's inspection is an informal check — not a required inspection unless it constitutes a return to service after A&P-level work. However, if the A&P formally inspects the work and determines an additional entry is warranted (for example, signing off that the installation was verified), that entry would be their own professional judgment and not a regulatory requirement in this scenario. The original pilot maintenance entry per 43.9 is what legally returns the aircraft to service. If the A&P had performed any corrective action during that check, a separate 43.9 entry under their certificate would be required.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A(c); 14 CFR 43.9; 14 CFR 43.13

issues: Answer asserts that fuel line installation requiring torque specification from maintenance manual exceeds pilot-performed preventive maintenance, but 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix A(c) lists 'Replacement of prefabricated fuel lines' without qualification regarding installation complexity or manual requirements. The regulation does not explicitly exclude installations requiring torque specifications. While reasonable interpretation may suggest this exceeds simple preventive maintenance, the answer goes beyond what the regulation explicitly states and represents an interpolated standard rather than a clear regulatory requirement.
verification.suggested_correction: The answer should clarify that while 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix A(c) permits replacement of prefabricated fuel lines, the interpretation of whether a specific installation (particularly one requiring torque specifications and careful assembly procedures) falls within 'preventive maintenance' vs. requiring A&P oversight is a judgment call that may benefit from consultation with the FSDO or manufacturer guidance. The regulation itself does not explicitly exclude such installations from pilot authority.

questions.question: You perform an oil change on your helicopter and correctly make the maintenance logbook entry. Two months later, you sell the helicopter. The new owner's A&P discovers during the annual inspection that the oil filter you installed was not an approved part per the aircraft's TC Data Sheet — it was a generic automotive filter you sourced online. Walk me through the airworthiness and regulatory implications of that situation.
questions.answer: This is a serious airworthiness violation with multiple layers of regulatory exposure. First, 14 CFR 43.13(a) requires that maintenance use the methods, techniques, and practices approved in the manufacturer's current instructions or other FAA-accepted data. Installing a non-approved part violates this standard and means the preventive maintenance was never properly completed. Second, under 14 CFR 21.303, parts installed on type-certificated aircraft must be approved parts — either manufactured under an FAA Production Approval, a PMA (Parts Manufacturer Approval), or accepted under other FAA approval mechanisms. A generic automotive filter is none of these. Third, the aircraft was operated in an unairworthy condition during those two months — a potential violation of 14 CFR 91.7 for every flight. Fourth, if you knowingly installed an unapproved part, the logbook entry could constitute falsification of records under 14 CFR 43.9 and expose you to certificate action under 14 CFR 61.59; however, if you reasonably believed the filter was approved, the primary violations would be airworthiness and improper maintenance rather than falsification. The new owner's A&P must remove the unapproved part, install an approved filter with a new oil service, and make the appropriate maintenance record entries before the aircraft can legally fly.
questions.follow_up: Would your liability or regulatory exposure change at all if, instead of an oil filter, the unapproved part was a position light bulb — one of the items explicitly listed as pilot-preventive-maintenance in Appendix A(c)?
questions.follow_up_answer: The same principles apply — approved parts requirements under 14 CFR 21.303 do not change based on who installs the part. Preventive maintenance provisions in 43.3(g) authorize who may perform the task; they do not waive the requirement that parts installed on type-certificated aircraft must be FAA-approved. A non-approved bulb installed in a position light still renders the aircraft technically unairworthy. However, the practical risk severity is substantially lower than an unapproved oil filter, which directly impacts engine lubrication and could cause catastrophic engine failure. The FAA's enforcement discretion would likely reflect that difference in severity, but the regulatory violation exists in both cases.

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), what must a pilot do before flying a helicopter with an inoperative piece of equipment that is NOT on an approved MEL?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), the pilot must determine that: (1) the inoperative equipment is not required by the VFR day or night equipment list in 14 CFR 91.205, (2) it is not required by an AD or the RFM/POH, (3) it does not constitute a hazard to the helicopter, and (4) the equipment is either removed from the helicopter, rendered inoperative, or placarded INOPERATIVE. If deactivation requires maintenance (including removal), a certificated maintenance person must perform it. A record of the deferral must be made in the maintenance logbook.

questions.question: What equipment is required on a helicopter for day VFR flight under 14 CFR 91.205(b), and how does the night VFR equipment list differ?
questions.answer: For day VFR, 14 CFR 91.205(b) requires: airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic direction indicator, tachometer for each engine and rotor, oil pressure gauge for each pressure-lubricated engine, temperature gauge for each air-cooled engine, oil temperature gauge for each air-cooled engine, manifold pressure gauge for each altitude engine, fuel gauge for each tank, landing gear position indicator (if retractable), anti-collision light system, safety belts with metal-to-metal latching, and an ELT. For night VFR, 14 CFR 91.205(c) adds: approved position lights, an adequate source of electrical energy, and one spare set of fuses (or three of each kind required).

questions.question: What legal status does the FAA assign to an approved Minimum Equipment List (MEL), and why does that matter for the helicopter it is issued to?
questions.answer: The FAA considers an approved MEL to be equivalent to a Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) for the specific aircraft to which it is issued. This means the MEL is part of that aircraft's type design and is aircraft-specific — it cannot be transferred to another helicopter. The MEL legally permits flight with certain inoperative equipment that would otherwise be prohibited, provided the conditions and limitations in the MEL are followed. Operating under an MEL is an alternative to the 14 CFR 91.213(d) deferral process.

questions.question: During your preflight, you discover the rotor tachometer is inoperative. Your helicopter does not have an approved MEL. Can you defer this under 14 CFR 91.213(d) and depart? Walk me through your reasoning.
questions.answer: No. The rotor tachometer is specifically required for VFR flight under 14 CFR 91.205(b) for rotorcraft. Because it appears on the required equipment list in 91.205, it cannot be deferred under 91.213(d) — that provision only applies to equipment NOT required by 91.205 or the aircraft's operating limitations. Without an MEL that specifically allows deferral of the rotor tachometer, the helicopter is not airworthy and must not be flown until the tachometer is repaired. The FAA handbook (FAA-H-8083-21B) also explicitly identifies the rotor tachometer as non-deferrable when not listed in the MEL.

questions.question: Your helicopter has an approved MEL. The MEL lists a specific avionics item as deferrable for VFR day operations only. It is now 30 minutes after sunset and you need to depart. What do you need to consider before accepting this flight?
questions.answer: The MEL is divided by kinds of operations — day VFR, night VFR, IFR, etc. If the MEL only permits deferral of that avionics item during day VFR operations, you are NOT authorized to dispatch or depart for a night VFR flight with that item inoperative. Flying at night with the item deferred would be a violation of the MEL's conditions, which would mean you are operating outside the terms of what is essentially the aircraft's STC. The item must be repaired before a night VFR departure, or an alternative MEL provision must exist that permits night VFR operations with the deferral. This is the core function of the Kinds of Operation Equipment List (KOEL) — it identifies which equipment is required for each kind of operation.

questions.question: While airborne on a VFR cross-country, you notice a piece of equipment has failed. Can you apply the 14 CFR 91.213(d) deferral process in the air to continue the flight?
questions.answer: No. The 14 CFR 91.213(d) deferral process is a preflight/maintenance deferral mechanism — it is not intended for use on in-flight discrepancies. The FAA handbook explicitly states that maintenance deferrals under 91.213(d) are not used for in-flight equipment failures. In flight, the applicable procedures are the RFM/POH emergency and abnormal procedures. As PIC, you must follow those procedures and determine whether continued flight to your destination or diverting to the nearest suitable airport is the safest course of action. After landing, the item can then be evaluated for possible deferral before the next departure.

questions.question: A mechanic verbally tells you that a piece of equipment has been deactivated and is acceptable to defer under 91.213(d). There is an INOPERATIVE placard on the instrument, but you cannot find any logbook entry documenting the deferral. Are you legal to depart, and what are the exact recordkeeping requirements?
questions.answer: No, you should not depart without proper documentation. Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), when equipment is deferred under the no-MEL deferral provision, a record of the deferral must be made in the aircraft maintenance logbook. The placard alone is not sufficient — there must be a written maintenance logbook entry reflecting that the item has been found inoperative, deactivated if applicable, and determined not to be a hazard or required item. If deactivation involved any maintenance action (including removal), only a certificated maintenance person may perform and log that work. Without the logbook entry, the airworthiness basis for the deferral cannot be established, and departing would expose the PIC to violation of 91.213 and 91.7.
questions.follow_up: What happens to the deferral record when the aircraft maintenance logbook is not carried on board during the flight?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 91.417 requires maintenance records to be retained by the owner or operator, but they are not required to be carried aboard the aircraft during flight. However, the INOPERATIVE placard must be visible in the cockpit so the crew is aware of the deferred item. The logbook record stays with the aircraft's maintenance records. If an FAA inspector questions the deferral, the logbook entry is what legally establishes that the deferral was performed properly by a certificated maintenance person using the correct regulatory authority.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a Minimum Equipment List (MEL) and a Kinds of Operations Equipment List (KOEL), and describe a scenario where the KOEL would restrict a helicopter flight that the MEL alone might seem to permit.
questions.answer: The MEL is an FAA-approved document specific to a particular aircraft (functioning as an STC) that lists equipment items which may be inoperative under specified conditions while still maintaining airworthiness. The KOEL is a list within the RFM or approved operating documents that identifies the equipment required for each kind of operation the aircraft is authorized to conduct — such as day VFR, night VFR, or IFR. The KOEL derives from the aircraft's type certificate and operating limitations. A scenario where the distinction matters: an MEL may list a position light circuit breaker as deferrable for 'VFR day only.' Even if the MEL document doesn't use the word KOEL, that operational restriction means the position lights are on the night VFR KOEL. A pilot who sees the deferral in the MEL without reading the operational category restriction might incorrectly believe a night VFR departure is legal — but the KOEL-equivalent restriction within the MEL prohibits it. The KOEL effectively defines the envelope within which any MEL deferral must operate.
questions.follow_up: If a helicopter's RFM does not contain a KOEL, how does the pilot determine what equipment is required for night VFR operations?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the RFM does not contain a specific KOEL, the minimum equipment requirements default to the applicable FARs — specifically 14 CFR 91.205(b) for day VFR and 91.205(c) for night VFR. Any additional equipment listed as required in the RFM operating limitations also becomes mandatory. The pilot must cross-reference the RFM limitations section with 91.205 to compile the effective required equipment list for the intended kind of operation. In practice, many older or simpler RFMs do not contain a formal KOEL, so regulatory knowledge of 91.205 is essential for the PIC.

questions.question: What is a special airworthiness certificate, and how does it differ from a standard airworthiness certificate?
questions.answer: A special airworthiness certificate is issued for aircraft that do not meet the requirements for a standard airworthiness certificate. Categories include experimental, primary, restricted, limited, light-sport, and provisional. Unlike a standard certificate, a special airworthiness certificate comes with specific operating limitations that restrict how, where, and for what purpose the aircraft may be flown. These limitations are issued as part of the certificate and are legally binding on the pilot.

questions.question: Where would you find the specific operating limitations that apply to a helicopter operating under a special airworthiness certificate, and are you required to comply with them?
questions.answer: The operating limitations for a special airworthiness certificate are issued by the FAA as a separate document that accompanies the certificate. They may also be referenced in the aircraft's operating manual or logbook. Yes, compliance is mandatory — 14 CFR 91.9 requires the pilot in command to comply with all operating limitations applicable to the aircraft, which includes those issued with a special airworthiness certificate.

questions.question: An experimental helicopter has a placard in the cockpit stating 'Passenger Carrying Prohibited.' What is the regulatory basis for that restriction, and what happens if a pilot ignores it?
questions.answer: Operating limitations issued with an experimental certificate under 14 CFR 21.191 frequently prohibit carrying passengers, especially during initial flight testing phases. These limitations are FAA-issued legal documents. Violating them means the aircraft is being operated contrary to its airworthiness certificate, which constitutes a violation of 14 CFR 91.9 and 14 CFR 91.7. The pilot could face certificate action and the aircraft would be considered not airworthy at the time of the flight.

questions.question: You are about to fly a helicopter with an experimental airworthiness certificate for the purpose of flight training. The operating limitations state the aircraft may only be flown 'for the purpose for which the certificate was issued.' What do you need to verify before using this helicopter for dual instruction?
questions.answer: You must verify that the experimental certificate was specifically issued for an operating purpose that includes flight training. Experimental certificates are issued for specific purposes listed in 14 CFR 21.191, such as research and development, amateur-built, exhibition, air racing, crew training, or market survey. If the certificate was issued for, say, amateur-built or exhibition purposes, using it for commercial flight instruction would violate the operating limitations. You would need to review the actual operating limitations document accompanying the certificate to confirm the authorized purpose before conducting training.

questions.question: During your preflight of an experimental helicopter, you notice the operating limitations require a minimum crew of one pilot and state that flight over populated areas is prohibited. You are departing from a suburban airport and your route will briefly pass over a residential neighborhood. How do you handle this?
questions.answer: You cannot legally fly that route. The operating limitations issued with the special airworthiness certificate are legally binding under 14 CFR 91.9 and 91.319. Flight over populated areas is explicitly prohibited in those limitations, and a residential neighborhood qualifies as a populated area. You would need to plan an alternate route that avoids populated areas, or delay the flight until a compliant route is available. Proceeding as planned would render the aircraft non-airworthy and expose the pilot to FAA certificate action.

questions.question: A restricted category helicopter is approved for an aerial application (agricultural spraying) operation. The operator now wants to use the same helicopter for a sightseeing flight with paying passengers. What must you know before accepting that flight?
questions.answer: A restricted category certificate is issued for specific special purpose operations defined in 14 CFR 21.25, such as aerial application, aerial surveying, or patrolling. The aircraft's operating limitations will specify which special purpose operations are authorized. Carrying paying sightseeing passengers is not a listed special purpose, and 14 CFR 91.313 prohibits carrying persons for compensation or hire in a restricted category aircraft, and also prohibits carrying persons not essential to the flight unless the FAA has issued a deviation. The operator cannot legally use that helicopter for sightseeing flights with paying passengers without obtaining a different class of airworthiness certificate.

questions.question: You are flying an experimental amateur-built helicopter and during preflight you discover that the operating limitations require a specific flight test area be used during an initial phase of flight testing. That phase was completed six months ago and a new set of operating limitations was supposedly issued removing the geographic restriction. How do you verify you are operating under the correct, current operating limitations, and what is the consequence if the original restricted-area limitation is still the legally current document?
questions.answer: Operating limitations for experimental aircraft are amended by the FAA through a formal process — the operator must apply for and receive an updated limitations document. The new document should be physically present in the aircraft and should supersede the old one, clearly dated and signed by an FAA representative. You must verify that the limitations document in the aircraft is the most current FAA-issued version, which should reference completion of the Phase I testing and authorize Phase II (unrestricted) flight. If the old Phase I limitations are still the legally current document — meaning the FAA amendment was never formally issued or is not on board — you are legally bound by the Phase I geographic restriction regardless of what you believe was approved. Flying outside the designated test area without an updated document would be an operating limitations violation under 14 CFR 91.9 and 91.319.
questions.follow_up: If you discovered mid-flight that the limitations document on board is actually the old Phase I document, and you are already outside the designated test area, what is your immediate obligation?
questions.follow_up_answer: You are already in violation of the operating limitations, which means the aircraft is technically being operated in a condition not authorized by its airworthiness certificate. Your obligation is to land as soon as practicable at the nearest suitable area, not to continue the flight. Once on the ground, you must contact the FAA FSDO to clarify the status of the limitations and obtain the correct current document before any further flight. You should also consider whether an ASRS (Aviation Safety Reporting System) report is appropriate to document the inadvertent violation.

questions.question: An experimental helicopter's operating limitations state the aircraft must be maintained by the owner-builder or a certificated A&P mechanic familiar with the construction. The owner tells you the annual condition inspection was performed by an IA who has never seen the aircraft before. Is the aircraft airworthy, and does this affect whether you can legally fly it?
questions.answer: Experimental operating limitations commonly specify who may perform maintenance and condition inspections, and those requirements are legally binding. If the limitations require the condition inspection to be performed by the builder or a person familiar with the construction, and an IA unfamiliar with the aircraft performed it, the condition inspection may not satisfy the limitations — potentially rendering the maintenance action noncompliant with the aircraft's operating limitations. As PIC, you are responsible under 14 CFR 91.7 for determining the aircraft is in an airworthy condition before flight. If the maintenance does not comply with the operating limitations, the aircraft cannot be considered airworthy. You should not accept the aircraft for flight until the matter is resolved with the FAA FSDO, which has authority over experimental aircraft operations in its district.
questions.follow_up: What is the difference between a condition inspection on an experimental aircraft and an annual inspection on a standard category aircraft, and why does that distinction matter here?
questions.follow_up_answer: A standard category aircraft requires an annual inspection performed by an FAA-certificated A&P mechanic holding an Inspection Authorization (IA), following 14 CFR Part 43 standards and appendices. The experimental aircraft condition inspection, by contrast, is not governed by Part 43 in the same way — it is governed by the aircraft's specific operating limitations and any associated inspection procedures. The condition inspection confirms the aircraft is in a condition for safe operation, but the standards and who may perform it are defined by the experimental certificate's operating limitations, not by 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix D. This distinction matters because an IA's authority to perform an annual inspection on a standard aircraft does not automatically qualify them to perform a compliant condition inspection on an experimental aircraft if the operating limitations impose additional or different requirements.

questions.question: You discover an inoperative piece of equipment during your preflight. Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), what are the two conditions that must both be true before you can defer that item and legally depart?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), the equipment must: (1) not be required by the VFR-day Type Certificate (TC), the aircraft's equipment list, or the RFM/POH as mandatory; and (2) not be required by a specific airworthiness directive or by the applicable FARs for the type of operation being conducted. If both conditions are met, the item may be deactivated or removed, placarded INOPERATIVE, and the flight may proceed without it.

questions.question: If your helicopter does not have an FAA-approved MEL and you find an inoperative instrument during preflight, what placard requirement applies before you can legally defer it and fly?
questions.answer: The inoperative instrument or piece of equipment must be placarded INOPERATIVE before flight. This is required under 14 CFR 91.213(d). Additionally, if deactivating the equipment requires any maintenance action — including removal — a certificated maintenance person must perform that work before the placard is applied and the flight departs.

questions.question: What is the legal status of an FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List (MEL) relative to the aircraft's type certificate?
questions.answer: The FAA considers an approved MEL to be a Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) for that specific aircraft. This means the MEL legally allows the aircraft to operate in a configuration that differs from its original type certificate by permitting certain inoperative equipment to be deferred, provided all MEL procedures and conditions are followed.

questions.question: During your preflight you find that the rotor tachometer is inoperative. Your helicopter has no approved MEL. A fellow pilot tells you to just placard it and go — it's not listed anywhere as required. How do you evaluate whether he is correct, and what is the actual risk management decision here?
questions.answer: The fellow pilot's advice is incorrect and potentially dangerous. The rotor tachometer is a critical flight instrument in a helicopter — without it, you cannot reliably monitor Nr (rotor RPM), which is essential for safe autorotation and avoiding rotor stall or overspeed. Per the FAA-H-8083-21B, components not listed in the MEL as deferrable — and the rotor tachometer is specifically cited as a non-deferrable item — require repair before departure. Even if a legal argument could be made under 91.213(d), the risk management decision is clear: operating without rotor RPM indication is unacceptable. The flight should not depart until the tachometer is repaired.

questions.question: You are operating under Part 91 with an approved MEL. During preflight you find that the outside air temperature (OAT) gauge is inoperative. The MEL lists it as deferrable with no crew operating procedure (O) required. Before you defer it, what risk factors should you specifically evaluate as a helicopter pilot before accepting that deferral?
questions.answer: Even though the MEL permits deferral, the pilot-in-command must evaluate operational risk. Key factors include: (1) Whether the planned flight involves density altitude calculations where OAT is critical for helicopter performance — helicopters are especially sensitive to high DA; (2) Whether any portion of the flight involves icing conditions where OAT monitoring is essential for safety; (3) Whether performance charts in the RFM require OAT input for hover ceiling, climb, or power calculations. If the flight involves hot, high-altitude, or IMC conditions, accepting the deferral may be legal but operationally unwise. The PIC retains authority and responsibility to refuse a deferral if it introduces unacceptable risk.

questions.question: You discover during preflight that the cyclic trim system is inoperative on your Part 91 helicopter. The aircraft has no MEL. A maintenance technician is not immediately available. Walk me through your risk management process for this situation.
questions.answer: The FAA-H-8083-21B specifically identifies cyclic trim as a non-deferrable component. This means it cannot be deferred under 91.213(d) — the aircraft is not airworthy without it. The risk management process requires: (1) Recognize the legal issue — flight is prohibited without repair; (2) Assess mission pressure — do not allow schedule or passenger pressure to override the airworthiness determination; (3) Ground the aircraft until a certificated maintenance person inspects and corrects the discrepancy; (4) Document the finding in the maintenance logbook. There is no workaround under 91.213(d) for items specifically identified as non-deferrable — the flight does not go.

questions.question: During preflight, you discover that the engine tachometer is inoperative on a helicopter with an approved MEL. The MEL shows this item as deferrable, but the MEL entry has a Maintenance (M) procedure required before flight. The line mechanic tells you verbally that he completed the procedure but has not yet signed off the MEL control log. What is the risk management and legal issue here, and can you legally depart?
questions.answer: You cannot legally depart. An MEL Maintenance (M) procedure is not considered complete until it is properly documented — a verbal statement from the mechanic is not sufficient to establish compliance. The MEL is an STC and operates as a binding airworthiness document; the control log entry is part of the legal deferral process, not optional paperwork. Departing without the signed documentation means the deferral is not valid, and the aircraft is not airworthy for that flight. The risk management issue is also one of normalization of deviance — accepting verbal confirmations instead of documented compliance erodes the integrity of the airworthiness system. Wait for the mechanic to complete and sign the required maintenance record entry before departure.
questions.follow_up: If the mechanic completes and signs the MEL maintenance procedure entry but you later discover en route that the engine tachometer was not actually deactivated properly — it is intermittently showing false readings — what are your options?
questions.follow_up_answer: An MEL deferral procedure covers preflight maintenance actions — it does not apply to in-flight discrepancies. Per the FAA-H-8083-21B, in-flight discrepancies are handled using the RFM/POH emergency or abnormal procedures, not the MEL deferral process. As PIC under 14 CFR 91.3, you have authority to deviate from any FAR to the extent necessary to meet the emergency. Practically, you must evaluate whether the false readings are creating a safety of flight issue. If the false tachometer data could cause you to mismanage engine RPM or fail to recognize a real power problem, you should treat this as an abnormal situation, reference the RFM, and divert to the nearest suitable landing area to have the issue corrected before continuing flight.

questions.question: You are the PIC of a Part 91 helicopter flight and during preflight you discover that a navigation light is inoperative. You determine under 91.213(d) that it can be deferred for a VFR daytime flight. However, weather is forecast to deteriorate by late afternoon and you may need to extend the flight into night VMC. What is the full risk management picture here, and how does the time-of-day factor change your deferral decision?
questions.answer: This is a classic example of how a legal decision in one context becomes an illegal one in a different operating context. Navigation lights are required for night operations under 14 CFR 91.209. While the deferral under 91.213(d) may be valid for a strictly daytime VFR flight, it becomes invalid the moment the aircraft operates after sunset — at which point you are operating an aircraft that does not meet its required equipment for the operation being conducted. The risk management decision must account for the full scope of the planned mission, not just the initial departure conditions. If there is any realistic chance the flight extends into night, the navigation light must be repaired before departure. Continuing into night with a deferred navigation light exposes the PIC to violations of both 91.209 and 91.213, and creates a mid-mission airworthiness crisis. The ADM principle here: do not plan a flight around a 'probably' — if night operations are possible, treat them as certain.
questions.follow_up: Suppose you departed legally for a day VFR flight with the navigation light deferred, and due to an unexpected emergency you are forced to continue flight past official sunset to reach a safe landing area. Are you protected under any FAR provision?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes. Under 14 CFR 91.3(b), the PIC may deviate from any FAR to the extent necessary to meet an emergency. If a genuine in-flight emergency forces continuation into night, the PIC may legally operate without the required navigation light to the extent necessary to safely land. However, the PIC must submit a written report to the FAA upon request explaining the deviation. The key distinction is that this emergency deviation authority applies to unplanned, genuine in-flight emergencies — it does not retroactively authorize a departure that was planned with known likelihood of night operations. Intentionally exploiting 91.3(b) as a workaround for a foreseeable equipment issue would not be viewed favorably by the FAA.

questions.question: Where in this helicopter would I find the airworthiness certificate, and what information does it contain?
questions.answer: The airworthiness certificate must be displayed in the aircraft in a location visible to passengers and crew — typically mounted on the instrument panel or cockpit wall. It contains the aircraft registration number (N-number), aircraft make and model, serial number, category of airworthiness (e.g., Normal, Restricted), and the statement that it is airworthy only when maintained in accordance with applicable FAA regulations. A standard airworthiness certificate is valid indefinitely as long as the aircraft remains in an airworthy condition and maintenance is performed per 14 CFR parts 21, 43, and 91.

questions.question: Where is the registration certificate kept on this helicopter, and what does it tell you?
questions.answer: The registration certificate must be kept in the aircraft at all times per 14 CFR 91.203(a)(2). It is typically stored in a document pouch in the cockpit. It identifies the aircraft by make, model, and serial number, shows the N-number assigned to the aircraft, and lists the registered owner's name and address. The registration certificate is issued by the FAA Civil Aviation Registry in Oklahoma City. Note that aircraft registered after January 1, 2023 are renewed on a 10-year cycle; some previously-issued certificates may still operate under a 3-year renewal cycle until their next renewal. Check the expiration date on your specific certificate.

questions.question: The RFM sitting on the shelf in the office looks identical to the one in this helicopter. Can you use it during flight? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No. The RFM is specific to each individual helicopter — the title page must reflect the serial number and registration number of that specific aircraft. Per the Helicopter Flying Handbook, the RFM is tied to the individual airframe. Using an RFM from an identical model with a different serial number could result in missing or incorrect aircraft-specific data, supplements, or limitations. The correct RFM must be aboard the aircraft and current for that specific helicopter.

questions.question: During preflight, you open the document pouch and find the airworthiness certificate but cannot locate the registration certificate. The owner tells you it was accidentally left in the hangar office. What are your options?
questions.answer: You may not legally depart without the registration certificate aboard — 14 CFR 91.203(a)(2) requires it to be carried in the aircraft. You have several options: (1) retrieve the physical registration certificate before departing; (2) if the aircraft has a current digital registration, the FAA does accept the PDF version of a valid registration certificate as a substitute for the paper certificate; or (3) delay the flight until it is obtained. Claiming the document 'probably' exists is not acceptable — the document must be physically verifiable in the aircraft before flight. This is a no-go item for the PIC.

issues: Answer mentions 'digital registration' and 'PDF version' as acceptable substitute for physical registration certificate. While the FAA has introduced digital registration options, the regulatory language in 14 CFR 91.203(a)(2) still requires the certificate to be 'carried in the aircraft.' The status of digital/PDF registration certificates as satisfying this requirement is in transition and may vary by FAA office interpretation. This creates potential ambiguity for a private pilot candidate.
verification.suggested_correction: You may not legally depart without the registration certificate aboard — 14 CFR 91.203(a)(2) requires it to be carried in the aircraft. The safest course is to retrieve the physical registration certificate before departing. The FAA has introduced digital registration options in recent years, but you should confirm with your local FSDO or Flight Service Station whether a digital copy satisfies the 'carried in aircraft' requirement for your specific operation, as interpretation may vary.
verification.triage_note: The answer claims PDF/digital registration satisfies 14 CFR 91.203(a)(2), but the regulation explicitly requires the certificate to be 'carried in the aircraft' and FAA interpretation of whether digital copies satisfy this is still in flux and varies by FSDO; this creates regulatory ambiguity unfit for a high-stakes exam answer.

questions.question: You're preflighting a helicopter and notice the airworthiness certificate lists it as a 'Restricted' category aircraft. What does that mean for how and where you can fly it today?
questions.answer: A Restricted category airworthiness certificate limits the aircraft to special purpose operations defined at the time of certification — such as agricultural application, aerial survey, patrolling, weather control, or aerial advertising. The aircraft may not be used for general utility operations, and it may not be operated over densely populated areas or in a congested airway unless a waiver is obtained. As PIC, you must know the specific restrictions listed and ensure today's operation falls within those approved uses. This is distinct from a Standard airworthiness certificate, which permits normal utility operations without those limitations.

questions.question: Show me where the operating limitations for this helicopter are defined and tell me what authority requires you to comply with them.
questions.answer: Operating limitations are found in the FAA-approved Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM), specifically in Section 2 (Limitations). They are also communicated through cockpit placards — for example, the VNE placard, which varies with altitude and gross weight. Per 14 CFR 91.9, no person may operate a civil aircraft in excess of the limitations specified in the approved flight manual, markings, and placards. The PIC is responsible for knowing and complying with these limitations before and during flight. Additionally, any supplements in the RFM for installed equipment may impose additional limitations that are equally binding.

questions.question: You're doing a preflight on a helicopter you've never flown before and you locate the airworthiness certificate — but the N-number on it doesn't match the N-number painted on the aircraft's tail. Walk me through exactly how you'd handle this situation and what it means for airworthiness.
questions.answer: This is a serious discrepancy and a definitive no-go condition. The airworthiness certificate must correspond to the specific aircraft you are about to fly — an N-number mismatch means either the aircraft has been re-registered and the certificate was not updated, the certificate was placed in the wrong aircraft, or there is a more serious paperwork or regulatory issue. Steps: (1) Stop the preflight immediately — do not fly. (2) Notify the aircraft owner or operator. (3) Contact the FAA Civil Aviation Registry to verify the current registration status of both N-numbers. (4) Contact an A&P or IA as needed. Flying with mismatched documentation could mean the aircraft is not legally registered under that N-number, lacks a valid airworthiness certificate, or both — making any flight illegal under 14 CFR 91.203.
questions.follow_up: What if the owner tells you the FAA just issued a new N-number but the paperwork 'is being processed' — is there any circumstance where you could still legally fly?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. There is no grace period provision for mismatched airworthiness and registration information during the re-registration process. The aircraft must have matching, current, valid documents aboard before it can be legally operated. The owner's claim that paperwork is 'being processed' does not create an exception under 14 CFR 91.203. The pilot would need confirmation from the FAA Registry that the specific N-number has been officially issued and a valid airworthiness certificate reflecting that N-number is in the aircraft before flight. Operating without proper documentation exposes the PIC to certificate action and potential civil penalties.

questions.question: During your preflight document check, you find the airworthiness certificate, registration, and RFM all appear to be in order. However, looking at the maintenance logbooks, you see the last annual inspection (100-hour for a for-hire operation) was completed 112 hours ago and you're about to fly a passenger for hire. What do you do, and how does this affect the legal airworthiness of this helicopter?
questions.answer: The aircraft is not legally airworthy for this operation and may not be flown for hire. Under 14 CFR 91.409(b), aircraft operated for hire or flight instruction are required to have an inspection every 100 hours of time in service. Exceeding that limit by 12 hours without an intervening inspection makes the aircraft non-airworthy for commercial operations. The fact that the airworthiness certificate is still physically present does not mean the aircraft is legally airworthy — the certificate is only valid when the aircraft is maintained in accordance with applicable regulations. You must decline the flight, ground the aircraft, and have it inspected before any for-hire flight. Note: the 10-hour overflight provision in 91.409(b) only applies when in-flight to reach a maintenance facility — it does not apply prospectively to justify continuing operations.
questions.follow_up: You're told this helicopter is only used for private operations under part 91 with no compensation involved — does the 100-hour inspection requirement still apply?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. The 100-hour inspection requirement under 14 CFR 91.409(b) applies only to aircraft used for hire (carrying passengers or cargo for compensation) or for flight instruction for hire. For purely private part 91 operations with no compensation, only the annual inspection (every 12 calendar months) is required under 14 CFR 91.409(a). However, if the aircraft is operated under an FAA-approved progressive inspection program or is subject to an AD requiring more frequent inspections, those requirements still apply regardless of whether compensation is involved.

questions.question: During preflight, you discover a placard in the cockpit that reads 'INOPERATIVE' on the fuel quantity gauge. Walk me through what you need to verify before you can legally depart under 14 CFR Part 91.
questions.answer: First, confirm the placard is present — inoperative equipment must be placarded INOPERATIVE per 14 CFR 91.213. Then determine whether the fuel quantity gauge is required by the aircraft's type certificate, airworthiness directives, or the RFM/POH for the operation you're conducting. Under 91.213(d), if it is not required for flight under VFR day conditions and its deactivation does not affect airworthiness, it may be deferred. You must also confirm the equipment was properly deactivated — if deactivation required maintenance or removal, a certificated maintenance person must have performed it. If the helicopter has an FAA-approved MEL, check whether the fuel gauge is listed as deferrable and comply with the MEL conditions. Note: fuel quantity gauges are only required to read accurately at empty (14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1)), so their serviceability must be evaluated in context of your fuel planning.

questions.question: Who is ultimately responsible for determining whether a helicopter is airworthy before flight, and where is that responsibility established?
questions.answer: The Pilot-in-Command (PIC) is responsible for ensuring the helicopter is in an airworthy condition before each flight. This responsibility is established under 14 CFR 91.7(b), which states that the PIC of a civil aircraft is responsible for determining whether that aircraft is in condition for safe flight. The PIC must also discontinue flight when an unairworthy condition is discovered. Additionally, 14 CFR 91.409 addresses inspection requirements and 91.417 covers maintenance records — both support the PIC's ability to make that determination.

questions.question: During preflight you want to use the 14 CFR 91.213(d) deferral provision — not an MEL — to defer an inoperative piece of equipment. What are the basic steps you must follow?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), to defer inoperative equipment without an MEL you must: (1) Determine the equipment is not required by the aircraft's type certificate, airworthiness directive, or applicable regulations for the intended operation. (2) Determine the inoperative equipment does not constitute a hazard to the aircraft. (3) Remove or deactivate the equipment — if this requires maintenance, a certificated maintenance person must perform it. (4) Placard the inoperative equipment as 'INOPERATIVE.' Only then may you depart with that item deferred. You must also ensure the equipment is not required for the specific conditions of flight (e.g., a night flight requires lighting equipment that would otherwise be deferrable for day VFR).

questions.question: Scenario: You're doing a preflight and find the cyclic trim system is inoperative. Maintenance hasn't been done, there's no MEL on board, and your next flight is a routine Part 91 cross-country. Can you defer this and depart? Walk me through your decision process.
questions.answer: No — you cannot defer the cyclic trim and depart. Here's the process: First, check whether the helicopter has an FAA-approved MEL. If it does, look up whether cyclic trim is listed as deferrable with associated conditions. If there is no MEL, you use the 14 CFR 91.213(d) process. However, the Helicopter Flying Handbook specifically identifies cyclic trim as an example of a component that is NOT deferrable under 91.213(d) because it is integral to flight safety. Cyclic trim affects aircraft controllability throughout flight. Additionally, under 91.213(d), if deactivation or removal requires maintenance, a certificated maintenance person must perform it — you cannot simply placard it yourself if deactivation involves more than flipping a circuit breaker in a published procedure. The helicopter is not airworthy for this flight. You must ground the aircraft and obtain proper maintenance before departure.

issues: The answer claims cyclic trim is 'specifically identified' in the Helicopter Flying Handbook as non-deferrable under 91.213(d), but this specific reference is not verifiable in standard FAA handbooks. While cyclic trim is indeed critical to flight safety and would likely not be deferrable, the claim of a specific handbook reference should be verified.
The statement about cyclic trim not being deferrable is correct in conclusion but the evidentiary basis cited (specific handbook identification) requires confirmation against FAA-H-8083-21B.
verification.suggested_correction: The answer conclusion is sound: cyclic trim cannot be deferred because it is integral to aircraft control and safety, and any maintenance would require certificated personnel. However, soften the claim about specific handbook identification unless the exact reference can be cited verbatim. State instead: 'Cyclic trim is essential to flight control and therefore is not deferrable under 91.213(d) because its inoperability would constitute a hazard to the aircraft.'

questions.question: Scenario: You're preflighting and you find the aircraft's annual inspection expired two days ago. The helicopter looks visually perfect. How do you determine airworthiness, and what are your options?
questions.answer: An expired annual inspection means the aircraft does not meet the airworthiness requirements under 14 CFR 91.409(a), which requires an annual inspection every 12 calendar months for aircraft not operated under a progressive inspection program. An aircraft with an expired annual is legally unairworthy regardless of its visual condition — airworthiness is not determined by appearance alone. Your options are: (1) Obtain an annual inspection from an A&P mechanic with Inspection Authorization (IA) before flying. (2) Determine if the aircraft is enrolled in a progressive inspection program (14 CFR 91.409(d)) that may supersede the annual requirement. (3) Contact an IA or FSDO about obtaining a Special Flight Permit (14 CFR 21.197) only if you need to fly it to a maintenance facility — this is limited to ferrying the aircraft for repairs, not for normal operations. You may not depart for a routine cross-country under these conditions.

questions.question: Scenario: You're at a remote off-airport landing site and during post-landing inspection you notice a hydraulic fluid leak that wasn't present before departure. You need to determine airworthiness for the return flight. What is your process, and does 14 CFR 91.213(d) apply here?
questions.answer: No — 14 CFR 91.213(d) is a maintenance deferral provision for pre-flight planning purposes; it does not apply to in-flight or post-flight discrepancies discovered during a flight sequence. For in-flight or newly discovered discrepancies, the Rotorcraft Flight Manual emergency and abnormal procedures take precedence. Your process should be: (1) Consult the RFM/POH for guidance on hydraulic system abnormalities and what conditions require grounding. (2) Assess the severity — is it a slow seep or an active leak? Where is the fluid coming from? (3) If the RFM does not provide a dispatch provision and the system is leaking, the helicopter is likely not airworthy for flight. (4) Contact your maintenance provider, company operations, or the local FSDO for guidance. (5) Consider ground transportation, another aircraft, or a Special Flight Permit if the aircraft needs to reach a maintenance facility. Do not simply depart because the aircraft flew in with no symptoms — the condition has changed.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7(b); 14 CFR 91.213(d); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8; RFM abnormal procedures

questions.question: Scenario: The helicopter has an FAA-approved MEL. During preflight you identify two separately inoperative items. Item A is listed in the MEL as deferrable with a condition that a specific placard be placed on the instrument panel. Item B is also listed as deferrable but requires a functional test by a certificated A&P before departure. The A&P did the test yesterday but did not make a logbook entry. Is the helicopter airworthy? What's the specific issue and how do you resolve it?
questions.answer: The helicopter's airworthiness is questionable specifically because of Item B. The MEL is an FAA-approved document that constitutes a supplemental type certificate (STC) for that aircraft — its conditions are mandatory, not optional. If the MEL requires a functional test by a certificated A&P before departure, that test and its results must be documented in the aircraft maintenance records per 14 CFR 43.9, which requires a description of work performed, date, name, signature, and certificate number of the person performing the work. Without a logbook entry, there is no legally traceable record that the required MEL condition was satisfied, even if the test was physically performed. You cannot self-certify that the condition was met. To resolve it: Have the A&P make the appropriate maintenance record entry before departure. For Item A, ensure the required placard is installed exactly as specified in the MEL — deviation from MEL conditions renders the deferral invalid and the aircraft unairworthy.
questions.follow_up: The FAA says the MEL is treated like an STC for that aircraft. What practical implications does that have for how you use and deviate from MEL provisions in the field?
questions.follow_up_answer: Because the FAA treats an approved MEL as a supplemental type certificate for that specific aircraft, the MEL conditions are part of the aircraft's type design for the purpose of legal operation. This means: (1) You cannot pick and choose which MEL conditions to follow — all conditions for a deferral must be satisfied exactly as written, or the deferral is invalid and the aircraft becomes unairworthy for that flight. (2) You cannot apply MEL procedures from a different aircraft of the same model — the MEL is specific to that individual aircraft's registration and serial number. (3) Adding items to the MEL or changing deferral conditions requires FAA FSDO approval — a pilot or operator cannot informally expand the MEL. (4) If an operator's MEL is more restrictive than the FAA Master MEL (MMEL), the more restrictive operator MEL controls. (5) If an item is not listed in the MEL at all, it cannot be deferred under the MEL — you must use 91.213(d) if applicable, or the aircraft must be repaired.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 43.9; 14 CFR 91.213; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8; MMEL/MEL policy

questions.question: Scenario: During preflight you find a rotor tachometer that is reading erratically and you suspect it may be intermittently inoperative. A fellow pilot says, 'Just defer it under 91.213(d) — it probably works fine most of the time.' How do you evaluate this, and what makes this situation more complicated than a straightforward 91.213(d) decision?
questions.answer: This situation is more complicated for several reasons. First, the Helicopter Flying Handbook specifically identifies the rotor tachometer as an example of equipment that is NOT deferrable under 91.213(d) — it is critical to safe helicopter operations because the pilot must monitor rotor RPM to prevent overspeed or underspeed conditions that could lead to loss of control. Deferring it would be inappropriate regardless of the 91.213(d) checklist. Second, the 'intermittent' nature creates an additional problem: an intermittently inoperative instrument may meet the legal definition of inoperative during the portion when it is not reading, but the pilot cannot predict when it will fail in flight. This is an airworthiness risk that the deferral process does not account for. Third, the fellow pilot's use of the word 'probably' is a red flag — as the Helicopter Flying Handbook ADM chapter notes, if an action will only 'probably' work, you should choose an option you know will work. The correct decision is to ground the helicopter and have the rotor tachometer inspected and repaired by a certificated maintenance person before flight. The aircraft is not airworthy in its current condition.
questions.follow_up: If the rotor tachometer is inoperative and you're already airborne when you discover this, does 91.213(d) now apply, and what is your correct course of action?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — 14 CFR 91.213(d) is a pre-departure maintenance deferral provision and explicitly does not apply to discrepancies discovered during flight. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook is clear that for in-flight discrepancies, the RFM/POH emergency and abnormal procedures govern. With a rotor tachometer failure in flight, you should: (1) Immediately reference the RFM abnormal procedures for tachometer failure, which will provide guidance on how to manage RPM by reference to other instruments, sound, and feel. (2) Assess whether the aircraft can be safely flown to the nearest suitable landing area. (3) Declare an emergency if warranted — a failed rotor tachometer in a helicopter is a serious safety concern because the pilot loses direct indication of a critical flight parameter. (4) Land as soon as practicable and do not depart again until the tachometer has been inspected and repaired with proper maintenance records.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7(b); 14 CFR 91.213(d); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapters 8 and 13; RFM abnormal procedures

issues: The answer claims the Helicopter Flying Handbook 'specifically identifies the rotor tachometer as an example of equipment that is NOT deferrable under 91.213(d)' but this specific reference cannot be independently verified as stated.
While the conclusion is almost certainly correct (rotor RPM monitoring is critical to helicopter safety and not deferrable), the cited reference to a specific handbook example should be verified.

The follow-up answer correctly addresses in-flight emergency procedures but uses the term 'declare an emergency if warranted' which is appropriately cautious but could benefit from clarity that tachometer loss in flight is typically a serious event requiring immediate descent and landing.
verification.suggested_correction: Main answer: Remove the claim of specific handbook identification unless the exact reference can be cited. Instead state: 'The rotor tachometer is critical to safe helicopter operations because the pilot must monitor rotor RPM to prevent overspeed/underspeed conditions. Equipment critical to flight control and safety cannot be deferred under 91.213(d).' The remainder of the answer is sound and the advisory against 'probably working' is excellent judgment.

questions.question: During preflight, you discover a piece of equipment on your Part 91 helicopter is inoperative. Walk me through the two methods available to you under 14 CFR 91.213 for determining whether you can legally depart.
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.213, there are two methods. First, if the aircraft has an FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List (MEL), you check whether the inoperative item is listed as deferrable. If it is, you follow the MEL's required procedures — which may include deactivating the equipment and placarding it INOPERATIVE — and then operate under the conditions and limitations of the MEL. Second, if no MEL exists, you use the 91.213(d) deferral provision: you check that the equipment is not required by the day-VFR equipment rules (91.205), not required by the aircraft's type certificate, Airworthiness Directive, or any other rule applicable to the operation. If it meets all four criteria, you may deactivate it (with a certificated maintenance person if deactivation requires maintenance), placard it INOPERATIVE, and depart.

questions.question: After determining an inoperative piece of equipment can be deferred, what two physical actions must you take before the helicopter can legally depart?
questions.answer: You must (1) deactivate the inoperative equipment — if deactivation requires any maintenance action, including removal of a circuit breaker or removal of a component, that work must be performed by a certificated maintenance person; and (2) placard the inoperative equipment as 'INOPERATIVE' in a location visible to the crew. Both steps are required — placarding alone without deactivation is not sufficient where deactivation is required by the deferral procedure.

questions.question: Your helicopter has an FAA-approved MEL. During preflight you find the rotor tachometer is inoperative. You look it up and it is not listed in the MEL as a deferrable item. What does that tell you, and what must you do?
questions.answer: If the rotor tachometer is not listed in the MEL as deferrable, it means it cannot be deferred under that MEL. Per FAA-H-8083-21B, components not listed in the MEL as deferrable require repair before the aircraft can depart. The helicopter is not airworthy for flight until the rotor tachometer is repaired. You must ground the aircraft and arrange for maintenance. The rotor tachometer is also a critical flight instrument — monitoring rotor RPM is essential for safe helicopter operation.

questions.question: You're preparing for a VFR cross-country in your Part 91 helicopter with no MEL on board. During run-up you notice the outside air temperature gauge is inoperative. Apply the 91.213(d) four-part test and tell me your decision.
questions.answer: Apply the 91.213(d) four-part test: (1) Is it required for day-VFR flight under 91.205? — No, an OAT gauge is not listed in 91.205(b) as required for day VFR. (2) Is it required by the aircraft's type certificate data sheet or the approved Rotorcraft Flight Manual? — You must check the specific RFM; if it is listed as required equipment, it cannot be deferred. Assuming it is not. (3) Is it required by an Airworthiness Directive? — Check applicable ADs; assuming none. (4) Is it required by any other rule applicable to the operation? — For a standard VFR cross-country, likely not. If all four checks pass, you may deactivate it if needed, placard it INOPERATIVE, and depart legally. However, you should note that OAT data may be relevant to density altitude and performance calculations, so you need an alternate means of obtaining that information before flight.

questions.question: You're planning an IFR flight in a helicopter equipped with an approved MEL. You discover the autopilot is inoperative. The MEL lists it as deferrable under Category C, which requires repair within 10 calendar days. Today is day 11 since the discrepancy was written up. What is the status of this aircraft, and what are your options?
questions.answer: The aircraft is not airworthy for the intended IFR operation. A Category C MEL item must be repaired within 10 calendar days of the discrepancy being entered in the maintenance record. Once that window has expired without repair, the deferral authority under the MEL has lapsed — the item is no longer legally deferred, and the aircraft cannot fly until the autopilot is repaired. There is no option to re-defer under 91.213(d) for items with an approved MEL; the MEL is controlling. You must ground the aircraft and have the autopilot repaired before any further flight. Additionally, even if it were within the deferral window, flying IFR with an inoperative autopilot may create significant workload and risk factors that require serious consideration.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.213(a); MEL procedural requirements; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8

questions.question: You're on a VFR flight in your Part 91 helicopter and you notice the fuel quantity gauge reads empty, but you know you departed with full fuel just 30 minutes ago on a flight that should have 2 more hours of endurance. You suspect the gauge has failed. Using proper procedures, how do you handle this as an in-flight equipment discrepancy?
questions.answer: First and most importantly, the 91.213(d) deferral provision is not used for in-flight discrepancies — that process applies only to preflight decisions on the ground. In flight, you follow the Rotorcraft Flight Manual emergency and abnormal procedures for fuel system or fuel quantity gauge malfunctions. You should cross-check your fuel state using all available means: fuel flow gauge, time since departure, known fuel quantity at takeoff, and fuel burn rate from the POH. Declare the situation to ATC if uncertain, and consider landing at the nearest suitable airport to have the aircraft inspected by a maintenance technician before continuing. Do not continue the flight if there is any genuine uncertainty about actual fuel state. After landing, the discrepancy must be addressed — either repaired or properly deferred under 91.213 before the next departure.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.213; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8; applicable RFM emergency/abnormal procedures

questions.question: You're the PIC of a Part 91 helicopter with no MEL. During preflight you find the cyclic trim system is inoperative. A fellow pilot tells you that you can just defer it using 91.213(d) since it's not on the required equipment list for day VFR. How do you evaluate that advice, and what is your actual decision-making process?
