The two main categories are: (1) NOTAM (D) — Distant NOTAMs, which cover airport and navaid information such as closed taxiways, runway closures, inoperative lighting, and displaced thresholds; and (2) FDC NOTAMs — regulatory in nature, issued by the FAA Flight Data Center, covering TFRs, chart amendments, and instrument procedure changes. Both must be checked before any air taxi operation.

questions.question: What is an airport diagram and why is it particularly important for a helicopter pilot performing an air taxi at an unfamiliar towered airport?
questions.answer: An airport diagram is a scaled, overhead-view chart depicting the physical layout of an airport including runways, taxiways, ramps, terminals, hangars, control tower, fuel facilities, and helipads. For helicopter air taxi operations at an unfamiliar towered airport, it is critical because ATC will issue taxi/air taxi instructions using taxiway designator names and routing. Without familiarity with the airport diagram, a pilot may become disoriented, inadvertently cross an active runway, or enter a runway without clearance — which constitutes a runway incursion. Airport diagrams are found in the Chart Supplement and on terminal area charts.

questions.question: You are planning an air taxi from the ramp to a remote helipad on the opposite side of a towered airport. Upon checking NOTAMs, you find a NOTAM stating 'TWY B CLSD.' How does this affect your air taxi planning, and what steps do you take?
questions.answer: A NOTAM closing Taxiway Bravo means that taxiway is unavailable for use by any aircraft, including helicopters performing an air taxi. This affects my routing from the ramp to the helipad because my planned path may be blocked. Steps include: (1) Review the airport diagram to identify an alternate air taxi route that avoids Taxiway Bravo; (2) Contact Ground Control prior to air taxi and advise them of the intended destination and request routing — ATC will provide an air taxi route that avoids the closed taxiway; (3) Confirm any alternate routing is safe for helicopter operations (obstacle clearance, surface type, wake turbulence avoidance from fixed-wing traffic); (4) Remain at or below 25 feet AGL for air taxi unless terrain or obstacles require higher, and always maintain awareness of wake turbulence from other aircraft. This illustrates why current NOTAM review is a required preflight action under 14 CFR 91.103.

questions.question: During your preflight planning for an air taxi operation at a non-towered airport, what specific information from the Chart Supplement and NOTAMs would you look for that directly affects how you conduct the air taxi?
questions.answer: From the Chart Supplement I would look for: traffic pattern direction and altitude, preferred helicopter operating areas or helipads, CTAF frequency, fuel availability and type, any noise abatement procedures specific to helicopters, hours the airport is attended, and any special notices regarding ground vehicle or pedestrian activity. From NOTAMs I would check for: temporary flight restrictions (TFRs) in the vicinity, any construction on taxiways or ramps that could affect my path of movement, pavement closures, inoperative lighting (for dusk/night ops), and any obstacles that may have been recently reported near the movement area. At a non-towered airport, all of this information is especially critical because there is no ATC to provide real-time guidance or conflict advisories during the air taxi.

questions.question: You are conducting an air taxi at a busy airport and ATC clears you to 'air taxi via alpha to the helipads.' You are unfamiliar with this airport and did not review the airport diagram prior to departure. What regulatory and safety implications does this create?
questions.answer: Failing to review the airport diagram prior to departure has both regulatory and safety implications. Regulatory: 14 CFR 91.103 requires pilots to become familiar with all available information pertinent to the flight, which includes airport diagrams for airports being used. This is a mandatory preflight action, not optional. Safety: Without the airport diagram, I cannot visualize where Taxiway Alpha leads, where the helipads are located, or what other runways, taxiways, or hot spots intersect my route. This significantly increases the risk of a runway incursion — one of the most dangerous events at an airport. If I become lost or disoriented on the movement area, I should immediately stop (or hover in place), advise ATC of my position and that I am unfamiliar with the airport, and request progressive taxi instructions. The correct action is to have the airport diagram on hand and reviewed before beginning movement.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.103; AIM 4-3-18; FAA Runway Safety Program

questions.question: A regulatory NOTAM amends the instrument approach procedure for the airport you intend to use, but you are planning a VFR air taxi — not an instrument approach. As the pilot in command, are you required to review this NOTAM, and does it have any relevance to your air taxi operation?
questions.answer: Yes, under 14 CFR 91.103, the pilot in command is required to review all available information pertinent to the flight — this does not exclude regulatory NOTAMs simply because the operation is VFR. A NOTAM amending an instrument approach could be relevant to a VFR air taxi in several ways: (1) It may indicate changes to obstacle or terrain data near the airport, which affects situational awareness even during VFR ops; (2) It could contain or reference a TFR that restricts airspace over the airport; (3) If IFR traffic is simultaneously using that approach while you are air taxiing, amended minimums or course changes could affect where instrument traffic appears relative to your position; (4) In some cases, NOTAMs address environmental, construction, or equipment changes that have indirect effects on VFR operations. The standard of care under 91.103 requires PIC awareness of all relevant NOTAMs regardless of flight rules.
questions.follow_up: If you find a TFR in a FDC NOTAM that covers the exact area of your planned air taxi, but the TFR exempts airport operations — does that exemption automatically apply to your air taxi?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not necessarily. TFR exemptions must be read carefully and in their entirety. Some TFRs exempt 'aircraft departing from or arriving at' the primary airport within the TFR, but an air taxi moving between two points on the same airport grounds may or may not fall within the plain language of that exemption depending on how it is written. A pilot must read the exact NOTAM language — if the exemption is ambiguous, the correct action is to contact the responsible ATC facility or FSS to get a clarification before operating. Assuming an exemption applies without confirming its exact scope is a common and dangerous error.

questions.question: The Chart Supplement shows that a particular airport has a designated helicopter operating area and preferred helicopter routes. ATC clears you to air taxi via a fixed-wing taxiway route instead of the published helicopter route. Are you required to follow ATC's instruction, and what factors should you consider before accepting or requesting a different clearance?
questions.answer: In controlled airspace, you are required to comply with ATC instructions unless doing so would create a safety hazard, in which case 14 CFR 91.3 (PIC authority) allows deviation to the extent necessary for safety. That said, before simply accepting the clearance, I should consider: (1) Whether the fixed-wing taxiway route poses any hazards specific to helicopters — such as rotor clearance from structures, jet blast exposure, or crossing active runways that the helicopter route was designed to avoid; (2) Whether the rotor downwash may create foreign object debris (FOD) hazards on taxiways not designed for helicopters; (3) Whether fixed-wing aircraft are in close proximity on that taxiway and wake turbulence or clearance is a concern. If the assigned route is safe, I can accept and comply. If I have a specific safety concern, the correct action is to advise ATC: 'Unable that routing, requesting helicopter route Alpha due to [reason].' ATC will generally accommodate the request. The Chart Supplement helicopter routing exists for a reason, and deviation from it by ATC instruction does not eliminate the PIC's responsibility to assess safety.
questions.follow_up: If you accept ATC's clearance to use the fixed-wing taxiway and you subsequently discover a rotor clearance issue mid-air taxi, what are your immediate options and obligations?
questions.follow_up_answer: Immediately stop forward movement and hover in place. Advise ATC: 'N[callsign] is stopped on Taxiway [X], unable to continue — requesting alternate routing due to rotor clearance conflict.' Under 14 CFR 91.3, the PIC has final authority in an emergency or safety-of-flight situation, and halting an air taxi to prevent a collision or rotor strike is well within that authority. After the flight, if ATC-assigned routing was unsafe, the pilot should file an ASRS (Aviation Safety Reporting System) report and may also file an ATC complaint through the FSDO. This scenario also highlights the importance of reviewing the airport diagram and helicopter routing before departure so that rotor clearance issues on alternate routes can be anticipated and briefed with ATC on the ground.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.123; AIM 4-3-17; FAA Chart Supplement

questions.question: What is the difference between an air taxi clearance and a ground taxi clearance, and which one would ATC typically issue to a helicopter operating below 100 feet AGL on an airport?
questions.answer: An air taxi clearance authorizes a helicopter to fly at low altitude, typically at or below 100 feet AGL, using flight in ground effect (IGE) or out of ground effect (OGE) to move from one point to another on or near an airport. A ground taxi clearance instructs an aircraft to move on the taxiways or ramp surface under its own power while remaining on the ground. ATC issues air taxi instructions to helicopters because helicopters are designed to maneuver in flight rather than rolling on the ground. The pilot-in-command retains the right to request ground taxi if the situation warrants it.

questions.question: At what altitude ceiling is a helicopter generally expected to remain during an air taxi operation, and who is ultimately responsible for obstacle clearance during that operation?
questions.answer: During air taxi operations, helicopters are expected to remain at or below 100 feet AGL. The pilot-in-command is ultimately responsible for obstacle clearance and safe separation from other aircraft, vehicles, and personnel. ATC air taxi instructions are based on known traffic and conditions, but they do not relieve the pilot of the responsibility to see and avoid obstacles or other hazards throughout the maneuver.

questions.question: When ATC issues an air taxi instruction, what specific information is the pilot expected to read back to ensure the clearance is correctly understood?
questions.answer: The pilot is expected to read back the essential elements of the air taxi instruction, including the destination or routing, any hold short instructions, and any altitude or altitude restriction specified. Specifically, any instruction to hold short of a runway must always be read back verbatim. This ensures ATC can confirm the pilot received and understood the clearance correctly before the helicopter begins moving.

questions.question: You are air taxiing across a large Class D airport and ATC says, 'hold short of runway 27L.' You are in a hover at 50 feet AGL and realize you could fly over runway 27L at that altitude without physically crossing its surface. Are you permitted to do so without additional clearance?
questions.answer: No. A hold short instruction applies to the entire runway environment, including the airspace above it. Flying over an active runway at 50 feet AGL without a specific crossing clearance would violate the hold short instruction and constitute a runway incursion. Runway incursion rules and ATC clearances apply to the runway and its protected area as a whole. The pilot must remain clear of the runway and its associated airspace until ATC issues a crossing clearance, even during an air taxi at low altitude.
questions.regulatory_ref: AIM 4-3-17; AIM 4-3-19; 14 CFR 91.129; FAA Airport/Facility Directory general information

questions.question: During an air taxi at a towered airport, the tower frequency suddenly goes quiet and you receive no response on two successive radio calls. You are mid-route between the FBO ramp and your departure pad with no hold short instructions pending. What should you do and what regulatory principle applies?
questions.answer: The pilot-in-command should attempt to contact ATC on the appropriate frequency, including attempting the ground frequency or the approach/departure frequency if available. If communication cannot be re-established, the pilot should look for light gun signals and comply with them. For an air taxi (ground/low-altitude movement), the safest course is to proceed to a clear, safe area and stop/hover while awaiting light gun signals or attempting to re-establish contact. Under 14 CFR 91.3, the PIC has final authority and must exercise sound aeronautical judgment. Note: 14 CFR 91.125 applies to flight operations within Class D airspace; during an air taxi, ground control procedures and light gun signals take precedence until communication is restored or the pilot transitions to flight operations.

questions.question: A helicopter is cleared to air taxi to the east ramp 'via taxiway alpha, hold short of runway 09.' Midway through the air taxi, the pilot realizes a direct routing would be faster but would cross over an uninstructed taxiway intersection. May the pilot deviate from the ATC-assigned routing and, if so, what must the pilot do?
questions.answer: No, the pilot may not deviate from the ATC-assigned routing without prior ATC approval. The air taxi clearance specifies the route, and the pilot must follow that routing or request an amended clearance from ATC before deviating. Operating on an unapproved route could conflict with other traffic or clearances that ATC has coordinated. If the pilot believes a different route is operationally preferable, they should request the amended routing from ATC before changing course.

questions.question: A pilot air taxiing at a towered airport is issued instructions to proceed to a specific pad 'without delay.' Wind conditions have shifted significantly, and the pilot assesses that proceeding immediately at the requested speed in a hover at 50 feet would exceed a safe power margin for current conditions. The pilot believes a brief stop and reassessment is necessary. Does ATC's 'without delay' instruction override the pilot's aeronautical judgment, and what is the appropriate response?
questions.answer: No. Under 14 CFR 91.3(a), the pilot-in-command has final authority and responsibility for the safe operation of the aircraft. 'Without delay' is an ATC instruction to expedite movement and is not a clearance to operate unsafely. The pilot must advise ATC immediately of the inability to comply, stating the reason (e.g., power margin concern due to wind shift), and request an amended clearance or a brief delay. ATC cannot override PIC aeronautical judgment on matters of aircraft safety. The correct phraseology would be: 'Tower, [callsign] is unable to comply with the without-delay instruction due to wind conditions, request brief delay or amended routing.'
questions.follow_up: If ATC responds by saying 'You are required to comply with ATC instructions,' how should the pilot respond and what regulatory authority supports that response?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot should calmly but firmly respond that compliance with the instruction as issued would compromise aircraft safety and that 14 CFR 91.3(a) gives the PIC final authority for safe operation. The pilot should state their amended request and comply as soon as safely possible. Additionally, 14 CFR 91.3(b) provides that in an emergency requiring immediate action, the pilot may deviate from any rule to the extent necessary to meet that emergency. If safety is genuinely at risk, the PIC's authority is paramount, and ATC must accommodate a safe alternative.

questions.question: You are air taxiing at a non-towered airport and receive a CTAF call from a fixed-wing aircraft stating it is on a two-mile final for runway 27. Your air taxi route would bring you to within 200 feet of the runway 27 threshold at approximately the same time the fixed-wing would land. There is no ATC involved. What limitations govern your air taxi, and how should you handle this conflict?
questions.answer: At a non-towered airport, there is no ATC clearance for air taxi — the pilot operates under 14 CFR 91.113 right-of-way rules and self-separates using the CTAF for situational awareness. Under 91.113, an aircraft on final approach to land has the right of way over other aircraft in flight or on the surface. The helicopter must yield, stop its air taxi, and allow the fixed-wing to land before proceeding. The pilot should broadcast intentions on CTAF and hold clear of the runway environment. Additionally, at a non-towered airport, the pilot must comply with any applicable airport traffic pattern and may not enter a runway environment without reasonable assurance it is clear.
questions.follow_up: At a non-towered airport, is a helicopter air taxiing at 50 feet AGL considered 'in flight' for the purpose of right-of-way rules under 14 CFR 91.113, and does this distinction matter in your scenario?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, a helicopter air taxiing at 50 feet AGL is considered in flight under 14 CFR 91.1 definitions — an aircraft is in flight from the moment it lifts off until it comes to rest after landing. Therefore, the helicopter is subject to the in-flight right-of-way rules of 91.113. This distinction matters because it means the fixed-wing aircraft on final approach has right-of-way over the helicopter in flight, requiring the helicopter to give way. If the helicopter were ground taxiing, the same practical result applies, but the legal basis differs.

questions.question: What does a yellow 'H' painted on a helipad surface indicate, and is it a mandatory marking?
questions.answer: The yellow 'H' is the standard touchdown and liftoff (TLOF) area designation marking on a helipad, indicating the approved landing/departure surface for helicopters. It is not federally mandated by FAR but is a standard per FAA Advisory Circular 150/5390-2 for heliport design. Its presence identifies the primary landing surface and helps pilots align the aircraft during approach and departure.

questions.question: What is the difference between a FATO and a TLOF on a heliport, and why does the distinction matter during an air taxi?
questions.answer: The FATO (Final Approach and Takeoff Area) is the defined area over which the final phase of approach to a hover is completed and from which takeoff is initiated. The TLOF (Touchdown and Liftoff Area) is a load-bearing surface within or adjacent to the FATO where the helicopter actually lands. During air taxi operations, the pilot must be aware that the FATO may be larger than the structural TLOF — taxiing or hovering over the FATO at altitude is acceptable, but ground contact must only occur on the TLOF to avoid structural damage.

questions.question: You are conducting an air taxi across a towered airport and need to cross Runway 28L. You see a sign with a red background and white '28L–10R' inscription. What does this sign tell you, and what action is required before proceeding?
questions.answer: A red background with white text indicates a mandatory instruction sign — in this case, a runway designation sign marking the entrance to Runway 28L–10R. You are at the boundary of an active runway. Before crossing, you must hold at this point and obtain explicit ATC clearance to cross the runway, even if currently cleared for air taxi. Entering an active runway without clearance constitutes a runway incursion. This sign does not grant permission; it identifies the runway threshold and serves as a mandatory hold-short boundary reference.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.129; FAA AC 150/5340-1M (Standards for Airport Markings); AIM 2-3-8

questions.question: While air taxiing along a designated helicopter air taxi route at a large international airport, you notice yellow chevrons painted on the pavement beneath your flight path. What do these markings mean, and do they have any operational significance for a helicopter at low-level hover taxi altitude?
questions.answer: Yellow chevrons (V-shaped or arrow-pattern markings) on airport pavement indicate areas that are unusable for aircraft ground operations — they mark closed or unserviceable pavement, blast pads, overrun areas, or displaced areas not approved for landing, taxi, or stopping. For a helicopter conducting a hover taxi (air taxi at low altitude above the surface), the pilot is not in ground contact and these markings indicate the surface below should not be used as an emergency or unplanned landing area. The chevron markings are relevant because if a mechanical problem required an immediate landing, that area is structurally unsuitable or operationally prohibited. The pilot should plan air taxi routes that keep suitable emergency landing surfaces below the flight path when possible.

questions.question: A rooftop helipad at a hospital has a published TLOF weight limit of 12,500 lbs and is marked with a circle containing the number '12.5.' Your loaded helicopter weighs 11,800 lbs. ATC clears you to land. Is this clearance alone sufficient authority to land, and what other information must you verify before touching down?
questions.answer: ATC clearance is not sufficient authority by itself — it provides separation and sequencing but does not authorize operations that violate aircraft limitations, heliport restrictions, or regulations. Before landing, you must verify: (1) the weight limit marking — '12.5' in a circle means the maximum gross weight is 12,500 lbs, so your 11,800 lb helicopter is within limits; (2) the D-value (rotor diameter limitation) — the helipad must be large enough to accommodate your aircraft's rotor diameter; (3) any published NOTAMs for the helipad; (4) structural certification documentation if required by your operator; and (5) any local restrictions published in the Chart Supplement (A/FD) or on the approach procedure. The pilot in command, not ATC, is responsible for ensuring the landing surface is appropriate under 14 CFR 91.3.
questions.follow_up: If the weight limit circle showed '8.5' instead of '12.5,' and your helicopter weighs 11,800 lbs, could you legally land there if you declared an emergency?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.3(b), a pilot in command may deviate from any rule to the extent necessary to meet an emergency. If a genuine emergency required landing at a helipad with an 8,500 lb weight limit and your aircraft weighs 11,800 lbs, you could legally land by declaring an emergency. However, you must be aware of the serious structural risk to the helipad and potential collapse. After landing, you must submit a written report to the FAA per 91.3(c) if requested. The 'emergency' must be genuine — landing overweight on a restricted helipad without a true emergency would be a regulatory violation and potentially expose the operator to liability for helipad damage.

questions.question: Name at least four visual indicators you would look for on the ground or in the environment to determine wind direction and speed before beginning an air taxi.
questions.answer: Common visual wind indicators include: windsocks or wind tees at airports, smoke from chimneys or industrial stacks, flags or banners, dust or debris being blown across the surface, ripples or waves on water, movement of tree branches or tall grass, and the drift of other aircraft during takeoff or landing. Each provides directional information; windsocks additionally provide a rough indication of speed based on how fully extended they are.

questions.question: Why is it important for a helicopter pilot to identify wind direction before conducting an air taxi, and which direction should you generally plan to air taxi relative to the wind?
questions.answer: Wind direction is critical because a helicopter in a hover or air taxi is most controllable when headed into the wind. A headwind reduces the groundspeed required to achieve the airspeed necessary for translational lift (typically 16–24 knots), improving rotor efficiency. Heading into the wind also avoids the adverse control conditions (pitch and yaw coupling, reduced tail rotor effectiveness) associated with quartering or tailwind air taxi. You should plan to air taxi into the wind whenever possible to maintain the best control margin and avoid control challenges.

questions.question: You are air taxiing at an unfamiliar helipad that has no windsock or wind tee. Describe how you would use environmental cues during the hover to confirm actual wind direction, and explain how the helicopter's behavior will help you identify a crosswind or tailwind condition.
questions.answer: During the hover, you can observe smoke, flags, tree movement, or surface debris to estimate wind direction. Once transitioning to air taxi, the helicopter may show a tendency to align with the wind (weathervaning), though this depends on fuselage design and wind speed and is not a guaranteed indicator. If a crosswind is present, you will notice the helicopter drifting laterally — requiring cyclic input opposite the drift to maintain track. A tailwind condition reduces tail rotor effectiveness and may require increased left pedal input (for counterclockwise rotor systems) to maintain heading; directional control may feel sluggish and response times may be slower. You should slow down, re-evaluate, and if possible reposition to air taxi into wind.

questions.question: During your preflight walkaround at a busy terminal helipad, you observe smoke from a nearby building drifting in a different direction than the airport windsock is pointing. How do you reconcile conflicting visual wind indicators, and which would you give more weight to for your air taxi planning?
questions.answer: Conflicting wind indicators can result from localized effects such as building-induced turbulence, channeling between structures, or thermal activity. The windsock is typically positioned in an open area to represent the prevailing surface wind most relevant to aircraft operations, so it is generally the more reliable reference for overall wind direction. However, smoke from an adjacent building reflects local flow that could affect your specific air taxi path. The correct approach is to give priority to the windsock for the general plan, but mentally note the local anomaly and remain prepared for variable or gusty conditions along the taxi route — especially near buildings or obstacles that can cause mechanical turbulence.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; Chapter 13 (ADM and situational awareness)

questions.question: You are departing a remote off-airport site with no wind measurement equipment. The site is surrounded by trees approximately 30 feet tall. Describe how you would use the tree canopy and any other available visual cues to assess wind before beginning your air taxi to the departure point.
questions.answer: You can observe the movement of the tree canopy to gauge wind speed and direction — leaves rustling and small branches swaying indicate light winds (around 7–10 knots), while larger branches moving indicate 15+ knots. Dust or loose debris being lifted gives directional information. You can also perform a brief hover-in-ground-effect check: note any drift and the pedal input required, which reveals crosswind and torque compensation demands. The direction in which you must apply cyclic to hold position reveals the wind direction. Additionally, any nearby water surfaces (lakes, streams) will show ripple patterns that move in the direction the wind is blowing — the ripple movement indicates the downwind direction, allowing you to infer the upwind direction. Combining multiple cues gives the most reliable wind assessment at sites without instruments.

questions.question: During an air taxi at a hover altitude of approximately 10 feet, the helicopter suddenly begins drifting right without a corresponding crosswind visible in the windsock or surrounding environment. What are the possible explanations, and how does this demonstrate the limitation of relying solely on visual wind indicators during low-altitude maneuvering?
questions.answer: Unexpected drift to the right, absent an obvious visual wind indicator change, can result from: (1) a surface-level wind gust or shift not yet reflected in the windsock due to response lag; (2) mechanical turbulence or an eddy produced by a nearby structure that is not visible from the cockpit; (3) a temporary reduction in tail rotor effectiveness or thrust, causing the aircraft to yaw in the direction of uncorrected main rotor torque (for standard U.S. helicopters with counterclockwise rotor rotation, this produces a right yaw); or (4) pilot input error or a sudden control input correction that induces lateral movement. This highlights the core limitation of visual indicators — windsocks respond to average conditions and may lag behind rapid gusts, and they cannot reveal micro-scale turbulence or eddies. Pilots must continuously monitor actual aircraft behavior (control inputs required, drift rate, yaw tendency) as the most real-time wind indicator available, rather than fixating on static environmental cues.
questions.follow_up: If this rightward drift happened consistently every time you passed the same point along your air taxi route, what hazard would you suspect, and what would be your course of action?
questions.follow_up_answer: Consistent drift at the same location strongly suggests a repeatable environmental flow pattern — most likely mechanical turbulence or a channeled wind effect caused by a building, terrain feature, or parked aircraft creating an eddy. This is predictable but potentially dangerous because the effect may be stronger at certain wind speeds. The correct action is to identify the source of the disturbance, increase hover altitude if possible to get above the eddy, adjust the air taxi route to avoid the area, or slow down significantly when passing through it. If the drift is severe and uncontrollable at any reasonable altitude, the route should be abandoned and an alternate path selected. This falls under risk management — recognizing a recurrent hazard and acting before it becomes an incident.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; Chapter 13 (ADM/risk management)

questions.question: During an air taxi, which aircraft lights are required to be illuminated when operating on or near the movement area of an airport at night?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.209, all position lights (navigation lights) must be illuminated from sunset to sunrise. Additionally, an anti-collision light system (rotating beacon or strobe lights) must be on whenever the engine is running, unless the pilot-in-command determines that the anti-collision lights would constitute a hazard. For air taxi operations at night, both position lights and the anti-collision system should be operating.

questions.question: What does the anti-collision light system on a helicopter consist of, and what is its primary purpose during air taxi?
questions.answer: The anti-collision light system consists of one or more approved red or white rotating beacons or strobe lights. Its primary purpose is to make the helicopter conspicuous to other aircraft and ground vehicles. During air taxi, the anti-collision system helps other pilots and ground personnel identify a helicopter that is in motion with its engine running, reducing the risk of collision.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.209; 14 CFR Part 23/27 (aircraft certification standards for lighting)

questions.question: You are conducting a daytime air taxi across a busy helipad area with multiple ground crew working in the vicinity. Your anti-collision strobe lights are very bright. What lighting consideration should you make, and does the regulation give you any flexibility?
questions.answer: Yes — 14 CFR 91.209(b) allows the pilot-in-command to turn off anti-collision lights if they determine those lights would be hazardous to safety. In this scenario, extremely bright strobes could temporarily blind or disorient ground crew in close proximity, creating a greater hazard than operating without them. The PIC may turn the strobes off in this specific situation. However, the rotating beacon (if installed separately) is generally less blinding at close range than high-intensity strobes, so using the beacon instead of white strobes may be a practical compromise. The decision must be based on a genuine safety hazard, not convenience.

questions.question: During a night air taxi from the ramp to the runway at a non-towered airport, another pilot radios asking for your position. You are using only your position lights. What additional lighting action should you consider and why?
questions.answer: You should turn on your landing light and consider pulsing it or leaving it on to make yourself more conspicuous. Although not required by regulation in non-hire night operations, using the landing light during air taxi significantly improves visibility to other pilots and ground operators. Additionally, at a non-towered airport with no ground lighting control, conspicuity is a major collision avoidance factor. The FAA recommends using all available lighting to enhance see-and-avoid capability. Turning on taxi/landing lights also helps you illuminate your own path and detect obstacles during the air taxi.

questions.question: You're doing a preflight at dusk and notice that one of the three position lights — the left red navigation light — is inoperative. Can you legally depart for a short night air taxi to the maintenance hangar across the field?
questions.answer: No. Under 14 CFR 91.209(a), no person may operate an aircraft from sunset to sunrise unless it has the lighted position lights required by 14 CFR Part 91. Position lights (red left, green right, white aft) are required equipment for night operations. An inoperative position light means the aircraft does not meet the equipment requirements for night operation. Additionally, 14 CFR 91.213 governs inoperative equipment; if there is no approved MEL for the aircraft, you must reference 14 CFR 91.213(d), which requires that inoperative equipment not required for the kind of operation being conducted be placarded and deactivated — but night-required position lights are indeed required for night ops, so the aircraft is not airworthy for a night air taxi. The correct action is to defer the flight until the light is repaired or daylight permits a daytime taxi.

questions.question: During a night air taxi at a towered airport, the tower controller asks you to 'hold position' and then seems unaware of where you are despite you advising your location. What lighting actions can you take to improve your conspicuity, and what is the regulatory basis for each?
questions.answer: Several actions are available: (1) Turn on the landing light — no specific regulatory requirement in non-hire night operations but strongly recommended per AIM guidance and best practice; it makes the helicopter visible from the tower cab and to other aircraft. (2) Verify position lights are on per 14 CFR 91.209(a) — these are required and should already be illuminated. (3) Verify anti-collision lights are on per 14 CFR 91.209(b)/91.205(b)(11). (4) If equipped with a searchlight or controllable landing light, you can direct it toward the tower cab briefly to draw attention. (5) Increase radio communication — advise tower of your exact position using specific taxiway/ramp references. The broader safety principle from FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 12 is to use every available lighting resource to maximize conspicuity during night operations, because the visual environment is degraded and other parties (ATC, other pilots) have reduced ability to locate you.
questions.follow_up: If the tower tells you to turn off your strobes because they are affecting the approach end of a runway, and you comply, have you violated 14 CFR 91.209?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — and this is a nuanced point. 14 CFR 91.209(b) already provides a PIC safety exception, but ATC instructions also carry authority under 14 CFR 91.123, which requires pilots to comply with ATC clearances and instructions. If ATC instructs you to extinguish strobes because they are creating a hazard to landing aircraft, you are legally and operationally justified in complying. The FAA's intent in 91.209(b) is to allow flexibility when lights create more hazard than they prevent — an ATC instruction reinforces exactly this scenario. You should acknowledge the instruction, turn off the strobes, and if feasible, leave the rotating beacon on for continued conspicuity at a lower intensity.

questions.question: What are the two methods of air taxiing a helicopter, and how do they differ in terms of altitude and speed?
questions.answer: Air taxiing can be done as a hover taxi or as a low-altitude air taxi. A hover taxi is conducted at hover altitude (typically 3–5 feet AGL) at a slow walking pace, keeping the helicopter within ground effect. A low-altitude air taxi is conducted above effective translational lift height — generally under 100 feet AGL — at speeds appropriate for the conditions, but not exceeding a safe airspeed where a safe landing could not be made if the engine fails.

questions.question: During an air taxi, what is the pilot's primary responsibility regarding ATC communications and clearances at a towered airport?
questions.answer: At a towered airport, the pilot must obtain an air taxi clearance from ATC before beginning movement. The pilot must maintain two-way radio communication with the tower throughout the taxi, comply with all ATC instructions, and not enter any taxiway, runway, or movement area without explicit clearance. The pilot is also responsible for verifying their position on the airport surface.

questions.question: What does the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook identify as the key factors a pilot must continuously monitor while air taxiing?
questions.answer: While air taxiing, the pilot must continuously monitor: rotor RPM, engine instruments (torque, temperature, oil pressure), altitude above the surface, airspeed and groundspeed, rotor clearance from obstacles (hangars, other aircraft, terrain, personnel), wind direction and velocity, and the intended taxi route. The pilot must also remain aware of wake turbulence from other aircraft and downwash effects on people and property on the ground.

questions.question: You're air taxiing across a large ramp area when a 15-knot crosswind picks up from your 3 o'clock position. Describe specifically how you would adjust your cyclic, collective, and pedal inputs to maintain directional control and a stable hover taxi.
questions.answer: With a crosswind from the right, you must apply right cyclic into the wind to prevent the helicopter from drifting left. The cyclic lean into the wind counteracts the lateral push of the crosswind on the fuselage and rotor disk. Collective is adjusted to maintain the desired hover altitude — wind effectively increases translational lift, so slight collective reduction may be needed. Pedals are used to maintain heading aligned with the intended taxi route, compensating for any weathervaning tendency. The key is to continuously make small, smooth control inputs rather than large corrections, keeping the helicopter tracking the desired ground path.

questions.question: While air taxiing at a busy general aviation airport, another helicopter is parked 40 feet to your left. What specific pilot actions and scanning techniques should you use to ensure adequate rotor clearance?
questions.answer: The pilot should use a systematic outside scan, prioritizing the rotor disk clearance on all sides — not just the direction of travel. Specifically: confirm rotor-to-obstacle distance before initiating any lateral movement; slow groundspeed to allow more reaction time; use a ground guide if available and the environment warrants it; avoid any sideward or rearward drift toward the parked helicopter; use pedal turns slowly to maintain visual reference of the rotor arc. Inside the cockpit, power and RPM should be confirmed in normal range, but the majority of pilot attention must remain outside. Remember that main rotor blades flex under load and may have less clearance than they appear.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.13

questions.question: You are air taxiing over a surface covered with loose gravel and dry grass. What aeronautical decision-making considerations should guide your altitude and airspeed selection during this taxi?
questions.answer: The pilot must consider the downwash effect on loose debris — flying too low over gravel or dry grass risks FOD ingestion into the engine intake, damage to the tail rotor, and creating hazards for people and aircraft nearby. The appropriate response is to increase hover altitude to reduce downwash velocity at the surface, or reroute to avoid the area entirely. Dry grass also presents a fire hazard from exhaust heat. ADM here requires anticipating the hazard before entering the area, not reacting after damage occurs. If no safe routing is available and surface conditions are hazardous, delaying the taxi until the area is cleared or conditions improve is the most conservative and correct choice.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 9 and 13; 14 CFR 91.13

questions.question: A student pilot tells you that during an air taxi, they keep their eyes primarily on the engine gauges to make sure everything stays in the green. What is wrong with this approach, and how would you correct it as their instructor?
questions.answer: This is a dangerous habit pattern. During air taxi, the pilot's primary scan must be outside the cockpit — monitoring rotor clearance from obstacles, tracking ground path, watching for personnel and vehicles, and assessing wind effects. Engine gauges during a stabilized hover taxi do not change rapidly enough to require continuous fixation. The correct technique is to use periodic, brief instrument scans to confirm engine parameters are normal, while devoting the majority of visual attention to the external environment. The student should be retrained to develop an 'outside-in' scan discipline: establish a stable hover, glance at instruments to confirm normal, then return outside. Fixating inside during a dynamic, close-quarters maneuver like air taxiing is a setup for a rotor strike or ground collision.
questions.follow_up: What FAA concept supports the idea that a pilot's workload management during low-altitude maneuvering should prioritize outside visual reference over instrument monitoring?
questions.follow_up_answer: Single-Pilot Resource Management (SRM), as described in FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13, identifies workload management as a core component. During high-workload, low-altitude phases like air taxiing, the pilot must triage attention appropriately — outside reference and situational awareness take priority because hazards in the external environment (obstacles, personnel, other aircraft) are immediate and unforgiving. Instrument deviation during a stable hover is recoverable; a rotor strike is not. SRM teaches pilots to allocate cognitive resources to the highest-consequence task first.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 9 and 13

questions.question: During an air taxi at an unfamiliar airport, you receive an instruction from ground control to 'taxi via Alpha to the runup area.' You are in a helicopter and unfamiliar with the layout. What are your specific obligations and the correct pilot actions?
questions.answer: The pilot is responsible for understanding ATC instructions before complying with them. If the taxi route is unclear, you must immediately request clarification — for example, 'Ground, Helicopter N123AB, unfamiliar with airport layout, request progressive taxi instructions.' Do not begin movement while uncertain of your route, as inadvertent runway incursion is a serious safety risk. Before departure, the pilot should have reviewed the airport diagram (available via Chart Supplement, ForeFlight, or printed airport diagram) so the taxi route can be confirmed once ATC provides it. If you do begin taxiing and become unsure of position, stop in a safe location and advise ATC of your situation. Runway incursion awareness and position confirmation are the pilot's responsibility regardless of ATC guidance. If an incursion occurs despite these precautions, immediately exit the runway by the shortest safe path and advise ATC. Pilots may self-report through NASA ASRS (Aviation Safety Reporting System) within 10 days to receive limited immunity from certificate action under 49 U.S.C. § 44703(d), provided the FAA has no independent knowledge of the incident.
questions.follow_up: If while air taxiing you inadvertently cross a hold short line and enter a runway without clearance, what are your immediate actions and your subsequent obligations?
questions.follow_up_answer: Immediately exit the runway without delay by the shortest safe path, then advise ATC of the incursion. Comply with any ATC instructions. After the flight, if the incursion involved a risk of collision or ATC determines it was a surface incident, the pilot may be subject to an Aviation Safety Hotline report or enforcement action under 14 CFR 91.129 (operations at controlled airports) or 14 CFR 91.13 (careless or reckless operation). Pilots are encouraged to self-report through NASA ASRS within 10 days of the incident to receive limited immunity from FAA certificate action, per 14 CFR Part 91 Advisory Circular guidance. Honest, prompt communication with ATC and self-reporting are the correct professional responses.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.129; 14 CFR 91.13; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9; NASA ASRS program

questions.question: What is the primary difference between air taxiing and hover taxiing in a helicopter?
questions.answer: Air taxiing is performed at a low altitude — typically 10–50 feet AGL depending on obstacles and terrain — to maintain the benefits of ground effect and allow faster movement over longer distances. Hover taxiing is conducted at hover altitude (3–5 feet AGL) at a slow walking pace. Air taxiing is more efficient for longer distances but requires greater awareness of obstacles, traffic, and terrain.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; AIM 4-3-17

questions.question: At a towered airport, what must a helicopter pilot do before air taxiing from the ramp to a takeoff point?
questions.answer: The pilot must contact ground control (or clearance delivery if required) and obtain a taxi/air taxi clearance before moving. The pilot should state their position, intended route or destination on the airport, and type of aircraft. ATC will issue a clearance or instructions, which may include a specific routing, altitude restriction, or hold-short instruction. The pilot must read back all hold-short instructions and runway crossing clearances.

questions.question: At a nontowered airport, what self-announcement calls should a helicopter pilot make when air taxiing, and on what frequency?
questions.answer: At a nontowered airport, the pilot should make position/intention broadcasts on the CTAF (Common Traffic Advisory Frequency). A typical call includes the airport name, aircraft type and call sign, current location, and intended movement — for example: '[Airport name] Traffic, Helicopter [call sign] air taxiing from the north ramp to runway 27 departure end, [airport name].' These broadcasts keep other traffic informed, especially since helicopter movements on an airport surface may not be where fixed-wing traffic expects aircraft to be.

questions.question: You're air taxiing across a large towered airport and ATC clears you to cross Runway 18L. Before crossing, what are your responsibilities, and what happens if you do not receive an explicit crossing clearance?
questions.answer: Before crossing any runway at a towered airport, you must have an explicit clearance to cross that specific runway — no exceptions. If ATC clears you to a point on the other side of a runway without explicitly clearing you to cross the runway itself, you must hold short and request the crossing clearance. You should read back the runway crossing clearance including the runway designation. ATC phraseology does not imply crossing authorization — if you are unsure, ask. Incursions can occur even at towered airports when pilots assume clearance is implied in their route.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.129; AIM 4-3-18; FAA Runway Incursion Avoidance guidance

questions.question: During an air taxi at a busy nontowered airport, another pilot asks you via CTAF to 'hold position' while they land on the runway you're approaching. You are flying a helicopter — do you have to comply?
questions.answer: Technically, pilot-to-pilot CTAF requests carry no regulatory authority — only ATC at a towered airport can issue binding instructions. However, the professional and safety-conscious response is to comply or coordinate. At a nontowered airport, right-of-way rules under 14 CFR 91.113 apply: an aircraft on final approach to land has the right-of-way over one in flight or taxiing. If your air taxi route would conflict with the landing aircraft's path, you are required to give way regardless of any CTAF communication. Cooperative use of CTAF is essential to safe operations.

questions.question: You're air taxiing at a towered airport and ground control instructs you to follow a Citation jet that is taxiing to Runway 9. What specific hazard must you consider as a helicopter pilot following a jet on the ground?
questions.answer: Jet blast is a significant hazard. A turbine-powered aircraft — especially at idle thrust — can produce a powerful rearward jet exhaust that can easily destabilize or even overturn a light helicopter. The pilot must maintain adequate separation behind the jet, be aware of when the jet is stationary and may apply power (which increases blast intensity), and be prepared to stop or reposition if the jet holds short or runs up its engines. As a general rule, a helicopter should never be positioned directly behind a turbine-powered aircraft during ground operations. Additionally, if the jet turns, the blast direction changes — the pilot must continuously track the jet's orientation.

questions.question: At a towered airport, ground control clears you to air taxi via a route that takes you through a fixed-wing aircraft's run-up area. As you approach, you see a Cessna 172 stationary with its engine running and prop wash coming directly toward you. Ground didn't mention this aircraft. What are your obligations and what should you do?
questions.answer: Your clearance does not relieve you of the responsibility to see and avoid other aircraft or ground hazards under 14 CFR 91.113. Even with a valid ground clearance, you are required to exercise good judgment. Prop wash from a fixed-wing aircraft, while less severe than jet blast, can still cause control difficulties for a light helicopter at low altitude. You should stop clear of the affected area, advise ground control of the conflict ('Ground, [call sign], holding short of the run-up area, traffic in our path'), and request amended routing or instructions. Ground control may not have been aware of the conflict, and this communication protects both you and the other aircraft.
questions.follow_up: If ground control acknowledges but tells you to continue as cleared because the Cessna is 'about to move,' and the Cessna is still running up engines when you get there — what do you do?
questions.follow_up_answer: You exercise pilot-in-command authority under 14 CFR 91.3 and hold your position until it is safe to proceed. A controller clearance does not override the pilot's responsibility for safety. You advise ground control: '[call sign] holding, unable to proceed safely at this time.' 14 CFR 91.3(a) makes the PIC directly responsible for and the final authority regarding safe operation of the aircraft — no clearance from ATC compels a pilot to operate in a manner that creates a hazard.

questions.question: You're air taxiing at a nontowered airport and you notice your chosen route will take you below the approach path for Runway 27, which has traffic in the pattern. There's no published taxi route for helicopters at this airport. How do you determine a safe air taxi altitude and routing, and what factors must you consider?
questions.answer: At a nontowered airport without published helicopter taxi routes, the pilot must use judgment to avoid conflicts with fixed-wing traffic in the pattern. Fixed-wing aircraft typically operate in a standard 1,000-foot AGL traffic pattern. The helicopter pilot may conduct air taxi at 25–100 feet AGL to remain well clear of this pattern but must continuously monitor CTAF and be prepared to give way to any aircraft on final approach per 14 CFR 91.113(g). The pilot should: (1) monitor CTAF continuously; (2) choose an air taxi altitude well below expected approach traffic — typically 25–100 feet AGL; (3) route laterally clear of the runway extended centerline if possible; (4) make CTAF broadcasts stating position and intentions; (5) be prepared to land and wait if a conflict develops. The pilot must never assume that altitude separation ensures safety—a fixed-wing pilot on final approach may not see a low helicopter below.
questions.follow_up: What if the only practical route to the fuel pump requires you to cross the Runway 27 extended centerline while a Piper Cherokee is on a 1-mile final? What is the correct action?
questions.follow_up_answer: The aircraft on final approach has the right-of-way under 14 CFR 91.113(g). You must give way — hold your position clear of the extended centerline until the Cherokee has landed and is clear of the runway environment. Announce your position and intentions on CTAF so the Cherokee pilot is aware of you, but do not proceed across the final approach path until it is unambiguously safe to do so. Attempting to 'beat' the landing aircraft is not acceptable regardless of how quickly you believe you can cross.

questions.question: When air taxiing a helicopter across an active runway at a towered airport, what communication is required before you cross?
questions.answer: You must receive an explicit ATC clearance to cross the runway. A taxi or air taxi clearance does NOT automatically authorize you to cross an active runway. You must hold short until the tower specifically clears you to cross. This applies to helicopters the same as fixed-wing aircraft operating on the surface.

questions.question: What is the recommended altitude to maintain when air taxiing a helicopter over a runway or taxiway?
questions.answer: The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook recommends air taxiing at a height of approximately 3 to 5 feet AGL — low enough to remain in ground effect but high enough to avoid prop/blade strike hazards and debris. When overflying a runway, the helicopter should remain low enough to avoid conflicting with fixed-wing traffic patterns while still clearing surface obstacles and jet blast hazards.

questions.question: At an uncontrolled airport, if you need to air taxi your helicopter over an active runway to reach the ramp, what is your primary responsibility before doing so?
questions.answer: At an uncontrolled airport, there is no ATC to issue a crossing clearance. The pilot is responsible for: (1) self-announcing intentions on the CTAF frequency, (2) visually scanning for traffic in the pattern and on final approach, and (3) ensuring the runway is clear of all traffic before crossing. The pilot-in-command bears full responsibility for avoiding collision.

questions.question: You are air taxiing your helicopter at a towered airport and the ground controller clears you to 'air taxi to the ramp via taxiway Alpha.' The direct route crosses runway 27, which is active. Can you cross runway 27 without further clearance?
questions.answer: No. A ground control taxi or air taxi clearance does NOT constitute authorization to cross an active runway, regardless of whether the route appears to go across it. You must hold short of runway 27 and contact ground or tower for an explicit runway crossing clearance. Runway incursions are one of the most serious safety hazards at airports, and this rule applies equally to helicopters air taxiing at low altitude.

questions.question: You're air taxiing a helicopter over a runway at a busy airport. A Cessna on a 2-mile final is cleared to land on the same runway. What should you do, and what factors affect your decision?
questions.answer: You must immediately clear the runway and give way to the landing aircraft. Fixed-wing aircraft on final approach have the right-of-way. As the more maneuverable aircraft, the helicopter must yield. You should move off the runway laterally, land if necessary, or accelerate clear of the runway environment. Factors affecting the decision include your position on the runway, available lateral clearance, surface conditions, and the Cessna's closure rate. Communicate your actions to ATC immediately.

questions.question: When overflying a runway during an air taxi, what specific hazards are unique to helicopters that a fixed-wing pilot would not encounter?
questions.answer: Helicopter-specific hazards when overflying a runway include: (1) Rotor downwash — the helicopter's rotor wash can stir up FOD, debris, or loose material that can damage the rotor system or be ingested; (2) Jet blast or propwash from fixed-wing aircraft can cause sudden loss of rotor RPM control or unexpected pitch/roll inputs; (3) Low inertia rotor systems can lose RPM rapidly if power is interrupted during the crossing; (4) Tail rotor clearance — the tail rotor may be at a height that is difficult to see and can strike runway lights, signs, or other low obstacles during slow maneuvering; (5) Vortex ring state vulnerability if the pilot descends too steeply to cross low.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot is cleared to air taxi over runway 18/36 at night. Runway edge lighting is on, and there is no moon. The pilot decides to cross at 10 feet AGL to stay clear of pattern traffic. What risks does this introduce, and what altitude and technique would you recommend?
questions.answer: Crossing at 10 feet AGL at night introduces significant risks: (1) Runway edge lights and taxiway lights create spatial disorientation hazards — the pilot may misjudge height or drift laterally into the light fixtures; (2) At night, depth perception and peripheral cues are degraded, making it difficult to judge tail rotor and skid clearance over lights; (3) 10 feet AGL is borderline — the pilot is near ground effect but possibly not fully in it, creating an unstable hover corridor; (4) Any power loss at 10 feet AGL over a runway at night leaves very little recovery margin. Recommended technique: cross at the minimum safe height (3–5 feet AGL, fully in ground effect) to maximize rotor efficiency and power margin, proceed at a deliberate lateral speed, keep the crossing angle as perpendicular to the runway centerline as practical to minimize time in the runway environment, and use all available lighting cues while maintaining instrument cross-check.
questions.follow_up: If the helicopter loses engine power at 8 feet AGL while crossing the runway at night, what is the correct immediate action and what factors determine whether a safe landing is achievable?
questions.follow_up_answer: Immediately lower collective to cushion the descent and autorotate to the runway surface — the runway is actually the ideal emergency landing surface in this scenario. At 8 feet AGL with forward motion, a running or sliding landing on the runway may be achievable. Factors affecting outcome include: (1) Rotor RPM at time of failure — low inertia systems decay fast and leave minimal cushion; (2) Forward airspeed — any translational velocity aids autorotation and allows a roll-on landing; (3) Aircraft weight and density altitude — heavier aircraft drain RPM faster; (4) Tail rotor position relative to ground — preventing dynamic rollover during touchdown is critical. The pilot must avoid pulling collective in a panic, which would accelerate RPM decay and result in a hard landing.

questions.question: A new helicopter pilot tells you: 'I always cross runways at 50 feet AGL during air taxi so I have plenty of obstacle clearance and nobody can accuse me of being on the runway.' What is wrong with this reasoning, and what operational and regulatory problems does it create?
questions.answer: This reasoning is flawed on multiple levels: (1) Regulatory — at 50 feet AGL, the helicopter is no longer air taxiing; it is flying. FAA air taxi operations are intended to remain near the surface, typically 3–5 feet AGL. At 50 feet, the pilot may be operating in the traffic pattern altitude environment and must be coordinated with ATC accordingly. (2) Traffic conflict — at 50 feet AGL on approach paths, the helicopter could conflict with fixed-wing aircraft on short final, especially at non-towered airports. (3) Performance — at 50 feet, the helicopter is above effective ground cushion for most designs, reducing power efficiency and increasing fuel burn and vulnerability to power loss. If an engine fails at 50 feet AGL with no forward airspeed, the pilot is in the most dangerous part of the height-velocity diagram for many helicopters. (4) Communication — if the pilot told ATC 'air taxi,' ATC expects near-surface movement; operating at 50 feet without coordination could violate the ATC clearance and create a runway incursion risk for arriving or departing traffic. The correct procedure is to air taxi low and in coordination with ATC, not self-impose arbitrary altitudes without briefing.
questions.follow_up: Where on the height-velocity diagram would a helicopter operating at 50 feet AGL with near-zero airspeed typically fall, and what does that mean for emergency options?
questions.follow_up_answer: 50 feet AGL with near-zero airspeed places the helicopter squarely in the 'dead man's curve' or high-hover/low-speed danger zone of the H-V diagram for most light helicopters. In this region, a power failure does not leave enough altitude to accelerate to best autorotation airspeed, and the rotor RPM will decay before the helicopter can build translational lift. The result is an uncontrolled descent with insufficient rotor energy to flare and cushion. This is why low air taxi near the surface is preferable — at 3–5 feet AGL, a power failure allows immediate collective reduction and a near-zero-damage touchdown on the surface below, well clear of the H-V danger zone.

questions.question: What is the Height/Velocity (H/V) diagram, and what does it represent for a helicopter pilot?
questions.answer: The H/V diagram, sometimes called the 'dead man's curve,' is a chart published in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for each helicopter that defines combinations of altitude and airspeed from which a successful autorotation and landing cannot reliably be made following an engine failure. It has two main avoid regions: (1) a low-altitude avoid region, where insufficient altitude exists to complete any autorotation regardless of airspeed, and (2) a high-altitude/low-airspeed avoid region, where adequate altitude exists but insufficient forward airspeed prevents effective energy conversion during autorotation. Operating outside these shaded zones gives the pilot the best chance of a successful autorotation if the engine fails.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual (aircraft-specific)

questions.question: Why does the H/V diagram have a 'low-speed/high-altitude' avoid region in addition to the more commonly known low-altitude region?
questions.answer: The low-speed/high-altitude avoid region exists because at those combinations there is insufficient forward airspeed to execute a flare that arrests the descent rate. Although altitude is available, the pilot lacks the forward speed needed to complete an autorotation flare and cushion to a safe landing. During autorotation, forward airspeed is converted into rotor inflow that maintains rotor RPM; without adequate forward speed, the pilot cannot decelerate vertical descent or build the rotor energy necessary to arrest the sink rate before ground contact. The high-altitude/low-speed region is most relevant for hovers above a certain height (often around 100 feet AGL for many light helicopters, but this varies by aircraft).
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; aircraft-specific RFM

questions.question: Where would you find the specific H/V diagram and avoid altitudes/airspeeds for the helicopter you are flying today?
questions.answer: The H/V diagram is found in the aircraft's Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM), typically in the Limitations or Performance section. It is aircraft-specific, meaning the values differ between helicopter models and even between gross weight conditions. The pilot must reference the RFM for the specific helicopter being flown, as using generic values from another aircraft could be hazardous.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 27.79 / 29.79 (Rotorcraft Flight Manual requirements); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: During an air taxi operation, you are asked to transit across a large ramp at a hover altitude of approximately 75 feet AGL at near-zero groundspeed because of congestion below. How does the H/V diagram apply here, and what is your decision?
questions.answer: A 75-foot AGL hover at near-zero airspeed falls squarely within the high-hover avoid region of most light helicopter H/V diagrams (the exact altitude varies by aircraft). At that combination of altitude and airspeed, an engine failure would likely not allow sufficient time or rotor energy to successfully complete an autorotation. The pilot should consult the aircraft's RFM to confirm whether this altitude/speed combination is in the avoid zone. If it is, the pilot should either descend to a low hover (below the avoid zone, typically under about 10 feet for many aircraft) or accelerate to a translational airspeed that exits the avoid region. Congestion below does not justify accepting an unacceptable risk — the pilot should coordinate with ground personnel or ATC to find an alternate route or technique that keeps the aircraft outside the H/V avoid zone.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; aircraft-specific RFM; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/risk management)

questions.question: Your helicopter is loaded to near maximum gross weight for an air taxi segment. How does gross weight affect your H/V avoid zones compared to operating at a lighter weight, and why?
questions.answer: At higher gross weights, the H/V avoid zones typically expand — the unsafe altitude band becomes larger and the minimum safe airspeed to exit the avoid region may increase. This is because a heavier helicopter has a higher power demand and greater inertia, requiring more rotor energy and more time/altitude to arrest a descent during autorotation. The rotor system must work harder to decelerate and set down safely. Many RFMs publish separate H/V diagrams or tables for different gross weight conditions. The pilot must use the correct chart for actual loading. Operating at or near max gross weight at low altitude and low airspeed significantly narrows the margin for a successful autorotation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; aircraft-specific RFM (gross weight H/V corrections)

questions.question: A pilot plans an air taxi from one pad to another across open terrain. The route is short enough to fly entirely at a low hover (5 feet AGL) or they could climb to 500 feet AGL and fly the route at normal cruise airspeed. From an H/V diagram perspective, which profile is safer, and what factors would influence that decision?
questions.answer: Both profiles can be acceptable if properly executed relative to the H/V diagram. A 5-foot AGL low hover keeps the helicopter below the high-hover avoid zone, where a power failure would result in a low-energy impact but with survivable potential if surface conditions are acceptable. The 500-foot AGL / cruise-airspeed profile keeps the aircraft well above the high-hover avoid zone with sufficient altitude and airspeed to enter and complete an autorotation. The low hover is safer over a smooth, obstruction-free surface but is operationally slow and exposes the aircraft to brownout/debris hazards. The 500-foot cruise profile requires adequate autorotation landing areas along the route. A pilot must assess: surface conditions, available autorotation landing zones, obstacles, wind, gross weight, density altitude, and the specific aircraft's H/V diagram boundaries. The intermediate altitudes (roughly 10–100 feet AGL at low airspeed for many light helicopters) are typically the most hazardous.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (risk management)

questions.question: A pilot argues that the H/V diagram only applies to single-engine helicopters and that flying a light twin-engine helicopter during air taxi means they don't need to consider H/V avoidance at all. How do you evaluate that position, and what are the limits of that reasoning?
questions.answer: This position is partially correct but dangerously incomplete. Twin-engine helicopters do have improved engine-failure survivability, and some RFMs for certified twin-engine helicopters show a reduced or eliminated H/V avoid zone under OEI (One Engine Inoperative) conditions at certain gross weights and density altitudes. However, the reasoning fails for several reasons: First, even twin-engine helicopters can experience dual-engine failures (fuel exhaustion, contamination, or catastrophic transmission failure). Second, the H/V diagram in the RFM for a twin-engine helicopter still exists and must be consulted — the boundaries may simply differ from a single-engine aircraft. Third, OEI performance is highly sensitive to density altitude, gross weight, and which performance category (Category A or B) the operation is being conducted under. Category A operations require defined takeoff and landing profiles that inherently manage H/V exposure; Category B operations do not guarantee OEI climb capability at all points. The pilot must reference the specific aircraft's RFM and applicable category of operation, not make blanket assumptions based on engine count. [For follow-up: Category A operations (14 CFR Part 29 subpart B) require multi-engine helicopters to be operated using approved takeoff and landing profiles that guarantee the ability to either continue flight or land safely following a single-engine failure at any point during the profile. This effectively manages H/V exposure by design. Category B operations do not guarantee OEI climb capability at all points; a single-engine failure may require an immediate landing. Category B can apply to both Part 27 Normal Category and Part 29 transport category helicopters. During air taxi in a Category B multi-engine helicopter, the pilot must still respect H/V avoidance principles because an engine failure may not be survivable from certain altitude/airspeed combinations.]
questions.follow_up: What is the difference between Category A and Category B helicopter operations, and how does that distinction relate to H/V exposure during air taxi?
questions.follow_up_answer: Category A (14 CFR Part 29, Transport Category) operations require multi-engine helicopters to be operated using approved takeoff and landing profiles that guarantee the ability to either continue flight or land safely following a single-engine failure at any point during the profile. This effectively manages H/V exposure by design — the profiles keep the aircraft on a path where OEI performance is assured. Category B operations (14 CFR Part 27, Normal Category) do not guarantee OEI climb capability at all points; a single-engine failure may require an immediate landing. Therefore, during air taxi in a Category B multi-engine helicopter, the pilot must still respect H/V avoidance principles because an engine failure may not be survivable from certain altitude/airspeed combinations, similar to a single-engine aircraft.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 27.79, 29.79 (H/V limitations); 14 CFR 29.1 (Category A/B definitions); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; AC 29-2C (Certification of Transport Category Rotorcraft)

questions.question: During an air taxi briefing, you note that today's density altitude at the departure helipad is significantly higher than standard. The aircraft's published H/V diagram was established at standard conditions. How does high density altitude affect the practical application of the H/V diagram, and what adjustments should you make?
questions.answer: High density altitude degrades helicopter performance in several ways that directly worsen H/V exposure: reduced power available, reduced rotor efficiency, and increased true airspeed for any given indicated airspeed. During an autorotation at high density altitude, the rotor system is less efficient at converting potential energy into lift, the rate of descent in autorotation tends to be higher, and the flare/deceleration phase requires more altitude to execute effectively. This means the published H/V diagram — typically established at or near sea level standard conditions — may be optimistic at high density altitudes. The avoid zone effectively expands upward and outward. While most RFMs do not publish separate H/V diagrams for all density altitude conditions, the FAA and helicopter manufacturers generally advise that pilots should treat the avoid region as larger under high-DA conditions and apply a conservative buffer. Additionally, if gross weight is near maximum and DA is high, the pilot should seriously consider delaying the flight, reducing weight, or choosing a flight profile that maximizes distance from H/V avoid zones (i.e., gaining translational airspeed quickly during departure rather than climbing vertically).
questions.follow_up: If the RFM does not explicitly publish H/V corrections for high density altitude, what is your regulatory and practical obligation as pilot-in-command when operating in conditions that may expand the effective H/V avoid zone?
questions.follow_up_answer: As PIC under 14 CFR 91.3, the pilot is directly responsible for and the final authority on the operation of the aircraft. This includes the duty not to operate in a manner that exceeds the demonstrated safety envelope even when explicit guidance is absent. The pilot must use sound ADM and risk management: consult the RFM for any DA-related performance notes, apply conservative buffers to the published H/V diagram, consider whether the mission can be replanned to avoid extended time in marginal altitude/airspeed combinations, and recognize that 'the book doesn't prohibit it' is not an adequate safety analysis. The pilot can also consult the manufacturer's customer support or applicable ACs for additional guidance. Ultimately, if conditions raise genuine doubt about safe autorotation capability from a given altitude/airspeed profile, the conservative and legally defensible decision is to modify the flight profile to reduce that risk.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3 (PIC responsibility); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (density altitude effects on autorotation); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, risk management); aircraft-specific RFM

questions.question: During an air taxi, what does 'situational awareness' mean in practical terms for a helicopter pilot?
questions.answer: Situational awareness (SA) is the accurate, real-time perception of your position, altitude, surrounding obstacles, other traffic, aircraft performance state, and environmental conditions — and the ability to project how those factors will change in the near future. During air taxi, it means knowing where you are on the airport, where other aircraft or vehicles are, your hover altitude and drift, and what is ahead of you along the taxi route. Loss of SA occurs when any of those mental pictures become inaccurate or incomplete, which can lead to collision, obstacle strike, or controlled flight into terrain.

questions.question: Name three common sources of distraction that can occur during an air taxi that have nothing to do with the outside environment.
questions.answer: Common cockpit-internal distractions during air taxi include: (1) radio communications — responding to ATC or passengers takes attention away from aircraft control; (2) checklist or chart management — looking down in the cockpit while hovering; and (3) avionics or GPS programming — attempting to enter data while the aircraft is airborne. Each of these diverts the pilot's eyes and cognitive attention from maintaining precise position, altitude, and clearance from obstacles, which is especially demanding during low-altitude maneuvering.

questions.question: What is the 'error chain,' and why is it especially relevant during air taxi operations?
questions.answer: The error chain is a sequence of individually manageable events or decisions that, when combined, lead to an accident. No single link is necessarily fatal, but each one narrows options and increases risk. Air taxi is particularly susceptible because it involves sustained low-altitude flight in congested areas with frequent communications, variable surface winds, nearby obstacles, and ground traffic — multiple stressors that can stack up rapidly. Recognizing and breaking even one link (e.g., stopping the taxi to respond to a radio call rather than multitasking) can prevent the chain from progressing to an accident.

questions.question: You are air taxiing across a busy ramp when ATC calls with a complex re-route clearance at the same time a passenger asks you a question. How do you prioritize your tasks to avoid losing situational awareness?
questions.answer: The immediate priority is aircraft control — maintain altitude, speed, and clearance from obstacles without interruption. The helicopter must be stabilized or brought to a hover before splitting attention with communications. Use the SRM principle of workload management: aviate first, communicate second, navigate third. Acknowledge the passenger with a brief non-verbal signal (e.g., raised hand) to pause them. Copy the ATC clearance using standard read-back, writing down key elements if needed. Only after the aircraft is in a controlled stable position should you engage the passenger fully.
