What specific runway incursion risk management protocols apply under Low Visibility Operations, and how do they differ from normal conditions?
questions.answer: Under Low Visibility Operations (LVO) at Category II/III airports, 14 CFR 91.129 and FAA Order JO 7110.65 Chapter 3 require enhanced procedures. ATC will issue explicit crossing or hold short instructions for every runway, even inactive ones—no 'proceed via' shortcuts; you must read back every runway hold short instruction verbatim. ATC may require position reports at specific points and will restrict the movement area to aircraft with operational lighting and radio contact. Some airports have airport surface detection equipment (ASDE) coverage, but this is airport-dependent, not universally required. As a helicopter pilot, you must have a current airport diagram and visually confirm each hold short point before crossing. In LVO, do not transition to hover-taxi near runway edges—this places you outside the protected area identified by lighting and signage. Remain in ground-taxi mode, taxi at reduced speed, keep exterior lights on, and do not proceed past any hold short point without explicit clearance and positive visual identification of the marking.
questions.follow_up: If ATC issues a runway crossing clearance during LVO and you lose visual contact with the centerline lights midway across the runway, what do you do?
questions.follow_up_answer: Stop immediately. Advise ATC of your position and that you have lost visual reference. Do not attempt to continue across the runway without visual confirmation of the centerline or edge. ATC will stop all traffic and provide assistance—potentially dispatching airport vehicles with radio contact to guide you. The risk of a collision from an aircraft on approach is real; stopping and communicating is always safer than continuing blindly. This scenario reinforces why thorough pre-taxi briefing, familiarity with the airport diagram, and slow deliberate movement are critical in LVO conditions.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.129; AC 91-73B; AC 120-57; FAA Order JO 7110.65 Chapter 3; AIM 4-3-19

questions.question: During ground taxi in a wheel-equipped helicopter, why is speed particularly critical when making turns?
questions.answer: During turns, the outer wheel travels a larger arc than the inner wheel. If taxi speed is too high during a turn, centrifugal force acting through the helicopter's center of gravity can cause the inside wheel to become a pivot point, raising the lateral moment arm and increasing rollover risk. This is the classic setup for dynamic rollover. Slower speed during turns reduces the lateral moment arm effect and keeps the helicopter stable.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover)

questions.question: You're taxiing a wheeled helicopter across a large ramp toward the runway. Wind is a direct 15-knot quartering tailwind. How does this affect your speed management and turn technique?
questions.answer: A tailwind during taxi is dangerous because it reduces the relative airflow through the rotor from the front, which decreases the cyclic effectiveness normally used to maintain rotor tilt and control. With a tailwind, you must slow down even further than normal because the effective control input is reduced, and the rotor is less able to counter momentum or lateral forces. During turns, you should make gentler, wider arcs to minimize centrifugal force and avoid creating a pivot condition. Additionally, the collective should be kept lower to prevent the tailwind from increasing rotor lift and making the helicopter light on the wheels.

questions.question: During taxi, you realize you're approaching an intersection faster than intended and need to slow down. What is the correct technique to reduce speed, and what incorrect technique could create a new hazard?
questions.answer: The correct technique is to reduce collective smoothly to decrease the power and resultant speed, use gentle cyclic input to help slow forward motion, and apply wheel brakes gradually and symmetrically if available. The incorrect and dangerous technique would be to apply abrupt or asymmetric braking, which can cause one wheel to lock or become a pivot point and trigger dynamic rollover — especially if the rotor is producing significant lift. Jerky or aggressive cyclic input in an attempt to stop quickly can also cause mast bumping on semi-rigid rotor systems. Speed management must be anticipatory, not reactive.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11

questions.question: A fellow pilot tells you that on a wheeled helicopter with good brakes, taxi speed doesn't really matter because you can always stop quickly. How would you address this flawed reasoning with specific hazards?
questions.answer: This reasoning is flawed for several reasons. First, hard or asymmetric braking at speed can lead to dynamic rollover by creating a fixed pivot point at one wheel while rotor lift and momentum act laterally. Second, abrupt braking can cause the rotor to flap forward on low-inertia rotor systems, increasing blade-ground clearance risk. Third, when the helicopter is 'light on the wheels' — a condition where rotor lift is near hover level — braking effectiveness is dramatically reduced regardless of brake quality. Finally, at higher speeds, the time available to recognize and react to surface hazards is compressed. Speed management is about sustained awareness and control margin, not reliance on stopping ability.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11

questions.question: Explain how speed during a wheeled taxi turn interacts with the critical rollover angle concept, and at what point does the pilot lose the ability to prevent dynamic rollover using cyclic?
questions.answer: Dynamic rollover occurs when a helicopter begins rotating about a fixed point — typically one wheel — and the roll rate exceeds the pilot's ability to arrest it with opposite cyclic. The critical rollover angle is the point of no return: typically around 5–8 degrees of lateral tilt depending on the helicopter type. At speeds above a safe walking pace during turns, centrifugal force transfers lateral moment to the inside wheel, increasing the chance of it becoming the pivot. Once roll begins and the lateral center of gravity moves beyond the wheel base, cyclic input alone cannot generate enough force to stop the roll — the rotor thrust line has shifted outside the support base. The FAA notes that once the critical rollover angle is reached, recovery is impossible. This is why speed control and flat, shallow turns are essential — they prevent reaching the threshold angle in the first place.
questions.follow_up: If you feel the inside wheel beginning to lift during a turn at taxi speed, what is the single most important corrective input?
questions.follow_up_answer: The single most important input is to reduce collective immediately to remove rotor lift and reduce the lateral moment driving the rollover. Applying opposite cyclic alone may be insufficient or even counterproductive if the helicopter is past the critical angle. Lowering collective reduces the total thrust vector, lowers the center of gravity effect, and lets gravity return the helicopter to all wheels on the ground. This must be done promptly — the window for recovery is very small and narrows rapidly once roll begins.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover)

questions.question: On a hot day at a high-density altitude airport, you are taxiing a wheeled helicopter near max gross weight. How does density altitude change the risk calculus for taxi speed and turns, and would you adjust your normal taxi technique?
questions.answer: At high density altitude near max gross weight, the rotor must work harder to produce the same lift, meaning the collective must be higher for a given rotor RPM. This increased collective setting means the rotor is generating more lift even at lower-than-hover collective positions during taxi, making the helicopter lighter on its wheels sooner — sometimes with only small collective increases. This narrows the margin between controlled ground roll and becoming airborne or light enough to trigger dynamic rollover. Additionally, antitorque thrust is reduced in thin air, meaning tail rotor authority during turns is diminished. For taxi technique: reduce speed more than normal, especially before turns; anticipate the collective position carefully to avoid inadvertent lift; use even shallower turn radii; and be extra smooth on all controls to prevent unintended rotor thrust changes. The system state offers less margin for error.
questions.follow_up: If at high density altitude during taxi the helicopter becomes unexpectedly light on the wheels and begins drifting left in a crosswind, what is the correct sequence of inputs?
questions.follow_up_answer: First, reduce collective smoothly to re-establish firm ground contact and reduce rotor lift — this is the priority because it removes the condition allowing drift. Second, apply right pedal to counter any left yaw tendency from the increased collective/torque relationship. Third, use cyclic to maintain directional alignment and resist the crosswind. Do not increase collective to try to hover out of the situation unless fully committed to a hover — an inadvertent partial hover in crosswind conditions at high DA near gross weight significantly increases dynamic rollover and settling risk. The goal is to get weight firmly back on the wheels and then re-evaluate.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-25B Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (Density Altitude)

questions.question: What does 'thrust vector' mean in the context of taxiing a wheel-gear helicopter, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Thrust vector refers to the direction in which the main rotor disk is tilted, which determines the direction and magnitude of the horizontal force applied to move the helicopter during ground taxi. By tilting the cyclic, the pilot tilts the rotor disk and directs lift/thrust in the desired direction — forward, aft, or laterally. It matters because an incorrect or excessive thrust vector can cause the helicopter to accelerate too rapidly, create uneven loading on the landing gear, or produce a tendency toward dynamic rollover, especially during turns or on slopes.

questions.question: You are taxiing a wheel-gear helicopter on a wet, downward-sloping taxiway. You apply forward cyclic to maintain taxi speed, but the helicopter begins accelerating. What is the risk and how should you manage thrust vector and brakes in this scenario?
questions.answer: On a downward slope, gravity assists forward movement, so even a neutral or slightly forward thrust vector can cause the helicopter to accelerate beyond safe taxi speed. The risk is loss of directional control, brake overheating, or a collision with another aircraft or obstacle. The correct risk management approach is to reduce forward cyclic input — possibly transitioning to a slightly aft or neutral thrust vector — to reduce the gravitational acceleration, while applying steady, even brake pressure to control speed. Avoid pumping brakes aggressively, as this can cause directional instability. If taxi speed becomes uncontrollable on the slope, the safest option may be to transition to a low hover taxi.

questions.question: During a wheel-gear taxi turn to the right on a narrow taxiway, you apply right cyclic to direct the thrust vector into the turn. What specific dynamic rollover risk does this create, and how do you mitigate it?
questions.answer: When applying lateral cyclic into a turn during wheel-gear taxi, the rotor disk tilts toward the inside of the turn, directing the thrust vector laterally. This increases the lateral force component on the downwind side landing gear, which can act as a pivot point. If the inside gear catches or the brakes are applied unevenly during the turn, the helicopter can rapidly begin to roll over the inside gear — this is a dynamic rollover scenario. The rollover tendency is amplified if collective is too high. To mitigate: use minimum collective required to keep weight on the wheels without becoming light, apply smooth and coordinated cyclic — not aggressive lateral inputs — use differential braking gently to assist the turn rather than depending on lateral cyclic, and avoid any abrupt control inputs during the turn.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover); Chapter 9

questions.question: A student pilot is taxiing a wheel-gear helicopter and instinctively uses cyclic aggressively to steer left and right during taxi rather than using the anti-torque pedals for directional control and brakes for speed control. What hazard does this habit pattern create regarding thrust vector management?
questions.answer: Using aggressive lateral cyclic inputs to 'steer' during ground taxi incorrectly directs the thrust vector side-to-side rather than maintaining a steady, controlled forward vector. This creates a rocking or 'wallowing' motion that loads and unloads the landing gear asymmetrically, increasing dynamic rollover risk. It also makes speed control erratic because the thrust magnitude changes with each cyclic input. Directional control during wheel-gear taxi should primarily come from the nose wheel steering (if equipped), differential braking, and anti-torque pedals — not from lateral cyclic inputs. The pilot should be trained to maintain a consistent, modest forward thrust vector using cyclic and control speed with brakes.

questions.question: During wheel-gear taxi in a crosswind, a pilot applies into-wind cyclic to prevent the upwind skid from lifting — but this helicopter has wheel-type gear, not skid gear. How does the risk calculus for thrust vector and brake use change specifically for wheel-gear helicopters in a crosswind compared to skid-gear helicopters, and what is the specific rollover risk the pilot must manage?
questions.answer: In a skid-gear helicopter, into-wind cyclic during a crosswind prevents the upwind skid from lifting off the ground. In a wheel-gear helicopter, the wheels roll freely, so the risk profile shifts: into-wind cyclic still helps counteract the tendency of the upwind side to become light, but now the wheel-gear's ability to roll means that if the cyclic input is excessive or the brakes are released, the aircraft can begin to skitter or drift laterally downwind. The specific rollover risk is that the downwind wheel(s) become the inadvertent pivot point — if the upwind wheel lifts even slightly and a brake is applied asymmetrically or a gust hits, the helicopter can rapidly roll over the downwind gear. Brake use must be even and symmetrical to prevent one wheel from locking and creating a pivot. The thrust vector must be balanced: enough into-wind cyclic to keep all wheels loaded, but not so much that the forward taxi vector is significantly compromised or lateral drift toward obstacles increases.
questions.follow_up: If the crosswind is strong enough that you cannot keep the upwind wheels loaded while also maintaining directional control on a narrow taxiway, what is your risk mitigation option as the pilot in command?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the crosswind is strong enough to create an unmanageable rollover risk or directional control problem during wheel-gear taxi, the safest mitigation is to transition to a low hover taxi, where all wheels clear the surface and the pilot can fully use cyclic, collective, and pedals to manage the crosswind as a flight control problem rather than a ground handling problem. Alternatively, the pilot should consider requesting a different taxi route with less crosswind exposure, stopping and waiting for conditions to improve, or requesting a pushback/repositioning with ground crew assistance. The PIC has the authority and responsibility under 14 CFR 91.3 to delay or modify the taxi if safety is in question.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11; 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: You are taxiing a wheel-gear helicopter and the brakes feel soft and less responsive than normal — they may be fading due to heat from a previous series of stop-and-go landings. You still need to taxi approximately 1,500 feet to the ramp. Walk me through your risk management decision-making for thrust vector and brake use for the remainder of the taxi.
questions.answer: Brake fade is a serious safety risk because it can result in complete brake failure with no warning. The risk management process should be: First, immediately reduce taxi speed to the absolute minimum necessary — this reduces kinetic energy and the braking force required to stop. Second, adjust the thrust vector to as close to neutral as possible — reduce forward cyclic significantly so that forward momentum is driven primarily by what is needed to maintain slow creep, not by active thrust. Third, plan for stopping: identify obstacles, taxiway intersections, and other aircraft ahead and mentally plan increased stopping distances. Fourth, avoid any downslope sections if possible — if unavoidable, use a slightly aft thrust vector to oppose gravity. Fifth, consider communicating with ground control about the brake condition and requesting priority to reach the ramp, or stopping in a safe location on the taxiway and notifying maintenance. The underlying principle is that with degraded brakes, the thrust vector becomes the primary speed control tool — forward cyclic must be treated with extreme conservatism. If brakes fail entirely, the pilot must be prepared to transition to a low hover to regain full flight control authority.
questions.follow_up: After landing and shutting down, what is your obligation as PIC regarding the brake fade condition before this helicopter is flown again?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.7, no person may operate an aircraft that is not in airworthy condition. The PIC must ground the aircraft and write up the brake fade condition in the maintenance logbook or squawk sheet (per the operator's maintenance program). The aircraft cannot be returned to service until a certificated A&P mechanic or the appropriate maintenance authority has inspected and determined the brakes airworthy. If operating under Part 135 or an air carrier certificate, MEL procedures and maintenance control must be contacted. The PIC is responsible for not releasing the aircraft to flight operations until the discrepancy is resolved.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: Why is the tail rotor considered the highest-risk rotor component for a ground strike during wheel-taxi operations?
questions.answer: The tail rotor is dangerous during taxi because it is located at the rear of the aircraft where the pilot has limited or no direct visibility, it rotates at high RPM and is virtually invisible in operation, it sits relatively low to the ground on most helicopter models, and it sweeps a path that can easily intersect with obstacles such as ground equipment, fuel hoses, tie-down chains, or personnel who approach from behind. Because the pilot cannot see it directly, situational awareness and ground crew communication are critical.

questions.question: You are ground taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter through a congested ramp area. A fuel truck is parked on your left and a Cessna is parked on your right with its wing at approximately main rotor height. How do you assess and manage this situation before proceeding?
questions.answer: Before entering the narrow passage, stop and visually assess the clearance on both sides. Determine the main rotor diameter and compare it to the available lateral space between the fuel truck and the Cessna's wing. If the passage is not clearly wider than the rotor disc with an adequate safety margin, do not attempt to taxi through — reposition or request ramp marshaling assistance. If you determine there is sufficient clearance, taxi at the slowest controllable speed, keep RPM in the normal operating range to maintain control authority, apply cyclic as needed to counter any wind effect on the disc, and assign a ground observer if available to monitor clearances on both sides. Never assume a gap is wide enough without a deliberate calculation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/Risk Management)

questions.question: During taxi, you notice that a ground crewmember is walking toward the rear of your helicopter from the right side while your tail rotor is turning. What is your immediate action and why?
questions.answer: Immediately bring the helicopter to a stop using the wheel brakes and, if necessary, reduce collective to idle/ground idle setting. Do not continue moving toward or away from the person while the tail rotor is turning and they are in proximity to the rear of the aircraft. Signal the crew member to stop with hand signals or via radio. The tail rotor hazard zone extends from roughly the right rear to directly behind the aircraft, and it is virtually invisible at operating RPM. Movement of the helicopter while someone is in that zone dramatically increases the risk of a fatal strike. Once the crewmember is confirmed clear of the tail rotor arc, you may resume taxi.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11 (Hazards)

questions.question: You are taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter across uneven terrain — specifically a ramp with a pronounced downslope to your left. How does this surface irregularity affect both airframe and rotor clearance risks, and what specific control technique addresses each?
questions.answer: On a left-downsloping surface, the airframe risk is dynamic rollover — the left gear becomes a potential pivot point if the helicopter slides or tips, and inertia combined with collective input can create a rollover moment that exceeds the cyclic's ability to correct. The rotor clearance risk is that the main rotor disc, if left neutral, will be tilted relative to the ground surface, reducing clearance on the left (lower) side where the ground is closer to the rotor arc. Control technique: apply right cyclic to keep the rotor disc approximately level relative to the horizon rather than the sloped ground surface, minimizing the left-side rotor-to-ground clearance reduction. Simultaneously, keep taxi speed slow, avoid any abrupt collective changes, and if the slope is severe, consider stopping and reassessing whether ground taxiing is appropriate versus repositioning via air taxi. The pilot must manage both risks simultaneously — neither can be ignored.
questions.follow_up: At what point does a side slope become a hard limit for ground taxiing, and where would you find that specific limitation for your helicopter?
questions.follow_up_answer: There is no single FAA-universal slope limit for all helicopters — the specific maximum allowable side slope for ground taxi operations is an airframe-specific limitation found in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for that particular helicopter model. It is typically listed in the Limitations section. Some RFMs also address slope limits in the Normal Procedures section. If the RFM does not specify a limit, the manufacturer's guidance and company operations specifications (if applicable) govern. When in doubt, the conservative decision is to conduct an air taxi instead, which eliminates the ground slope/rollover risk entirely. As the pilot in command, you are responsible under 14 CFR 91.9 and 91.13 to operate within all RFM limitations.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover); 14 CFR 91.9; Aircraft RFM Limitations Section

questions.question: A student pilot asks why they can't simply look outside at the rotor blades during taxi to visually confirm adequate clearance. What is the fundamental flaw in that strategy, and how should clearance actually be managed?
questions.answer: The fundamental flaw is that rotor blades in motion are largely or completely invisible — at operating RPM, they cannot be tracked individually by the human eye. Additionally, the pilot's field of view from the cockpit does not cover the full rotor disc arc, especially near the tail, and does not include the tail rotor at all. Attempting to 'watch the blades' creates a dangerous heads-down fixation that pulls attention away from ground traffic, ramp obstacles, and aircraft movement. Proper clearance management relies on: (1) pre-taxi planning — knowing the rotor diameter and mentally mapping it against obstacles before moving; (2) systematic visual scanning of the environment in the direction of intended travel and laterally; (3) using ground personnel or a safety observer for clearance guidance in congested areas; (4) applying correct cyclic inputs based on wind and surface conditions rather than reactive control after observing blade proximity; and (5) maintaining a taxi speed slow enough to stop before reaching any obstacle. Clearance must be ensured before entry into a confined space, not monitored reactively while transiting it.
questions.follow_up: If a ground observer is giving you taxi signals and you are uncertain whether the tail rotor has adequate clearance based on their signals, who has final authority and what should you do?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot in command retains final authority at all times under 14 CFR 91.3. A ground observer provides guidance, but their signals do not transfer legal or operational responsibility to them. If you have any doubt about tail rotor clearance based on the observer's signals — for example, if they appear to be focused on the nose while you cannot confirm tail rotor clearance — you must stop. Communicate clearly with the observer about what specific clearance you need them to monitor. If you cannot get reliable confirmation of tail rotor clearance, do not proceed. The PIC must never surrender situational awareness to a ground observer or assume their signals account for all hazards. Stopping and reassessing is always the correct decision when uncertainty exists.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.3 (PIC Final Authority); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM)

questions.question: Before beginning a wheel taxi in a helicopter, what checklist should you complete, and why is this step considered non-negotiable by the FAA?
questions.answer: The before-taxi or pre-taxi checklist specific to the helicopter being operated must be completed before any ground movement begins. This checklist typically covers flight controls for correct movement and freedom, engine and rotor instruments within normal ranges, flight deck configuration, brakes check, and any wheel-gear specific items such as shimmy dampeners and nose wheel steering. It is non-negotiable because undetected anomalies—such as a binding cyclic or low hydraulic pressure—can lead to loss of control during taxi. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that checklists are a systematic safeguard against omission errors.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9; aircraft manufacturer's POH/RFM checklist section

questions.question: What is the difference between using a 'do-list' (flow) and a printed checklist during wheel taxi operations, and which does the FAA consider the actual checklist?
questions.answer: A flow, or 'do-list,' is a memorized sequence a pilot performs to set up the cockpit by memory and habit. The printed checklist is then used to verify that every item was accomplished correctly. The FAA considers the printed checklist to be the authoritative reference. Using a flow alone without verifying against the printed checklist is not compliant with the checklist-completion standard. During wheel taxi prep, a pilot may flow through instruments and controls, but must cross-check against the POH/RFM checklist before releasing brakes for ground movement.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.9 (operating per flight manual limitations)

questions.question: Name at least four items that are typically verified on a wheel-type helicopter's before-taxi checklist that would not appear on a skid-type helicopter's checklist.
questions.answer: Items unique to wheel-type helicopters on a before-taxi checklist typically include: (1) parking/wheel brake pressure or condition check, (2) nose wheel steering engagement or free-caster mode selection, (3) shimmy dampener check or condition (if applicable), (4) wheel chocks removed and gear pins stowed, (5) hydraulic brake system pressure within limits, and (6) ground handling wheels removed (on some models). These items reflect the unique mechanical and hydraulic systems involved in wheeled landing gear that skid-equipped helicopters simply do not have.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9; applicable POH/RFM for wheel-equipped helicopter

questions.question: You are taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter to the runway and halfway to the runway you notice you skipped the cyclic and collective freedom-of-movement check on the before-taxi checklist. What is the correct action, and what are the potential consequences of continuing without addressing it?
questions.answer: The correct action is to stop the helicopter safely, set the parking brake, and complete the missed checklist item by verifying full cyclic and collective movement with no binding, sticking, or restriction. Continuing without this check risks discovering a flight control anomaly at a critical moment—such as during takeoff or in flight—when consequences could be fatal. A cyclic that binds due to an overlooked maintenance issue or foreign object could cause immediate loss of control. The FAA's ADM guidance stresses that continuing when a known checklist omission exists is an error-chain link that should be broken immediately.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 and Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); 14 CFR 91.7 (aircraft airworthiness)

questions.question: During a wheel taxi checkride in an unfamiliar wheel-equipped helicopter model, how would you demonstrate proper checklist usage even if your flow through the cockpit items was already complete before the examiner called 'cleared to taxi'?
questions.answer: Even if the cockpit flow was completed mentally or physically beforehand, I would verbally call out or physically reference the printed before-taxi checklist item by item, confirming each item aloud and pointing to or indicating each control or instrument. This challenge-and-response or read-and-do method demonstrates that I am using the checklist as verification, not just memory. On a checkride, examiners look for evidence that the checklist was actually consulted, not assumed. Skipping the printed checklist in favor of memory—even if accurate—does not meet the ACS skills standard of 'completing the appropriate checklist.'
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9; ACS PH.V.D Skills requirement

questions.question: ATC issues you a taxi clearance while you are still partway through your before-taxi checklist. How do you handle completing the checklist versus complying with ATC in a timely manner?
questions.answer: Checklist completion takes priority over immediate compliance with a taxi clearance when safety items remain unverified. The correct technique is to acknowledge the taxi clearance to ATC ('Hold short, [call sign] will advise when ready to taxi'), finish the checklist completely, and then begin taxiing. You should never begin taxiing with flight controls, instruments, or braking systems unverified just to avoid a perceived ATC delay. ATC expects pilots to be ready before requesting taxi, but controllers would always prefer a brief hold over a pilot taxiing with an incomplete safety check. This reflects proper workload management under SRM principles.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (SRM/workload management); 14 CFR 91.123 (ATC clearance compliance); AIM 4-3-18

questions.question: A student pilot you are mentoring argues that completing the before-taxi checklist on a wheel-equipped helicopter is 'just going through the motions' because the helicopter was just flown an hour ago and nothing has changed. How do you refute this argument technically and operationally, and what specific scenario would illustrate the risk?
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.7 requires the pilot in command to determine that the aircraft is in an airworthy condition before flight, and 14 CFR 91.9 requires operation within the limitations of the flight manual—which includes the required checklists. If an incident investigation revealed the pilot knowingly or negligently skipped checklist items, the FAA could pursue certificate action under 14 CFR 91.13 (careless or reckless operation) or 49 U.S.C. 44709 (reexamination/certificate action). Additionally, if the helicopter's POH/AFM designates certain checklist items as Required Actions within the Airworthiness Limitations section, bypassing them could constitute a violation of 14 CFR 43.16 and affect the aircraft's airworthiness status under its type certification, compounding PIC liability under 91.7.
questions.follow_up: What FAA regulation or standard specifically holds the pilot responsible for ensuring the checklist was completed, and how could that affect certificate action if an incident occurred because a checklist item was skipped?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 91.7 requires the pilot in command to determine that the aircraft is in an airworthy condition before flight, and 14 CFR 91.9 requires operation within the limitations of the flight manual—which includes the required checklists. If an incident investigation revealed the pilot knowingly or negligently skipped checklist items, the FAA could pursue certificate action under 14 CFR 91.13 (careless or reckless operation) or 49 U.S.C. 44709 (reexamination/certificate action). Additionally, if the helicopter's POH/AFM designates certain checklist items as Required Actions, bypassing them could void the airworthiness of the aircraft under 14 CFR 21.183 limitations, compounding liability.

questions.question: During a checkride, you complete what you believe is the before-taxi checklist, but the examiner tells you that you used the 'before engine start' checklist instead of the 'before taxi' checklist. The helicopter is running and ready to move. What does this reveal about your checklist discipline, and what is the correct recovery?
questions.answer: Using the wrong checklist reveals a breakdown in checklist selection discipline—a higher-order skill than simply running items. The correct before-taxi checklist may contain items not present on the before-engine-start checklist, such as brake pressure check, nose wheel steering confirmation, rotor engagement verification, or instrument scanning confirmation. The correct recovery is to immediately acknowledge the error without defensiveness, locate and identify the correct before-taxi checklist by tab or section header, and complete it from the beginning—even if some items overlap with what was already checked. On a checkride, examiners are evaluating whether a pilot can self-correct and demonstrate procedural integrity, not just whether they can memorize a list.
questions.follow_up: If the POH for your specific helicopter does not have a separate 'before taxi' checklist—only 'before engine start' and 'before takeoff'—how do you address the ACS requirement to complete the appropriate checklist for taxi?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the manufacturer's POH/RFM does not include a dedicated before-taxi checklist, the appropriate checklist is whatever the manufacturer designates as the pre-movement ground check—which may be embedded within the 'after engine start' or a combined checklist. The ACS standard requires completing what is 'appropriate,' meaning the pilot must use the checklist that the manufacturer's AFM/POH and any applicable supplements or SOPs designate for that phase of operation. The pilot should be prepared to explain this to an examiner and reference the specific POH section. If an operator has a company SOP that adds a before-taxi checklist, that document also becomes applicable under 14 CFR 91.9 and any applicable Part 135 operating certificate requirements.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.9; ACS PH.V.D Skills; applicable POH/RFM

questions.question: What does the term 'hotspot' mean on an airport diagram, and how should that affect your taxi planning as a helicopter pilot?
questions.answer: A hotspot is a location on an airport movement area with a history of, or potential for, runway incursions or surface incidents. Hotspots are marked on airport diagrams with a circled number and described in the Chart Supplement. As a helicopter pilot taxiing on the surface, you should identify all hotspots on the diagram before taxiing, brief yourself on the associated risk, and exercise extra vigilance — including a head-up scan — when transiting those areas.
questions.regulatory_ref: AIM 2-3-8 (Airport Hot Spots); FAA Airport/Facility Directory (Chart Supplement)

questions.question: Where can you obtain a current airport diagram for a destination airport before departing on a cross-country that will end with a wheel-taxi to the ramp?
questions.answer: Current airport diagrams can be obtained from several sources: the FAA's free Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide and downloadable airport diagrams at faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav; the Chart Supplement (formerly A/FD) for the appropriate region; aviation apps and EFBs that pull FAA-sourced data; and some GPS/moving map avionics. The chart must be current — FAA terminal procedure publications and airport diagrams are updated on the 28-day AIRAC cycle. Outdated diagrams may not reflect recent taxiway or ramp construction.

questions.question: You are cleared to taxi to the run-up area at an unfamiliar Class D airport. ATC says 'taxi via Alpha, hold short of Runway 28.' You have the airport diagram open on your EFB. Walk me through how you use that diagram from your current ramp position to the hold-short line.
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.129(d) and (g)

questions.question: You are taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter at a towered airport and you realize the taxiway you are on does not match what you see on the airport diagram. What do you do?
questions.answer: I stop the helicopter immediately in a safe position — clear of runways and intersections if possible. I re-orient myself on the airport diagram, comparing visible signage, taxiway markings, and landmarks to my charted position. If I cannot positively confirm my location, I contact ground control, advise them I am unsure of my position, and request progressive taxi instructions. I do not guess or proceed without positive situational awareness, because an incorrect assumption could lead to a runway incursion. ATC has surface detection radar at many airports and can assist. The key is to stop, assess, and communicate — not to continue while confused.

questions.question: You are planning to taxi a wheel-equipped helicopter at a small general aviation airport that has no published airport diagram. How does this change your pre-taxi preparation and situational awareness strategy?
questions.answer: If no airport diagram is published, I use the best available alternatives: a satellite imagery view on an EFB or mapping application to familiarize myself with the ramp, taxiway, and runway layout; the Chart Supplement entry for the airport, which often describes the taxiway and runway configuration in text; and NOTAMs for any construction or closures. If I am unfamiliar with the airport, I may ask the FBO for a ramp diagram or request progressive taxi instructions from the CTAF or UNICOM. During taxi, I increase vigilance by slowing down, scanning for runway markings, and treating all hard-surface areas as potentially active runways until confirmed otherwise.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.103 (preflight action); AIM 4-3-18; FAA Chart Supplement

questions.question: You are wheel-taxiing a helicopter at a large Class B airport at night. The tower clears you to 'cross Runway 15, then taxi via Echo and Delta to the south ramp.' When you look at the airport diagram, you count three runways you will pass near on that route. How do you confirm which crossing was authorized and which were not?
questions.answer: Runway guard lights — also called 'wig-wag' lights — are alternating flashing yellow lights installed at taxiway/runway intersections to warn pilots they are approaching a runway. They can be in-pavement (embedded in the taxiway surface) or elevated on both sides of the taxiway. Additionally, runway hold-short positions are marked with elevated red stop bar lights at many airports. At airports equipped with a Surface Movement Guidance and Control System (SMGCS), red stop bar lights remain illuminated until ATC issues a crossing clearance and activates the green lead-on lights. This ATC-controlled feature is available at select major airports; pilots should not assume all airports with stop bars have remotely controlled systems. Regardless of stop bar type, a pilot must never cross an illuminated red stop bar without explicit ATC clearance. If I see alternating flashing yellows or red stop bars in my path, I stop immediately regardless of my positional awareness on the diagram.
questions.follow_up: What lighting cue on the airport surface should immediately alert you that you are approaching a runway hold-short position, even if you have lost track of where you are on the diagram?
questions.follow_up_answer: Runway guard lights — also called 'wig-wag' lights — are alternating flashing yellow lights installed at taxiway/runway intersections to warn pilots they are approaching a runway. They can be in-pavement (embedded in the taxiway surface) or elevated on both sides of the taxiway. Additionally, runway hold-short positions are marked with elevated red stop bar lights at many airports, which remain illuminated until ATC issues a crossing clearance and activates the green lead-on lights. If I see alternating flashing yellows or red stop bars in my path, I stop immediately regardless of my positional awareness on the diagram.
questions.regulatory_ref: AIM 2-1-9 (Runway Guard Lights); AIM 2-3-5 (Taxi Clearances); AIM 4-3-18 (Runway Incursion Avoidance); 14 CFR 91.129

questions.question: What is the difference between a castoring nosewheel and a steerable nosewheel on a wheel-equipped helicopter, and how does that affect how you taxi?
questions.answer: A castoring nosewheel swivels freely and is not directly linked to the anti-torque pedals; directional control on the ground is achieved through differential braking and cyclic inputs. A steerable nosewheel is linked to the anti-torque pedals, allowing the pilot to steer the helicopter on the ground similarly to a fixed-wing aircraft nosewheel. On a castoring nosewheel helicopter, you must use the brakes more actively for directional control. On a steerable nosewheel, pedal inputs translate directly to nosewheel direction.

questions.question: On a helicopter with a tailwheel-type landing gear, what is the general rule for whether the tailwheel should be locked or unlocked during straight-ahead ground taxi?
questions.answer: During straight-ahead ground taxi, the tailwheel is typically locked to provide positive directional control and prevent the tail from swinging out. The tailwheel lock keeps the tailwheel aligned with the helicopter's longitudinal axis. It is unlocked when tight turns or repositioning maneuvers require the tailwheel to swivel freely. The specific procedures depend on the aircraft's flight manual (POH/RFM), which must always be the primary reference.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; applicable aircraft RFM

questions.question: You are taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter with a castoring nosewheel and need to make a sharp 90-degree turn to the right at a taxiway intersection. Walk me through the control inputs you would use, specifically addressing nosewheel position.
questions.answer: With a castoring nosewheel, there is no lock to manage because the nosewheel swivels freely. To execute the sharp right turn: apply right cyclic to lean the rotor disk slightly in the direction of the turn, use right brake to initiate and control the turn rate, and modulate the collective as needed to maintain slight ground contact pressure without becoming airborne. The castoring nosewheel will naturally follow the turn direction once the brake and cyclic inputs pivot the helicopter. The pilot should avoid excessive speed into the turn, use smooth brake application, and keep rotor RPM in the normal range throughout. After completing the turn, resume straight-ahead taxi.

questions.question: During a pre-takeoff check, you verify the nosewheel lock is engaged for taxi, but now you are about to transition from ground taxi to a hover taxi or liftoff. What must you do with the nosewheel lock and why?
questions.answer: Before transitioning to a hover taxi or liftoff, the nosewheel lock must be disengaged (unlocked). If the nosewheel lock is left engaged and the helicopter lands or touches down in a position other than perfectly aligned with the direction of travel, the locked nosewheel can cause the landing gear to side-load, potentially leading to dynamic rollover or gear damage. Additionally, if the helicopter lands with a locked nosewheel while drifting laterally, the aircraft can tip or roll. The RFM will specify the exact checklist step, but the general principle is: unlock before any operation where the helicopter may depart the ground or where landing direction may not match the nosewheel direction.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover); applicable aircraft RFM

questions.question: You are repositioning a tailwheel-equipped helicopter on a ramp with limited space. The lineman wants you to make a very tight 180-degree turn. What would you do with the tailwheel lock for this maneuver, and what risk must you manage?
questions.answer: For a very tight 180-degree turn, the tailwheel lock should be disengaged (unlocked) to allow the tailwheel to swivel freely, enabling the tightest possible turning radius. With the tailwheel locked, the turning radius is larger and the aircraft may not be able to complete the turn in the available space without dragging or side-loading the tailwheel. The primary risk to manage is dynamic rollover — any time a wheel is constrained or catches while the helicopter has some lateral lift component, the aircraft can roll over the contact point. The pilot must keep ground speed very slow, apply smooth cyclic and pedal inputs, and monitor rotor RPM throughout. If at any point the tail drags or catches, stop immediately and reassess.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11; applicable aircraft RFM

questions.question: On an aircraft with both a tailwheel lock and a steerable nosewheel system, a student consistently leaves the tailwheel lock engaged throughout the entire flight operation, including during slope landings and departure from unimproved surfaces. As an examiner, what specific hazard does this create, and how would you expect an applicant to demonstrate proper tailwheel lock management during a practical test?
questions.answer: Leaving the tailwheel lock engaged during slope landings and departures from unimproved surfaces creates serious dynamic rollover risk. On uneven terrain, if the helicopter touches down while drifting or at an angle to the landing direction, the locked tailwheel cannot swivel to accommodate the actual ground track — it becomes a fixed pivot point. This can apply a rolling moment to the helicopter, and if the rotor is still producing lift (or the collective is raised), the aircraft can roll over the locked tailwheel. On departure from uneven ground, a locked tailwheel can catch on a ridge, rock, or soft spot, again creating an uncontrolled pivot. During the practical test, the applicant must demonstrate: (1) referencing the RFM for the specific lock/unlock checklist items; (2) unlocking the tailwheel prior to any operation on surfaces where the landing direction may not be perfectly controlled; (3) engaging the tailwheel lock only during straight-ahead taxi on prepared surfaces as specified by the RFM; (4) verbalizing their decision-making rationale clearly when transitioning between locked and unlocked states.
questions.follow_up: The applicant argues that keeping the tailwheel locked at all times actually improves directional control and reduces workload. How do you respond, and what is the fundamental aerodynamic principle that makes this argument dangerous?
questions.follow_up_answer: The argument misunderstands the dynamic rollover hazard. Dynamic rollover occurs when a wheel or skid becomes a fixed pivot point while the rotor produces a lateral lift component. A locked tailwheel on anything other than a perfectly flat, prepared surface can become exactly that fixed pivot. The critical principle is that a helicopter's rotor can produce a rolling moment that, once the rollover angle exceeds roughly 5–8 degrees (the specific critical rollover angle varies by aircraft and is listed in the RFM), cannot be corrected by any control input — the aircraft will roll over regardless of what the pilot does. The locked tailwheel reduces directional workload only in the narrow scenario of straight taxi on smooth pavement; in every other scenario it introduces a constraint that can initiate an unrecoverable rolling moment. Reducing workload is never a valid justification for accepting an unrecoverable accident risk.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover); applicable aircraft RFM

questions.question: What is the purpose of keeping the landing gear in contact with the surface during a surface taxi in a wheel-type helicopter?
questions.answer: Maintaining ground contact keeps the helicopter in the taxi mode rather than transitioning to a hover, which reduces power requirements and increases directional control stability. It also minimizes exposure to dynamic rollover risk, reduces the chance of unexpected lift-off, and prevents the helicopter from becoming airborne in gusty wind conditions. Ground contact provides a mechanical stabilizing reference that helps prevent loss of directional control.

questions.question: When surface-taxiing with a direct tailwind, how should you position the cyclic?
questions.answer: With a direct tailwind, move the cyclic to a slightly forward position to lean the rotor disk into the relative wind — which is coming from behind the helicopter. This counteracts the tendency of the tailwind to push the nose up and lift the tail, which could cause the helicopter to become unstable or even tip. Aft cyclic would be the worst input in this situation because it would amplify the destabilizing effect of the tailwind on the rotor disk.

questions.question: You're surface-taxiing a wheel-type helicopter and a 20-knot crosswind is coming from your left. Describe exactly how you position the cyclic and explain the aerodynamic reason for that input.
questions.answer: With a left crosswind, tilt the cyclic into the wind — meaning left cyclic. This positions the rotor disk so it tilts into the relative wind, reducing the aerodynamic lifting force on the upwind (left) side of the disk. Without this correction, the crosswind would push under the retreating blade side (or the upwind side depending on rotor direction), creating an asymmetric lift condition that could tip the helicopter away from the wind or cause a lateral rollover tendency. By leaning the disk into the crosswind, you counteract that asymmetric force and keep the fuselage level and the gear on the ground.

questions.question: You are taxiing a wheel-type helicopter and the wind shifts from a headwind to a right quartering tailwind while you are moving. What control corrections do you make, and what loss-of-control risk are you now managing?
questions.answer: As the wind shifts to a right quartering tailwind, transition the cyclic forward (to counteract the tailwind component pitching the nose down) and right (to counteract the right crosswind). The primary risk you are now managing is dynamic rollover: the right crosswind unloads the left (upwind) wheel while the tailwind pitches the nose, making the right (downwind) wheel the pivot point. If cyclic correction is insufficient or delayed, the helicopter can tip over the downwind wheel. Pedal inputs may also be needed to counteract yaw. Early, smooth cyclic correction is essential before the upwind wheel lightens significantly.

questions.question: During a surface taxi in gusty conditions, you notice the upwind wheel is starting to lighten. What does this tell you about your cyclic position, and what do you do to correct it?
questions.answer: The upwind wheel lightening tells you that the rotor disk is not tilted sufficiently into the wind — the cyclic correction is inadequate. The wind is generating more lift on the upwind side of the rotor than you are compensating for, which raises the upwind landing gear. Immediately add more cyclic input into the wind to tilt the disk further into the relative airflow, increasing the counteracting aerodynamic force on that side. You should also verify that collective is not creeping up. A lightening upwind wheel is an early warning sign of an impending dynamic rollover — if uncorrected, the helicopter can tip over the downwind wheel as a pivot point. The correct response is prompt but smooth cyclic into the wind.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11

questions.question: You're surface-taxiing a wheel-type helicopter with a strong left quartering tailwind. The main rotor turns counterclockwise when viewed from above. Explain how the combination of wind direction, rotor rotation direction, and cyclic position interact to create the greatest rollover risk in this scenario, and how you manage all three factors simultaneously.
questions.answer: With a counterclockwise rotating main rotor and a left quartering tailwind, the blade moving aft on the right side of the aircraft is the retreating blade, and the blade moving forward on the left is the advancing blade. The left quartering tailwind creates a lifting force on the upwind (left) side of the rotor disk while simultaneously pushing airflow under the tail and left side of the aircraft. The retreating blade on the right already produces less lift due to lower relative airspeed, and the wind from the left further amplifies the asymmetry. To counteract this, you need right and forward cyclic — right to lean the disk into the left crosswind component, and forward to counteract the tailwind component trying to raise the nose or pitch the disk aft. The rollover risk is greatest toward the right (downwind) side because the right main wheel becomes the potential pivot point. Simultaneously, you must keep collective low to prevent inadvertent lift-off that would eliminate ground friction as a stabilizing factor. Taxi speed should be slow so that abrupt inputs are not required. The pilot must be aggressive with right cyclic but smooth — any hesitation allows the left wheel to unload and sets up an unrecoverable rollover condition.
questions.follow_up: At what point during a surface taxi dynamic rollover does it become unrecoverable, and what is the critical control response before that point?
questions.follow_up_answer: Dynamic rollover becomes unrecoverable when the helicopter reaches the critical rollover angle — typically around 8 degrees of bank with the gear on the surface. At that angle, the moment created by the rotor thrust component exceeds the restoring moment available from the rotor, and the helicopter will continue to roll regardless of corrective inputs. Before reaching that angle, the only correct response is immediate, aggressive cyclic into the roll (toward the high side) combined with simultaneous reduction of collective to reduce total thrust. Once past the critical angle, reducing collective actually makes the situation worse because it removes the last remaining corrective force. This is why early recognition — indicated by wheel lightening — is essential. Once rolling, the window for recovery is measured in fractions of a second.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11

questions.question: A student surface-taxiing a wheel-type helicopter in a crosswind consistently positions the cyclic away from the wind instead of into it, believing they need to 'lean away' from the force pushing on them. How do you explain the correct aerodynamic logic, and what observable aircraft behavior would occur if they continued the incorrect technique?
questions.answer: The student's instinct is treating the helicopter like a boat or car — leaning away from a push. But the rotor disk is an aerodynamic surface, not a rigid sail. When you apply cyclic away from the wind (downwind), you tilt the rotor disk away from the wind, which actually increases the angle of attack on the upwind side and decreases it on the downwind side. This amplifies the asymmetric lift — more lift is generated on the upwind side — which further unloads the upwind wheel and loads the downwind wheel. The correct logic is: you tilt the disk into the wind to flatten the angle at which the wind strikes the upwind portion of the disk, reducing the net lifting force. Think of it like angling a wing into relative wind to control where lift goes, not away from it. If the student continued the incorrect technique, the observable behaviors would be: progressive unloading of the upwind wheel, the helicopter wanting to drift downwind, increasing tendency to yaw into the wind (weathervane), and ultimately the upwind wheel fully lifting, which could lead to dynamic rollover over the downwind main wheel as a pivot point. In severe crosswinds, the helicopter could tip over within seconds of the upwind wheel fully clearing the surface.
questions.follow_up: If this student then over-corrects with extreme into-wind cyclic to compensate, what new risk does that create?
questions.follow_up_answer: Extreme into-wind cyclic causes the rotor disk to tilt aggressively into the wind, which can cause the rotor blade to strike the tail boom or airframe (blade clearance violation) if the disk tilts far enough — particularly on low-inertia rotor systems. Additionally, with extreme cyclic displacement, effective translational lift may cause the helicopter to begin drifting into the wind and the nose may pitch in an unexpected direction. The rotor thrust vector is now pointed significantly sideways, which reduces the vertical component of lift and can cause unintended collective response. The pilot may also lose smooth collective control while fixating on the cyclic correction. The correct technique is a moderate, timely correction into the wind — enough to keep the wheels planted equally — not a maximum displacement input. Smooth, early control inputs are always superior to delayed, extreme corrections.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11

questions.question: What is the purpose of the brakes when taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter, and how do they differ from how you'd slow down a skid-equipped helicopter?
questions.answer: On a wheel-type helicopter, the wheel brakes are used to slow or stop the aircraft during ground taxi, similar to how you would use brakes on a fixed-wing aircraft. On a skid-equipped helicopter, brakes are not available — slowing or stopping requires reducing cyclic back toward neutral and reducing collective to lower rotor thrust. The availability of wheel brakes gives the pilot direct speed control independent of rotor inputs.

questions.question: You're taxiing a wheel-equipped helicopter on a slight downhill slope toward the fuel pit and your taxi speed is beginning to increase more than desired. Walk me through the exact sequence of control inputs you'd use to reduce speed without stopping.
questions.answer: First, apply moderate aft cyclic to reduce the forward tilt of the rotor disk, which reduces the horizontal component of rotor thrust pulling the helicopter forward. Simultaneously, you can use light brake pressure to help check the speed. If the slope is steep enough, a slight reduction in collective can further reduce overall rotor thrust. The key is coordination — aft cyclic first to reduce forward drive, then brakes as needed to match the desired taxi speed. Avoid applying excessive aft cyclic, which could risk mast bumping or tail strike at low airspeeds.

questions.question: During wheel taxi, you increase collective slightly to cushion over a rough section of taxiway and you notice Nr begins to decay toward the lower limit of the green arc. Your helicopter has a manual throttle. What is your response, and what is the consequence if you do not act?
questions.answer: On a manually throttled helicopter, the pilot must manually increase throttle to compensate for the added load on the rotor when collective pitch is increased. If Nr is decaying toward the lower limit of the green arc, the pilot should smoothly increase throttle to restore RPM to the middle of the normal range. The consequence of inaction is continued RPM decay into the caution or warning range. If RPM drops below the minimum for safe flight, the helicopter would be unable to lift off safely if required. At critically low RPM, rotor stall becomes a hazard — the rotor loses lift suddenly, and recovery at low altitude may be impossible, making prevention through proper throttle management essential.

questions.question: A student tends to use only the brakes to control taxi speed and ignores the cyclic entirely. What hazard does this introduce, and how do you correct this technique?
questions.answer: Relying solely on brakes without cyclic coordination is problematic for several reasons. If the brakes are applied aggressively with a forward cyclic position still in, the rotor disk continues pushing the helicopter forward even while the wheels are being braked, creating a nose-low pitching tendency and putting uneven stress on the landing gear. Additionally, using only brakes to control speed leads to stop-and-go taxi instead of smooth speed management. The correction is to have the student use aft cyclic input to reduce forward rotor thrust simultaneously with brake application — this creates smooth, coordinated deceleration. Think of cyclic as the primary speed manager and brakes as the fine-tuning tool.

questions.question: You're demonstrating taxi technique to a student and you briefly apply aft cyclic while taxiing at a moderate speed to slow down. The student asks why you didn't just use the brakes and save rotor wear. How do you explain the coordinated use of all three controls — cyclic, collective, and brakes — and when each takes priority during a taxi?
questions.answer: This is a great teaching moment. Cyclic is the primary directional and speed control during taxi — it tilts the rotor disk and determines how much horizontal thrust the rotor pushes the helicopter forward or backward. Collective sets the overall power level and rotor thrust, and on level ground should generally be kept low enough to keep the helicopter firmly on the wheels but high enough to allow controllable movement. Brakes are the fine-tuning and emergency stopping tool — they should not be the primary speed regulator. If a pilot uses brakes as the primary speed control while leaving forward cyclic in, they create a tug-of-war between the rotor pulling forward and the brakes fighting back, which stresses the landing gear, causes uneven wear, and reduces smooth control. Priority order: use cyclic first to manage speed and direction, use collective to manage rotor load and prevent unintended lift, and use brakes to make fine adjustments or to stop. All three should be coordinated together, not used in isolation.
questions.follow_up: If the helicopter POH or RFM specifies a maximum taxi speed, where does that limit come from and what controls help you stay within it?
questions.follow_up_answer: The maximum taxi speed in the RFM is typically set by landing gear structural limits, tire speed ratings, or aircraft stability considerations during ground roll. It is not an aerodynamic limit. Staying within this limit is primarily managed through aft cyclic (reducing forward thrust) and brake application — collective should be kept low to minimize rotor lift contribution. If taxi speed begins to approach the limit, aft cyclic and braking should be applied together to decelerate smoothly.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; Aircraft RFM/POH for specific speed limits

questions.question: What is the primary control input a pilot uses to manage main rotor RPM while taxiing a helicopter equipped with wheel-type landing gear on the ground?
questions.answer: The collective is the primary control for managing rotor RPM and powerplant output during ground taxi. Raising the collective increases blade pitch and load on the rotor system, which can cause Nr to decay if not matched with a corresponding increase in throttle (on non-governed systems). Lowering the collective reduces pitch and load, allowing RPM to climb. On governor-equipped helicopters, the governor automatically adjusts fuel flow to maintain the target RPM as collective is adjusted.

questions.question: Why is low rotor RPM considered a critical hazard during ground taxi in a wheeled helicopter, even though you are not in flight?
questions.answer: Low rotor RPM during ground taxi is dangerous because if an emergency liftoff becomes necessary — for example, to avoid a ground obstacle or taxiing aircraft — the rotor must be at or near normal operating RPM to provide adequate lift and control response. The FAA emphasizes that rotor RPM must be maintained in the normal operating range at all times the helicopter is operating. Additionally, operating below the normal RPM range risks damage to the powerplant and drivetrain. The primary concern during ground taxi is ensuring sufficient rotor energy is available for immediate control response if needed.

questions.question: You are taxiing a wheeled helicopter across a large ramp on a hot day. You notice your Nr has crept to the upper edge of the normal range. What is causing this, and what corrective action do you take?
questions.answer: On a hot day at low density altitude effect on engine output, if the governor is functioning, it should be holding Nr steady — but if the helicopter is on a slight downslope or the collective is lowered to reduce taxi height, reduced blade pitch lowers the load on the rotor and Nr can climb toward the upper limit. The corrective action is to slightly raise the collective to add blade pitch and increase rotor load, which will bring Nr back into the middle of the normal (green arc) range. On non-governed systems, reducing throttle slightly would also be appropriate. The pilot should cross-check the engine torque and temperature gauges to ensure all powerplant parameters remain within limits while adjusting.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; aircraft-specific RFM

questions.question: During wheel taxi, you increase collective slightly to cushion over a rough section of taxiway and you notice Nr begins to decay toward the lower limit of the green arc. Your helicopter has a manual throttle. What is your response, and what is the consequence if you do not act?
questions.answer: On a manually throttled helicopter, the pilot must manually increase throttle to compensate for the added load on the rotor when collective pitch is increased. If Nr is decaying toward the lower limit of the green arc, the pilot should smoothly increase throttle to restore RPM to the middle of the normal range. The consequence of inaction is continued RPM decay into the caution or warning range. If RPM drops below the minimum for safe flight, the helicopter would be unable to lift off safely if required. At critically low RPM, rotor stall becomes a hazard — the rotor loses lift suddenly, and recovery at low altitude may be impossible, making prevention through proper throttle management essential.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11

questions.question: How does the coordination of cyclic, collective, and pedals during a wheel taxi turn affect the powerplant and Nr, and what must the pilot monitor to keep all parameters within limits?
questions.answer: During a wheel taxi turn, the pilot uses cyclic to tilt the helicopter slightly in the direction of turn, differential braking or forward/aft cyclic to steer (depending on helicopter design), and pedals to counteract torque changes. When collective is adjusted — even slightly — the load on the rotor and engine changes, affecting Nr and powerplant torque. The pilot must monitor: (1) Nr on the tachometer to ensure it stays within the green arc; (2) engine torque or manifold pressure/fuel flow to stay within limits; (3) turbine outlet temperature (TOT) or EGT on turbine helicopters to avoid exceedances during any power additions. Smooth, coordinated inputs prevent Nr fluctuation during turns.

questions.question: You are wheel-taxiing a turbine helicopter and the governor fails, causing Nr to begin climbing above the normal range. The helicopter is mid-ramp with aircraft and equipment nearby. Walk me through your immediate action sequence to control Nr and powerplant speed without losing situational awareness of your surroundings.
questions.answer: With governor failure and Nr climbing above the normal (green arc) range, the immediate actions are: (1) Smoothly increase collective to add blade pitch and load the rotor, which will resist Nr climb; (2) Simultaneously reduce throttle/fuel control to reduce engine output — specific procedures vary by aircraft type; consult the RFM/AFM emergency procedures for your helicopter's fuel control system (some turbines require throttle movement, others fuel control lever override); (3) Monitor Nr, torque, and TOT/TGT simultaneously to ensure you are not overloading the drivetrain while reducing RPM; (4) Maintain situational awareness by keeping a slow, controlled taxi pace or stopping in place if clear — do not allow the emergency management to distract you into taxiing into obstacles or personnel; (5) Once Nr is stabilized manually, taxi clear of congested areas and shut down per RFM. Overspeed of Nr risks exceeding rotor and gearbox limits, which can cause structural damage or rotor separation. Post-flight: Under 14 CFR 91.7, a governor failure must be corrected by an FAA-certificated AMT or repair station and logged per 14 CFR 43.9 and 43.11 before the aircraft is returned to service.
questions.follow_up: After landing and shutting down following a governor failure, what is the regulatory requirement before flying the aircraft again?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.7, the pilot in command is responsible for determining the aircraft is in an airworthy condition prior to flight. A governor failure is a system malfunction that must be addressed by an FAA-certificated aviation maintenance technician (AMT) or repair station. The aircraft may not be returned to service until the discrepancy is corrected and an appropriate logbook entry is made per 14 CFR 43.9 and 43.11. The aircraft must be returned to its type certificate configuration before flight.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9 and Chapter 11; 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 43.9; 14 CFR 43.11

questions.question: When wheel-taxiing a helicopter along a centerline, which primary control inputs are you using to keep the track within the 4-foot tolerance?
questions.answer: Cyclic is the primary control for directional tracking — lateral cyclic steers the helicopter left or right to stay on the centerline, and fore/aft cyclic controls taxi speed. Anti-torque pedals control heading (yaw) to keep the nose aligned with the direction of travel. Collective is managed to keep the helicopter sufficiently light on its wheels for responsive directional control while maintaining enough ground contact for rolling traction and preventing inadvertent liftoff. The coordination of all three controls is required to maintain precise track.

questions.question: Why is it easier to drift off a specified track in a helicopter with wheel-type landing gear compared to a skid-equipped helicopter during ground taxiing?
questions.answer: Wheeled helicopters can roll freely in any direction because the wheels offer little lateral friction resistance. A skid-equipped helicopter has significant ground drag that resists sideward movement. In a wheeled helicopter, even a small uncorrected crosswind component or an unintended lateral cyclic input can cause the aircraft to drift sideways across the pavement quickly, making the 4-foot tolerance more challenging to maintain and requiring continuous active correction.

questions.question: You are wheel-taxiing down a taxiway with a 15-knot direct crosswind from the left. Describe the specific control technique you would use to maintain the centerline within 4 feet.
questions.answer: Apply left lateral cyclic into the wind to counteract the tendency to drift right. The amount of cyclic depends on wind strength — enough to prevent lateral drift without overcorrecting and tracking left of centerline. Use anti-torque pedals to keep the nose aligned with the direction of travel so the helicopter tracks straight rather than weather-vaning into the wind. Reduce collective slightly if needed to keep wheels firmly on the ground and maintain rolling traction. Continuously scan the centerline ahead and make small corrective inputs early — large corrections create overcorrection cycles that are harder to manage within the 4-foot standard.

questions.question: During a practical test wheel-taxi demonstration, you notice your helicopter has drifted 3.5 feet right of the centerline. What is the correct recovery technique, and what common mistake should you avoid?
questions.answer: Apply gentle left lateral cyclic to initiate a slow drift back toward centerline. As the helicopter begins tracking back left, neutralize or slightly reduce the correction so you don't overshoot and end up 4 feet to the left. The goal is a gradual, controlled return to centerline — not a sharp snap correction. The most common mistake is over-correcting: applying too much cyclic input causes the helicopter to swing past centerline and then drift the other direction, creating an oscillating pattern that is difficult to control and will likely exceed the 4-foot tolerance on the opposite side. Small, early inputs are the key to staying within limits.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9; PH ACS Task V.D

questions.question: You are executing a 90-degree turn on the taxiway during a wheel-taxi checkride task. How do you maintain the 4-foot track standard through the turn rather than just on the straight sections?
questions.answer: During the turn, you must follow the inside or center of the taxiway turn radius as defined by the centerline or as directed. Begin the turn by applying lateral cyclic in the direction of the turn while using pedals to coordinate the heading change. Manage taxi speed by reducing it before the turn so the helicopter doesn't swing wide — the inertia of the wheeled undercarriage can cause tracking to the outside of the turn. Anticipate the turn entry point slightly before the centerline arc begins to account for the helicopter's rolling inertia. Keep collective at a level that maintains rotor partially loaded for steering response without becoming airborne. Watch the nose position relative to the centerline continuously and be prepared to modulate cyclic pressure throughout to stay within the 4-foot tolerance as the turn arc changes radius. Complete the turn aligned with the new centerline before allowing speed to increase.

questions.question: What visual reference do you use to confirm your wheeled helicopter is properly stopped at a hold short line?
questions.answer: The pilot looks directly down and to the side to confirm the main wheels are just behind and clear of the hold short line. Because the cockpit is forward of the main gear on most wheeled helicopters, the pilot should know the specific offset distance between the cockpit and the main gear for their aircraft. Additionally, the pilot verifies that the rotor disc — the most forward-extending part of the aircraft — does not overhang the line, often by using peripheral visual references such as wingtip or blade position relative to taxiway edge markings.

questions.question: What does a double solid yellow line with a dashed yellow line adjacent to it on the taxiway surface indicate, and on which side must the helicopter hold?
questions.answer: That marking is a runway holding position marking (hold short line). The solid lines are always on the side where the aircraft must hold — in other words, aircraft must stop on the side of the solid double lines and may not proceed past them toward the runway without ATC clearance. The dashed lines face the runway side, indicating it is permissible to cross from that direction.

questions.question: You are ground taxiing a wheeled helicopter and ATC instructs you to 'hold short of Runway 27 at Bravo.' As you slow to a stop, you notice your cockpit is directly over the hold short line. What action do you take and why?
questions.answer: You must back up or reposition so that the entire helicopter — including the main gear and the rotor disc — is clear of the hold short line on the non-runway side. The cockpit sitting over the line means the main gear is likely past the line, placing part of the aircraft in the runway safety area. You would use careful aft cyclic combined with collective to back the helicopter away from the line until the main gear and rotor disc are clearly behind it. Then advise ATC if needed. Operating past a hold short line without clearance is a runway incursion, which is a serious safety and regulatory violation.

questions.question: ATC clears you to taxi to the runway and hold short of an ILS critical area marking. How do you recognize that marking and where do you stop relative to it?
questions.answer: The ILS critical area boundary is marked by a yellow ladder-style marking (two solid yellow lines with evenly spaced perpendicular rungs) painted on the taxiway surface, along with a sign showing 'ILS CRITICAL AREA.'
