If your situation is marginal and you are still evaluating, a brief advisory like '[Callsign], power check, may need to go around' gives ATC early awareness. Never sacrifice aircraft control for radio communication, but inform ATC as soon as it is safe to do so.

questions.question: You are inbound for a steep approach at a non-towered airport and you hear another pilot announce he is on a two-mile final for the same runway in a Cessna 172. Your steep approach will require a steeper glidepath and slower final speed. How do you coordinate via radio to safely sequence yourself?
questions.answer: Broadcast on CTAF acknowledging the traffic: '[Airport name] traffic, Helicopter N123AB has traffic in sight, will follow the Cessna on final, will hold position [describe your position] to allow separation, [airport name].' If you determine you cannot safely sequence behind the 172 or timing is problematic, announce you are extending or holding off to allow the fixed-wing to land first. Your steep approach profile means you will slow significantly more than the 172 on final, which increases the risk of conflict if you attempt to squeeze in ahead or too close behind. Clear, proactive radio communication prevents a mid-air conflict.

questions.question: During a steep approach to a towered airport, ATC instructs you to 'keep your speed up to the threshold' to accommodate a Boeing 737 on a three-mile final behind you. You know that complying with this instruction conflicts with your steep approach technique and may compromise safety. What do you do, and what exactly do you say on the radio?
questions.answer: You are not required to accept an ATC clearance that compromises safety. Immediately advise ATC: '[Callsign] unable, conducting steep approach, cannot maintain speed. Request different sequencing or immediate clearance to land.' Under 14 CFR 91.3, you as pilot-in-command are responsible for the safe operation of the aircraft. ATC may not fully understand the speed limitations inherent in a helicopter steep approach. By declaring 'unable' and explaining your constraint, you give ATC the opportunity to hold the 737, extend your clearance, or provide an alternate solution. Never compromise your approach technique to accommodate ATC without first communicating your constraints.
questions.follow_up: If ATC responds by clearing the Boeing 737 to land and tells you to 'expedite clearing the runway,' but you are still in the steep approach and not yet committed to landing — what are your options and what do you say?
questions.follow_up_answer: You have the authority to execute a go-around at any point. Declare: '[Callsign] going around.' This is non-negotiable if safety is at risk. Under 14 CFR 91.3(a), PIC authority supersedes ATC instructions when safety requires deviation. After the go-around is established, contact ATC and explain the situation. You may also declare 'minimum fuel' or an emergency if applicable. Document the event with an ASRS report to provide immunity and share safety data. The key point: ATC issues instructions, but you — as PIC — are responsible for the safety of the flight.

questions.question: You are conducting a steep approach into a confined area during a cross-country when your radio fails. You are five miles from a towered airport and need to land there due to a low fuel state. Describe how you handle communications and what signals or procedures you use to comply with ATC requirements.
questions.answer: Squawk 7600 on the transponder immediately to declare a communication failure. Per 14 CFR 91.185 and AIM 6-4-1, in VFR conditions, proceed to the airport, rock wings to acknowledge light gun signals from the tower, and watch for steady green (cleared to land) or other light gun signals. Fly a normal or modified pattern and comply with light gun signals. Land and contact ATC by any means available (phone, FBO radio) after landing. Document the radio failure. For the steep approach specifically, if light gun signals are given, they apply to your approach just as with any aircraft — clear the active runway promptly after landing to allow the tower to manage other traffic. The core principle: squawk 7600, look for light gun signals, and comply.
questions.follow_up: If you are in IMC when the radio fails, how does the procedure change?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.185, in IMC with a radio failure, you fly the route with the highest priority: assigned route, expected route, filed route — in that order. For altitude, fly the highest of: MEA, assigned altitude, or expected altitude. Complete the approach using the IAF arrival time or EFC time, whichever is applicable, and land as soon as possible. Squawk 7600 throughout. The difference from VFR communication failure is that you cannot rely on light gun signals in IMC and must adhere strictly to the IFR lost comm procedures to safely navigate to landing.

questions.question: Before beginning a steep approach, what three environmental factors must you assess regarding the landing zone?
questions.answer: You must assess: (1) wind direction and conditions — to determine your approach heading and anticipate any tailwind, crosswind, or gusty conditions that affect control and ETL loss; (2) landing surface — to evaluate firmness, slope, debris, and whether you can safely set down or hover OGE; and (3) obstacles — to identify anything along the approach path or around the landing area that constrains your angle, abort options, or departure route.

questions.question: Why is wind direction particularly important when selecting your approach heading for a steep approach?
questions.answer: A headwind is preferred because it reduces groundspeed, lowers the airspeed at which ETL is lost, and provides the most favorable lift-to-power ratio during the approach. A tailwind component on a steep approach is especially dangerous because it increases groundspeed, causes ETL to be lost at a higher altitude than normal, and demands more power — potentially exceeding available power before reaching the landing zone. A direct headwind approach also gives the pilot the greatest go-around margin.

questions.question: What is the significance of identifying obstacles before starting a steep approach, and at what point in your planning should that assessment happen?
questions.answer: Obstacle identification must occur during the high reconnaissance — before committing to the approach. Obstacles define the angle of approach required, the abort corridor, and the departure path. On a steep approach, the flight path is already steeper than normal, so any obstacle that was not identified beforehand could block the only escape route. During the recon you confirm obstacle height, position relative to the approach path, and whether a go-around can safely clear them if the approach must be abandoned.

questions.question: You are setting up for a steep approach into a small clearing. The wind sock shows winds from the south at approximately 12 knots, but the only obstacle-free entry corridor is from the west. Walk me through how you weigh the wind condition against the obstacle geometry to choose your approach heading.
questions.answer: First, I quantify the crosswind component if I approach from the west with a 12-knot south wind — that gives me a full 12-knot crosswind at 90°, which is significant on a steep approach where speed and control margins are already reduced. I then check whether approaching from the south (into the wind) is truly blocked by obstacles or just more challenging. If a southerly approach is feasible with a steep enough angle to clear obstacles, I take it — headwind always wins when power margin is tight. If the southern corridor is genuinely blocked by obstacles that cannot be cleared at any practical approach angle, I accept the crosswind approach from the west but plan for drift correction throughout, account for the crosswind's effect on rotor thrust efficiency, and ensure I have a clear abort path upwind. I also verify OGE hover capability before committing, since a crosswind steep approach demands more power than a headwind approach.

questions.question: During your low reconnaissance of a confined area, you observe that the landing surface has a mix of dry grass and soft wet soil on the downslope side. How does this landing surface assessment affect your steep approach planning and your intended touchdown point?
questions.answer: Wet soft soil on the downslope side raises two concerns: dynamic rollover risk if a skid settles unevenly, and the possibility of the helicopter sinking or tipping as power is reduced. I would aim my touchdown point toward the dry, firmer grass area and avoid the soft soil entirely. If the slope is beyond a safe limit (generally 8–10° for most helicopters), I would not attempt the landing at all. I also consider that a soft surface can mask a slope that appears level — once skids contact and sink, a hidden slope becomes a rollover hazard. My steep approach angle and power reduction timing must place me precisely on the firm surface, not allow drift toward the soft zone. I would also brief a go-around decision point prior to touchdown if the surface condition looks worse on short final.

questions.question: You are on short final for a steep approach and you notice the treetops on the left side of your approach corridor are moving significantly while the clearing itself appears calm. What does this tell you, and how do you adjust your approach?
questions.answer: Moving treetops at altitude while the clearing is calm indicates wind shear — there is likely a significant wind gradient between the treetop level and the surface. As I descend below the treeline, I will likely lose a headwind component, which means airspeed will suddenly decrease, ETL will be lost earlier than planned, and the helicopter may sink unexpectedly or require a rapid power increase. I adjust by carrying slightly more airspeed than normal entering the approach to provide a buffer, remaining alert for an abrupt airspeed drop, and being ready to apply collective quickly. I also reassess whether available power supports a go-around if the sink rate becomes uncontrollable. If the shear is severe and I lose confidence in a safe outcome, I abort before entering the confined area and reassess surface wind by other means.

questions.question: During a steep approach recon, you identify that the only into-wind corridor has a single 60-foot tree directly on the centerline about 150 feet short of the intended landing spot. The surrounding terrain allows no deviation around it. Walk me through how you use wind, surface, and obstacle data together to make a go/no-go decision and, if go, how you modify the approach.
questions.answer: I integrate all three factors simultaneously. Wind: into-wind is the safest approach heading for power margin — that's confirmed. Surface: I've already assessed it as firm and suitable. Obstacle: the 60-foot tree on centerline is the critical constraint. My first determination is whether I can clear it with a steeper-than-normal angle and still arrive over the landing spot with enough altitude to transition to a hover or controlled touchdown — without exceeding OGE power requirements. I calculate the required approach angle from the tree's top to my intended touchdown point. If the angle forces me to cross the tree with very little clearance, I then ask: if I lose ETL immediately after clearing that tree, do I have enough power and rotor RPM to arrest the descent and land safely in the remaining 150 feet? If the answer is no, or if I am uncertain, the decision is no-go — the obstacle eliminates the necessary safety margin for a steep approach. If I determine I can clear the tree with at least 10–15 feet of buffer and still have abort options, I go — but I pre-brief my go-around decision point as the tree itself: if I'm not stabilized and configured to clear it by that point, I execute the go-around before crossing it, not after.
questions.follow_up: What happens to your go-around options after you've crossed that tree and are now inside the confined area — and how does that affect the risk calculus before you ever start the approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: Once I cross the obstacle and enter the confined area below the treeline, my go-around options are severely constrained or eliminated — I may only be able to execute a vertical or near-vertical abort if power allows, or I'm committed to landing. This means the real go/no-go decision must be made before crossing the obstacle, not after. The risk calculus shifts the decision point earlier in the maneuver: I must be committed only when I'm confident the approach is stable, power is adequate, and I can land safely — because once I'm inside, the margin for error collapses to near zero. This is the core reason the FAA requires a thorough reconnaissance before any confined area or steep approach: the commitment point happens before entry, not during.

questions.question: A pilot tells you they plan to do a steep approach into a sloped landing zone with a 7-degree downslope, a gusty crosswind of 15 knots, and a surface covered in loose gravel and debris. They say they're comfortable with each factor individually. What is your assessment, and how do you explain the compounding risk of combining all three?
questions.answer: Each factor is individually manageable at or near its limit, but the combination creates compounding risks that multiply rather than simply add together. The 7-degree slope is within most helicopter limits, but combined with a gusty crosswind, the pilot must hold cross-controls to prevent drift — and if a gust relaxes suddenly, the helicopter may shift laterally into the downslope, dramatically increasing dynamic rollover risk. The loose gravel and debris add a third hazard: ingestion of foreign object debris (FOD) into the engine or tail rotor, and unpredictable skid behavior on touchdown if rocks shift. Now add the gusty crosswind to ETL loss on a steep approach — gusts can cause abrupt airspeed changes that force power corrections at the worst moment, just as you're trying to manage slope and surface simultaneously. The pilot's comfort with each factor in isolation is irrelevant; what matters is whether they've analyzed the scenario as a system. In this case, I would counsel the pilot that the combined risk exceeds the safety margins available, and the correct decision is to not attempt the approach until at least one of the three conditions improves — ideally the wind.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot argues that their performance data shows they have plenty of power available for this approach, why is excess power alone insufficient to mitigate the combined risk you described?
questions.follow_up_answer: Power availability addresses only one dimension — the ability to maintain rotor RPM and generate lift. It does not mitigate dynamic rollover, which is a function of lateral center of gravity shift and skid contact geometry on a slope, not power. It does not prevent FOD ingestion from debris, which is a function of rotor downwash and surface material regardless of power setting. And it does not compensate for the control workload created by simultaneous slope, crosswind, and gusty conditions — which is a human factors and piloting capacity issue. Accidents happen when pilots conflate 'I have power' with 'I have margin.' The FAA's ADM framework specifically addresses this: each risk factor must be evaluated individually and collectively, and the presence of one safety buffer does not neutralize compounding hazards in other categories.

questions.question: When selecting a termination point for a steep approach, what are the two primary characteristics you look for in that spot before committing to the approach?
questions.answer: You want a termination point that is (1) large enough and firm enough to safely accept the helicopter — free of obstacles that could interfere with the rotor disk or tail rotor — and (2) positioned so that if a go-around becomes necessary before reaching it, you still have adequate power margin and obstacle clearance to execute one. The spot must allow you to bring the helicopter to a stable hover or touchdown without drifting into terrain, trees, wires, or other hazards.

questions.question: On a steep approach, at what point during the maneuver should you have your termination point positively identified and committed to — before starting the approach or once you are on final?
questions.answer: You must positively identify and commit to the termination point before beginning the approach — ideally during a high and low reconnaissance. Once you start a steep approach and lose ETL at a higher altitude than a normal approach, your options narrow quickly. Waiting until you are already on a steep final to decide where you are going is too late to safely evaluate wind, surface conditions, slope, and go-around options.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Reconnaissance Procedures and Steep Approach

questions.question: Why does wind direction matter when selecting your termination point for a steep approach?
questions.answer: Wind direction determines which heading gives you into-wind advantage during the slow-speed and hover phase of the termination. Because you lose effective translational lift (ETL) at a higher altitude on a steep approach than a normal approach, you need whatever wind assistance is available to support hover power requirements. Terminating into the wind also helps prevent an unexpected tailwind or quartering tailwind condition during the critical low-speed segment, which can degrade tail rotor effectiveness and complicate directional control.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Steep Approach; Chapter 11, Loss of Tail Rotor Effectiveness

questions.question: You are performing a steep approach into a small clearing surrounded by tall trees. There are two possible termination points: Point A is in the center of the clearing but requires you to fly directly over the tallest trees on final, and Point B is near the upwind edge of the clearing with a slightly lower obstacle on final but a more confined landing area. Walk me through how you decide which point to use.
questions.answer: First, I evaluate whether my helicopter can hover OGE at the density altitude present — if not, I need a point that allows an OGE hover or a running landing. For Point A, I assess whether I have sufficient power to clear the tall trees on final AND still have collective reserve remaining when I arrive at the termination point — if clearing those trees burns most of my available power, I may arrive with no margin to stop. For Point B, the lower obstacle reduces the power demand on final, preserving more collective reserve at the termination point, but I must confirm the confined area is large enough for a safe hover and touchdown and that there is adequate room to avoid dynamic rollover if I need to adjust. I also consider go-around paths from each point — which one allows a safe abort if performance is less than expected? The point that leaves me the most power reserve at termination and the clearest go-around path wins, even if the approach geometry is slightly less ideal.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Steep Approach and Confined Area Operations

questions.question: During your steep approach, you arrive over your selected termination point and realize the surface is softer than it appeared from altitude — possible soft mud or wet grass hiding standing water. How does this information change your actions at the termination point?
questions.answer: A soft or saturated surface introduces the risk of dynamic rollover if a skid digs in, and also creates a potential settling or sinking hazard after touchdown. At this point I have several options: (1) execute a go-around and re-evaluate, selecting an alternate firmer termination point; (2) if the helicopter must land there, I transition to a very slow, nearly vertical descent into a smooth touchdown with minimum lateral movement, keep collective ready to respond immediately to any settling, and prepare to depart at the first sign of instability. I would also brief any crew or passengers before touching down. The preferred decision is to go around if a clearly safer surface is available — accepting a poor termination point because you are already over it is a classic link in an accident chain.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Steep Approach; Chapter 11, Dynamic Rollover; Chapter 13, ADM

questions.question: Your helicopter's performance charts show you are marginal for an OGE hover at today's density altitude. You've selected a termination point at the base of a slope inside a confined area. What specific surface and terrain factors at that termination point must you evaluate before committing to this approach?
questions.answer: With marginal OGE hover performance, the termination point evaluation becomes critical: (1) Slope angle — the point must be within the helicopter's approved lateral and longitudinal slope limits to prevent dynamic rollover risk; if the slope exceeds limits, I cannot use that point. (2) Surface firmness — I need a surface firm enough to hold the skids without sinking, which could trap me and create rollover risk; soft ground at a slope is especially dangerous. (3) Rotor clearance — at a confined area base-of-slope position, I must ensure no terrain or vegetation enters the rotor disk as I descend the steep angle; the tail rotor must also clear the slope. (4) Go-around path — with marginal power I must know exactly where I will climb if I abort; a box canyon or rising terrain behind me may eliminate the go-around option entirely, which may mean this termination point is unsuitable regardless of other factors.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Steep Approach, Slope Operations, Confined Area Operations

questions.question: You select a termination point at the far end of a small confined clearing because it gives you the most obstacle clearance on final. Your instructor points out that the same termination point places your tail rotor within six feet of a tree line when you are in a hover. How does tail rotor proximity to terrain or obstacles factor into termination point suitability, and what is the minimum safe consideration?
questions.answer: Tail rotor clearance is a non-negotiable factor in termination point selection. The tail rotor operates in a zone that is difficult for the pilot to see directly, and its tip-path plane can be deceptively close to obstacles during a hover. If a tail rotor strikes an obstacle, the result is typically catastrophic loss of directional control and structural failure. The termination point must provide adequate clearance for the tail rotor in all axes — not just at the hover point, but accounting for any rearward drift during deceleration. 'Adequate clearance' is not a fixed regulatory number but is operationally defined as enough margin that a normal control input or a slight drift cannot result in a strike. The practical standard is to maintain at least one rotor blade length of clearance from any solid obstacle during hover operations in confined areas, and more if wind or turbulence is a factor. A termination point that maximizes obstacle clearance on final but puts the tail rotor at risk is not a suitable termination point — the approach geometry must be rethought.
questions.follow_up: If during your high reconnaissance you cannot positively confirm tail rotor clearance at your intended termination point from altitude, what are your options before committing to the approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: If I cannot positively confirm tail rotor clearance from altitude, I must not commit to that termination point. My options are: (1) select an alternate termination point within the clearing where I can confirm clearance; (2) if safety and regulations permit and it is operationally feasible, conduct a ground reconnaissance by landing at a safe adjacent area and walking the confined area to physically measure and assess clearances; (3) if neither is possible, declare the area unsuitable and divert to a site I can properly evaluate. The decision to proceed without confirmed clearance is not an acceptable risk — the consequences of a tail rotor strike are nearly always fatal.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Confined Area Operations and Steep Approach; Chapter 13, ADM and Risk Management

questions.question: A student selects what appears to be an excellent termination point during reconnaissance — firm surface, into-wind, good obstacle clearance, clear go-around path. On short final during the steep approach, the student calls the point 'good' and continues without re-evaluating. As the examiner, what are you looking for in that moment, and what error is the student potentially making?
questions.answer: The student is making the classic 'plan continuation bias' error — also called get-there-itis applied to a landing zone. A termination point selected during reconnaissance is a conditional selection, not a locked-in commitment. On short final, conditions can change: animals or people may have entered the zone, wind may have shifted, shadows that appeared solid may now reveal a hazard, or rotor wash interaction with terrain may reveal unexpected turbulence. What I am looking for as an examiner is a pilot who continuously re-evaluates the termination point throughout the approach — not just at the start — and who is genuinely prepared to execute a go-around at any point if conditions deteriorate. The test question I ask myself watching this approach is: 'Does this pilot have a real abort plan, or are they committed to landing no matter what?' If they called the point 'good' and stopped looking, they have mentally landed before they have physically landed, which is one of the most dangerous mindsets in confined area and off-airport operations.
questions.follow_up: At what point on a steep approach is it too late to execute a safe go-around, and how should that boundary influence termination point selection during reconnaissance?
questions.follow_up_answer: There is a point on every steep approach — often called the 'committed point' or the point of no-return — below which the helicopter no longer has sufficient altitude, airspeed, or power margin to successfully climb out over the obstacles it just descended past. This point varies with density altitude, gross weight, obstacle height, and approach angle. Because a steep approach loses ETL earlier and at a higher altitude than a normal approach, the committed point is reached earlier in the maneuver. During reconnaissance, the termination point must be selected with this boundary in mind: if available power is marginal, the go-around option disappears sooner, which means the termination point must be even more carefully chosen — it must be one I am highly confident I can reach safely, because my ability to change my mind shrinks faster than on a shallower approach. Pilots who do not account for this shrinking decision window during site selection are gambling on execution rather than planning for success.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Steep Approach and Maximum Performance Takeoff; Chapter 13, ADM — Plan Continuation Bias

questions.question: What is the maximum allowable approach angle for a steep approach, and how does this angle compare to a normal approach angle on final?
questions.answer: The maximum approach angle for a steep approach is 15°. A normal approach is typically flown at approximately 8-10°, so a steep approach is noticeably steeper — roughly 50% or more steeper than normal. The 15° maximum is a regulatory/standards boundary defined in the ACS and reinforced in the Helicopter Flying Handbook.

questions.question: During a steep approach, at what point in the descent does the helicopter lose effective translational lift (ETL), and why does this matter for your collective management?
questions.answer: On a steep approach, the helicopter loses ETL at a higher altitude above the surface compared to a normal approach, because the steeper angle causes airspeed to decrease more rapidly over a shorter ground track. This means the pilot must begin increasing collective earlier than on a normal approach to compensate for the loss of translational lift and maintain rotor RPM and controlled rate of closure. Failing to anticipate this can result in a hard landing or settling.

questions.question: What does 'proper rate of closure' mean during a steep approach, and what visual cues do you use to judge it?
questions.answer: Proper rate of closure means the helicopter is descending toward the intended landing point at a controlled, consistent rate — not too fast (which risks a hard landing or loss of control) and not too slow (which wastes the purpose of the steep approach). Visual cues include the apparent movement and expansion of the landing point in the windshield, the angle of the slope relative to the horizon, and the rate at which obstacles in the foreground appear to drop away. The landing point should appear to remain stationary relative to a reference point on the windshield while the surrounding terrain rises toward the helicopter.

questions.question: You're flying a steep approach into a confined area at 12° and notice that your approach angle feels too flat to clear the trees on the near edge but you're still within the 15° limit. You add aft cyclic to steepen the approach. What are the three things you must do simultaneously or immediately after to maintain a stabilized approach?
questions.answer: When you steepen the approach with aft cyclic: (1) Increase collective slightly to counter the blade flapping and rotor thrust reduction that comes with the aft cyclic input, preventing a sudden drop in rotor RPM and maintaining altitude momentarily while the new approach angle is established. (2) Adjust pedals (antitorque) to maintain trim/coordinated flight, since collective change affects torque. (3) Immediately re-reference the intended landing point to confirm the new angle will clear the obstacle and that rate of closure remains appropriate — you may need to reduce airspeed further and manage power to prevent the descent from accelerating past a controlled rate. The key is that no single control input is made in isolation on a steep approach.

questions.question: During your steep approach at approximately 13°, you notice your rate of closure has become excessive — you're descending faster than intended and you're getting close to the surface. Walk me through your corrections to regain a stabilized approach without transitioning into a go-around.
questions.answer: To correct an excessive rate of closure on a steep approach without going around: (1) Increase collective gradually to add power and reduce the descent rate — this is the primary control to arrest the sink. (2) Simultaneously add forward cyclic slightly if needed to convert some of that descent into forward motion and redistribute energy, though be cautious not to overshoot the landing point. (3) Adjust pedals to maintain trim as collective increases. (4) Continuously monitor rotor RPM to ensure it stays in the green arc. (5) Re-assess the approach angle and closure rate — if the correction cannot stabilize the approach before reaching the flare point, execute a go-around. The critical point: do not allow the situation to deteriorate hoping it will fix itself. If you cannot establish proper rate of closure with controlled inputs, go around.

questions.question: You've established a 14° steep approach and everything looks good, but as you pass through approximately 50 feet AGL you realize the wind has shifted and you now have a tailwind component. How does this change your energy state and what immediate control adjustments must you make to maintain proper rate of closure?
questions.answer: A tailwind component at 50 feet AGL on a steep approach significantly increases your groundspeed and therefore your rate of closure over the ground, while also reducing the rotor's effective translational lift and aerodynamic efficiency. This creates a higher-energy state that can quickly lead to an overshoot or hard landing. Immediate adjustments: (1) Recognize that the landing point will appear to expand faster in the windshield — this is your visual cue of increased closure rate. (2) Increase collective to manage descent rate and arrest any tendency to sink rapidly as airspeed bleeds off. (3) Apply aft cyclic to slow the groundspeed and reduce rate of closure over the landing point. (4) Be alert that the loss of headwind means ETL may degrade faster than anticipated, requiring more aggressive collective input. (5) If a stabilized approach cannot be re-established within the remaining altitude, execute a go-around — do not attempt to salvage a deteriorating approach at 50 feet with a tailwind.

questions.question: An applicant consistently establishes the correct 12-14° approach angle initially but then allows the angle to gradually shallow to 8° by midpoint on every attempt. As an examiner, what specific control habit or perceptual error is most likely driving this, and how would you diagnose it during the debrief?
questions.answer: The most likely cause is a visual fixation error combined with an instinctive power addition habit. As the pilot descends and the ground references expand, there is a natural tendency to perceive the approach as steeper than it actually is — this is a well-documented spatial disorientation issue on steep approaches. The pilot then unconsciously relaxes aft cyclic and/or adds forward cyclic to 'reduce the steepness,' combined with collective additions that further flatten the approach. Another contributor is premature anticipation of the flare: the pilot begins mentally transitioning to a normal approach profile before reaching the intended steepening zone. To diagnose in debrief: ask the pilot at what point they noticed their sight picture changing, and whether they were cross-checking their approach angle against a fixed external reference (tree line, obstacle top) or relying solely on feel. Ask them to describe what they were looking at between initial establishment and midpoint. Fixation on the landing spot rather than scanning the approach angle against background references is typically the root cause.
questions.follow_up: If you determine the pilot's sight picture is the problem, what specific technique or exercise would you assign before their next attempt to correct the angle-shallowing tendency?
questions.follow_up_answer: Assign a ground reference exercise before flight: have the pilot stand at a point 50-100 feet from a vertical structure (tree, building) and physically estimate what a 12° and 15° slope looks like against that reference — this calibrates their internal visual model. In the aircraft, instruct them to select a fixed external reference point (top of obstacle, treeline break) and maintain that reference point at a consistent position in the windshield throughout the approach rather than looking at the landing spot. Additionally, assign them to verbalize their approach angle check every 10-15 seconds during practice approaches using checkpoint cross-referencing. This forces active monitoring rather than passive drift. Some instructors also use a marked spot on the chin bubble or a chinstrap reference to help pilots see the angle relative to the horizon objectively.

questions.question: You are on a steep approach at exactly 15° in a high-density altitude environment. The approach angle is at the maximum allowable limit and you still have 500 feet AGL to descend. Your power margin above hover is very small. What factors could cause the approach to become unrecoverable without a go-around, and what is the physiological warning you might experience before reaching a critical point?
questions.answer: At maximum approach angle (15°) in a high-density altitude environment with minimal power margin, the following factors can push the approach toward unrecoverable: (1) Loss of ETL occurs at a higher altitude than at sea level, and the power required to compensate exceeds available power — the pilot cannot add enough collective to arrest the descent. (2) Any tailwind or downdraft further erodes the power margin and accelerates closure rate. (3) Rotor RPM decay: if the pilot adds collective to arrest descent but the engine cannot respond quickly enough (turbine spool-up lag or piston throttle lag), RPM may droop into a region where rotor efficiency degrades, compounding the problem. (4) Vortex ring state risk increases if the pilot applies excessive collective in a descending attitude with low airspeed and high rate of descent — this is a real hazard on the back side of a steep approach in low-power conditions. The physiological warning the pilot may experience before reaching a critical state is a 'sinking feeling' — the controls feel mushy and less responsive, the helicopter does not respond to collective inputs as expected, and the landing point begins expanding rapidly in the windshield despite aft cyclic inputs. This is the last perceptible warning before a potential hard landing or vortex ring state entry. Go-around must be initiated immediately at this recognition.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot recognizes they are entering vortex ring state during this steep approach recovery attempt, what is the specific recovery procedure and why is altitude the critical variable?
questions.follow_up_answer: Vortex ring state recovery requires: (1) Immediately apply forward cyclic to increase airspeed — this moves the rotor system out of its own downwash and restores normal airflow through the disk. (2) Do NOT increase collective — adding collective in vortex ring state increases the recirculating vortex and worsens the condition. (3) Allow the helicopter to accelerate through ETL; once translational lift is restored, normal collective control effectiveness returns. Altitude is the critical variable because the recovery requires a finite altitude loss before airspeed increases enough to break out of the vortex ring state — estimates range from 100 to several hundred feet depending on onset severity and aircraft type. On a steep approach at low altitude (say, 100-200 feet AGL) in a high-density altitude environment, there may simply not be enough altitude to complete the recovery before ground contact. This is why recognition must come early and the go-around decision must be made proactively, not reactively.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Vortex Ring State)

questions.question: During a steep approach to a confined area, what does 'maintaining proper ground track' actually mean in practical terms?
questions.answer: Maintaining proper ground track means the helicopter follows a straight line over the ground from the entry point to the intended touchdown spot, regardless of wind. The flight path over the ground should not drift left or right of the desired track. This is distinct from the helicopter's heading — the nose may be crabbed into the wind, but the actual path across the ground remains aligned with the landing area centerline.

questions.question: What two primary crosswind correction methods can a helicopter pilot use to maintain ground track during a steep approach, and what is the key difference between them?
questions.answer: The two methods are the crab method and the side-slip (forward slip) method. In the crab method, the pilot points the nose into the wind so the helicopter tracks straight over the ground, then aligns the nose with the landing area just before touchdown. In the side-slip method, the pilot holds the nose aligned with the ground track while using lateral cyclic to slip into the wind to cancel drift. The key difference is that the crab keeps the fuselage angled into the wind throughout, while the side-slip keeps the fuselage aligned with the track but requires continuous lateral cyclic correction. Most helicopter approaches use a combination technique — crab during the approach, transitioning to alignment at termination.

questions.question: On a steep approach, at what point during the maneuver does loss of ETL occur, and how does that event specifically affect your ability to hold the desired ground track?
questions.answer: On a steep approach, loss of effective translational lift (ETL) occurs at a higher altitude above the ground than it does on a normal approach because the steeper descent angle causes the helicopter to slow below approximately 16–24 knots of airspeed sooner. When ETL is lost, the helicopter experiences increased vibration and a tendency to settle. The pilot must increase collective to compensate for the loss of lift, and this torque change requires an immediate antitorque pedal correction to prevent the nose from yawing. If that pedal correction is not made promptly, the nose will swing and the helicopter will drift off the desired ground track.

issues: The statement that ETL loss occurs at 'a higher altitude above the ground' on a steep approach needs clarification. ETL is lost at the same airspeed (typically 16-24 knots) regardless of approach angle, but the steep approach may reach that airspeed sooner in the descent. The answer conflates airspeed with altitude, which could confuse students about the actual mechanism.

The answer correctly identifies that loss of ETL requires collective increase and pedal correction, but the phrasing 'the nose will swing and the helicopter will drift off the desired ground track' oversimplifies—the nose swing (yaw) from torque increase is the primary issue, not directly a ground track drift issue until yaw misalignment occurs.
verification.suggested_correction: Clarify: 'On a steep approach, loss of ETL occurs at the same airspeed as a normal approach (approximately 16-24 knots), but the steeper descent angle may cause the helicopter to reach that airspeed sooner. When ETL is lost, the reduced rotor efficiency requires increased collective pitch. This increased collective demand increases engine torque, requiring immediate antitorque pedal correction to prevent nose yaw. If the yaw correction is not made, the nose will swing, misaligning the fuselage with the desired ground track and causing drift.'

questions.question: You are on short final for a steep approach into a narrow clearing. The wind is 15 knots from your left. As you descend through ETL, the nose swings right and the helicopter begins to drift left of the intended touchdown point. Walk me through your control inputs to reestablish the correct ground track without overshooting the landing area.
questions.answer: First, correct the yaw: apply left pedal to stop the nose swing to the right and re-align the fuselage or re-establish the crab angle into the wind. Simultaneously, use right cyclic to stop the leftward ground drift and reestablish the track toward the touchdown point. Because you are also managing the collective increase through the ETL transition, you must coordinate all three: left pedal with the collective increase to manage torque/yaw, right cyclic to arrest lateral drift, and continued forward cyclic management to maintain the glidepath angle. Avoid large cyclic inputs — at this phase of a steep approach with low airspeed and high power demand, abrupt lateral inputs can displace the glidepath and create a height/power management problem. If the correction is not achievable without overflying obstacles or compromising the touchdown point, execute a go-around.

questions.question: You are flying a steep approach into a confined area surrounded by tall trees. There is a right crosswind. As you descend below the treeline, you notice the effective wind is now calm — the trees are blocking it. How does this wind shear affect your ground track management and what do you do?
questions.answer: Above the treeline you were carrying a left crab (or left cyclic side-slip) to correct for the right crosswind. Once you descend into the sheltered area and the wind suddenly drops off, your existing crosswind correction becomes an overcorrection — the helicopter will now drift left of your intended ground track because the right cyclic or left crab you were holding is no longer needed. You must quickly recognize the loss of crosswind effect: immediately reduce the crosswind correction input, re-centering the cyclic laterally while reestablishing a neutral heading or track alignment. Additionally, you may experience a brief loss of groundspeed and lift since you lose the headwind component, so be prepared to add collective to arrest any unexpected descent rate increase. This scenario reinforces why a proper reconnaissance is critical — identifying windbreaks that can cause sheltered shear zones on the approach.

questions.question: During a steep approach with a left crosswind, you notice you are consistently drifting right of the touchdown point throughout the approach — not just at ETL. What is the most likely cause, and how do you correct it during the approach versus adjusting for the next attempt?
questions.answer: Consistent drift to the right throughout the approach — not just near ETL — indicates that the crosswind correction is insufficient. You are under-correcting for the left crosswind, meaning you are not crabbing enough to the left or not holding enough right-into-wind cyclic. During the approach: apply additional left cyclic (if using side-slip technique) or increase the left crab angle to place the nose further into the wind, stopping the rightward drift first, then re-tracking to the left to re-acquire the intended ground track to the landing point. For the next attempt: during the reconnaissance or as you establish the approach, better assess the crosswind component and establish the crab angle earlier and more aggressively. A useful reference is to note a landmark (rock, stump) aligned with your intended track — if that reference is drifting, you are off ground track. Also verify you are beginning the approach from the correct upwind position so drift does not accumulate before you even reach the clearing.

questions.question: On a steep approach with a direct crosswind, as you apply left antitorque pedal at ETL transition to manage torque, the nose moves left — now the wind is more of a tailwind component. Explain the compounding effect this has on ground track control and how you prevent it from turning a manageable crosswind into a critical situation.
questions.answer: This is a compounding control interaction that is easy to miss. When you apply left pedal to counteract increased torque at the ETL transition, the nose yaws left. If the wind was originally from the right (requiring right crab), yawing the nose left now opens the helicopter to more direct tailwind exposure. A tailwind during a steep approach has two negative effects on ground track: first, it increases groundspeed, causing the touchdown point to appear to move away from you and making the approach angle look shallower than it is; second, groundspeed increases the kinetic energy and landing rollout distance in a running landing, or requires more deceleration energy in a hover termination. The combined result is that what started as a manageable right crosswind can quickly become a partial tailwind — increasing groundspeed and pushing you past the intended landing point. Prevention requires anticipating the torque change before losing ETL: pre-position the nose appropriately by beginning pedal correction before the yaw occurs, and use coordinated cyclic to maintain the crab angle rather than allowing the pedal input to drive the heading. If the nose does yaw left excessively, immediately correct with right pedal while re-establishing the crab with left cyclic.
questions.follow_up: At what point during a steep approach would a tailwind component become severe enough to require a go-around rather than a continued attempt at correcting the ground track?
questions.follow_up_answer: There is no single defined airspeed threshold for this decision — it is a judgment call based on several converging factors. However, you should execute a go-around when: (1) your groundspeed has increased to the point where you cannot arrest forward movement before the intended landing point; (2) you have consumed your available power margin managing the correction and have no cushion left; (3) the glidepath has become uncontrollable — you are either too high and fast or too low with insufficient collective authority; or (4) you are below ETL with a tailwind and cannot slow the helicopter to a hover within the available landing area. The FAA guidance is clear: on steep approaches, if doubt exists about power availability or the ability to terminate safely, the go-around must be executed without hesitation. Delay compounds the problem because you are lower, slower, and have less maneuvering energy available.

questions.question: You complete a reconnaissance on a confined area and determine the only safe approach corridor requires a direct 90-degree crosswind approach on a steep angle, landing between two tall obstructions that limit your ability to crab. The trees form a narrow slot. How do you maintain ground track in that slot, and what is the fundamental limit of using the crab technique in this scenario?
questions.answer: In a narrow slot with obstructions on both sides, the crab technique has a critical limitation: the helicopter fuselage is yawed sideways relative to the slot, meaning the tail rotor or main rotor disc may approach the obstacle on the upwind side even though the cockpit appears centered on the track. In a narrow corridor, tail rotor clearance is the controlling concern. For this reason, you would likely use a side-slip (forward slip) crosswind technique rather than a crab — holding the fuselage aligned with the slot centerline and using lateral cyclic to cancel wind drift. This keeps the helicopter's longitudinal axis parallel to the obstacle walls, maximizing rotor disc and tail clearance within the slot. The control technique is: hold right cyclic into the wind (for a left crosswind) to prevent drift, while keeping the nose pointed straight at the landing point with neutral or slight pedal. This requires continuous lateral cyclic throughout the descent. The limitation is that the side-slip technique demands precise cyclic coordination and becomes increasingly fatiguing and less precise at the low airspeed of the steep approach final segment. If drift cannot be stopped with available cyclic travel without compromising attitude, the approach is not safe and a go-around is mandatory.
questions.follow_up: If the helicopter POH specifies a maximum demonstrated crosswind component, how does that figure apply to a steep confined area approach versus a normal runway landing?
questions.follow_up_answer: The maximum demonstrated crosswind component listed in the POH is established during testing on a prepared surface — typically a runway — under controlled conditions at normal approach angles and airspeeds. It is not a structural or absolute limit; it is the maximum crosswind at which the test pilot was able to maintain directional control during the landing certification testing. In a steep approach to a confined area, this figure is still a useful reference but must be treated conservatively for three reasons: (1) the approach is conducted at lower airspeed than a normal approach, meaning aerodynamic crosswind correction authority (cyclic effectiveness) is reduced; (2) obstacles may physically constrain the crab angle available, removing the most effective correction method; and (3) the confined area may have variable or sheltered wind conditions that cannot be precisely assessed from altitude. Prudent practice is to treat the demonstrated crosswind value as an upper boundary in ideal conditions and apply a conservative margin — perhaps 50–70% of that value — for confined area steep approaches. If the actual crosswind exceeds your conservative limit for the conditions, identify an alternate approach corridor or decline the operation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; POH/AFM applicable aircraft section

questions.question: During a steep approach, what happens to main rotor RPM (Nr) as you increase collective to arrest the increased rate of descent that occurs when you lose effective translational lift at a higher altitude than normal?
questions.answer: Increasing collective pitch increases the drag load on the main rotor blades, which tends to decrease Nr. The engine must respond by increasing torque to maintain RPM within normal limits. The pilot must monitor Nr and ensure the throttle (or engine governor) is keeping pace with the collective input. If power available is insufficient or the governor is slow to respond, Nr can decay toward the low end of the normal range or below.

questions.question: On a steep approach, at what point on the approach profile does the pilot typically need to make the most aggressive collective management to prevent Nr from decaying below normal limits?
questions.answer: The critical point is when effective translational lift (ETL) is lost, which on a steep approach occurs at a higher altitude above the landing area than during a normal approach. As the helicopter decelerates through ETL, rotor efficiency decreases and more collective pitch is required to maintain a controlled descent rate. This sudden increase in collective demand can pull Nr low if not anticipated. The pilot must increase collective earlier than on a normal approach to stay ahead of the Nr decay.

questions.question: What does 'Nr within normal limits' mean in practical terms, and where do you find the normal operating range for your specific helicopter?
questions.answer: Nr within normal limits means the main rotor RPM is operating within the green arc shown on the tachometer, as defined by the manufacturer for normal flight operations. The specific RPM range (and any caution or redline ranges) is found in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) or Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) for the specific aircraft, typically in the Limitations section and displayed on the tachometer instrument itself. Operating outside normal limits — either too high or too low — can compromise rotor lift, structural integrity, and aircraft control.

questions.question: You are established on a steep approach at 3:1 glide ratio. As you cross through ETL, you raise collective to manage your descent rate, and you notice Nr beginning to bleed into the low caution range. What are your immediate priorities and options?
questions.answer: Immediate priorities: (1) Arrest the Nr decay — if the helicopter has a manual throttle, increase throttle to add power; if governor-equipped, ensure the governor is engaged and functioning. (2) Reduce collective slightly to decrease rotor blade drag and allow Nr to recover. (3) Simultaneously use aft cyclic to manage the descent rate while collective is briefly reduced. If Nr continues to decay toward a low rotor RPM condition, execute a go-around immediately — do not attempt to salvage the approach with decaying Nr. Low rotor RPM close to the ground on a steep approach is a precursor to a loss of control or hard landing. Power margin and altitude at that point must be assessed against the RFM limitations.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 11 (Emergencies); RFM Limitations

questions.question: A student pilot tends to fixate on the landing spot during steep approaches and forgets to cross-check the engine instruments, leading to an undetected Nr decay. As the instructor, how would you explain the relationship between steep approach control inputs and the engine/rotor instrument scan?
questions.answer: On a steep approach, the pilot is making frequent and sometimes large collective changes to manage an aggressive glide path and a higher-than-normal rate of descent. Each collective increase adds pitch to the rotor blades, increasing aerodynamic drag on the rotor system. If the engine's power output doesn't keep pace — due to governor lag, power limits, or throttle management — Nr will drop. The pilot must include torque gauge, Nr/engine RPM tachometer, and manifold pressure or turbine indicators in their instrument scan throughout the approach, not just at the beginning. Fixating on the landing spot is a common trap that allows Nr to decay silently until the helicopter enters the low RPM caution range or triggers a warning horn. A disciplined cross-check — landing zone, instruments, landing zone — prevents this.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Advanced Flight Maneuvers); Chapter 11 (Low Rotor RPM)

questions.question: You are conducting a steep approach into a confined area on a hot day at a high-density altitude airport. Your preflight power check showed you were near OGE power limits. How does this condition affect your ability to maintain Nr within normal limits during the steep approach, and what technique adjustments would you make?
questions.answer: At high density altitude with temperatures above standard, engine power output is reduced. If you are already near OGE hover limits, you have a very narrow power margin during the approach. As you lose ETL and demand more collective to manage descent rate, the engine may be unable to supply the additional torque needed to maintain Nr without the RPM decaying. Technique adjustments include: (1) Plan a shallower approach if obstacle clearance permits — a less steep profile reduces the severity of collective inputs required through ETL. (2) Carry slightly higher airspeed into the approach to delay ETL loss and give the engine more time to respond. (3) Accept a slightly higher touchdown groundspeed if necessary. (4) Identify a clear abort path before beginning the approach. (5) Monitor torque and Nr continuously. If Nr approaches the bottom of the green arc and torque is at or near maximum, execute the go-around immediately — you cannot trade altitude for RPM recovery if you are already close to the ground.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; Chapter 8 (Helicopter Performance, Density Altitude)

questions.question: During a steep approach evaluation, a candidate maintains a stabilized profile but consistently operates Nr at the very bottom of the green arc throughout the final portion of the approach. The approach results in a safe landing each time. Would you pass or fail this performance, and why?
questions.answer: This performance would not meet the standard. Operating Nr consistently at the bottom of the green arc during a steep approach demonstrates inadequate power management, even if the landing itself is safe. The standard requires Nr be maintained 'within normal limits,' which implies operating in a stable, safe portion of the normal range — not riding the threshold between normal and caution. A consistent bottom-of-green-arc Nr means the pilot has no remaining recovery margin: any additional collective demand (gust, obstacle avoidance, steeper than anticipated final), governor response lag, or slight temperature increase could push Nr into the caution range or trigger a low rotor RPM condition close to the ground. The safe landing was the result of conditions cooperating, not of competent technique. The candidate must demonstrate anticipatory collective management that keeps Nr comfortably within the normal band, not merely avoids an exceedance.
questions.follow_up: The candidate argues that the RFM says the entire green arc is 'normal limits' and they never left it. How do you respond?
questions.follow_up_answer: Technically, the candidate is correct that the green arc defines normal limits, and no regulatory violation occurred. However, the ACS skill standard requires the pilot to 'maintain' Nr within normal limits, which implies active management and control — not passive tolerance of marginal conditions. An examiner evaluates whether the pilot demonstrated the skill and judgment expected of a certificated pilot, not just whether a limitation was technically not violated. Consistently operating at the threshold of a caution range when better technique was available reflects inadequate anticipation and power management. The practical test standard also requires the examiner to evaluate whether the applicant exercised sound judgment; repeatedly allowing Nr to drift to the bottom of normal under controlled conditions suggests the pilot would likely exceed limits under actual operational stress. The remedial discussion should focus on anticipating collective demands earlier in the approach profile.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 11; ACS PH.VI.D Skills Standard; FAA-S-ACS-17 Practical Test Standards

questions.question: During a steep approach in a turbine helicopter with a dual-engine FADEC system, a candidate states they don't need to actively monitor Nr because 'the computers handle it.' Evaluate this statement and explain the pilot's actual responsibility for Nr management on a steep approach.
questions.answer: This statement reflects a dangerous overreliance on automation. While FADEC systems in turbine helicopters do automate fuel scheduling and can respond quickly to power demands, they do not eliminate the pilot's responsibility to monitor and maintain Nr within limits. FADECs have operational limits, response lags, and potential failure modes. On a steep approach, large and rapid collective inputs can temporarily outpace even a well-functioning FADEC, causing transient Nr excursions. Additionally, FADEC authority limits may prevent the system from supplying unlimited torque — if the engine is torque-limited or at a power margin boundary, the FADEC will protect the engine and Nr may still decay. Pilot responsibilities include: (1) Monitoring Nr and torque instruments throughout the approach; (2) Pacing collective inputs to allow the FADEC to respond; (3) Recognizing any FADEC advisory or failure annunciations that would degrade automatic control; (4) Understanding the specific RFM limitations and FADEC logic for the aircraft type. Automation manages the engine; the pilot manages the approach.
questions.follow_up: What specific failure mode or condition could cause a FADEC-equipped turbine helicopter to experience Nr decay on a steep approach even with both FADEC channels operational?
questions.follow_up_answer: Even with FADEC fully operational, Nr can decay if the demanded power exceeds the engine's actual available output — which FADEC cannot create power that doesn't exist. Specific conditions include: (1) Operating at or above maximum continuous power (MCP) — the FADEC will limit fuel flow to protect the engine, and if collective demand exceeds available power, Nr will decay; (2) Hot-section temperature (TGT/ITT/TOT) limiting — FADEC may reduce fuel flow to protect turbine temperature, reducing available torque; (3) Single-engine inoperative during a steep approach in a twin — if one engine fails, total available power is halved and the remaining FADEC may not compensate fully at high power demand; (4) Compressor bleed air extraction (anti-ice, air conditioning) reducing available shaft power; (5) Fuel control unit transient lag during very rapid collective application. In all these cases, the pilot's active monitoring and proactive power management are the only safeguard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 11; RFM for specific turbine aircraft (FADEC limitations section); 14 CFR 27.361 / 29.361 (Engine Torque Limits)

questions.question: The ACS requires you to terminate a steep approach at the surface or in a stabilized hover within plus or minus 4 feet of your intended point. What does 'stabilized hover' mean in the context of meeting that standard?
questions.answer: A stabilized hover means the helicopter is stationary over the termination point with altitude, heading, and position all under control — no drifting, no continued climb or descent, and rotor RPM in the normal operating range. The ±4 foot standard means your hover must be established within 4 feet laterally and longitudinally of the designated spot, and at a consistent hover altitude (typically skid height or 2-3 feet AGL) without hunting or chasing the controls.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; PH ACS Task VI.D

questions.question: At what point during a steep approach does effective translational lift (ETL) typically dissipate, and how does that affect your arrival at the termination point?
questions.answer: During a steep approach, ETL is lost at a higher altitude than during a normal approach because you are decelerating more rapidly and at a steeper angle. This means you must increase collective earlier and more aggressively than on a normal approach to arrest the increased rate of descent that accompanies ETL loss. Failing to anticipate this results in a hard landing or arriving short of the intended termination point, violating the ±4 foot standard.

questions.question: When terminating a steep approach to the surface rather than a hover, what three things should be true at the moment of touchdown to consider the arrival within the ACS standard?
questions.answer: At touchdown, the helicopter should: (1) contact the surface at or within ±4 feet of the designated termination point, (2) be in a level attitude with all gear contacting simultaneously (no dynamic rollover risk), and (3) have a rate of descent that results in a controlled, smooth touchdown — not a hard landing. The aircraft must also be tracking in the correct direction with no significant lateral drift at contact.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; PH ACS Task VI.D

questions.question: You are on a steep approach and you realize at about 50 feet AGL that you have significantly overshot your intended termination point by what looks like 10 feet. What is your best course of action, and why is attempting to correct at that stage risky?
questions.answer: At 50 feet AGL with a 10-foot overshoot already established on a steep approach, the safest option is typically to execute a go-around rather than attempt a last-minute correction. Trying to slide the aircraft back toward the point requires aft cyclic, which will increase the nose-high attitude and may cause an uncontrolled rate of descent, especially since ETL has likely already been lost. Additionally, aggressive lateral or aft cyclic corrections close to the ground increase dynamic rollover risk on touchdown. A go-around allows you to reposition and fly the approach correctly from the beginning, keeping the arrival within the ±4 foot standard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; PH ACS Task VI.D

questions.question: You are conducting a steep approach into a confined area. As you near the termination point, you notice the helicopter is drifting left about 2 feet. How do you correct it without busting the ±4 foot standard, and what is the risk if you over-correct with right cyclic close to the ground?
questions.answer: A small, smooth right cyclic input should arrest the drift and re-center the aircraft over the termination point. The correction must be proportional — just enough to stop the drift, then neutralize. If you over-correct with aggressive right cyclic close to the ground while simultaneously increasing collective to check the descent, you risk inducing dynamic rollover to the right, particularly if the skid contacts the surface while the aircraft still has lateral momentum. The key is smooth, early corrections well before reaching the termination point rather than chasing the drift in the final few feet.

questions.question: You are flying a steep approach in high-density altitude conditions. You've already checked that you can hover OGE at your landing point. How does density altitude specifically affect your ability to arrive precisely at the termination point within ±4 feet?
questions.answer: At high density altitude, the helicopter is operating closer to its power limits. As ETL dissipates on the steep approach, you need a significant collective increase to arrest the descent, but reduced air density means less rotor efficiency — so you need more collective for the same lift. This causes the aircraft to respond more sluggishly to collective inputs, making precise rate-of-descent control harder. There is also less power margin available to arrest an undershoot. The result is a higher tendency to arrive short or with a higher-than-desired sink rate, both of which can push you outside the ±4 foot standard or result in a hard landing. Precise power management and anticipation of ETL loss must happen earlier.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapters 10 and 11; FAA-H-8083-25B Pilot's Handbook Chapter 4

questions.question: During your checkride steep approach, you arrive at the designated termination point and establish what you believe is a stabilized hover, but you are 5 feet left of the cone and 3 feet in front of it. You are within the vertical hover altitude standard but outside the lateral/longitudinal standard. The examiner asks you to evaluate your own performance. Walk me through your honest assessment and what caused the miss.
questions.answer: An honest self-assessment would acknowledge the arrival was outside the ±4 foot standard laterally. The most common causes for this type of miss are: (1) incorrect aim point selected during the approach — if the aim point drifted or was never precisely fixed, the aircraft will track to the wrong spot; (2) an uncorrected crosswind or drift that wasn't identified and neutralized early enough on final; (3) fixating on the rate-of-descent management through ETL loss and losing awareness of tracking accuracy; or (4) a late power correction that caused an inadvertent lateral control input. The correction for future attempts is to establish a definite aim point early, maintain coordinated tracking throughout the approach, and make lateral corrections smoothly before the last 50 feet AGL.
questions.follow_up: If you had arrived 5 feet left but exactly on the longitudinal mark, and the examiner says 'that's close enough' — should you accept that assessment?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. The ACS standard is clear: ±4 feet. Five feet of lateral displacement exceeds the standard, and accepting a 'close enough' evaluation from an examiner would be inappropriate — an examiner cannot simply waive a published ACS standard. The correct response as a pilot is to acknowledge the bust honestly, understand the cause, and demonstrate the maneuver to standard on a subsequent attempt. Accepting a substandard performance as passing sets a dangerous precedent for actual operational precision in confined areas where a 5-foot error could mean striking an obstacle.
questions.regulatory_ref: PH ACS Task VI.D; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10

questions.question: You are executing a steep approach to a pinnacle landing point. You arrive at the termination point in a stabilized hover exactly at the ±4 foot standard, but then you notice the surface has a slight slope you didn't see during your high and low reconnaissance. You are at hover altitude. What is your decision process before setting down, and how does the arrival standard interact with the slope landing procedure?
questions.answer: Arriving at the termination point within the ACS standard is only the first part of the task — a stabilized hover within ±4 feet confirms approach accuracy, but it does not obligate you to complete the landing if conditions at the termination point are unsafe. Upon noticing the slope, the decision process is: (1) assess the degree of slope — can the helicopter land safely without exceeding the lateral rollover threshold for the specific aircraft (typically around 8-10 degrees depending on the helicopter)? (2) Determine if there is sufficient tail clearance for a slope landing given rotor disk tilt; (3) If the slope is within limits, transition to slope landing technique — touch the upslope skid first while maintaining rotor RPM and level attitude with cyclic, then lower the downslope skid; (4) If slope exceeds limits or is uncertain, execute a go-around and conduct a more detailed low reconnaissance. The ACS arrival standard is met by the hover; the subsequent decision about landing is a separate judgment. Meeting the ±4 foot standard in the hover and then executing a safe go-around is a fully acceptable outcome.
questions.follow_up: If the slope is within limits and you begin the slope landing by touching the upslope skid, at what point is dynamic rollover risk highest, and what control input can initiate it?
questions.follow_up_answer: Dynamic rollover risk is highest at the moment one skid is on the ground and the other is still airborne — the on-ground skid becomes a pivot point. At that moment, if the pilot applies lateral cyclic toward the low (downslope) side, or if the collective is raised while lateral cyclic is displaced toward the low side, the aircraft can begin rolling over the grounded skid. The roll rate can exceed the pilot's ability to correct with opposite cyclic because the grounded skid eliminates one degree of freedom. On a slope landing, cyclic must be held into the upslope side throughout the entire landing sequence, and collective must be lowered smoothly — not raised — once the first skid contacts.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapters 10 and 11; PH ACS Task VI.D

questions.question: When conducting a steep approach to a helipad located on or adjacent to an airport, what does 'runway incursion avoidance' mean for you as a helicopter pilot?
questions.answer: Runway incursion avoidance means ensuring that neither the helicopter nor its rotor system enters an active runway, taxiway, or other movement area without proper ATC clearance. Even when approaching a helipad, the flight path must be planned to avoid crossing active runways or taxiways unless specifically authorized by ATC. The pilot must maintain situational awareness of other traffic and movement areas throughout the approach.

questions.question: What is the definition of a runway incursion, and give one example of how it could occur during a steep approach to an airport helipad?
questions.answer: A runway incursion is any occurrence at an aerodrome involving the incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle, or person on the protected area of a surface designated for landing and takeoff. During a steep approach to an airport helipad, an example would be the pilot beginning the approach without obtaining clearance to cross Runway 27, resulting in the helicopter flying through the runway protected area while another aircraft is on final. This can happen when the pilot is focused on the approach profile and fails to monitor ATC communications or request a crossing clearance.

questions.question: When does the runway incursion avoidance requirement apply during a steep approach, and when is it considered 'not applicable'?
questions.answer: The runway incursion avoidance requirement applies whenever the steep approach is conducted at a towered or non-towered airport where active runways, taxiways, or other designated movement areas exist and where the approach path could intersect those surfaces. It is considered 'not applicable' when the approach is made to an off-airport landing zone — such as a remote pinnacle, confined area, rooftop helipad, or private property — where no runway or aerodrome infrastructure is present and no other aircraft operations on controlled surfaces are a factor.

questions.question: You are conducting a steep approach to a helipad inside the airport perimeter at a non-towered airport. Another aircraft is on a long final for Runway 18, which your approach path crosses at low altitude. Walk me through the specific actions you take to avoid a runway incursion.
questions.answer: First, I would have obtained a complete airport diagram or reviewed the airport layout during preflight to identify all potential conflict points. On the CTAF, I would announce my position and intentions clearly, including that my approach path crosses Runway 18. I would monitor CTAF continuously to track the traffic on final. Before crossing the runway protected area, I would make an explicit call such as 'Helicopter N123AB crossing Runway 18 for helipad' and visually confirm the runway is clear in both directions. If there is any doubt about the spacing or intent of the fixed-wing traffic, I would extend my approach, orbit, or hold clear of the runway until separation is assured. I would not allow the time pressure of the approach profile to compromise the hold-short discipline.

questions.question: During a steep approach to a hospital helipad located just off the departure end of Runway 10 at a towered airport, ATC clears you for the approach but does not specifically clear you to cross Runway 10. What do you do?
questions.answer: I would not cross Runway 10 without an explicit crossing clearance. An approach clearance to the helipad does not automatically authorize crossing any runway. I would contact the tower and request a specific runway crossing clearance before my flight path intersects the runway protected area. If unable to resolve the clearance prior to reaching the runway boundary, I would slow or orbit clear of the runway, ensure I have the traffic picture, and hold my position until ATC issues explicit crossing clearance. I would not assume the clearance was implied — runway crossings require specific, unambiguous authorization from ATC at controlled airports.

questions.question: How does the high pilot workload inherent in a steep approach — managing power, ETL loss, approach angle, and landing spot — create a specific runway incursion risk, and what technique do you use to manage it?
questions.answer: A steep approach demands more active power management than a normal approach because effective translational lift (ETL) is lost at a higher altitude, requiring an earlier and larger collective increase. This increased workload narrows attention to the approach profile and landing spot, creating a significant risk that the pilot will miss ATC instructions, fail to monitor other traffic, or neglect to hold short of a crossing runway. To manage this, I complete all ATC communications and obtain any necessary crossing clearances before beginning the approach. I conduct a thorough reconnaissance of the intended flight path and identify any runway conflict points prior to committing to the steep profile. During the approach I maintain the habit of visual scanning to either side for movement on crossing surfaces, and I do not allow fixation on the landing spot to eliminate runway awareness. If at any point I cannot maintain both approach control and runway situational awareness, I execute a go-around.

questions.question: You receive a landing clearance from tower for the helipad, begin your steep approach, and midway through the approach you see a ground vehicle has entered and stopped on the taxiway that crosses directly beneath your intended flight path. ATC has not called traffic. What is your decision-making process and exact course of action?
questions.answer: I would immediately initiate a go-around — collective up, maintain rotor RPM, transition forward cyclic to arrest descent and accelerate as conditions allow, and climb clear of all obstacles. I would simultaneously advise tower: 'Tower, N123AB going around, vehicle on taxiway.'
