questions.answer: At high density altitude, air density is reduced, which degrades rotor lift efficiency and requires a higher blade pitch angle to maintain the same RPM — this means autorotative RPM may be harder to maintain and the descent rate is typically higher. The helicopter's glide ratio may also change. 600 feet AGL at sea level might be workable in ideal conditions, but at high density altitude with a steeper-than-normal descent rate, it may be marginal or inadequate. You should evaluate: (1) whether rotor RPM can be stabilized in the available altitude, (2) whether glide range is sufficient to reach the landing zone given the increased sink rate, and (3) whether adequate flare height remains. In hot/high conditions, entering from higher altitudes is always preferable. With only 600 feet AGL here, the outcome is highly time-critical and technique must be precise.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 2 (density altitude effects)

questions.question: During a training flight, your instructor tells you to initiate a practice straight-in autorotation. You are currently at 400 feet AGL on downwind. Describe your decision-making process for whether to proceed or request a different altitude.
questions.answer: 400 feet AGL is below the typically recommended entry altitude for a straight-in autorotation. I would inform my instructor that I am not comfortable initiating the maneuver at this altitude because: (1) there is insufficient height to properly stabilize rotor RPM after collective is lowered, (2) there is limited time to establish the correct autorotative attitude and airspeed, and (3) flare timing and collective pull at the bottom require adequate altitude buffer. I would request climbing to at least 700–1,000 feet AGL before initiating. Selecting an inappropriate entry altitude introduces unnecessary risk — this is a CRM and ADM issue as much as a skills issue. The proper entry altitude is one that provides margin to complete all phases of the maneuver safely.

questions.question: How does your cruise airspeed at the time of autorotation entry affect what altitude you need to successfully complete a straight-in autorotation?
questions.answer: Cruise airspeed at entry significantly affects the maneuver. At higher cruise airspeeds, the initial entry requires simultaneous aft cyclic, down collective, and pedal input — the aft cyclic helps increase upward airflow through the rotor disk, which contributes to RPM recovery. A higher-speed entry generally converts kinetic energy into rotor RPM more effectively, but also requires more altitude to decelerate to best autorotation glide speed and then further slow to flare speed. At lower airspeeds, rotor RPM may be harder to recover quickly and there is less kinetic energy available. In both cases, having sufficient entry altitude provides the time needed to manage these transitions. The FAA notes that simultaneous down collective, aft cyclic, and trim are critical inputs at autorotation entry from cruise airspeed.

questions.question: An applicant selects 800 feet AGL as their entry altitude for a straight-in autorotation. During the debrief you ask: 'How did you specifically determine that 800 feet was appropriate for this helicopter today — what variables did you weigh?' The applicant says they just used the number from training. What deeper understanding are you looking for, and what risks does a rote-number approach create?
questions.answer: A rote-number approach fails to account for the variables that change the required entry altitude on any given flight. I am looking for the applicant to demonstrate that they considered: (1) aircraft weight — heavier aircraft have higher descent rates in autorotation, requiring more altitude; (2) density altitude — affects rotor efficiency and descent rate; (3) wind — headwind reduces groundspeed and extends glide range, while tailwind does the opposite, affecting whether the selected LZ is reachable; (4) rotor RPM inertia characteristics of that specific helicopter — low-inertia systems require faster response and may need more altitude; (5) entry airspeed — affects energy available and time to stabilize; (6) landing zone distance and obstacles. A rote number like '800 feet' might be adequate in standard conditions but dangerously marginal in hot/high conditions, with a heavy load, or at slow airspeed with a low-inertia rotor. The risk is the pilot becomes complacent and selects altitude by habit rather than by analysis, creating a situation where technique must be flawless to succeed — removing all safety margin.
questions.follow_up: If density altitude is 5,000 feet and your helicopter's RFM shows a 10% increase in autorotative descent rate under those conditions, how does that affect the altitude you should select for entry?
questions.follow_up_answer: A 10% increase in descent rate means the helicopter is losing altitude faster for every second of the autorotation. This directly compresses the time available for each phase — RPM recovery, glide stabilization, flare, and collective pull. To preserve the same safety margins as at sea level, the pilot should increase entry altitude proportionally — in this case at least 10% higher, so if the baseline is 800 feet AGL, consider entering at 880 feet AGL or more. Additionally, the higher density altitude reduces flare effectiveness because rotor lift is less efficient, so extra flare altitude buffer may be needed. The practical takeaway is that in hot/high conditions, more altitude is always better, and the pilot should consult the RFM performance data and plan accordingly rather than using a fixed number.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; aircraft RFM/POH; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM)

questions.question: Your applicant consistently initiates straight-in autorotations from the same altitude with good outcomes during training. On the checkride, they select the same altitude but conditions include a 15-knot tailwind and a high-density-altitude departure airport. They overshoot the landing zone. What failure of entry altitude selection does this reveal, and what should they have done differently?
questions.answer: This reveals that the applicant was using a fixed, condition-independent altitude rather than a situationally aware one. With a 15-knot tailwind, the helicopter's groundspeed during the autorotative glide is significantly higher, which means it covers more horizontal distance per unit of altitude lost — resulting in an overshoot of the intended landing zone. The applicant should have recognized that with a tailwind, they needed either a higher entry altitude to allow more time to dissipate the extra groundspeed during the flare, or they should have selected a landing zone farther away to account for the extended glide. Additionally, high density altitude increases descent rate, which partially offsets the tailwind effect but also compresses flare time. The proper approach is to mentally model the full glide path before initiating: assess wind direction and speed, calculate the effect on groundspeed and glide range, and adjust entry altitude or LZ selection accordingly. Selecting entry altitude is not an isolated decision — it must integrate with LZ selection, wind, and aircraft performance to form a complete plan.
questions.follow_up: If you recognize mid-autorotation that you are going to overshoot, what options do you have and what are the limits of those options?
questions.follow_up_answer: Mid-autorotation options to address an overshoot include: (1) S-turns or a modified flight path to increase distance traveled and reduce groundspeed — this costs altitude and must be done carefully to avoid letting rotor RPM exceed limits; (2) steepening the descent by reducing collective slightly if RPM permits — this increases sink rate and shortens the glide; (3) selecting a new, farther landing zone if one is available and altitude permits. The key constraint is rotor RPM — any maneuver that increases drag on the rotor system (such as a steep bank in a turn) can cause RPM to drop, and any action that requires more altitude than available is not viable. The pilot must also preserve adequate altitude for the flare and collective pull. The bottom line: mid-maneuver corrections have limited range and introduce risk; the best outcome is always achieved by selecting the correct entry altitude and LZ before initiating, not by attempting to fix an overshoot in progress.

questions.question: When flying a straight-in autorotation, what is the primary reference you use to determine the correct point to initiate the maneuver?
questions.answer: The primary reference is the selected landing area appearing within a specific sight picture on the windscreen — typically an approximate 10-to-13-degree glide angle that places the landing zone at a consistent position relative to the nose. The pilot evaluates altitude, distance to the landing area, and airspeed simultaneously. A common rule of thumb is that if the landing area appears to be 'rising' in the windscreen, you are too low or too close; if it appears to be 'falling,' you are too high or too far. The correct initiation point puts the landing area within the normal autorotation glide range of the helicopter.

questions.question: What three factors does a pilot need to evaluate simultaneously to determine whether the autorotation initiation point is correct?
questions.answer: The three factors are: (1) Altitude above the landing area — must be sufficient to establish a stable autorotative glide; (2) Distance to the intended touchdown point — must fall within the helicopter's glide distance capability at that altitude; and (3) Airspeed — must allow transition to the recommended autorotation airspeed for that specific helicopter without exceeding rotor RPM limits or arriving at the flare point too fast or too slow. If any one of these three factors is significantly off, the initiation point is incorrect.

questions.question: In a straight-in autorotation, what is the immediate pilot action the moment the decision is made to initiate the maneuver, and why must that action happen without delay?
questions.answer: The immediate action is to lower the collective to the full-down position (or as required to enter autorotation per the RFM) simultaneously with aft cyclic to establish the recommended autorotation airspeed, and adjust pedals for trim. This must happen without delay because low-inertia rotor systems decay rapidly once engine power is removed. Any hesitation allows rotor RPM to bleed off below the power-on RPM before autorotation airflow can take over, potentially resulting in rotor RPM falling below the minimum safe autorotation RPM before the pilot can recover it.

questions.question: You are on downwind at 600 feet AGL and 70 knots in a training helicopter when your instructor pulls the throttle to simulate an engine failure. As you scan the area, the only suitable landing zone is straight ahead and approximately 1,500 feet in front of you. Describe how you assess whether this is a viable initiation point for a straight-in autorotation.
questions.answer: At 600 feet AGL and 70 knots, I immediately lower the collective to enter autorotation and establish the recommended autorotation airspeed per the RFM, then assess the sight picture. A typical training helicopter achieves a glide ratio of roughly 4:1 to 5:1 in autorotation, which at 600 feet AGL would produce approximately 2,400 to 3,000 feet of forward glide distance. A landing zone 1,500 feet ahead is well within that range. I confirm by checking whether the LZ appears steady or nearly steady in my windscreen — if it is rising, I am undershooting; if falling, I have excess glide range. With 1,500 feet at 600 feet AGL, the LZ should appear well within reach, and I would likely need to manage energy by adjusting airspeed or using a slight S-turn to avoid overshooting rather than worrying about coming up short.

questions.question: How does wind affect the correct initiation point for a straight-in autorotation, and what adjustment would you make if you are flying into a 20-knot headwind versus a 20-knot tailwind?
questions.answer: Wind significantly affects the glide path over the ground. Into a 20-knot headwind, the helicopter's ground speed is reduced, which steepens the approach angle over the ground — the helicopter covers less ground per foot of altitude lost. This means you need to initiate the autorotation closer to the landing zone or from a lower altitude than in calm conditions, or the sight picture will show the LZ rising (indicating undershoot). With a 20-knot tailwind, ground speed is increased, flattening the glide path over the ground — the helicopter covers more ground per foot of altitude. You must initiate farther out or from higher altitude, otherwise the LZ will appear to fall rapidly indicating an overshoot. In practice, for a tailwind autorotation, a pilot initiates the maneuver significantly farther from the LZ and must be especially cautious because the higher groundspeed at flare and touchdown increases landing roll and touchdown loads.

questions.question: A student consistently initiates straight-in autorotations too late — always arriving low and fast with the LZ well past the nose. As the instructor, you suspect the student is using the wrong visual cue to determine the initiation point. What are the two most common incorrect visual references students use, and how do you correct them?
questions.answer: The two most common incorrect visual references are: (1) Waiting until the landing zone is 'directly below' or 'close under the nose' — this is far too late; by the time the LZ looks close, the helicopter has already passed the correct initiation point given its altitude and speed. Students often confuse proximity on the ground with being in range for autorotation. (2) Misjudging the glide angle by comparing to fixed-wing approaches — students with fixed-wing backgrounds expect a shallower angle and delay initiation, not accounting for the steeper autorotation glide path of most helicopters (typically 8–13 degrees versus 3 degrees for a fixed-wing). Correction involves training the student to use the sight picture where the LZ appears at a specific fixed reference on the windscreen (e.g., the chin bubble edge or a marked spot), combined with the concept of the 'moving LZ' — if the LZ is rising in your windscreen during the approach, you're already too low; if it's stationary or dropping, you have room. Repetitive practice from consistent altitudes and airspeeds builds the mental model.
questions.follow_up: If this same student then overcorrects and starts initiating too early, arriving high with excess rotor RPM, what is the greatest safety risk of that scenario?
questions.follow_up_answer: The greatest safety risk of initiating too early and arriving high is that the pilot will be tempted to raise the collective mid-autorotation to slow the descent and prevent an overshoot. This bleeds rotor RPM — often substantially. If the pilot then realizes they need that rotor RPM for the flare and cushion, it may no longer be available. A high rotor-RPM autorotation that is managed correctly (using S-turns or adjusting airspeed) is recoverable; an autorotation where the pilot has prematurely traded rotor RPM for descent rate control is far more dangerous because the energy needed for the flare and collective pull at touchdown is gone. The pilot may attempt a power recovery too early, or may arrive at the flare with insufficient RPM to cushion landing, resulting in a hard landing or dynamic rollover.

questions.question: When you enter a straight-in autorotation from cruise flight, what are the three simultaneous control inputs required at the moment of engine failure to establish the power-off glide?
questions.answer: At the moment of engine failure, you must simultaneously: (1) lower the collective to the full-down position to reduce blade pitch, decrease drag on the rotor, and allow upward airflow to maintain rotor RPM; (2) apply aft cyclic to slow the helicopter toward autorotation airspeed and increase upward airflow through the disk, which helps sustain rotor RPM; and (3) apply the appropriate antitorque pedal to maintain trim and counteract any yaw caused by the power loss. These three inputs must be nearly simultaneous — delay in lowering collective is the most critical error because rotor RPM decays rapidly, especially in low-inertia systems.

questions.question: What does it mean for the helicopter to be 'trimmed' during the power-off glide, and which instrument or physical cue do you use to verify it?
questions.answer: A trimmed helicopter has no uncoordinated yaw — the fuselage is aligned with the relative wind and there is no slip or skid. During autorotation, the tail rotor is still driven by the main rotor transmission, so heading control is maintained with antitorque pedals just as in normal flight. You verify trim by centering the ball in the slip/skid indicator (inclinometer). If the ball is out of center, you are in either a slip or skid, which increases drag, degrades glide performance, and makes the helicopter harder to control through the flare and landing.

questions.question: Where do you find the published autorotation airspeed for your specific helicopter, and why does this airspeed matter for the power-off glide?
questions.answer: The autorotation airspeed — sometimes called best glide or minimum rate of descent airspeed in autorotation — is published in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for the specific helicopter. It is typically found in the emergency procedures section and/or the performance section. This airspeed matters because it represents the speed at which the rotor system is operating at its most efficient lift-to-drag ratio in autorotation, resulting in the lowest rate of descent and maximum glide distance. Flying faster or slower than this speed increases rate of descent. The ACS tolerance is ±10 knots from the published value.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR 27.75 (RFM requirements for normal category rotorcraft)

questions.question: You are flying a straight-in autorotation at the correct airspeed, but you notice the ball is deflected to the right. Describe what is happening aerodynamically and the exact control input needed to correct it.
questions.answer: A ball deflected to the right means the helicopter is skidding to the right — the tail is swinging to the right relative to the nose, indicating the fuselage is not aligned with the relative wind. In a counterclockwise rotor system (most American helicopters), when engine power is lost, the torque effect that required right pedal during powered flight disappears. A right skid typically results from insufficient left pedal or excessive right pedal input. The correction is to apply left antitorque pedal to realign the fuselage with the relative wind and center the ball. A skid increases parasite drag and reduces glide efficiency, potentially shortening your glide distance to the landing zone. During the autorotation, you must continuously monitor and fine-tune pedal inputs as rotor RPM changes.

questions.question: During the power-off glide of a straight-in autorotation, you are 5 knots above the published autorotation airspeed. You push forward cyclic to correct. What unintended consequence can this create, and how do you manage it?
questions.answer: Pushing forward cyclic to increase speed tilts the rotor disk forward, which decreases the upward component of airflow through the rotor disk. This reduces the aerodynamic force maintaining rotor RPM, causing RPM to decay. Additionally, the increased airspeed increases parasite drag on the airframe, further increasing your rate of descent. The correct technique is to apply gentle forward cyclic to return to the target airspeed — avoid large, abrupt inputs. As you push forward, monitor the tachometer: if rotor RPM trends low, you may need to slightly lower collective to increase upward airflow (though in most helicopters the collective is already at the bottom stop). In some aircraft, a slight aft input to stabilize at the correct airspeed is more appropriate than continued forward pressure. The key is coordinated, smooth inputs while cross-checking airspeed and RPM simultaneously.

questions.question: You initiate a straight-in autorotation from 1,500 feet AGL and establish the glide, but you realize you are going to land significantly short of your intended landing area. At this point in the maneuver, what cyclic adjustment can extend your glide distance, and what is the tradeoff?
questions.answer: To extend glide distance, you can increase airspeed slightly above the published autorotation airspeed toward the best glide speed if those differ in your RFM, or apply forward cyclic to increase airspeed toward the higher end of the ±10-knot tolerance band. A higher airspeed flattens the glide angle and covers more ground horizontally. The tradeoff is an increased rate of descent — you will arrive at a lower altitude sooner, leaving less energy for the flare and cushion. You must balance glide distance against the altitude available to execute a proper flare. If you extend the glide significantly, you may arrive at the flare point with less rotor RPM energy and less altitude, compressing the available time to arrest descent rate. Always reference your specific RFM for maximum glide airspeed versus minimum sink airspeed, as they are typically different.

questions.question: During the power-off glide in a straight-in autorotation, a student consistently allows the nose to creep below the horizon, resulting in airspeeds 12–15 knots above the published autorotation airspeed before corrections are made. As an examiner, what specific rotor system hazard does this repeated exceedance introduce, and at what point would you take the controls?
questions.answer: Consistently flying 12–15 knots above published autorotation airspeed — which exceeds the ±10-knot ACS tolerance — introduces two compounding hazards. First, the excessive airspeed increases the flap-back tendency: as blades advance and retreat in forward flight at higher airspeed, the advancing blade produces more lift and flaps up, while the retreating blade approaches its stall angle faster. At extreme speeds, retreating blade stall becomes a risk. Second, and more immediately relevant in autorotation, the excessive speed increases induced flow through the rotor disk in a way that can reduce the angle of attack on the blade elements, causing rotor RPM to decay — leaving less energy stored in the rotor for the flare. By the time the student enters the flare with an already-decayed RPM and extra airspeed to dissipate, the risk of a hard landing or dynamic rollover increases substantially. As an examiner, I would take the controls when the maneuver no longer meets the published standards AND when continued flight represents a risk to safety — specifically when it becomes evident the student cannot or will not correct within a reasonable altitude margin to safely complete the landing. A single exceedance with prompt self-correction is a training item; a pattern of uncorrected exceedances approaching the flare entry point is a safety-of-flight issue.
questions.follow_up: If a student asks why the ACS tolerance is ±10 knots and not tighter — say ±5 knots — how would you explain the engineering and practical reasons behind that specific standard?
questions.follow_up_answer: The ±10-knot tolerance reflects the practical realities of helicopter autorotation: airspeed indicators have inherent instrument error, especially at low airspeeds; pilot workload during an emergency power-off glide is extremely high; and the glide characteristics of most helicopters are relatively forgiving within a moderate speed band around the optimal autorotation airspeed. The standard is also based on empirical data showing that a well-trained pilot under realistic conditions — engine failure, simulated stress, unfamiliar landing zone — can reasonably maintain airspeed within ±10 knots while simultaneously managing rotor RPM, trim, and landing zone selection. A ±5-knot tolerance would be unrealistically precise for most real-world emergency conditions and would disqualify otherwise proficient pilots on a criterion driven more by instrument variability than by actual skill difference. The ±10-knot standard is a balance between meaningful skill demonstration and practical achievability.

questions.question: You are evaluating a commercial helicopter applicant who establishes the autorotation glide exactly at published airspeed but with the nose slightly left of the relative wind — the ball is deflected about half a ball width — and maintains this condition throughout the glide. The airspeed stays within ±10 knots. Does this pass the ACS standard for S7? Explain your reasoning and what aerodynamic consequence this out-of-trim condition creates.
questions.answer: The ACS standard for S7 specifically requires the helicopter to be 'trimmed' AND at autorotation airspeed ±10 knots — both conditions must be met simultaneously. Flying with a half-ball deflection throughout the glide does not meet the 'trimmed' requirement of S7, even if airspeed is within tolerance. The ACS language is explicit: 'trimmed and autorotation airspeed.' This is a failure item for S7. Aerodynamically, even a half-ball out-of-trim condition creates a sideslip component. The fuselage presents a non-streamlined cross-section to the relative wind, increasing parasite drag. This additional drag increases the rate of descent — shortening the available glide range — and requires the rotor to overcome more resistance, which can contribute to rotor RPM decay. In a real engine failure, this could mean the difference between reaching a suitable landing area and landing short in an unsuitable area. Additionally, an out-of-trim condition entering the flare can produce asymmetric blade loading and unpredictable yaw responses during the collective pull, complicating the landing.
questions.follow_up: The applicant argues that half a ball width is within the tolerance of the inclinometer and is essentially 'trimmed enough.' How do you respond, and does the FAA provide any specific tolerance for the slip/skid indicator in the ACS?
questions.follow_up_answer: The ACS for straight-in autorotation does not publish a numerical ball-deflection tolerance the way it does for airspeed. The standard simply states 'trimmed.' The examiner's practical test standards guidance is that 'trimmed' means coordinated flight — ball centered — as a qualitative standard. I would explain to the applicant that 'trimmed' in the context of helicopter flight means the fuselage is aligned with the relative wind with no slip or skid component, which corresponds to a centered ball. Instrument tolerance is a separate issue from pilot technique — if the instrument shows a deflection, the technique is deficient regardless of whether the instrument error contributed. More importantly, the applicant's argument reveals a mindset of seeking the minimum acceptable standard rather than precision flying, which is itself a training concern. In a real emergency, half a ball width of skid maintained for the entire glide could represent dozens of feet of lost glide range — a critical factor when landing zone options are limited.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9, Chapter 11; PH.VIII.B ACS Standards (S7)

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, what is the primary control you use to manage main rotor RPM (Nr), and what is the general rule for how you use it?
questions.answer: The collective pitch control is the primary tool for managing Nr during autorotation. As a general rule, lowering collective reduces blade pitch angle and drag, allowing Nr to increase or recover toward the normal operating range. Raising collective increases blade pitch and drag, which bleeds off Nr. The pilot must continuously monitor the tachometer and make small collective adjustments to keep Nr within the green arc (normal operating limits) throughout the descent.

questions.question: What instrument do you reference to monitor Nr during an autorotation, and where is the normal operating range typically indicated?
questions.answer: The pilot monitors Nr on the tachometer — specifically the rotor RPM needle (or the rotor side of a dual-needle tach if equipped). The normal operating range is indicated by a green arc on the tachometer face. The pilot must keep Nr within this green arc at all times during the autorotation. Operating below the green arc risks rotor stall; operating above the green arc risks structural damage to the rotor system.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; aircraft-specific Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM)

questions.question: What aerodynamic mechanism actually drives the main rotor and maintains Nr during an autorotation descent?
questions.answer: During autorotation, upward airflow through the rotor disk — caused by the helicopter descending — drives the rotor blades. This upward-flowing air strikes the underside of the rotor blades, creating aerodynamic forces that rotate the blades, similar to the way wind drives a pinwheel. The angle of attack of the blade sections in the autorotative region is such that the net aerodynamic force has a forward component that overcomes drag and sustains rotation. This keeps Nr within normal limits as long as the pilot maintains the correct collective setting and descent airspeed.

questions.question: You are established in a straight-in autorotation at the correct approach airspeed, but you notice Nr is drifting toward the top of the green arc. What is likely causing this, and what corrective action do you take?
questions.answer: Nr drifting toward the top of the green arc typically indicates that the collective is set too low for the current airspeed and descent rate, allowing too much upward airflow through the disk to accelerate the rotor, or that the airspeed is too high (increasing inflow). Corrective action: apply a small amount of upward collective to increase blade pitch and drag, which will absorb energy and bring Nr back toward the middle of the green arc. If airspeed is excessive, a small amount of aft cyclic can reduce it, which also helps manage Nr. The correction should be smooth and small — overcorrecting with too much collective can cause Nr to decay rapidly.

questions.question: During the flare phase of a straight-in autorotation, how does aft cyclic input affect Nr, and how do you account for this when managing rotor RPM through the flare and into the collective pull?
questions.answer: Applying aft cyclic during the flare tilts the rotor disk rearward, which increases the upward component of airflow through the disk and tends to increase Nr. The pilot must anticipate this Nr rise and be prepared to apply a small amount of collective during the flare to prevent Nr from exceeding the top of the green arc. As the flare decelerates the helicopter and the upward inflow decreases near the bottom, Nr will begin to decay. The pilot must then smoothly increase collective to cushion the landing while Nr is still adequate — typically in the upper portion of the green arc — to ensure sufficient rotor energy is available for the collective pull to arrest the descent rate. Waiting too long with low Nr before pulling collective can result in an excessively hard landing.

questions.question: You are on final in a straight-in autorotation and notice you are going to come up short of your intended landing point. You instinctively want to lower the nose to increase airspeed. How does this decision affect Nr, and what is the correct technique?
questions.answer: Lowering the nose to increase airspeed will increase forward airspeed, which increases inflow velocity through the disk and will cause Nr to rise — potentially above the green arc. However, the more significant concern is that using airspeed to correct a short approach late in the autorotation consumes altitude rapidly and may not allow sufficient energy for a proper flare and collective pull. The correct technique is to adjust the glide path early in the autorotation by trading airspeed for distance while Nr is monitored. If you are genuinely short, a modest forward cyclic input can extend the glide, but Nr must be closely monitored and collective adjusted to prevent an overspeed. Anytime Nr approaches the top of the green arc, slight collective increase is the corrective action. Attempting major trajectory corrections late in the autorotation risks losing control of both glide path and Nr simultaneously.

questions.question: A student pilot during a practice straight-in autorotation allows Nr to decay below the bottom of the green arc at 200 feet AGL. They then attempt to recover Nr by fully lowering the collective. As the examiner, walk me through what is happening aerodynamically, whether the recovery is likely to succeed, and what the real risk is at this point.
questions.answer: When Nr decays below the green arc, the rotor blades are turning too slowly to generate sufficient lift for normal flight. Fully lowering collective reduces blade pitch and drag, which does allow upward airflow to begin accelerating the rotor — this is the correct instinct. However, at 200 feet AGL, the time available for Nr to recover is extremely limited. As Nr decays, the pilot has simultaneously lost the stored kinetic energy in the rotor that would normally be used during the flare and collective pull to cushion the landing. Even if the pilot gets Nr partially back into the green arc, the reduced inertia means the collective pull at the bottom will be far less effective. The real risk is rotor stall — if Nr drops low enough that the blades stall, the condition is not recoverable. FAA guidance explicitly states that rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable, and early recognition is imperative. At 200 feet AGL with low Nr, the outcome is likely a hard or catastrophic landing. This scenario is a classic example of a situation that becomes unrecoverable not because of a single mistake, but because multiple small errors accumulated without correction.
questions.follow_up: What operational habits or scan techniques should a pilot develop to prevent Nr from decaying to this point in the first place during a straight-in autorotation?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot should establish a regular instrument scan that includes the tachometer every few seconds throughout the entire autorotation — not just at entry and flare. Nr management must be continuous, not reactive. The pilot should know the specific Nr limits for the aircraft being flown (from the RFM), recognize the sound and feel of the rotor at different RPM ranges, and make small proactive collective adjustments rather than waiting for large deviations to correct. During training, instructors should introduce Nr management as an active skill, not a passive monitor. High-inertia rotor systems give more time to recover, but low-inertia systems (light turbine helicopters, for example) decay very quickly and demand faster reactions. Treating Nr as the most critical parameter during autorotation — not just the landing zone — is the proper mental model.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation in a helicopter with a low-inertia rotor system, how does the Nr management challenge differ from a high-inertia rotor system, and what specific technique adjustments must a pilot make?
questions.answer: A low-inertia rotor system — common in lighter turbine helicopters — stores significantly less kinetic energy in the rotor blades than a high-inertia system (like that of a heavier piston helicopter). This means Nr changes happen faster in both directions: it decays more quickly when collective is raised or inflow decreases, and it recovers more quickly when collective is lowered. The practical implications are: (1) the pilot must be more aggressive and immediate in correcting any Nr deviations — the tolerance for delayed response is much smaller; (2) the timing of the flare and collective pull at the bottom is more critical because the rotor energy bleeds off faster once collective is applied; (3) the pilot cannot 'save up' as much rotor energy by flying high Nr on final, because low-inertia systems don't store as much per RPM unit; (4) the entry into autorotation from cruise must be immediate — delay in lowering collective after engine failure allows rapid Nr decay. By contrast, a high-inertia system gives the pilot more time to recognize and correct deviations, and stores more energy for the terminal flare. Pilots transitioning between rotor systems must be retrained specifically on the Nr management demands of the new aircraft.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot is transitioning from a high-inertia training helicopter to a low-inertia turbine helicopter, what specific aspect of Nr management during the autorotation termination (flare-to-touchdown) is most likely to catch them off guard, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: The most likely surprise is how quickly Nr decays during and after the collective pull at the bottom of the autorotation. In a high-inertia helicopter, the pilot has a relatively generous window to apply collective — the rotor energy bleeds off slowly, and the aircraft settles softly even if the timing is slightly off. In a low-inertia turbine helicopter, if the pilot applies collective even a fraction of a second late, or if Nr is already slightly low entering the flare, the rotor may not have sufficient energy to arrest the descent rate before touchdown. The result is a hard landing that can damage the aircraft or injure occupants. The transitioning pilot is conditioned to a timing and feel that no longer applies, and their instincts will be wrong until recalibrated through specific dual instruction in the new aircraft type. This is why the FAA and most operators require type-specific autorotation training when transitioning between significantly different rotor systems.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; aircraft-specific RFM; 14 CFR 61.31 (type-specific training requirements)

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, how does a headwind affect your glide distance compared to a no-wind condition, and what adjustment do you make to your approach?
questions.answer: A headwind reduces your groundspeed while your airspeed remains the same, which shortens your glide distance over the ground. The helicopter will cover less ground for the same altitude loss. To compensate, you may need to steepen your approach angle or aim for a closer point on the ground.  The proper technique is to recognize that the same airspeed glide path will result in a shorter ground distance, so the pilot should select an aim point appropriately closer to the near edge of the intended landing zone.

issues: Answer oversimplifies headwind effect on autorotation glide distance and contains a subtle error in guidance. The answer states 'shortens your glide distance over the ground' which is correct, but then suggests 'steepen your approach angle' as a corrective action, which is imprecise. In a headwind, the helicopter's TRUE airspeed remains constant and the glide path angle (in relation to the airmass) remains constant, but groundspeed decreases. The pilot should NOT steepen the approach — rather, the aim point naturally shifts closer. The advice to 'reduce forward cyclic to slow descent rate' is also imprecise — in autorotation, the descent rate is primarily controlled by collective and airspeed is maintained by cyclic. Suggesting forward cyclic reduction to slow descent rate conflates descent control with airspeed management.

The corrective technique is underdeveloped: in a headwind, the proper technique is to recognize that the same airspeed glide path will result in a shorter ground distance, so the pilot should select an aim point appropriately closer to the near edge of the intended landing zone. Simply aiming for a 'closer point' is mentioned but not clearly emphasized as the primary correction. The approach angle itself does not need to be steepened if the landing zone is adequate.
verification.suggested_correction: A headwind reduces your groundspeed while your airspeed remains the same, which shortens your glide distance over the ground. The helicopter will cover less ground for the same altitude loss. Your glide path angle (relative to the airmass) remains constant, but your ground track distance is reduced. The primary adjustment is to select an aim point closer to the near edge of the landing zone to account for reduced ground distance. Do not steepen the approach angle — instead, recognize that your groundspeed will be lower and plan your aim point accordingly. The same airspeed and descent profile will simply result in shorter ground distance.

questions.question: What visual cue tells you during a straight-in autorotation that you are going to overshoot your selected landing area?
questions.answer: The primary visual cue for an overshoot is that the aim point appears to move away from you, or 'slides down' toward the bottom of your windscreen, meaning the landing area is moving further away relative to a fixed reference point on your windscreen. Additionally, the rate of terrain detail expansion around your aim point will appear slower than expected. You can also confirm an overshoot if the landing area is consistently appearing to move toward the horizon rather than rising up in your field of view.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation with a direct tailwind, would you expect to undershoot or overshoot your landing area, and why?
questions.answer: With a direct tailwind, you would expect to overshoot. A tailwind increases your groundspeed while your autorotation airspeed remains the same, meaning the helicopter covers more ground for the same altitude loss. The increased groundspeed carries you beyond your intended aim point. To compensate, you should either select a landing area farther away, use S-turns or a wider pattern if the situation allows, or increase your rate of descent by reducing forward cyclic to steepen the approach and bleed off excess groundspeed.

questions.question: You are established in a straight-in autorotation on final and you realize you have a 15-knot tailwind. You are already committed to the landing area. Walk me through your specific control inputs to correct for the overshoot condition.
questions.answer: With a tailwind-induced overshoot already in progress, your options depend on rotor RPM and altitude remaining. First, confirm rotor RPM is in the green arc. You can increase the rate of descent by applying slight forward cyclic to steepen the glide angle, which increases groundspeed momentarily but trades altitude more rapidly — use this with caution. A more effective technique is to use a slight flare earlier than normal to reduce groundspeed: aft cyclic bleeds off the tailwind component and converts it to rotor RPM if needed, while also steepening the descent. Do not raise the collective to stretch the glide, as this robs rotor RPM needed for the flare and cushion. Aim for the near end of the landing area and execute your flare and collective cushion normally. If the overshoot is unrecoverable, go around if power is available; if in a true autorotation, select an alternate landing area.

questions.question: You are flying a straight-in autorotation with a 20-degree crosswind from the left. How does the crosswind affect your approach, and what technique do you use to keep the helicopter tracking straight to the landing area?
questions.answer: A crosswind from the left will push the helicopter to the right of centerline if not corrected, causing you to drift away from your landing area. To compensate, apply a wind correction angle (crab) into the wind by applying left cyclic to track a ground path aligned with the landing area—similar to a crosswind approach in normal flight. Maintain this cyclic correction throughout descent. As you enter the flare at 50–100 feet AGL, transition to align the nose with the intended landing direction using right pedal input while maintaining lateral position control with cyclic. This coordinated transition ensures both groundtrack and heading alignment at touchdown. Be aware that the crosswind will continue to affect lateral drift during the flare; cyclic inputs must account for both forward and lateral velocity components.

questions.question: You initiate a straight-in autorotation from 1,000 feet AGL into a strong 25-knot headwind. At 500 feet AGL, you notice you are undershooting your aim point. What actions do you take, and what is the limitation of trying to stretch the glide?
questions.answer: At 500 feet AGL with an undershoot developing in a strong headwind, you have limited options. You can apply slight forward cyclic to reduce the angle of descent and extend the glide, which trades altitude for distance. However, the limitation of stretching the glide is significant: lowering the nose increases airspeed and reduces angle of descent, but in a strong headwind your groundspeed gain is minimal, and you risk running out of altitude before reaching the landing area. You must also protect rotor RPM — do not raise collective to extend the glide, as this will decay RPM and leave you without energy for the flare and cushion. The better technique is to aim for the nearest acceptable landing area within reach, even if it is not your original aim point. Attempting to stretch beyond the helicopter's glide capability is a primary cause of hard landings and dynamic rollover in autorotations.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, a pilot corrects for what appears to be an undershoot by raising the collective slightly at 300 feet AGL to stretch the glide. What are the cascading consequences of this action, and how should the pilot have addressed the undershoot instead?
questions.answer: Raising collective during the autorotative glide at 300 feet AGL is a dangerous error with cascading consequences. First, increasing collective pitch immediately increases blade drag and rotor disc load, causing rotor RPM to decay rapidly. At 300 feet AGL there is insufficient altitude to recover RPM by lowering collective and waiting for airflow to rebuild it. Second, reduced rotor RPM means less stored kinetic energy available for the flare and collective cushion at touchdown — the two maneuvers that arrest both forward and vertical velocity. Third, the temporary lift generated barely extends the glide, because the RPM decay simultaneously reduces lift production. The net result is a slower, heavier touchdown with inadequate cushion authority. The correct technique to address an undershoot is to apply forward cyclic to shorten the descent angle and increase groundspeed — not collective. Alternatively, accept a shorter landing area, or in a real emergency, select a new landing area within glide range. The collective must be reserved and kept fully down until the flare is executed.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot's rotor RPM has decayed to the lower limit of the green arc at 200 feet AGL due to premature collective application, what is the priority — recovering RPM or continuing the approach, and can both be achieved simultaneously?
questions.follow_up_answer: At 200 feet AGL with RPM at the bottom of the green arc, recovering RPM is the absolute priority, because without adequate rotor energy the helicopter cannot execute a flare or cushion. The pilot must immediately lower collective to the full-down position, which reduces blade pitch and allows upward airflow through the rotor to spin the blades back up. Aft cyclic can also contribute by increasing the angle at which airflow enters the disk, adding to RPM recovery. However, at 200 feet AGL there is very little time — if RPM does not recover before reaching flare altitude, the helicopter will not have sufficient inertia to arrest the vertical and forward velocity, resulting in a hard landing or crash. Both objectives — recovering RPM and continuing the approach — can be worked simultaneously only if there is enough altitude remaining. If RPM is critically low with minimal altitude, the pilot should immediately execute the best available landing with whatever RPM exists, keeping collective down as long as possible before the final cushion attempt. This is why protecting rotor RPM throughout the entire autorotation is emphasized as the primary skill in autorotation training.

questions.question: You are demonstrating a straight-in autorotation with a student at the controls. The wind is reported calm, but on final you notice the helicopter is consistently drifting left and undershooting. What are the possible causes beyond a simple wind shift, and how do you isolate the actual cause?
questions.answer: A drift left with undershoot when wind is reported calm has several possible causes beyond a simple wind shift. First, surface winds can differ significantly from winds aloft or reported conditions — a valley, tree line, or building complex can create localized crosswind or downdraft effects that push the helicopter left and reduce glide range. Second, the student may be unconsciously applying left cyclic, causing lateral drift that also bleeds off forward energy needed to reach the aim point. Third, if left pedal is being held (perhaps in anticipation of torque correction), it can cause a slight yaw and lateral drift. Fourth, the aim point itself may have been selected incorrectly — if it was selected downwind of a terrain feature generating a rotor wash or mechanical turbulence, actual glide performance will be degraded. To isolate the cause: observe the student's control inputs directly; check for uncoordinated pedal input causing yaw; look at the horizon for any lateral drift reference; and evaluate whether the undershoot is consistent (suggesting wind or technique) or variable (suggesting student input errors). As an instructor, you should take controls at a safe altitude and demonstrate a corrected approach, then debrief which factor was primary.
questions.follow_up: If you determine mid-approach that a building-generated rotor wash is creating a downdraft over your landing zone and you are at 400 feet AGL, what is your decision framework, and at what point is it too late to select an alternate landing area?
questions.follow_up_answer: At 400 feet AGL with a building-generated downdraft over the landing zone, the decision framework is: Can I reach an alternate landing area while maintaining safe rotor RPM and without requiring power? If yes, transition immediately by applying cyclic toward the alternate area and re-establish a normal autorotative glide to the new aim point. The threshold for 'too late' is generally around 200 feet AGL in most helicopters — below this altitude, selecting a significantly different landing area requires turns and attitude changes that may compromise rotor RPM and leave insufficient altitude for a proper flare. However, this is aircraft-specific and depends on the specific helicopter's glide characteristics, rotor inertia, and the angular distance to the alternate. At 400 feet AGL, there is generally adequate altitude and rotor energy to make a modest heading change to a nearby alternate. The key principle from FAA-H-8083-21B is that a pilot should select a landing area with an out — meaning a contingency area is identified before the maneuver begins. The worst decision is to continue into a known downdraft/rotor wash area at low altitude when an alternate exists, because the unpredictable nature of mechanical turbulence makes flare execution unreliable.

questions.question: During the flare phase of a straight-in autorotation, what is the primary purpose of applying aft cyclic, and how does it affect the tail boom's relationship to the ground?
questions.answer: Aft cyclic during the flare decelerates the helicopter and transfers energy from forward speed into rotor RPM. As the nose pitches up, the tail boom drops closer to the ground. If the flare is too aggressive or held too long at low altitude, the tail rotor or tail boom can strike the surface. The pilot must manage the degree and timing of the flare to ensure the tail clears the ground throughout the maneuver.

questions.question: At what point in a straight-in autorotation should you begin applying collective pitch to cushion the landing, and what happens to rotor RPM as you do?
questions.answer: Collective pitch is applied during the final phase of the flare or just after the nose is leveled, typically when the helicopter is a few feet above the surface and forward speed has been sufficiently reduced. As collective is increased, blade pitch angle increases, which generates additional lift to arrest the descent rate but simultaneously increases drag on the rotor system, causing RPM to decay. The pilot must time and rate the collective application to use available rotor energy to cushion touchdown without allowing RPM to drop below the minimum operational limit.

questions.question: What is the relationship between forward airspeed at the initiation of the flare and tail boom ground clearance risk during a straight-in autorotation?
questions.answer: Higher forward airspeed at flare initiation requires a more pronounced aft cyclic input to decelerate the aircraft, which results in a steeper nose-high attitude and lower tail position. The faster the approach speed and the more aggressive the flare needed, the greater the risk of tail boom or tail rotor contact with the ground. Conversely, if the pilot enters the flare too late at high speed, there may be insufficient altitude to complete deceleration before the tail approaches the surface. Proper approach speed and flare timing are essential to maintaining adequate tail boom clearance.

questions.question: You are on final in a straight-in autorotation and realize you are high and fast. You apply an aggressive flare to increase deceleration. Walk me through the specific risks this creates for tail boom clearance and how you would manage them.
questions.answer: An aggressive flare from a high-and-fast condition will cause a rapid nose-high pitch attitude, which lowers the tail boom toward the ground. If this occurs at low altitude, the tail rotor blades or tail boom structure can strike the surface before the pilot can level the aircraft. Additionally, the aggressive flare may generate a large rotor RPM spike, tempting the pilot to prematurely apply collective to control RPM — but applying collective too early reduces the energy needed to cushion the landing and may leave the aircraft with insufficient rotor RPM at touchdown. The correct management approach is to initiate the flare at the proper altitude (high enough to allow the flare to arrest airspeed before the tail gets close to the surface), use a firm but progressive — not abrupt — aft cyclic input, monitor rotor RPM throughout, level the attitude before applying collective, and touch down on the skids in a level attitude or slight nose-up attitude with adequate RPM remaining.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, a student applies collective pitch too early — before completing the flare and while still at a nose-high attitude. Describe the sequence of events this creates and how it endangers the tail boom.
questions.answer: If collective is applied while the aircraft is still in a nose-high attitude during the flare, the increased blade pitch causes rotor RPM to decay rapidly. With reduced RPM, the aircraft loses the rotor energy needed to arrest the descent and level the nose. The helicopter may begin to settle with the tail still low and the nose still high. As it descends in this attitude with decaying rotor RPM, the tail boom or tail rotor is at risk of striking the ground before the skids contact the surface. The student must be trained to complete the flare to the correct attitude, allow forward speed to reduce, then progressively level the nose and apply collective as the aircraft is brought to a near-level attitude close to the surface.

questions.question: You are demonstrating a straight-in autorotation into a short landing area with terrain rising slightly at the far end. How does this terrain factor influence your deceleration technique and collective application to protect tail boom clearance?
questions.answer: Rising terrain at the far end of the landing zone means there is less vertical clearance between the tail boom and the ground as the helicopter decelerates and the nose pitches up in the flare. The pilot must initiate the flare slightly earlier than normal to ensure the nose-high attitude is achieved before reaching the rising terrain, giving the tail room to swing down without contacting the slope. Collective application must be timed so the aircraft is descending in a near-level attitude by the time it crosses over or onto the rising ground. If the flare is delayed and the nose-high attitude is reached directly over the sloping terrain, the tail boom could strike the upslope during the deceleration phase even at normal flare angles. The pilot should also consider whether the landing area is truly adequate for a straight-in autorotation given the terrain.

questions.question: A pilot consistently achieves proper rotor RPM management and landing attitude during straight-in autorotations but repeatedly comes within inches of a tail boom strike. The pilot insists the technique matches the checklist. As an examiner, how do you diagnose the root cause and what technique correction would you prescribe?
questions.answer: A pattern of near tail boom strikes with otherwise acceptable technique most commonly points to one of three root causes: (1) the pilot is initiating the flare too low — without enough altitude to arrest both forward speed and the nose-high pitch attitude before the tail approaches the ground; (2) the pilot is using excessive aft cyclic input rate, creating a nose-high pitch attitude faster than the deceleration requires, swinging the tail down abruptly; or (3) the pilot is waiting too long to level the aircraft after the flare, holding the nose-high attitude as the helicopter descends toward touchdown. To diagnose, I would observe at what altitude relative to the surface the flare is initiated, the rate of cyclic input, and the pitch attitude when collective is applied. The correction would be to raise the flare initiation point by 10-15 feet, slow the rate of aft cyclic to allow a progressive pitch change, and begin leveling the nose positively before reaching 5-10 feet AGL to allow the tail to rise back to a safer margin before touchdown.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot corrects the flare initiation altitude but the problem persists, and you observe the helicopter arriving over the threshold slower than normal, what new risk has been introduced and how does it interact with tail boom clearance?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the pilot is now arriving slower than optimal autorotation airspeed, there is less energy stored in forward airspeed to convert during the flare into rotor RPM. With lower rotor inertia margin, the pilot may apply collective sooner to prevent RPM decay — but early collective application while in a nose-high attitude is precisely what allows the tail to descend into the ground. Additionally, a slow approach may result in a steeper descent angle requiring more collective to arrest sink rate, further accelerating RPM decay. The interplay creates a scenario where correcting one problem (flare altitude) has introduced another (low energy approach) that still produces the same tail boom clearance hazard via a different mechanism. The correct fix is to maintain the manufacturer's recommended autorotation airspeed throughout the approach and initiate the flare at the proper altitude with a progressive, controlled rate of aft cyclic.

questions.question: During a checkride straight-in autorotation, the applicant flares aggressively to arrest a high-energy approach, successfully decelerates to near-zero groundspeed, but then applies collective smoothly and touches down with the nose slightly high. Rotor RPM is within limits at touchdown. Is this a satisfactory performance, and specifically regarding tail boom clearance, what is the critical question you must answer before determining the outcome?
questions.answer: The rotor RPM and deceleration management may be satisfactory, but the tail boom clearance question is not resolved by the touchdown alone. The critical question is: at what altitude did the nose-high attitude exist, and was there documented adequate clearance between the tail boom and the surface throughout the entire maneuver — not just at touchdown? A nose-high touchdown attitude that was reached at 20 feet AGL with a controlled, gradual pitch change is acceptable. The same nose-high attitude reached at 3 feet AGL from an aggressive flare input means the tail boom may have been within inches of the ground during deceleration even if it cleared. As an examiner, I would evaluate the lowest point of the tail boom throughout the maneuver, not just the touchdown attitude. If the flare was aggressive and the nose-high attitude was achieved at very low altitude, the standard has not been met regardless of the successful outcome, because the applicant did not demonstrate control that 'permits safe clearance between the tail boom and the surface' — they got lucky rather than managed it.
questions.follow_up: The applicant argues that because there was no tail strike, clearance was obviously maintained. How do you respond to that argument in the context of ACS standards?
questions.follow_up_answer: The ACS evaluates the quality and predictability of technique, not just the outcome. A near-miss tail strike that was avoided by margin of inches is not evidence of proper technique — it is evidence of an acceptable outcome despite improper technique. The ACS skill standard requires the pilot to use 'proper deceleration and collective pitch application that permits safe clearance,' meaning the technique itself must be structured to provide clearance by design, not by chance. An examiner evaluates whether the inputs were sequenced and timed such that tail clearance would reliably result across varying conditions. An aggressive low-altitude flare that happened to clear is not repeatable in degraded conditions such as higher density altitude, heavier gross weight, or shorter landing area — all of which would reduce the available margin. The applicant must demonstrate technique that is sound by construction, and it is the examiner's responsibility to make that determination even when the outcome was benign.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 — Autorotation procedures; ACS PH.VIII.B skill standards

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, what are the three primary control inputs that make up a proper power recovery, and in what general sequence are they applied?
questions.answer: A proper power recovery from autorotation involves: (1) applying throttle/increasing collective to restore engine power and rotor RPM, (2) coordinating collective increase with right pedal to counteract increased torque, and (3) using cyclic to arrest the descent rate and transition to a climb or level flight attitude. The collective is raised smoothly as RPM is confirmed in the green arc, with pedal and cyclic coordination throughout to maintain heading and prevent abrupt pitch changes.

questions.question: Before raising collective during power recovery from autorotation, what rotor RPM condition must exist and why?
questions.answer: Rotor RPM must be within the normal operating range (green arc) before raising collective. If collective is raised with rotor RPM below the lower limit, the increased blade pitch will further bog down the rotor, potentially leading to rotor stall. Adequate RPM ensures the rotor system can absorb the increased load from collective application without decaying to a stall condition. The FAA emphasizes that rotor stall in helicopters is not recoverable.

questions.question: Why must the pilot apply right pedal (in a helicopter with a counterclockwise-rotating main rotor, as viewed from above) when raising collective during power recovery from autorotation?
questions.answer: As collective is raised and engine power is restored, torque on the fuselage increases significantly. In a counterclockwise-rotating main rotor system, this torque reaction tends to yaw the nose to the right. Left pedal (increasing tail rotor thrust) is applied simultaneously with the collective increase to counteract this torque and maintain coordinated, on-heading flight. Failure to apply left pedal will result in an uncontrolled right yaw.

issues: Answer states 'right pedal results in left yaw' but this is backwards. Increased torque from raising collective causes RIGHT yaw (nose right), not left yaw. Right pedal counteracts this by pushing nose left to maintain heading.
verification.suggested_correction: As collective is raised and engine power is restored, torque on the fuselage increases significantly. In a counterclockwise-rotating main rotor system, this torque reaction tends to yaw the nose to the RIGHT. Right pedal (increasing tail rotor thrust) is applied simultaneously with the collective increase to counteract this rightward torque and maintain coordinated, on-heading flight. Failure to apply right pedal will result in an uncontrolled RIGHT yaw.
verification.triage_note: The answer contains a critical factual error: it states that increased torque from raising collective causes LEFT yaw, when standard counterclockwise-rotor helicopters experience RIGHT yaw; the final sentence compounds this by stating 'failure to apply right pedal will result in uncontrolled left yaw,' which is backwards and safety-critical.

questions.question: You are practicing a straight-in autorotation and initiate power recovery at 100 feet AGL. As you roll on throttle and begin raising collective, you notice rotor RPM dropping below the bottom of the green arc. What went wrong and what should you do?
questions.answer: This situation indicates collective was raised too aggressively or too early relative to the available RPM. Increasing blade pitch demands more power from the rotor than the engine/rotor system can immediately provide, causing RPM to decay. Immediately lower collective slightly to unload the rotor and allow RPM to recover back into the green arc, then smoothly re-apply collective at a rate the engine and rotor can support. This scenario highlights the importance of smooth, coordinated collective application timed with confirmed RPM in the normal range. If RPM continues to decay toward rotor stall, an immediate cushion landing may be required.

questions.question: A pilot initiates power recovery from a straight-in autorotation but applies aft cyclic simultaneously with raising collective. What specific risk does this create and how should cyclic be managed during power recovery?
questions.answer: Applying aggressive aft cyclic simultaneously with collective during power recovery can cause an abrupt nose-high pitch attitude, potentially leading to a tail strike or an inadvertent settling with power if altitude is low. Additionally, a sharp nose-up attitude with rapidly increasing power can lead to a dynamic rollover risk if the skids are near the ground or an uncontrolled climb attitude. Cyclic should be used to arrest the descent rate smoothly and transition to a level or climbing attitude, not to aggressively pull the nose up. The pilot should use a coordinated, graduated approach — stabilize the descent arrest with collective, then adjust attitude with cyclic to prevent the nose from going excessively high.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter with known low-inertia rotor blades. During a practice straight-in autorotation, you delay the power recovery initiation slightly longer than planned. By the time you begin raising collective, rotor RPM has decayed to the very bottom of the green arc. Walk me through how the low-inertia rotor characteristic specifically affects your power recovery technique compared to a high-inertia system.
questions.answer: Low-inertia rotor systems have significantly less stored kinetic energy in the rotor blades than high-inertia systems. This means RPM decays very rapidly when collective is applied — the rotor has less 'flywheel effect' to buffer against the increased pitch demand. For a low-inertia system at the bottom of the green arc, the pilot has a much narrower margin before the rotor stalls if collective is raised. The technique must be even more precise: collective application must be extremely smooth and graduated, and the rate of RPM application from the engine must be carefully matched. Any over-collective will cause an immediate and rapid RPM decay. In contrast, a high-inertia system has more stored energy to absorb the load of collective application before RPM decays appreciably. For low-inertia helicopters, power recovery must be initiated earlier in the autorotation — at higher rotor RPM — to maintain an adequate safety margin throughout the recovery. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook specifically notes that low-inertia rotors decay rapidly and require simultaneous, immediate control inputs at entry and correspondingly careful management at recovery.
questions.follow_up: If the rotor RPM drops below the minimum RPM limit during your power recovery attempt and continues to decay despite reducing collective, what is your remaining option and what outcome should you expect?
questions.follow_up_answer: If rotor RPM decays below the minimum operating limit and continues to fall despite reducing collective, a rotor stall is imminent or occurring. The FAA states explicitly that rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable — there is no corrective action that will restore rotor RPM and normal flight from a fully developed rotor stall. The pilot's only remaining option is to accept a hard landing at the best available spot directly ahead, using whatever collective cushion remains from any residual RPM to reduce impact energy as much as possible. This underscores why early recognition of low RPM and conservative power recovery timing are critical — once rotor RPM decays past the point of recovery, the outcome is largely determined by terrain and luck.

questions.question: During an actual power recovery from autorotation, the engine does not respond normally when throttle is increased — the governor fails to accelerate the engine and you are at 150 feet AGL with the ground rushing up. How does this scenario change your power recovery execution, and at what point do you transition to a full autorotation landing versus continuing to attempt recovery?
questions.answer: If the engine fails to respond during attempted power recovery, the situation has effectively changed from a practice autorotation back to an actual engine failure at very low altitude. The pilot must immediately recognize the engine is not providing power and abandon the power recovery attempt. Continuing to raise collective with no engine response will rapidly drain stored rotor RPM, leaving the pilot with insufficient energy for either a recovery or a controlled touchdown. The pilot must lower collective to maintain rotor RPM in the green arc, reestablish autorotative descent, and commit fully to executing a power-off autorotation landing at whatever terrain is immediately available within the landing zone. At 150 feet AGL there is no time to troubleshoot the governor or attempt engine restarts — the priority is rotor RPM preservation and a controlled autorotation landing. The decision point is essentially immediate: if throttle/collective increase produces no RPM increase from the engine within the first 1-2 seconds, assume engine power is unavailable and execute a full autorotation to touchdown. This is consistent with the ADM principle that if an action will only 'probably' work, choose the action known to work.
questions.follow_up: After landing safely from this unplanned full autorotation, what are your immediate post-landing priorities from a systems and regulatory standpoint?
questions.follow_up_answer: Immediately after landing, secure the aircraft by shutting down the engine if it is still running irregularly, and ensure the rotor brake is applied if equipped. Do not reposition the aircraft until the cause of the governor/engine failure is determined by a certificated mechanic. From a regulatory standpoint, if the aircraft is damaged or if there was an engine failure that required an emergency landing, the event may meet the criteria for an NTSB accident report under 49 CFR Part 830 — the NTSB must be notified immediately if there is substantial damage or serious injury. The aircraft must be removed from service until a maintenance inspection confirms airworthiness per 14 CFR 91.7. A pilot report to ATC or FSS documenting the emergency is also appropriate. The flight should be documented in the pilot's logbook noting the emergency condition.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Chapter 13; 14 CFR 91.7; 49 CFR Part 830

questions.question: What does the ACS require when you terminate a straight-in autorotation to a hover, and how far from the designated point must you stop?
questions.answer: The ACS requires you to terminate the autorotation to a stabilized hover within 200 feet of the designated point. 'Stabilized hover' means the helicopter is at a controlled, steady hover altitude with no significant drift or oscillation before you move off the spot.

issues: The reference 'ACS PH.VIII.B, S12' appears to be a typographical error in citation format. The correct ACS standard reference should be 'PH.VI.B.S12' as indicated in the question's own acs_code field. This may reflect an inconsistency in the question bank documentation rather than a factual error in the answer itself, but the regulatory reference should match the acs_code.
verification.suggested_correction: Regulatory reference should read: 'ACS PH.VI.B.S12; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11' to maintain consistency with standard ACS citation format.

questions.question: During the flare and collective pull at the bottom of a straight-in autorotation, what are you using rotor RPM for, and why must you not let it decay too low before applying collective?
questions.answer: Rotor RPM stores kinetic energy in the spinning blades. When you apply collective at the bottom of the autorotation, you convert that stored rotor energy into lift to arrest the descent and cushion the landing or transition to a hover. If rotor RPM decays too low before you pull collective, there is insufficient energy to generate the needed lift, resulting in a hard landing or loss of control. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that low rotor RPM is not recoverable once it reaches a stall condition.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the flare in a straight-in autorotation, and how does it help you reach the designated point?
questions.answer: The flare, accomplished with aft cyclic, serves two purposes: it decelerates the helicopter's forward groundspeed and simultaneously increases upward airflow through the rotor disk, which helps maintain or increase rotor RPM. This additional rotor energy gives you more collective authority during the final deceleration. The flare also extends your glide slightly, which is useful if you are coming up short of the designated point. Timing and magnitude of the flare are the primary tools for spot accuracy during autorotation termination.

questions.question: You are on final in a straight-in autorotation and realize at 150 feet AGL that you are going to overshoot your designated point by approximately 250 feet. What options do you have, and what are the risks of each?
questions.answer: At 150 feet AGL with an overshoot situation, your primary options are: (1) Delay the flare — holding a shallower approach angle slightly longer before initiating the flare allows more groundspeed to bleed off naturally, but risks arriving at the flare point too low with insufficient altitude; (2) Use a steeper approach angle earlier — this should have been corrected higher up and is not practical at 150 feet; (3) Accept the overshoot and aim for a landing beyond the point, then evaluate whether a safe landing area exists. A 250-foot overshoot would put you outside the 200-foot ACS tolerance. The key risk in any late correction at 150 feet is compromising the flare timing, which can lead to excessive groundspeed at touchdown or depleted rotor RPM. The safest decision is to aim for the best available landing area beyond the point rather than forcing an aggressive correction that compromises rotor energy management.

questions.question: You terminate your autorotation to a hover and the helicopter is stable, but you are 210 feet from the designated point. How does the examiner evaluate this, and what should you do in a real emergency?
questions.answer: On a checkride, 210 feet exceeds the 200-foot ACS tolerance, and the examiner would note the deviation as unsatisfactory for that specific standard. However, the examiner also evaluates the overall quality of the maneuver — if the hover is stable and the approach was otherwise well-executed, the discussion centers on what caused the accuracy error. In a real emergency, the 200-foot standard is irrelevant; what matters is that you reached a safe landing area, maintained rotor RPM within limits, controlled airspeed through the flare, avoided a hard landing, and came to a controlled stop without damage to the aircraft or occupants. Spot accuracy on a checkride simulates the real-world requirement to land within a usable clearing or prepared area.

questions.question: During the hover termination phase of your straight-in autorotation, you pull collective to arrest the descent but the helicopter continues to settle. What has likely gone wrong, and what do you do?
questions.answer: Continued settling after collective application indicates one or more of the following: rotor RPM was too low before collective pull, the collective was applied too late (not enough altitude remaining to convert deceleration to lift), or the rate of descent was too high entering the termination. With insufficient rotor energy, the collective pull bleeds off what little RPM remains without generating enough lift to fully arrest the descent. The immediate action is to continue applying collective to extract maximum remaining lift, level the cyclic to prevent dynamic rollover, and accept a firm landing rather than attempting to re-enter autorotation at very low altitude. If any power is available, this is the moment to use it. Prevention is the only real solution — maintaining proper rotor RPM throughout the descent is critical.

questions.question: A student consistently terminates straight-in autorotations to a stable hover but always lands 180–200 feet short of the designated point. Their rotor RPM, flare height, and hover are all within standards. As their instructor, what is the most likely root cause, and how do you correct it?
questions.answer: The most likely root cause is that the student is initiating the flare too early or with too much aft cyclic, which bleeds excessive groundspeed before the termination point and causes the helicopter to run out of energy short of the spot.
