Second, assess rotor RPM and airspeed: if RPM is within limits, continue the turn only as necessary to align with the intended landing area, then roll wings level as soon as feasible to reduce load factor and conserve RPM. Third, select or confirm the landing area — the 180-degree autorotation should have already placed you aligned with the takeoff path or a designated zone. Fourth, manage airspeed with cyclic to stay at best glide/autorotation speed per the RFM. Fifth, execute a coordinated flare at the appropriate height to dissipate descent rate, then apply collective to cushion touchdown. Throughout, resist the urge to raise collective early — premature collective application bleeds rotor RPM irreversibly at low altitude.

questions.question: Your training helicopter has low-inertia rotor blades. How does this characteristic specifically increase risk if the engine actually fails during an autorotation with turns maneuver?
questions.answer: Low-inertia rotor systems store less kinetic energy in the rotor disk, meaning RPM decays much faster when lift demand increases (as in a banked turn) or when energy is consumed in flare and cushion. If an actual engine failure occurs mid-turn during practice autorotation on a low-inertia helicopter, the pilot has a very narrow time window to roll wings level, establish best autorotation airspeed, and manage the descent to touchdown — because the rotor RPM margin is thinner and decays faster. The FAA HFH specifically notes that low-inertia rotors decay rapidly, so any delay in control inputs or any increase in load factor from continued banked flight compounds the risk exponentially compared to a high-inertia system.

questions.question: As an instructor, you allow a student to perform autorotations with turns at 800 feet AGL. Mid-maneuver, the engine fails for real. What factors in your pre-maneuver planning should have mitigated this risk, and what factors now affect survivability?
questions.answer: Pre-maneuver risk mitigations should have included: selecting an entry altitude that allows sufficient height to complete the turn, align with a suitable landing area, and execute a flare and cushion — 800 feet AGL may be marginal depending on the helicopter type and rotor inertia. The pilot should have confirmed a suitable forced landing area directly ahead and within the autorotation glide envelope. Engine and rotor system health checks should have been completed. Survivability factors now include: current rotor RPM (is it in the green?), height above terrain (is there enough altitude for a flare?), proximity and suitability of the pre-selected landing zone, current airspeed, and whether the bank angle can be safely reduced in time to align with that zone. This scenario underscores the FAA requirement that autorotation entry altitudes account for actual engine failure contingencies, not just simulated recovery scenarios.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR 91.9 (operating within RFM limitations)

questions.question: A pilot argues that because the helicopter is already in autorotation when practicing autorotation with turns, an actual engine failure during the maneuver presents no additional risk compared to the simulated failure. Evaluate this argument and explain where it is flawed from a risk management standpoint.
questions.answer: This argument is dangerously flawed for several reasons. First, during a simulated autorotation, the instructor or pilot can always recover to powered flight if RPM decays, airspeed becomes uncontrolled, or the landing area becomes unsuitable — that safety valve disappears with an actual engine failure. Second, the turning component of the maneuver creates load factor demands on the rotor that accelerate RPM decay; in a simulated autorotation, adding power corrects this instantly, but in an actual failure, every degree of bank costs rotor energy that cannot be replaced. Third, the pilot's cognitive expectation during a practice maneuver is that a recovery will occur; recognition of an actual failure may be delayed by expectation bias ('the instructor is about to say recover'), costing critical altitude. Fourth, the entry altitude and position selected for training may not have been chosen with a true forced landing analysis — they may be adequate for the training maneuver but not for an unrecoverable emergency. The presence of autorotative state does not eliminate the unique risks introduced by an actual, irreversible powerplant failure.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot's rotor RPM is at the bottom of the green arc mid-turn when the actual engine failure occurs, and they are at 500 feet AGL, what specific control input sequence should they prioritize and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: At 500 feet AGL with RPM at the bottom of the green and an actual engine failure, the priority sequence is: (1) Ensure collective is fully down — any partial collective position increases blade pitch, worsens RPM decay immediately. (2) Roll wings level with coordinated cyclic and pedal inputs — reducing load factor to 1G is the fastest way to reduce rotor drag and allow RPM to recover toward mid-green. (3) Establish best autorotation airspeed for that helicopter (per RFM) — aft cyclic to the appropriate attitude increases upward airflow through the disk, which helps RPM recover. (4) Once RPM is stabilizing in the middle of the green, begin evaluating landing area alignment. At 500 feet AGL there is very little margin for delay — the flare must begin around 75-100 feet AGL (helicopter-specific), and any further RPM loss from continued bank or premature collective will eliminate the ability to cushion the landing. The student must understand that RPM recovery comes first, then heading/alignment, then flare — in that order.

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns at a confined area training site, the engine fails for real at the apex of a 90-degree turn. The only suitable landing zone is directly behind the helicopter's current nose position, requiring an additional 270 degrees of turn in autorotation to reach it. How should the pilot assess whether continuing to turn is a survivable option versus landing in the unsuitable area ahead?
questions.answer: The pilot must rapidly perform a mental energy budget: does sufficient rotor RPM, altitude, and airspeed exist to sustain an additional 270 degrees of banked autorotation and still retain enough rotor energy for a flare and cushion? The answer in most cases at typical training altitudes will be no — each additional degree of bank and each additional second of turn bleeds altitude and rotor RPM. The FAA HFH emphasizes that in actual autorotation emergencies, accepting an imperfect but survivable landing area is almost always preferable to attempting to reach an ideal zone at the cost of rotor energy and altitude. The pilot should roll wings level immediately, commit to the available surface ahead (even if soft, sloped, or obstructed), optimize autorotation airspeed, execute the best possible flare given rotor RPM state, and accept the survivable outcome. Attempting a 270-degree turn to reach the preferred zone risks rotor RPM depletion, loss of flare effectiveness, and zero-energy touchdown — a potentially fatal outcome in exchange for a better landing surface.
questions.follow_up: The pilot decides to land on the unsuitable terrain ahead and the helicopter contacts the ground with some lateral drift. What is the greatest dynamic hazard during ground contact in this scenario, and what control input minimizes it?
questions.follow_up_answer: The greatest hazard is dynamic rollover. With lateral drift at ground contact, one skid touches first and becomes a pivot point. If the pilot allows the collective to remain down and the drift continues unchecked, the helicopter can roll beyond its critical rollover angle — typically around 5-8 degrees — faster than the pilot can react. The correct input is: immediately apply cyclic into the slope (or into the direction of drift) to counter the rolling tendency, and resist raising collective to arrest the roll if doing so would over-torque a stopped or slowing rotor. If rollover is imminent and unstoppable, the pilot should reduce collective to eliminate lift and lower the fuselage to the ground as quickly as possible to minimize rotational energy. Post-contact, the pilot should roll throttle to idle (if not already failed) and execute emergency shutdown to prevent fuel-fed fire.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Dynamic Rollover); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Autorotation procedures)

questions.question: During an autorotation with a turn, what happens to rotor RPM if you are slow to roll out and the helicopter is still banked when you apply collective for the flare?
questions.answer: A banked attitude during the flare means the collective increase is being used to support the load factor of the turn rather than purely decelerating the descent. This creates a higher demand on rotor RPM at exactly the moment you need it most. Any pre-existing RPM decay that built up during the turn is compounded, increasing the risk of rotor RPM dropping below the minimum limit and potentially leading to blade stall on the retreating side.

questions.question: When rolling out of a turn during autorotation, what control input is required to compensate for the change in torque effect, and why?
questions.answer: During autorotation the tail rotor is still driven by the main rotor transmission and heading control is maintained with antitorque pedals the same as in normal flight. As you roll wings-level and rotor lift vector returns to vertical, the torque demand on the tail rotor changes. In most US-market helicopters with counterclockwise main rotor rotation, rolling out of a left turn typically requires right pedal adjustment and vice versa to maintain coordinated flight. Failing to trim properly can produce a slip or skid that wastes altitude and misdirects the landing approach path.

questions.question: Why is altitude judgment during rollout from a turn in autorotation more demanding than altitude judgment in a straight autorotation?
questions.answer: In a banked turn, the pilot's outside visual references are partially obscured, the horizon line appears tilted, and the rate of descent can be masked by the circular ground track. The rollout itself consumes altitude and time. If the pilot misjudges heading to the landing zone and is late rolling out, the remaining altitude for executing a proper flare and collective pull is reduced. Additionally, any RPM that has decayed during the turn leaves less energy margin. The combination of reduced altitude, degraded visual reference, and compressed time window makes the rollout phase a high-risk transition point.

questions.question: You are practicing an autorotation with a 180-degree turn. At 300 feet AGL you realize the rollout heading will be 30 degrees off the intended landing direction and you need additional cyclic to correct. Walk me through the risk you are accepting and what you should do.
questions.answer: At 300 feet AGL in autorotation you have very limited altitude remaining to execute a rollout, flare, and collective application. Applying additional cyclic at this point to chase the correct heading does three things: it temporarily increases rotor disk loading, it may cause further RPM decay if RPM is already trending low, and it delays the wings-level condition needed before initiating the flare. The risk is arriving at flare altitude with residual bank angle, low RPM, and incorrect energy management. The better decision is to accept the off-heading alignment if the landing area is safe enough, roll out promptly, monitor RPM, and execute a normal flare rather than over-control trying to nail the exact heading at the cost of a stable entry into the terminal phase.

questions.question: A student consistently completes the rollout from a 180-degree autorotation turn with excess airspeed — they are fast at rollout. What specific risk does this create in the terminal phase, and how would you brief them on correcting it?
questions.answer: Excess airspeed at rollout from the turn means the helicopter arrives at the flare point with higher groundspeed and potentially a steeper descent angle than planned. The student must use more aggressive aft cyclic input to arrest the descent, which transiently increases rotor disk angle of attack and can spike RPM above limits momentarily, then cause RPM to drop if the flare is held too long. The higher groundspeed also increases the risk of dynamic rollover or tail strike if touchdown occurs before airspeed is fully dissipated. I would brief the student to plan the turn entry so the rollout occurs with airspeed within the aircraft manufacturer's recommended autorotation airspeed range, to use the rollout as a tool to bleed excess airspeed to target speed rather than accepting whatever speed they have at rollout.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Autorotation), Rotorcraft Flight Manual procedures

questions.question: During rollout from a left turn in autorotation in a helicopter with counterclockwise main rotor rotation, the nose suddenly yaws left as the bank decreases. What caused this and what is the associated risk if uncorrected?
questions.answer: As the helicopter rolls out of a left bank, the horizontal component of lift diminishes and the load on the tail rotor changes. With counterclockwise rotor rotation, torque effect tends to yaw the nose left. If the pilot fails to apply right pedal during rollout, the nose yaws left, producing an uncoordinated skid condition. The risk is threefold: the skid degrades rotor efficiency and can reduce RPM, it introduces a lateral drift component into the approach path potentially directing the helicopter off the intended landing zone, and if significant nose-left yaw develops close to the ground during flare, the tail rotor can contact terrain or obstacles.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Autorotation), Chapter 9 (Pedals and Torque Compensation)

questions.question: A pilot rolls out of a 180-degree autorotation turn at a high density altitude airport and immediately notices rotor RPM is at the low end of the green arc. The pilot elects to sacrifice some flare to apply collective earlier and stop the RPM decay. Evaluate this decision — is it sound risk management, and what is the limiting factor they may be ignoring?
questions.answer: This decision reflects appropriate risk prioritization in principle — protecting rotor RPM is non-negotiable because a rotor stall is unrecoverable. Applying collective earlier to arrest RPM decay is correct when RPM is trending toward the red. However, the limiting factor the pilot may be ignoring is that at high density altitude, the rotor requires a higher collective angle to generate the same lift, meaning the RPM recovery will consume collective authority faster than at sea level. The pilot must also recognize that applying collective early shortens the flare, meaning groundspeed and descent rate at touchdown will be higher than normal. They must ensure there is sufficient landing area to accommodate a harder, faster landing, or convert to a run-on landing if ground and helicopter type permit. Trading RPM protection for flare adequacy at the wrong altitude or into an obstacle-laden area substitutes one risk for another.
questions.follow_up: If rotor RPM had already reached the low red line limit during the turn and the pilot could not recover it prior to the flare, what is the correct action and what helicopter design characteristic is most critical to that decision?
questions.follow_up_answer: If rotor RPM reaches the low red limit, the pilot must immediately lower collective to reduce rotor drag and allow upward airflow through the disk to restore RPM — even if this means a steeper descent temporarily. The most critical design characteristic is rotor system inertia. Helicopters with high-inertia rotor systems (typically two-bladed or heavier main rotors) have more stored kinetic energy and a slower RPM decay rate, giving the pilot more time to recover. Low-inertia systems decay faster and are more sensitive to delay. The pilot must know their specific aircraft's rotor inertia characteristics because the recovery window differs significantly between a Robinson R44 and a Bell 206, for example. Attempting a flare with RPM already in the red risks rotor blade stall, which is non-recoverable.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Autorotation, Rotor Stall, Density Altitude Effects), Rotorcraft Flight Manual limitations

questions.question: Explain how a skidding rollout versus a slipping rollout from an autorotation turn each creates a different risk profile for the terminal phase of the autorotation, and which is generally considered more dangerous and why.
questions.answer: A skid during rollout occurs when the rate of turn is too high for the bank angle — the helicopter's inertia exceeds the horizontal component of lift. In the terminal phase of autorotation this causes the tail to swing outward (for counterclockwise rotor, the tail swings right in a left turn rollout), which can misalign the approach path and create a lateral groundspeed component at touchdown, increasing dynamic rollover risk. A slip occurs when bank angle is excessive for the rate of turn — the helicopter sideslips into the turn. In the terminal phase, a slip causes the helicopter to drift sideways relative to the landing zone and can induce mast bumping risk in teetering rotor systems if the cyclic is displaced significantly off-center. Generally, a skid is considered more dangerous in the rollout-to-touchdown transition because the resulting tail-swing and lateral groundspeed can directly cause a rollover on touchdown if the skid is not corrected before ground contact, and the loss of coordinated flight at low altitude in autorotation severely limits recovery options. Both must be corrected with pedal inputs, but skidding rollouts are operationally the higher-priority hazard given their proximity to catastrophic ground contact outcomes.
questions.follow_up: In a teetering rotor helicopter such as a Robinson R22, what specific additional hazard does a slipping rollout create that is less of a concern in a fully articulated rotor system?
questions.follow_up_answer: In a teetering (semi-rigid) rotor system, the blades teeter around a single underslung hinge. During a slip, the pilot must apply significant lateral cyclic to correct the drift, and the combination of the teetering motion and off-center cyclic input under low-G conditions creates a risk of mast bumping — where the rotor hub contacts the mast. This can occur if the rotor disk unloads suddenly (even momentarily) and the blades flap excessively. Fully articulated rotor systems have individual flapping hinges for each blade, which absorb these inputs independently and are far less susceptible to mast bumping. In the Robinson specifically, Robinson has issued safety notices warning against pushovers and low-G maneuvers precisely because of the mast bumping vulnerability, making a slipping rollout at low altitude a particularly serious risk in that aircraft type.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (Slips and Skids), Chapter 11 (Low-G/Mast Bumping), Robinson Aircraft Safety Notices

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns, what categories of collision hazards should you be scanning for before and throughout the maneuver?
questions.answer: You must scan for other aircraft in the practice area (mid-air collision hazard), terrain and obstacles below and in the direction of turn (ground collision), power lines and towers that may not be visible until you are descending into them, and other traffic that may be conducting similar practice maneuvers in the same area. The turn itself changes your flight path heading and descent trajectory, so what was clear ahead may now be directly in your path.

questions.question: Why do power lines represent a particularly serious collision hazard during an autorotation with turns compared to normal powered flight?
questions.answer: During autorotation, you have no power to climb or accelerate out of a deteriorating situation. Power lines are often difficult to see from altitude because they are thin, blend with terrain backgrounds, and the supporting poles may not be visible until you are already committed to a descent path. In powered flight you can apply power and maneuver away; in autorotation your options are extremely limited. The turn also continuously changes your perspective, which can obscure previously identified hazards.

questions.question: What is the purpose of performing clearing turns before beginning an autorotation with turns during training, and how should they be executed?
questions.answer: Clearing turns are performed to scan the practice area for other aircraft, obstacles, and terrain before committing to a maneuver. They should be at least 90 degrees in each direction (or a 180-degree turn) at a safe altitude, allowing the pilot to visually clear the area above, below, and to the sides. During the clearing turns, the pilot should also mentally note the terrain and any obstacles below the intended practice altitude so they are not surprised during the descending autorotation.

questions.question: You are practicing autorotations with turns at a training area you use regularly. Another helicopter enters the area during your descent while you are 90 degrees through a 180-degree turn. What collision hazard factors are now compounding, and how do you manage them?
questions.answer: Multiple hazards are compounding: (1) Your flight path has changed 90 degrees due to the turn, so the other helicopter that was in your peripheral vision may now be ahead of you; (2) You are descending, shrinking the vertical separation quickly; (3) Your airspeed and rotor RPM demands during the autorotative turn are absorbing workload, reducing your scan capacity; (4) The other pilot may not see you because you are descending and may be below their scan. Management: immediately broadcast your position and intentions on CTAF or area frequency, initiate a power recovery if safe to do so to climb away from the conflict, maintain visual contact with the other traffic, and do not re-enter the maneuver until the area is clear and coordinated.

questions.question: How does the bank angle used during an autorotation with turns affect collision hazard risk, particularly regarding rotor clearance and terrain avoidance?
questions.answer: Increasing bank angle during an autorotation with turns increases the rate of descent and the rate of altitude loss, bringing the helicopter toward the ground and obstacles more quickly. Steeper banks also increase the load on the rotor system, requiring the pilot to manage rotor RPM more actively, which can distract from collision scanning. On the rotor clearance side, banked flight tilts the rotor disk, reducing ground clearance on the low side of the aircraft. In confined practice areas or near terrain, a steep bank can bring the rotor tips dangerously close to trees, towers, or rising terrain that appeared to be safely below the initial entry altitude.

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns, at what phase of the maneuver is the collision hazard risk highest, and why?
questions.answer: The collision hazard risk is highest during the mid-to-late turn phase as the helicopter is descending through the lower altitudes approaching the power recovery or landing. At this point, the pilot's workload peaks — managing rotor RPM, airspeed, altitude, and turn coordination simultaneously — which degrades the outside scan. The terrain, obstacles, and other traffic are now closer, leaving less time and space to react. Additionally, the heading has changed significantly from the original approach, potentially placing the helicopter on a trajectory toward obstacles that were previously not in the direct flight path.

questions.question: A student consistently clears the area before entry but then fixes their scan almost entirely inside the cockpit on rotor RPM and airspeed during the autorotation with turns. As an instructor, how do you assess this as a collision hazard risk, and what corrective strategy do you use?
questions.answer: This is a significant safety deficiency. The student has correctly identified the pre-entry clearing requirement but fails to maintain continuous outside visual scanning during the maneuver, which is where the real collision hazard exists. The area may be clear at entry but another aircraft can enter your airspace in seconds. The corrective strategy involves: (1) Pointing out that clearing turns are a starting point, not a complete collision avoidance solution; (2) Practicing instrument crosscheck rhythm explicitly — brief inside scan, extended outside scan — so the student normalizes it as a habit; (3) Using verbal callouts during training ('clear left, clear right, obstacle check') to build a structured scan discipline; (4) Introducing an intentional traffic scenario during practice to demonstrate how quickly a threat can appear. The underlying habit risk is that cockpit fixation becomes normalized, and this can translate to real-world autorotations where the terrain scan is just as critical.
questions.follow_up: The student argues that rotor RPM is the most critical thing to monitor during an autorotation, so the inside scan is justified. How do you respond?
questions.follow_up_answer: Rotor RPM is indeed critical and neglecting it is dangerous, but the argument presents a false choice. The correct answer is that both must be managed simultaneously. The rotor RPM normal operating range is a band, not a single number — the pilot should be trained to sense RPM through sound and vibration cues as a supplement to the gauge, which frees up visual scan capacity for outside reference. Cockpit fixation that results in a collision with terrain or another aircraft makes rotor RPM irrelevant. The skill being developed is precisely the ability to manage multiple, competing demands — instrument monitoring AND outside collision scan — which is the standard expected at the private and commercial helicopter level.

questions.question: You are conducting an autorotation with a 180-degree turn in an uncontrolled area with no established traffic pattern. Halfway through the autorotation, you realize your heading change has oriented the helicopter toward rising terrain with trees at approximately your current descent altitude. You are already below entry altitude with insufficient rotor inertia for a sustained climb. Walk me through your collision hazard decision-making at this point.
questions.answer: This is a genuine emergency scenario, not just a training management situation. The decision tree is: (1) Immediately assess whether a power recovery can arrest the descent before reaching the tree line — apply collective and throttle aggressively to recover; (2) If power recovery altitude and energy are marginal, determine whether continuing the turn past 180 degrees can redirect the flight path away from the obstacle; (3) If rotor RPM is sufficient, a shallow cyclic pull can extend the glide momentarily to clear the obstacle; (4) If none of these are viable, execute the best available forced landing into the least hazardous terrain before reaching the trees. The key lesson is that this scenario should never occur in a trained pilot — the pre-entry scan must include identifying all terrain at and below practice altitude within the full 360-degree arc of any planned turns, not just straight ahead. Rising terrain and trees are predictable, visible hazards that should be briefed and excluded from the maneuver area before entry.
questions.follow_up: What proactive decision — made before the autorotation entry — would have prevented this scenario entirely?
questions.follow_up_answer: Before initiating the autorotation, the pilot should have conducted a thorough reconnaissance of the practice area, specifically identifying the terrain profile at and below the intended practice altitude across all headings that the turn would produce. This includes identifying the heading the aircraft will be on at the completion of the turn, the terrain in that direction, and whether a power recovery altitude exists that keeps the aircraft clear of all obstacles throughout the maneuver. The entry should be refused if terrain clearance cannot be confirmed for every phase of the maneuver including the post-turn ground track. This is essentially the same reconnaissance principle applied to confined area operations — identify the abort point and ensure the exit path is clear before committing.

questions.question: What is the primary risk if a pilot applies collective pitch too early during the flare phase of an autorotation termination?
questions.answer: Applying collective too early during the flare bleeds off rotor RPM before the helicopter has decelerated sufficiently. This results in insufficient rotor energy remaining to cushion the final touchdown, leading to a hard landing or loss of rotor RPM below the recoverable range. The collective should be raised smoothly as the helicopter reaches the lowest point of the flare with RPM in the normal operating range.

questions.question: During an autorotation termination, what happens to rotor RPM if the pilot applies full collective too abruptly and too late, when the helicopter is already at low altitude and very low airspeed?
questions.answer: Applying full collective too abruptly and too late causes a rapid decay of rotor RPM because there is insufficient rotor kinetic energy remaining to absorb the sudden pitch increase demand. The result can be a hard, potentially uncontrolled touchdown with inadequate lift to cushion the landing. Low rotor RPM at touchdown removes the pilot's ability to make any corrective inputs.

questions.question: Why is it critical to ensure the helicopter is aligned with the intended landing direction before the final collective application during an autorotation termination?
questions.answer: Once the collective is raised to cushion the landing, rotor RPM drops rapidly and the pilot has very limited ability to make corrective heading or lateral control inputs. Any misalignment with the landing surface at that point cannot be effectively corrected and can result in a dynamic rollover, skid ground contact, or loss of control. The helicopter must be properly aligned, level, and decelerating before committing to the final collective pull.

questions.question: You are practicing autorotations with turns and roll out of the turn 50 feet lower than planned due to a steeper-than-expected descent rate. How does this affect your termination strategy, and what is the primary risk?
questions.answer: Rolling out of the turn lower than planned compresses the time available to complete the flare and execute a proper cushioned landing. The helicopter may have insufficient altitude to establish the correct flare attitude to decelerate, and the pilot may be forced to raise collective while still at an excessive rate of descent or forward speed. The primary risk is a hard landing or loss of directional control because the energy management sequence — flare, level, collective cushion — is disrupted. The pilot should recognize the compressed altitude margin early and adjust the flare initiation accordingly, accepting a faster groundspeed touchdown if needed to avoid a high-rate-of-descent contact.

questions.question: During an autorotation termination, the pilot notices rotor RPM is at the low end of the normal range as the helicopter approaches the flare point. What risk does this create, and how should the pilot modify the termination?
questions.answer: Low rotor RPM entering the flare means there is less kinetic energy stored in the rotor system. The rotor has reduced capacity to absorb the collective pitch increase needed to cushion the landing. The risk is that RPM will drop below the minimum safe level during the cushion phase, resulting in an uncontrolled hard landing. The pilot should prioritize recovering RPM — forward cyclic to trade altitude for RPM if altitude permits — or accept a higher groundspeed touchdown with a reduced collective cushion to avoid depleting what little rotor energy remains. If RPM cannot be recovered, a running landing is preferable to a full power-off stop.

questions.question: A student performs an autorotation with a 90-degree turn and consistently begins the flare too late during the termination. Beyond the obvious hard landing risk, what secondary hazard can develop if the late flare results in excessive forward speed at touchdown?
questions.answer: Excessive forward speed at ground contact creates the risk of dynamic rollover, especially if one skid contacts the ground before the helicopter is level and fully decelerated. The skid acts as a pivot point, and with residual forward momentum, the helicopter can roll over before the pilot can apply corrective cyclic. Additionally, excessive forward speed with low rotor RPM at touchdown limits the pilot's ability to use remaining rotor energy to counteract the roll. Ground contact with forward speed on uneven terrain also increases the risk of skid catching, which can initiate a rollover even on flat surfaces.

questions.question: During a power recovery from an autorotation with turns at a relatively low practice altitude, the pilot applies collective smoothly to arrest descent but simultaneously allows aft cyclic to remain from the flare attitude. The engine has re-engaged. What compounding risk develops, and how does rotor system type influence this outcome?
questions.answer: If the pilot holds aft cyclic while raising collective after engine re-engagement, the helicopter will pitch nose-high aggressively as both power and blade pitch demand increase simultaneously. This can lead to an unintended climb with decaying airspeed at low altitude, placing the aircraft in the region of reversed command with reduced recovery margin. Additionally, a rapid pitch-up with high collective in a low-inertia rotor system can overstress the rotor or cause mast bumping in a semirigid (teetering) rotor system if the fuselage pitches faster than the rotor disk can follow — a particularly dangerous characteristic of two-bladed teetering systems. In an articulated rotor system, this risk is lower but aggressive pitch-up with high power still creates a high blade loading condition. The pilot must coordinate leveling the cyclic to a neutral or slightly forward attitude simultaneously with the power recovery collective application.
questions.follow_up: If this same sequence occurred in a helicopter with a low-inertia rotor system at 50 feet AGL during the recovery, and the pilot recognized a nose-high, decelerating attitude — what are the available options and what is the constraint on each?
questions.follow_up_answer: At 50 feet AGL with a low-inertia rotor in a nose-high, decelerating state during power recovery, the options are severely limited. Forward cyclic to lower the nose risks a steep nose-low attitude very close to the ground. Reducing collective to manage blade loading will reduce lift and accelerate the descent toward the ground. Increasing power further to arrest descent may exceed torque limits or cause retreating blade stall if the nose is high and airspeed is very low. The fundamental constraint is that the helicopter is simultaneously inside the height-velocity (H/V) curve region, at low airspeed, and in a nose-high attitude — a combination where no single corrective input can address all threats at once. The FAA recognizes this as a reason why practice autorotations with full power-off touchdowns and low practice altitudes carry disproportionate risk compared to power recoveries begun at or above recommended recovery altitudes per the H/V diagram in the RFM.

questions.question: A pilot completes an autorotation with a 180-degree turn and rolls out aligned with the landing area, but due to the bank angle maintained during the turn, exits the turn with a higher-than-normal rate of descent and airspeed. During the termination flare, the pilot simultaneously uses aft cyclic to arrest the descent while raising collective to cushion. Why is this combined input a risk to rotor RPM management, and what does it tell you about the quality of the energy management throughout the maneuver?
questions.answer: Using aft cyclic to arrest a high rate of descent simultaneously with raising collective creates a dual demand on the rotor system: the aft cyclic increases blade loading by loading the disk to slow the rate of descent, and the collective pitch increase demands additional blade angle from blades that may already be near or at their efficient autorotative pitch. Both inputs simultaneously extract energy from the rotor, accelerating RPM decay. A properly executed autorotation should arrive at the flare point with rotor RPM in the upper third of the normal operating range specifically to have a reserve of kinetic energy for the termination cushion. The fact that the pilot needed to combine aft cyclic with collective at the termination point indicates that energy was lost during the turn — likely by banking too steeply (which increased disk loading and descent rate) or not managing airspeed in the normal autorotation range. It reflects a deficiency in the maneuver entry and execution, not just the termination.
questions.follow_up: If you were examining this applicant and this pattern repeated on a second attempt — arriving at the flare point high-rate-of-descent and fast every time — what systemic error in the autorotation entry or turn execution would you investigate first?
questions.follow_up_answer: The first area to investigate is the bank angle and airspeed management during the turn itself. Excessive bank angle during the 180-degree turn increases the load factor on the rotor disk, which increases induced power demand and accelerates the rate of descent beyond what a straight autorotation at the same airspeed would produce. If the applicant is also allowing airspeed to build during the turn rather than maintaining best autorotation airspeed (typically per the RFM), the descent rate will compound. The second area is the timing and altitude at which the turn was initiated — beginning the turn too high allows excess altitude to be lost to a steep bank rather than converted to rotor RPM via a proper entry airspeed. Examining the entry altitude, initial collective position, airspeed at roll-in, and bank angle throughout the turn would isolate whether the problem is technique (bank angle/speed control) or judgment (turn timing/altitude selection).

questions.question: During a practice autorotation with turns, at what point in the maneuver is a power recovery initiated, and what is the proper sequence and coordination of control inputs the pilot makes?
questions.answer: Power recovery is initiated at a safe altitude before touchdown—typically around 100 feet AGL or per the operator's training standard. The pilot must coordinate cyclic and collective inputs simultaneously: smoothly increase collective pitch to arrest descent rate while applying forward or level cyclic control to transition to level flight attitude, then increase throttle (or allow the correlator/governor to respond) to restore engine and rotor RPM to normal operating range. Collective pitch must be increased smoothly to avoid abrupt RPM spikes or structural stress to the rotor system.

questions.question: Why is rotor RPM management critical during the power recovery phase of an autorotation?
questions.answer: During autorotation, rotor RPM is maintained by airflow up through the rotor disk. When power is recovered, the pilot must ensure rotor RPM is within the normal green arc before raising collective aggressively. If rotor RPM is low when collective is raised, the blades may not have enough energy to arrest the descent, potentially leading to rotor stall. Conversely, if RPM is excessively high, raising collective too rapidly can cause an RPM overspeed or structural stress. The pilot must cross-check the tachometer throughout the recovery.

questions.question: What constitutes a go-around decision during a practice autorotation, and when should that decision ideally be made?
questions.answer: A go-around is the decision to apply power and transition back to normal flight rather than continuing to a landing. During a practice autorotation, the go-around decision should be made early enough — typically no lower than the minimum recovery altitude specified in the flight training program or RFM — to allow sufficient altitude for full power recovery, arresting the descent, and transitioning to a climb or level flight. Delaying the decision too long reduces the rotor RPM margin available to safely complete the recovery.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; operator minimums per RFM

questions.question: You are practicing an autorotation with a 90-degree turn and at the completion of the turn your rotor RPM is at the high end of the green arc. You initiate power recovery. Describe how you manage the collective during recovery and explain the risk of being too aggressive with it.
questions.answer: With rotor RPM at the high end of the green arc, you have good energy available, but you must still raise collective smoothly rather than aggressively. A rapid, large collective increase will load the rotor blades and cause RPM to decay sharply and quickly, potentially dropping below the green arc before engine power has fully restored torque. The risk is entering a low-RPM condition mid-recovery where the rotor no longer has sufficient energy to arrest the descent rate. The correct technique is a steady, controlled collective rise coordinated with throttle application, monitoring the tachometer to keep RPM in the normal range throughout the transition.

questions.question: During a power recovery from an autorotation with a 180-degree turn, the helicopter is still in a 20-degree bank when you begin applying collective. What risk does this create and how does it affect your go-around?
questions.answer: Initiating power recovery while still banked means the total lift vector is tilted, so a portion of the rotor thrust is directed horizontally rather than vertically. This reduces the effective vertical lift component available to arrest the descent, meaning you need more collective input than you would in wings-level flight to achieve the same deceleration of sink rate. Additionally, the banked attitude may cause the helicopter to continue turning or climb unevenly. The risk is an inadequate arrest of descent rate before the helicopter reaches the ground. Best practice is to roll wings level before or simultaneously with beginning the power recovery so that all available rotor thrust is directed vertically.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Chapter 2 (aerodynamics of turning flight)

questions.question: A student executes an autorotation with turns and arrives at the recovery altitude low and slow — airspeed is below ETL and the helicopter is at a nose-high attitude. What risks exist during the power recovery and go-around from this position?
questions.answer: Arriving low and slow below ETL creates several compounding risks during power recovery. First, without ETL airflow, the rotor is less efficient and requires more power to sustain or arrest descent, meaning the collective may need to be raised more aggressively to prevent ground contact — but aggressive collective input risks rotor RPM decay. Second, the nose-high attitude, if not corrected with forward cyclic, can allow the helicopter to climb steeply or even enter a settling-with-power condition if the rotor becomes over-pitched with insufficient RPM. Third, without ETL, a go-around requires transitioning back through ETL with coordinated cyclic and collective to avoid rotor RPM fluctuations. The pilot must simultaneously manage attitude, RPM, and power application — a very high workload at a critical altitude.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Chapter 10 (steep approach, ETL loss)

questions.question: During a training flight, you observe your student consistently initiating power recovery from autorotations at the same altitude regardless of rotor RPM status at that point. Why is using a fixed altitude as the sole criterion for power recovery a risk management failure, and what should the student be cross-checking instead?
questions.answer: Using only altitude as the trigger for power recovery creates a false sense of safety because altitude alone does not tell you whether the rotor system has the energy to safely complete the recovery. If rotor RPM is below the green arc at the recovery altitude — perhaps due to poor management during the turn, a wind gust, or slow entry — raising collective at that altitude with insufficient RPM may not arrest the descent before touchdown. The pilot must cross-check three things before and during power recovery: rotor RPM (within green arc), airspeed (and approximate energy state), and altitude (sufficient margin remaining). Recovery should be initiated when all three parameters support a successful go-around, not simply when the altimeter reads a predetermined number. If RPM is low, the student may need to delay the collective raise momentarily to allow RPM recovery through autorotative airflow before applying collective.
questions.follow_up: If rotor RPM has already decayed below the green arc at recovery altitude and the student raises collective anyway — what is the most likely outcome and what, if anything, can be done?
questions.follow_up_answer: If collective is raised with rotor RPM already below the green arc, the additional blade pitch loading will further reduce RPM rapidly, potentially into the yellow arc or beyond — potentially reaching rotor stall. Once rotor stall begins, it is not recoverable. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states explicitly that rotor stall in helicopters is not recoverable and early recognition of low RPM is imperative. At that point, if altitude still permits, the only option is to immediately lower collective to unload the blades and allow autorotative airflow to rebuild RPM, then attempt a landing from whatever energy remains. If altitude is insufficient, the outcome is likely a hard landing or loss of control. This reinforces that allowing rotor RPM to decay during the turn phase is the antecedent risk — not the recovery itself.

questions.question: During a practice autorotation with a 180-degree turn, the student completes the turn but the landing zone is now obscured by the helicopter's nose in a nose-low attitude. The student hesitates and delays the power recovery go-around for three to four seconds. Describe the cascading risk chain created by this hesitation and how it could affect the outcome.
questions.answer: A three-to-four second delay in initiating power recovery during an autorotation creates a dangerous cascade. First, altitude is consumed rapidly — a typical autorotation descent rate at idle can exceed 1,500 to 2,000 FPM, meaning 75 to 135 feet of altitude is lost in those seconds alone. Second, if the nose-low attitude is allowed to persist, airspeed builds and rotor RPM may rise toward the upper end of the green arc or into the yellow arc, requiring careful collective management to avoid overspeed on recovery. Third, if the student panics and raises collective sharply once they do initiate recovery, the rapid RPM decay from an oversped rotor being suddenly loaded creates an unpredictable situation. Fourth, the reduced altitude margin compresses the time available for a successful go-around, and the student is now in a high-workload environment with little room for error. The hesitation itself is a risk — situational awareness loss, task fixation, and startle effect are all contributing human factors. Proper risk management requires the pilot to have a predetermined minimum recovery altitude with no exceptions, and to not allow task overload from turn management to delay that go-around decision.
questions.follow_up: How does helicopter inertia type — low-inertia versus high-inertia rotor systems — affect the acceptable hesitation window during power recovery from an autorotation?
questions.follow_up_answer: Low-inertia rotor systems, such as those on light turbine helicopters with smaller rotor disks, store less kinetic energy in the rotor and therefore see RPM decay much more rapidly when autorotative airflow is disrupted or when collective is raised prematurely. A hesitation that might be manageable in a high-inertia system like a larger piston helicopter could be fatal in a low-inertia system because the energy reservoir available to arrest descent or sustain lift is depleted in seconds. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that simultaneous down collective, aft cyclic, and trim inputs at entry are critical for low-inertia rotors precisely because they decay rapidly. For power recovery, this means a low-inertia helicopter tolerates much less hesitation or RPM variance before the recovery window closes entirely. Pilots transitioning between rotor systems must account for this difference as a specific risk management item.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (autorotation entry, low-inertia rotors); Chapter 2 (rotor energy and RPM)

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns, what is meant by 'task prioritization,' and what should always be your first priority?
questions.answer: Task prioritization means consciously deciding which tasks demand immediate attention versus which can wait. During an autorotation with turns, the absolute first priority is flying the helicopter — specifically maintaining rotor RPM within limits and controlling the descent. Secondary tasks like clearing the landing area, communicating, or reconfiguring cockpit systems must never compete with rotor RPM management and aircraft control. If you allow a secondary task to distract you from rotor RPM, the consequence can be catastrophic and unrecoverable.

questions.question: What is spatial disorientation, and why is a pilot executing an autorotation with turns particularly vulnerable to it?
questions.answer: Spatial disorientation is the inability to correctly perceive the helicopter's attitude, altitude, or movement relative to the earth. During an autorotation with turns, the pilot is managing a rapidly changing situation — descending, banking, and monitoring rotor RPM simultaneously. The combination of unusual attitudes, changing G-forces during turn entry and rollout, and high workload can overwhelm the vestibular system, causing the pilot to perceive a false sense of level flight or bank angle. Visual references outside the cockpit are the primary defense; loss of a visual horizon during the maneuver significantly increases disorientation risk.

questions.question: Define situational awareness in the context of an autorotation with turns, and name three specific elements a pilot must track to maintain it.
questions.answer: Situational awareness (SA) during an autorotation with turns means having an accurate, continuously updated mental picture of the helicopter's condition and its environment. Three critical elements to track are: (1) Rotor RPM — must remain within the green arc at all times; (2) Altitude and descent rate — to judge when to initiate flare and collective cushion before ground contact; and (3) Heading and position relative to the intended landing area — turns during autorotation alter the approach path and can result in arriving at the landing site with excess speed, poor alignment, or insufficient altitude for a safe flare.

questions.question: You are practicing autorotations with 180-degree turns at altitude with your student. Halfway through the turn, ATC calls with traffic information that requires an immediate readback. How should you handle this situation, and what risk does acting on it immediately pose?
questions.answer: The correct action is to ignore the radio call — or briefly acknowledge with 'standby' — until you have completed the autorotation maneuver and rotor RPM, bank angle, and descent profile are stable. The risk of responding immediately is divided attention at a critical phase: during a 180-degree autorotation turn, cyclic bank and rotor RPM must be actively managed, and reaching for or keying the radio is a classic distraction that has led to rotor RPM decay and loss of control. After the maneuver is stabilized or the practice autorotation is terminated, you respond to ATC. Aviate — Navigate — Communicate is the correct hierarchy, and it applies fully during simulated emergencies.

questions.question: During a real emergency autorotation, you are executing a 90-degree turn to align with a road. Midway through the turn you notice rotor RPM decaying toward the bottom of the green arc. What caused this and what is the correct recovery action, given that you still need to complete the turn?
questions.answer: Rotor RPM decay during a turning autorotation is most commonly caused by: (1) excessive bank angle increasing the load on the rotor disk, (2) collective pitch being too high, or (3) allowing airspeed to drop below the best glide/autorotation speed. The correct recovery is to simultaneously lower collective to reduce pitch and blade drag, reduce bank angle slightly to unload the disk, and maintain or slightly increase airspeed using forward cyclic pressure. Do not abandon the turn abruptly — complete it with a shallower bank while recovering RPM. Landing at an angle to the road is preferable to arriving with rotor RPM below limits. The key lesson is that turns in autorotation require more active RPM management than straight descents.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot experiences an engine failure at 800 feet AGL while maneuvering and must execute an autorotation with a 180-degree turn to reach the only suitable landing area. Describe at least three specific scenarios where loss of situational awareness during this maneuver could result in a fatal outcome.
questions.answer: Three situational awareness failures that could be fatal: (1) Losing track of altitude — the pilot focuses on the turn and heading correction but fails to monitor altitude consumed during the maneuver, arriving at the landing site too low to complete a proper flare, resulting in hard ground contact. (2) Losing sight of the intended landing area mid-turn — the pilot becomes visually fixated on the instruments or cockpit items, exits the turn with an incorrect heading, and is now aligned with an unsuitable area (trees, structures) with insufficient altitude to correct. (3) Misjudging rotor RPM decay — fixating on completing the turn, the pilot ignores the low-RPM horn/light, arrives over the landing zone with rotor RPM in the red or below it, with no stored energy for a flare or cushion, resulting in uncontrolled descent.

questions.question: A student consistently performs acceptable straight-ahead autorotations but becomes task-saturated during autorotations with turns — she gets the turn started, but rotor RPM fluctuates widely and she frequently exits on the wrong heading. As the instructor, what specific cognitive error is she most likely making, and how would you restructure her training to address it?
questions.answer: The most likely cognitive error is 'task tunneling' or attention narrowing — she is fixating on the turn (bank angle and heading) to the exclusion of rotor RPM management, or vice versa. This is a classic symptom of an automation deficit: she has not yet built the procedural memory to manage RPM as a background task while executing the turn consciously. The training restructure should: (1) Start with partial-panel autorotation drills that force her to verbalize RPM every 5 seconds throughout the descent, building the habit of monitoring it even while turning. (2) Use a callout system — 'RPM — Bank — Heading' repeated on a cadence so no one item dominates attention. (3) Introduce turns at altitude with the engine running first, so she builds the scan pattern without the full emergency workload. (4) Debrief with a review of altitude and RPM trend data to show her objectively where attention lapses occurred. The goal is to make RPM scanning automatic so cognitive bandwidth is freed for the turn management.
questions.follow_up: Your student argues that she can handle autorotations fine in real emergencies because 'adrenaline sharpens focus.' How would you respond, and what does the research on stress and cognitive performance actually show?
questions.follow_up_answer: This is a dangerous misconception. Research on stress and cognitive performance consistently shows an inverted-U relationship (Yerkes-Dodson law) — moderate arousal improves performance, but high stress (such as a real engine failure) causes cognitive narrowing, tunnel vision, and breakdown of complex task sharing. A pilot who cannot manage the scan during a calm practice autorotation with a safety pilot aboard will almost certainly perform worse in an actual emergency, not better. Additionally, fine motor skills degrade under acute stress, making precise rotor RPM and collective management more difficult, not easier. The correct argument is: train until the correct procedure is automatic and stress-resistant, not rely on adrenaline to compensate for incomplete skill development.

questions.question: During a checkride, the applicant initiates a simulated autorotation with a 180-degree turn. At the 90-degree point, you deliberately call out 'I have a cramp in my leg — what do I do?' to introduce a distraction. The applicant immediately looks at you and begins to answer verbally. Rotor RPM starts to bleed slightly. What are you evaluating, and at what point would you take the controls?
questions.answer: You are evaluating the applicant's ability to maintain task prioritization and resist distraction during a high-workload, safety-critical phase of flight — directly addressing PH.VI.C.R15. The correct applicant response is to ignore or briefly deflect the distraction ('Not now, sir') and maintain eyes outside and hands active on the controls. Ideal behavior: no change to scan pattern, RPM stays in the green, turn continues normally. You would take the controls if: (1) Rotor RPM decays to or below the bottom of the green arc with no corrective action by the applicant, (2) Bank angle increases beyond safe limits with no correction, or (3) Altitude margin becomes unsafe for recovery and the applicant shows no awareness. A slight RPM fluctuation with immediate self-correction is not disqualifying — it may actually demonstrate good monitoring. An applicant who fully disengages from aircraft control to answer a social question fails this element because they demonstrated inability to maintain situational awareness and task prioritization when distracted.
questions.follow_up: The applicant passed the checkride overall but was visibly rattled by the distraction question. During the debrief, she asks whether it is 'legal' to intentionally distract a pilot during a practical test. How do you respond?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, it is both legal and expected. The ACS explicitly requires examiners to assess risk management elements including distractions and task prioritization (ACS PH.VI.C.R15). FAA Order 8900.2 and the ACS preamble authorize examiners to introduce realistic distractions during practical tests to evaluate whether applicants can manage them safely. The examiner is not creating an unsafe condition — the distraction is introduced while a safety pilot (the examiner) is prepared to intervene. The entire purpose is to evaluate whether the applicant has internalized 'aviate first' as a reflexive priority, not just as a verbal answer to an oral question. This is a higher standard than simply knowing the concept.

questions.question: Before conducting autorotation with turns practice, what is the purpose of completing a checklist, and what general items would you expect it to cover for this maneuver?
questions.answer: Checklists ensure the helicopter is properly configured and the crew is prepared before entering a practice autorotation. For autorotation practice, a pre-maneuver checklist typically covers: area clear of traffic and terrain, altitude sufficient for safe recovery, engine and rotor instruments in normal range, carb heat or engine anti-ice as applicable, fuel selector and mixture (if applicable) set correctly, doors and windows secured, and passenger/crew briefed. Checklists standardize procedures and reduce the risk of overlooking critical items prior to intentionally reducing power to the engine.

questions.question: At what point in the autorotation with turns maneuver sequence should you complete the applicable checklist — before, during, or after entry — and why does timing matter?
questions.answer: The checklist must be completed before initiating the maneuver. Once the collective is lowered at autorotation entry, the pilot's full attention must be on rotor RPM control, airspeed, heading, and landing area selection. Attempting checklist tasks after entry diverts attention during a time-critical phase when low inertia rotors can decay rapidly. Completing the checklist beforehand ensures all configurations are verified while workload is manageable.

questions.question: What is the difference between a manufacturer's checklist and a memory items list, and which one applies when entering an autorotation?
questions.answer: A manufacturer's checklist is a written, step-by-step reference document used to verify aircraft configuration at specific phases of flight. Memory items (sometimes called immediate action items) are critical emergency steps that must be accomplished from memory without reference to a checklist because of their time-critical nature. The immediate control inputs at autorotation entry — lowering collective, adjusting aft cyclic, applying pedal — are memory items that must be performed instantly. The written checklist for practice autorotations is completed before entry, during the setup phase, when there is time to reference it.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; helicopter flight manual emergency procedures

questions.question: You are setting up for an autorotation with turns practice maneuver at 3,000 feet AGL. Walk me through how you would use your checklist during the setup, and what specifically you are confirming before lowering the collective.
questions.answer: During setup, I would level off at the designated entry altitude and perform a clearing turn to check for traffic. I would then run through the pre-autorotation checklist, confirming: area clear of traffic in all quadrants, suitable landing area identified, altitude adequate for turn completion and recovery, engine instruments in normal range (temperature, pressure, RPM), fuel quantity and fuel selector confirmed, carb heat applied if in the carb icing range, doors latched, and any passengers briefed on the maneuver. I would also confirm I am outside any published H-V (height-velocity) curve restrictions for the entry altitude and airspeed. Only after all checklist items are verified do I establish the entry airspeed and lower collective.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) emergency/abnormal procedures

questions.question: During a practice autorotation with turns, you notice at about 500 feet AGL that you realize you forgot to confirm carb heat was applied before entry. What does this situation reveal about your checklist discipline, and how does it affect your options now?
questions.answer: This reveals a breakdown in pre-maneuver checklist discipline. At 500 feet AGL in an autorotation, it is too late to safely troubleshoot engine configuration issues — you are committed to the maneuver and must focus entirely on rotor RPM, airspeed, and landing area. Attempting to manipulate carb heat at this point diverts attention during the most critical phase of the autorotation. The correct response is to complete the autorotation or power recovery, land safely, and then debrief the checklist error. This situation underscores why checklists must be completed before entry: omissions cannot be safely corrected once you are in the descent.

questions.question: After completing a power recovery from an autorotation with turns, an examiner asks you what checklist you complete at that point. What is it, and what does it verify?
questions.answer: After a power recovery, a post-maneuver or power recovery checklist is completed. This typically includes: engine and rotor instruments back in normal ranges, throttle at full operating RPM, carb heat returned to cold (if applicable per the RFM), collective repositioned appropriately, all temperatures and pressures verified, and the aircraft reconfigured for normal flight. Some manufacturers specify that carb heat should be removed from heat once the engine is producing power to prevent induction system damage. The post-maneuver checklist closes the loop on configuration changes made during the maneuver setup.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual normal/abnormal procedures

questions.question: During the pre-autorotation checklist, you verify that the helicopter is well above the published height-velocity diagram for your airspeed. A student asks why the H-V diagram is a checklist consideration at all if this is just a practice maneuver. How do you explain the relationship between the H-V diagram and checklist compliance in this context?
questions.answer: The H-V diagram defines the combinations of altitude and airspeed from which a safe autorotation cannot be completed if a power loss occurs. During a practice autorotation, you are intentionally replicating a power-off descent, so if anything goes wrong during the maneuver — such as an actual engine failure, a rotor RPM exceedance, or a control problem — you need adequate altitude to recover. Confirming your entry altitude and airspeed are outside the shaded avoid area on the H-V diagram is a legitimate checklist consideration because it ensures you have enough energy margin to manage unexpected complications. Flying practice autorotations from inside the H-V avoid area removes your safety buffer if the practice maneuver becomes an actual emergency.
questions.follow_up: What happens to a helicopter's H-V diagram on a hot, high-density-altitude day compared to standard conditions, and how should that affect your checklist-driven altitude selection for the maneuver?
questions.follow_up_answer: High density altitude reduces rotor efficiency and engine power, meaning the helicopter requires more altitude to safely complete an autorotation because rotor RPM decays faster and lift generation is degraded. The published H-V diagram in most flight manuals is based on standard conditions at maximum gross weight. At high density altitudes, the avoid area effectively expands — a higher entry altitude provides a larger safety margin. During checklist preparation, the pilot should reference the RFM for any density altitude corrections to the H-V diagram and select an entry altitude that provides adequate buffer beyond the avoid area, not just the minimum published value.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual performance section; 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: You are the PIC conducting an autorotation with turns demonstration. Your student completed the pre-maneuver checklist verbally, but you noticed they skipped confirming a landing area below before entry. The student says, 'We're just doing a power recovery anyway, so it doesn't matter.' How do you respond, and what principle of checklist philosophy does this scenario illustrate?
questions.answer: I would tell the student that every item on the pre-autorotation checklist is completed as if the autorotation will go to the ground — because it might. An engine that fails to respond during power recovery, a rotor RPM exceedance requiring continued autorotation, or an unexpected mechanical issue could all turn a practice maneuver into a real one. Identifying a suitable landing area before entry is non-negotiable because that decision cannot be made effectively at 200 feet AGL under high workload. This scenario illustrates the principle that checklists are not completed based on expected outcomes — they are completed based on possible outcomes. The value of a checklist is precisely that it forces verification of items that seem unnecessary until the moment they are critically needed.
questions.follow_up: If the helicopter is over an urban area with no clear landing zone, should the autorotation practice be conducted anyway if all other checklist items are complete?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. A lack of a suitable landing area is a no-go item for practice autorotations regardless of other checklist compliance. The FAA expects pilots to select an appropriate practice area before initiating the maneuver, and the ability to identify a suitable landing area is itself part of the autorotation task. Over congested areas, the risk to persons and property on the ground in the event of an actual forced landing is unacceptable. The pilot in command is required under 14 CFR 91.3 to ensure the safety of the flight, which includes not conducting a maneuver that could result in a forced landing where no safe landing is possible. The correct action is to reposition to an area over open terrain before conducting the practice autorotation.

questions.question: During a practice autorotation with turns, when would you make a radio call on the CTAF, and what information must that call include?
questions.answer: You should broadcast your intentions before initiating the maneuver. A CTAF position report should include: your aircraft type and N-number, location relative to the airport (e.g., 'two miles south'), altitude, and intentions (e.g., 'practicing autorotation to runway 27, will terminate on short final and go-around'). This alerts other traffic in the pattern to your non-standard descent profile and expected go-around.

questions.question: What radio frequency would you use for position reporting during a practice autorotation at an uncontrolled airport?
questions.answer: At an uncontrolled airport, you would use the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF) for the airport. The CTAF is published on the sectional chart and in the Chart Supplement. If the airport has a UNICOM, that frequency typically serves as the CTAF. All position calls and intention broadcasts are made on this frequency to ensure other traffic in the area is aware of your operations.

questions.question: If you are practicing autorotations with turns at a towered airport, at what point during the maneuver would a radio call to the tower be expected?
questions.answer: At a towered airport, you must maintain two-way radio communication with the tower whenever operating in Class B, C, or D airspace per 14 CFR 91.129/91.130. The tower will typically clear you for the practice autorotation as part of your landing clearance or special VFR/pattern instruction. If the tower instructs you to go-around or if you decide to terminate early, you must communicate that immediately. You do not unilaterally call out position fixes unless directed to, but you must acknowledge all tower instructions and report any deviations from your cleared maneuver.

questions.question: You are on downwind in a busy pattern at an uncontrolled airport when you enter a practice autorotation with turns. During the maneuver, a Cessna calls a 3-mile final on the CTAF. How do you manage your radio calls without compromising rotor RPM control?
questions.answer: Cockpit resource management is key here. Rotor RPM, glide path, and landing zone alignment are the priority during an autorotation — those tasks cannot be interrupted. If you are flying solo, you should make your radio call at a stable point in the maneuver, ideally right after entry when the helicopter is established in the autorotative glide and before initiating the turn, because that is when workload is momentarily reduced. Keep the call brief: identify yourself, state your position and intentions, and acknowledge the Cessna's traffic if necessary. Never sacrifice aircraft control for a radio call — if you cannot safely transmit, do not transmit. The Cessna should see you visually and adjust, and your earlier position calls would have alerted traffic to your practice autorotation.

questions.question: During a practice autorotation with turns at an uncontrolled airport, you decide the landing zone is not going to work out and you need to execute a power recovery and go-around. When and what do you call on the CTAF?
questions.answer: As soon as you have applied power, established a positive rate of climb, and the immediate aircraft control demands allow, you should transmit on the CTAF. Your call should state your aircraft ID, that you are going around from your current position (e.g., 'short final runway 27'), and your intentions (e.g., 're-entering left downwind'). This is important because other traffic may have sequenced behind you expecting a landing, and the go-around changes the traffic flow. The call should be timely but not at the expense of managing the power recovery from the autorotation, which requires precise collective and pedal coordination.

questions.question: You are conducting a practice autorotation with a 180-degree turn at a remote practice area away from any airport. Is a radio call required, and if so, to whom and on what frequency?
questions.answer: No radio call is legally required in uncontrolled airspace away from an airport. 14 CFR 91.126 and related sections only mandate radio communication in the traffic pattern at specific airports or in designated airspace classes. However, best practice is to make a blind call on a relevant area frequency (check the Chart Supplement or sectional for published frequencies in the area) or, if no specific frequency is listed, on 122.5 MHz (the alternate air-to-air frequency) to alert other aircraft of your practice maneuvers. You should also brief your intentions with any instructor or observer before the flight. Just because it is not legally required does not mean it is not prudent—particularly since an autorotation with turns involves rapid altitude loss that other aircraft would not anticipate.

questions.question: During an actual engine failure in a helicopter, an applicant immediately keys the mic to call Mayday before lowering the collective. How would you evaluate this decision, and what does it tell you about their understanding of task prioritization during emergencies?
questions.answer: This represents a critical error in task prioritization and would be a disqualifying performance issue. In a helicopter autorotation, the first and most time-critical action after engine failure is to lower the collective immediately to reduce pitch angle on the rotor blades, allow upward airflow through the disk, and maintain rotor RPM. Rotor RPM decay in low-inertia systems can be catastrophic within seconds. A Mayday call, while important, is secondary — it does not help you survive the next 10 seconds. The correct sequence is: (1) immediately lower collective, (2) establish autorotative glide and stabilize, (3) attempt engine restart per checklist if altitude permits, (4) transmit Mayday when workload allows. This error suggests the applicant has not internalized the 'aviate, navigate, communicate' hierarchy and may have trained radio calls as a reflexive first response rather than understanding the aerodynamic urgency of rotor RPM preservation.
questions.follow_up: What rotor RPM indication would you accept before deciding a Mayday call is safe to make, and how does rotor inertia affect that decision?
questions.follow_up_answer: This depends on the specific helicopter's limitations per the POH/RFM, but generally once the autorotative glide is established, rotor RPM is in the green arc, and the aircraft is tracking toward a suitable landing zone, the pilot has a brief window to transmit. In high-inertia rotor systems (heavier blades), RPM decays more slowly after collective is lowered, giving slightly more time before a Mayday call becomes secondary. In low-inertia systems, RPM can decay to a dangerous level in as few as 2–4 seconds without immediate collective reduction — no amount of communication is worth that trade-off. The examiner would expect the applicant to know their aircraft's rotor inertia characteristics and why that drives the 'aviate first' principle more urgently in helicopters than in fixed-wing aircraft.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; AIM 6-3-1 (distress and urgency communications); 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: An applicant practices autorotations with turns at an uncontrolled airport and consistently makes radio calls at downwind, base, and final — but during the checkride, on a power-off 180 autorotation, they make no calls at all after entering from abeam the numbers. How do you evaluate this, and what would you expect to hear?
questions.answer: This is a nuanced evaluation. A power-off 180 autorotation from abeam the numbers is a high-workload maneuver with a compressed timeline — the pilot transitions from downwind to base to final very quickly, sometimes in under 30 seconds. During this window, managing rotor RPM, glide path, bank angle in the turn, and landing zone alignment are primary tasks. An absolute requirement for a base and final radio call during this specific maneuver may not be realistic or safe if it distracts from aircraft control. However, the applicant should have made a position report at the downwind entry or abeam the numbers stating intentions (e.g., 'practice power-off 180, runway 27'), and ideally a brief final call if workload permits. The evaluator should consider: did the pilot previously call their intentions? Did they omit calls due to high workload management, or did they simply forget radio discipline? If earlier calls were made and situational awareness of other traffic was maintained, the omission of base and final calls in this specific high-workload context may be acceptable. If no calls were made at any point, that is a deficiency in PH.VI.C.S2.
questions.follow_up: How would you determine whether the applicant's failure to call was good workload management versus a gap in radio discipline knowledge?
questions.follow_up_answer: Ask the applicant to debrief the maneuver immediately after. A pilot who managed workload intentionally will explain: 'I made my call on downwind and chose not to transmit again because I was focused on the turn and RPM management — I had no time for a non-essential transmission.' A pilot with a knowledge gap will typically not have a clear rationale, may say they forgot, or may not know what calls were expected. You can also observe whether they resumed normal CTAF calls on subsequent patterns. Real examiners look for intentional decision-making — aviate, navigate, communicate — versus simple omission. The former reflects competency; the latter may indicate the applicant does not understand radio communication requirements in the pattern.
