questions.answer: When directed to execute a power recovery, the pilot should: (1) smoothly roll on throttle to restore engine RPM and re-engage the drive system, (2) coordinate collective increase as engine power comes online to arrest the descent rate, (3) apply appropriate pedal input to counteract the increased torque, and (4) use cyclic to transition to a normal climb or level-off attitude. The recovery must be smooth and coordinated to avoid rotor RPM overshoot, blade stall, or loss of control.

questions.question: What is the purpose of terminating an autorotation approach with a power recovery rather than flying it to a full landing?
questions.answer: A power recovery termination allows the pilot to practice the entry, descent profile, and approach technique of autorotation while eliminating the risk of actual touchdown damage or hard landing in a confined or unsuitable area. It also permits evaluation of the pilot's ability to recognize the correct termination point, manage rotor RPM throughout the maneuver, and execute a smooth transition back to powered flight — all without requiring a designated landing zone. This is the standard evaluator-directed method during checkrides when full autorotation landings are not appropriate.

questions.question: During the autorotation descent prior to a power recovery, what rotor RPM range should you maintain, and why is this critical before applying power?
questions.answer: The pilot must maintain rotor RPM within the normal operating range specified in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) — typically depicted in the green arc on the tachometer. Maintaining proper RPM is critical because if RPM is too low at the moment of power recovery, the sudden torque application of the engine re-engaging can further bog down an already low rotor, risking rotor stall, which is unrecoverable. Conversely, excessive RPM increases stress on the rotor system. Proper RPM going into the recovery ensures a smooth, safe transition back to powered flight.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM limitations section

questions.question: You are executing an autorotation from 1,500 feet AGL and the evaluator calls for a power recovery at 300 feet AGL. As you apply collective to arrest the descent, you notice rotor RPM dropping below the normal range. What do you do, and what caused this?
questions.answer: Immediately reduce collective to unload the rotor and allow RPM to recover. The RPM drop was likely caused by applying collective too aggressively before engine power was fully restored — essentially asking the rotor to produce lift before the engine had sufficient torque to support it. The correct technique is to smoothly roll on throttle first, confirm engine power is coming online (RPM rising, torque responding), then coordinate the collective increase with available power. If RPM continues to drop despite reducing collective and engine power is confirmed restored, execute the emergency low-RPM recovery per the RFM. Rotor stall is unrecoverable — early recognition is imperative.

questions.question: During a power recovery at 200 feet AGL, you restore power and begin to climb out, but the helicopter starts yawing left and the nose continues to pitch up. What are the likely causes and how do you correct them?
questions.answer: The yaw to the left (assuming counterclockwise main rotor) suggests insufficient right pedal input to compensate for the rapidly increasing torque as power is restored. The nose pitch-up indicates the pilot has allowed collective to come up too fast or has applied aft cyclic without managing the transition. Corrections: apply right pedal to counteract torque, level the cyclic attitude to a normal climb attitude, and modulate collective smoothly to match the power being applied. The inputs during power recovery must be coordinated — pedal, cyclic, and collective must all be managed simultaneously. Abrupt or uncoordinated inputs at low altitude can result in a dangerous flight attitude with limited recovery margin.

questions.question: The evaluator directs you to perform a power recovery, but as you restore power you notice the engine RPM is not rising — power is not coming back. What is your course of action?
questions.answer: If power does not restore as expected, the pilot must immediately recognize this as an actual engine malfunction rather than a simulated one. Do not continue attempting to force a recovery with collective — doing so will rapidly decay rotor RPM. Instead, reduce collective back to autorotation position, re-establish the proper autorotation descent, and commit to a real autorotation landing on the most suitable available area. Simultaneously run the engine failure emergency checklist per the RFM if altitude permits, and declare a Mayday on the appropriate frequency. The transition from a simulated to an actual emergency requires immediate recognition and decisive action. The key is not fixating on restoring power — preserve rotor RPM and ensure a survivable touchdown.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM emergency procedures

questions.question: During a power recovery at a 'safe altitude' as directed by the evaluator, what factors should you as the pilot be assessing independently — beyond just following the evaluator's call — to determine whether the recovery can actually be safely executed at that altitude?
questions.answer: The pilot must independently assess: (1) current rotor RPM — if it is decaying below limits, the altitude directive may be irrelevant because a safe recovery may no longer be possible; (2) airspeed and glide profile — if the approach is steeper than normal or airspeed is outside the recommended autorotation range, additional altitude margin may be needed; (3) available power — in high-density altitude environments, the engine may not produce full rated power, meaning the recovery requires more altitude to arrest descent; (4) surface wind and any obstacles in the abort climb path; (5) the helicopter's current energy state — if collective has already been partially applied to cushion the approach, rotor energy may be partially depleted. The evaluator directs the recovery but the PIC retains authority and responsibility. If any of these factors indicate the recovery cannot be safely completed, the pilot must communicate that and continue to touchdown or to a height where recovery is certain.
questions.follow_up: If you're at a high-density altitude airport and the evaluator calls for power recovery at the same altitude as a sea-level training area, why might that specific altitude no longer be 'safe' for power recovery?
questions.follow_up_answer: At high density altitude, the engine produces less power due to reduced air density. The power-to-weight margin needed to arrest the descent rate and transition to a climb is significantly reduced. Additionally, rotor efficiency is lower, meaning more collective is required to generate equivalent lift, which further demands more engine torque. The same 200-foot recovery altitude that provides ample margin at sea level may be insufficient at 6,000 feet density altitude because the engine cannot respond quickly enough or produce sufficient power to arrest the descent before ground contact. The pilot must either discuss with the evaluator adjusting the recovery altitude for conditions or recognize the reduced margin and fly a shallower, more conservative autorotation profile.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 2 (aerodynamic factors); applicable RFM density altitude performance charts

questions.question: You execute a textbook power recovery at the directed altitude — rotor RPM is in the green, power is restored, you level off cleanly. The evaluator then asks you: 'What would have changed about that recovery if you had been 10 knots below your recommended autorotation airspeed going into it?' Walk me through the differences.
questions.answer: Flying 10 knots slow in autorotation has several compounding effects on the power recovery. First, at a lower airspeed the descent rate is higher — the rotor is producing less translational lift and more induced drag, so you are coming down faster and will need more power and altitude to arrest the descent. Second, the rotor RPM may actually be higher due to the steeper descent angle allowing more upward airflow, which could cause an overspeed risk if power is applied abruptly. Third, the helicopter is operating deeper in the region of reversed command — adding collective to recover requires significantly more power for the same lift response compared to being at the correct airspeed. Fourth, cyclic authority to transition to a climb attitude is reduced at slower airspeeds, and the aircraft may be closer to effective translational lift (ETL) challenges. The recovery must be executed more carefully: power applied more gradually, collective managed precisely, and more altitude buffer is required. A slow autorotation recovery is more demanding and less predictable than one conducted at the book-recommended airspeed.
questions.follow_up: If the airspeed were 10 knots too fast instead of too slow going into the power recovery, what different risks would you face?
questions.follow_up_answer: At 10 knots fast, the descent rate is generally lower and translational lift is higher, which can actually make the power recovery easier to arrest. However, the risks shift: rotor RPM may be lower due to reduced upward airflow in the shallower descent, meaning there is less stored rotor energy available. When power is applied, the engine must accelerate the main rotor system while simultaneously producing lift — if RPM is on the lower end of the green arc, abrupt collective application can bog the rotor before engine torque catches up. Additionally, at higher airspeeds the torque effect is amplified, requiring more aggressive right pedal input. Structural considerations also apply — if airspeed is near or above VNE, maneuvering with power application could exceed airframe or rotor system limits. The pilot must ensure the approach airspeed stays within the RFM-recommended autorotation airspeed range throughout the maneuver.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 2; applicable RFM autorotation airspeed data

tasks.title: Task C. Approach and Landing with One Engine Inoperative (OEI) (Simulated) (Multiengine Helicopter Only)

questions.question: When conducting an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, what is the primary goal of the pilot regarding power management on the operating engine?
questions.answer: The primary goal is to keep the operating engine within its approved OEI power limits (typically expressed as OEI continuous, 30-minute, or 2-minute ratings) while maintaining sufficient rotor RPM and controllable airspeed throughout the approach. The pilot must avoid exceeding torque, turbine temperature, or other engine limits while still producing enough power to maintain a controlled approach profile and arrest the descent for landing.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft Flight Manual OEI procedures

questions.question: What does the term 'OEI' stand for, and why is an OEI approach considered more critical than a normal two-engine approach in a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: OEI stands for One Engine Inoperative. An OEI approach is more critical because the remaining engine must carry the full power demand that was previously shared between two engines. This reduces available power margins significantly, limits the pilot's ability to arrest a high rate of descent or correct for errors, and narrows the corridor between a successful landing and an uncontrolled impact. Yaw control demands also increase due to asymmetric torque.

questions.question: What role does anti-torque (tail rotor) control play during an OEI approach, and how does it differ from a normal two-engine approach?
questions.answer: During an OEI approach, the single operating engine produces torque that the tail rotor must counteract. Because the operating engine is typically running at a higher power setting than either engine would during a normal approach, the tail rotor demand is greater, requiring more pedal input. If the failed engine was also contributing torque, the net torque load may shift unexpectedly depending on which engine failed. The pilot must anticipate and manage yaw aggressively using anti-torque pedals to maintain coordinated flight throughout the approach.

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter and lose one engine on final approach at 300 feet AGL with a 10-knot headwind. Your flight manual shows your helicopter is above the OEI hover ceiling for this DA and gross weight. Walk me through the key decision points and control inputs for completing the approach.
questions.answer: First, immediately identify and confirm the failed engine. Apply max continuous OEI power on the operating engine while maintaining rotor RPM in the green. Since you are above the OEI hover ceiling, a hover is not possible — plan for a run-on or roll-on landing to an appropriate surface. Maintain approach airspeed at or above the OEI minimum recommended approach speed from the AFM (typically around Vy or a published OEI approach speed) to retain translational lift as long as possible. On short final, gradually reduce collective to control descent rate while using aft cyclic to decelerate. Accept a higher-than-normal ground speed at touchdown and perform a run-on landing with collective cushion as the skids or wheels contact. Avoid abrupt collective reductions that could cause rotor RPM decay.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft Flight Manual emergency procedures

questions.question: How does the selection of approach angle and airspeed affect the success of an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter? What happens if you fly too steep or too slow?
questions.answer: A shallower approach angle and an airspeed at or above the published OEI approach speed (or Vy as a general reference) are preferred because they preserve translational lift, reduce the power demand on the operating engine, and allow more time for corrections. Flying too steep increases the rate of descent, which demands more power to arrest at the bottom — power the single engine may not be able to provide. Flying too slow risks the loss of translational lift and increases induced power requirements, potentially exceeding OEI engine limits or causing rotor RPM decay. Both conditions can lead to a hard landing or loss of control. The pilot should fly the approach angle and speed published in the AFM for OEI conditions.

questions.question: During OEI approach training, the instructor simulates the engine failure by reducing power on one engine to flight idle rather than actually shutting it down. What are the aerodynamic and handling implications the pilot must still account for, and what limitation does this simulation have compared to an actual OEI condition?
questions.answer: Even at flight idle, the simulated failed engine continues to produce some drag on the rotor system through the transmission and some residual torque, so the yaw and power demands are not precisely identical to a true engine-out condition. However, the simulation still requires the pilot to manage asymmetric torque, increased anti-torque pedal input, and reduced power margins realistically. The key limitation is that the idle engine may provide a small cushion of power not available in an actual failure, meaning the true OEI power margin could be slightly less than what the simulation reveals. Pilots must understand their specific helicopter's OEI procedures are calibrated for actual engine-out conditions, and simulation may make the maneuver slightly easier than reality.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR Part 61 training requirements

questions.question: A pilot conducts an OEI approach and attempts to transition to a hover at 10 feet AGL, but the operating engine reaches its torque limit before the helicopter fully arrests its descent. Explain the aerodynamic chain of events that follows and what options the pilot has at that moment.
questions.answer: Once the operating engine hits its torque limit, the pilot cannot add more collective to increase lift without risking an overtorque or over-temperature exceedance. If rotor RPM begins to decay due to the high power demand, lift decreases further, accelerating the descent. The helicopter will settle toward the ground with increasing rate of descent. The pilot's options are: (1) accept a firm but controlled touchdown — essentially a run-on or a hard landing — with collective cushion applied to soften contact as much as the engine allows; (2) if forward airspeed is still present, convert it into translational lift by lowering the nose slightly and using the ground effect to assist the arrest; (3) if altitude and airspeed permit, execute a run-on landing rather than attempting to hover. Attempting to hold a hover above OEI hover ceiling simply leads to controlled flight into terrain. The AFM hover ceiling charts exist precisely to define when a hover is or is not achievable.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot anticipates being above OEI hover ceiling before starting the approach, what should they have done differently in their approach planning?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot should have planned for a run-on or roll-on landing from the outset — selecting a landing area with adequate length for a ground run, maintaining a higher approach speed through short final to retain translational lift as long as possible, and committing to not stopping in a hover. The AFM OEI performance charts should have been consulted during preflight planning using current DA, gross weight, and OEI power available to determine whether a hover was feasible at the intended landing site. If not feasible, the pilot should have selected an alternate site with a suitable surface for a run-on landing or coordinated for emergency services if at a confined area.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft Flight Manual OEI performance charts

questions.question: During an OEI approach in a twin-engine helicopter, a candidate consistently lets rotor RPM decay 2–3% below the lower green arc limit during the flare and touchdown phase. As the examiner, what does this tell you about the candidate's understanding of OEI energy management, and what specific knowledge deficit are you identifying?
questions.answer: This pattern reveals the candidate does not understand that during the OEI flare and deceleration phase, rotor RPM is the primary energy reservoir. When collective is applied to arrest the descent and the single engine is at or near its limit, rotor RPM is 'spent' to supplement lift. Allowing it to drop below the green arc means the candidate is draining this reserve without a recovery path — if RPM drops below minimum controllable levels, rotor stall and loss of control become possible. The knowledge deficit is a failure to understand OEI power scheduling: the pilot must manage the collective to keep RPM in the green throughout the maneuver, accepting a firmer touchdown rather than sacrificing rotor RPM for a softer landing. The candidate may also not understand that rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable, unlike fixed-wing aerodynamic stalls, making early recognition and prevention of low RPM conditions absolutely critical.
questions.follow_up: What technique should the candidate use to prevent rotor RPM decay during the OEI touchdown phase, and what is the trade-off?
questions.follow_up_answer: The candidate should reduce collective earlier in the approach to bleed off descent rate before the final flare, accepting a higher approach speed and potentially a firmer touchdown rather than relying on a large collective pull at the bottom. The trade-off is a run-on or firmer landing versus preserving rotor RPM and avoiding a rotor stall. Some manufacturers also recommend maintaining a slightly higher approach speed on OEI approaches specifically to keep rotor RPM in the green and provide energy margin at the bottom. The pilot must accept that a perfect soft hover-landing is not the goal in an OEI emergency — a controlled landing with rotor RPM intact is the goal.

questions.question: How does high density altitude affect your ability to execute an OEI approach and landing in a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: High density altitude reduces air density, which decreases the remaining engine's power output and reduces rotor system efficiency. The surviving engine produces less power than it would at sea level, meaning you have less margin above minimum power required to maintain flight. The helicopter will also require a higher true airspeed for the same indicated airspeed, and hover power demands will be greater. In practical terms, this can shrink or eliminate your ability to maintain altitude or execute a powered approach, forcing a steeper, higher-energy approach and potentially requiring a run-on or sliding landing rather than a hover.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-1B Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge Chapter 10

questions.question: What effect does a strong tailwind have on an OEI approach compared to a calm wind condition?
questions.answer: A tailwind increases groundspeed for the same indicated airspeed, resulting in a shallower approach angle and greater ground distance covered. On an OEI approach, this means you arrive at the landing area with more horizontal energy that must be dissipated. A tailwind also reduces the effectiveness of any translational lift gained during approach, and if a go-around or balked landing is necessary, the tailwind reduces climb performance. Additionally, flaring into a tailwind provides less deceleration effect from the wind. For these reasons, OEI approaches should favor into-the-wind landing directions whenever operationally possible.

questions.question: How does outside air temperature relate to engine performance during an OEI emergency approach, and what does this mean for the pilot?
questions.answer: Higher outside air temperatures reduce air density, which directly reduces the power output of the remaining operating engine because less oxygen mass is available for combustion. This is a component of density altitude along with pressure altitude. In hot conditions, the surviving engine may already be operating closer to its maximum continuous power limit just to maintain a normal approach profile, leaving little torque margin for corrections, go-arounds, or unexpected obstacles. The pilot must anticipate reduced power margins and plan for a lower approach angle with a run-on or sliding landing to avoid exceeding engine limits or experiencing a hard landing.

questions.question: You're conducting an OEI approach to a mountain helipad at 7,500 feet MSL on a hot afternoon with a reported surface temperature of 35°C. The RFM shows your remaining engine is already near 90% torque in cruise. How do atmospheric conditions specifically alter your approach planning compared to a sea-level operation?
questions.answer: At 7,500 feet MSL with a 35°C surface temperature, density altitude will likely be 11,000–12,000 feet or higher. This means the remaining engine is producing significantly less than its sea-level rated power—possibly 20–30% less depending on engine type. The rotor system is also less efficient in thin air, requiring higher collective to generate the same lift. At 90% torque in cruise, you have almost no power reserve for slowing, maneuvering, or correcting errors. Planning changes include: selecting a shallower but energy-managed approach angle to avoid a steep dive requiring sudden collective reduction; targeting a run-on landing rather than a hover termination to avoid the high power demand of hovering OGE; identifying a longer, unobstructed landing area; and accepting that a go-around may not be possible—making the first approach a committed landing. Crew resource management and declaring the emergency early to ensure the LZ is clear are critical.

questions.question: During an OEI approach in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), how does the combination of reduced visibility and the atmospheric effects causing the engine failure complicate your emergency?
questions.answer: IMC during an OEI approach compounds the emergency significantly. If the engine failure was caused by icing conditions, the surviving engine and inlet may also be vulnerable to ice ingestion or power degradation, and the rotor system may have accumulated ice that increases weight and disrupts airfoil efficiency. Reduced visibility prevents visual terrain avoidance and landing zone assessment, forcing reliance on instruments and ATC. The pilot must transition to instrument flying while simultaneously managing single-engine procedures—a high workload scenario. Additionally, icing conditions can cause pitot-static errors affecting airspeed and altitude readouts, degrading the accuracy of approach profile monitoring. The pilot should squawk 7700, declare the emergency, request radar vectors to the nearest suitable facility with instrument approaches, and be prepared for a higher-than-normal approach speed to maintain rotor RPM and avoid ice accumulation stall.

questions.question: You experience an engine failure during a crosswind leg of a traffic pattern at a heliport. There is a 20-knot direct crosswind. How does this atmospheric condition specifically affect your OEI approach back to the heliport?
questions.answer: A strong crosswind during an OEI approach creates several challenges. First, maintaining coordinated flight with one engine inoperative already demands asymmetric power management; adding a crosswind means the remaining engine must compensate for both the asymmetric torque and the lateral wind correction, increasing its power demand. The antitorque system must also work harder to maintain heading against combined torque and crosswind effects, potentially approaching pedal limits on some aircraft. During the final approach, crabbing or slipping into the wind while managing single-engine power margins increases pilot workload. Drift correction must be precise because a sideward landing with significant groundspeed on one side increases the risk of dynamic rollover. The pilot should consider turning to a more favorable wind-aligned approach path if altitude permits, even if it means a longer routing.

questions.question: A multiengine helicopter with Category A certification loses one engine during a climb-out on a Category A profile on a cold, standard-pressure day at sea level. The crew notes that performance data in the RFM was developed under ISA conditions. How might an atmospheric condition still degrade actual OEI performance even in seemingly favorable cold-air conditions, and what is often misunderstood about cold weather and engine power?
questions.answer: Cold air is denser, which generally increases engine power output and rotor efficiency—this part is accurate and beneficial. However, there are important nuances that are commonly misunderstood. First, many turbine engines are flat-rated, meaning they are electronically or mechanically limited to a maximum torque or power setting regardless of ambient conditions. On a cold day, the engine may reach its flat-rated torque limit at a lower throttle position, meaning the pilot cannot extract additional power beyond the flat-rated limit anyway—the theoretical benefit of cold dense air is capped by the engine limiter. Second, cold temperatures increase the risk of fuel icing, inlet icing, or compressor icing that can rapidly degrade or eliminate engine power, especially in visible moisture. Third, if the Category A profile is followed precisely, the aircraft should be able to clear obstacles on one engine per the RFM—but only if the aircraft is at or below the published Category A takeoff weight for those conditions. Any deviation, such as being overweight or flying a non-Category A profile, invalidates the certification data entirely. The pilot must always verify that actual gross weight does not exceed the Category A OEI climb performance data for the given pressure altitude and temperature.
questions.follow_up: You mentioned flat-rating. If the engine is flat-rated, does that mean OEI performance is the same on a hot day versus a cold day?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not entirely. On a cold day, a flat-rated engine produces its maximum rated power with a larger temperature margin before reaching turbine temperature limits—meaning the engine can sustain that power longer without thermal stress. On a hot day, a flat-rated engine may still produce its rated power up to the flat-rating temperature limit, but above that limit (which the FAA calls the 'corner point' or 'breakpoint' temperature), the engine can no longer maintain rated power and output begins to decline. So OEI performance on a very hot day degrades even if the engine was previously described as 'flat-rated,' because the flat-rating only applies up to a certain temperature. This is why RFM performance charts show a bend or breakpoint in the power available curves at a specific outside air temperature.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR Part 29 (Transport Category Rotorcraft); RFM Chapter-specific performance data

questions.question: How does a microburst or severe wind shear encountered during an OEI final approach interact with the already-degraded performance margins of single-engine flight, and what makes this combination potentially unrecoverable?
questions.answer: During an OEI approach, the remaining engine is likely at or near its maximum continuous power setting, leaving little or no power reserve. A microburst or severe wind shear creates a rapid change in wind velocity—typically a headwind that suddenly becomes a tailwind as the aircraft passes through the shear boundary. In normal two-engine flight, pilots are taught to add power aggressively to counter the airspeed and lift loss caused by the transition to tailwind. On one engine, the power required to arrest the resulting descent may exceed what the single engine can produce at that moment. Additionally, the sudden airspeed loss reduces translational lift and can cause main rotor RPM to decay if the pilot is slow to lower the collective. The combination of increased power demand, reduced airspeed, descent rate development, and possible rotor RPM decay on a single-engine platform can create a sequence that exceeds the aircraft's recovery capability—especially at low altitude on final. This is why pre-approach planning must include checking PIREPs, METARs, and wind shear advisories, and why a go-around option should be identified before beginning the approach even in OEI emergencies. If wind shear is reported or suspected near the intended landing area, the pilot should consider diverting to an alternate site if fuel and performance allow.
questions.follow_up: If you detect wind shear during the OEI approach and decide to execute a go-around, what specific atmospheric factor might make that go-around more hazardous than the approach itself?
questions.follow_up_answer: During the go-around in wind shear, the aircraft may be transitioning from a headwind component back to a tailwind—or vice versa depending on the shear structure—while simultaneously requiring maximum power from a single engine to climb away. If the aircraft is in the tail-of-the-microburst (outflow) region, executing a climbing go-around means flying into increasing downdraft that directly opposes climb performance. The downdraft component of a microburst can exceed the climb capability of even a healthy two-engine helicopter; on one engine, this margin is further reduced. Additionally, the acceleration required to achieve best rate of climb speed from approach speed takes time and power, and in a microburst environment, there may not be sufficient altitude to complete that acceleration before terrain or obstacles become a factor. The pilot must weigh whether staying committed to the landing—even an imperfect one—is safer than attempting a go-around into unknown shear and downdraft conditions with a single engine.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM); AC 00-54 Pilot Wind Shear Guide

questions.question: Define a stabilized approach in the context of a multiengine helicopter OEI approach and landing. What are the key parameters that must be established and maintained?
questions.answer: A stabilized approach means the helicopter is established on a consistent, controlled flight path to the landing area with a constant approach angle, stable airspeed at or near the manufacturer's recommended OEI approach speed, controlled rate of descent, and coordinated flight — all before reaching the stabilization gate altitude defined in the aircraft's RFM. The stabilization gate altitude for OEI approaches is specified in the RFM and may differ from standard instrument approach gates because it reflects single-engine power limitations, terrain clearance, and obstacle avoidance requirements unique to that helicopter type. In an OEI condition, power margins are reduced, so stabilizing early at or above the RFM-defined gate altitude is critical to avoid overtaxing the remaining engine near the ground and to maintain adequate energy reserves for a go-around or emergency divert.

questions.question: Why is achieving a stabilized approach especially important when flying a multiengine helicopter with one engine inoperative, compared to a normal two-engine approach?
questions.answer: With one engine inoperative, the remaining engine is operating at or near its maximum continuous or contingency power rating, leaving little or no power reserve for large corrections. An unstabilized approach forces the pilot to make significant power or attitude adjustments close to the ground, where the single operating engine may be unable to respond adequately. This can lead to excessive sink rates, loss of rotor RPM, or an inability to arrest descent before touchdown. A stabilized approach allows the pilot to manage the reduced power margin predictably and reach a safe touchdown or go-around decision point in a controlled energy state.

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter and lose the left engine on a 3-mile final. You configure for OEI and continue the approach. At 400 feet AGL the airspeed is fluctuating between Vy and 20 knots above it, the descent rate varies between 200 and 700 fpm, and you're slightly left of centerline. Is this approach stabilized? What should you do?
questions.answer: No, this approach is not stabilized. By 300–500 feet AGL (the stabilization gate), airspeed must be steady at the manufacturer's recommended OEI approach speed, descent rate must be controlled and consistent with a normal approach profile (typically around 300–500 fpm for most profiles), and the aircraft must be on the correct lateral track. Fluctuating airspeed over a 20-knot range, a highly variable descent rate swinging from 200 to 700 fpm, and lateral deviation all indicate an unstabilized approach. The correct action is to execute a go-around or missed approach immediately. Attempting to salvage the approach below the stabilization gate with OEI is high-risk — the remaining engine is already heavily loaded, and further large corrections near the ground could result in exceeding engine limits, loss of rotor RPM, or an uncontrolled hard landing.

questions.question: How does operating in the 'region of reversed command' affect your ability to maintain a stabilized OEI approach, and how should you plan your approach speed to account for this?
questions.answer: In the region of reversed command (also called the back side of the power curve), additional power is required to prevent further airspeed decay — the aircraft is speed-unstable. Flying too slowly on an OEI approach puts the helicopter in this region, where even small speed reductions demand increasing power from the already heavily loaded remaining engine, which may not have capacity to respond. This can rapidly lead to an unrecoverable sink rate. To maintain a stabilized approach, the pilot should select an approach speed above the speed for minimum power (L/D MAX or best glide equivalent) — typically the manufacturer's recommended OEI approach speed, which balances obstacle clearance capability with a safe margin above the region of reversed command. Planning a shallower approach angle also reduces the power demand throughout the descent.

questions.question: During an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, how does your approach angle selection affect the stabilized approach and the energy management at the landing zone?
questions.answer: Approach angle directly determines the rate of descent and the airspeed-to-descent-rate ratio needed to maintain a stable profile. A steeper approach angle on OEI requires a higher power setting or a faster airspeed to prevent an excessive sink rate, and it creates a more demanding flare and deceleration phase near the ground where power reserves are most limited. A shallower approach angle reduces power demand during descent and allows for a more gradual flare, giving the pilot more time to transition to a hover or run-on landing using available translational lift. However, too shallow an approach reduces obstacle clearance capability. The ideal OEI approach angle balances obstacle clearance, power availability, and the ability to maintain a stable, constant angle — typically shallower than normal to reduce demands on the single remaining engine during the critical final phase.

questions.question: A candidate tells you that during an OEI approach, as long as they can visually see the landing zone and believe they can 'make it,' they don't need to worry about strict stabilized approach criteria — they just need to get the aircraft on the ground safely. How do you evaluate that reasoning, and what is the specific danger it represents in a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: That reasoning reflects a classic hazardous attitude — 'press-on-itis' or 'invulnerability' — and is precisely the kind of faulty ADM that the error chain concept warns against. The stabilized approach criteria exist because human perception of 'making it' is unreliable, especially under high workload, stress, and with degraded visual cues. In a multiengine helicopter with OEI, the remaining engine is at or near its contingency power limit. An unstabilized approach that the pilot believes they can 'salvage' often requires a sudden, large power demand very close to the ground — exactly when the single engine has the least margin and the pilot has the least time to recover. The specific danger is torque overshoot or exceedance of the remaining engine's limits, combined with rotor RPM decay or an uncorrectable sink rate below effective translational lift altitude. The stabilized approach gate is not a suggestion — it is a go/no-go decision point that removes the subjective bias of 'I think I can make it' from the equation.
questions.follow_up: If that pilot then argues that the RFM doesn't specifically define a stabilized approach gate altitude, does that mean no gate exists, and the pilot can use their own judgment?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. The absence of an explicit gate altitude in the RFM does not mean no standard applies. Standard industry practice and FAA guidance (FAA-H-8083-15B, FAA-H-8083-21B, and operator SOPs) establish stabilized approach criteria as a fundamental safety standard. For helicopter IFR operations, 14 CFR Part 135 operators are required to have approach and landing procedures in their Operations Specifications, and those typically define stabilization gates. For Part 91 operations, the pilot in command is responsible for determining that the approach is safe — and FAA guidance consistently states that a go-around must be executed if the approach is not stabilized by the defined gate. Additionally, the examiner would note that 'judgment' is only sound when it is informed by training, standards, and realistic assessment of aircraft performance — not wishful thinking under pressure. The RFM silence on gate altitude does not grant permission to fly an unstabilized OEI approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9; 14 CFR Part 135

questions.question: Explain how loss of translational lift during an OEI approach can disrupt a previously stabilized approach, and what the pilot must do to recognize and respond to this before it becomes unrecoverable.
questions.answer: Translational lift provides additional lift efficiency as the helicopter moves through the air at approximately 16–24 knots. As the helicopter decelerates through translational lift speed during the final phase of an OEI approach, rotor efficiency decreases and power demand increases — sometimes significantly. On a single operating engine already near its power limit, this sudden increase in power requirement can exceed available torque, causing an uncommanded sink rate that steepens the approach and drives the helicopter below the intended flight path. The approach may appear stable above translational lift speed but deteriorate rapidly below it. Recognition cues include: increasing sink rate without additional collective input, decreasing rotor RPM trend, torque at or exceeding limits, and a nose-high attitude with descending flight path. The pilot must anticipate this transition — not react to it after it occurs. Planning includes knowing the OEI hover ceiling, confirming the single-engine power available exceeds the power required to arrest descent through and below translational lift, and establishing a landing plan (run-on landing or sliding landing rather than a hover) if a full OEI hover is not within aircraft performance. If the sink rate becomes uncontrolled below effective translational lift altitude with insufficient power, the situation is approaching an autorotation entry scenario and may be unrecoverable without immediate decisive action.
questions.follow_up: If your performance charts show that OEI hover out of ground effect is not achievable at your current weight, does that automatically mean an OEI approach and landing is not possible?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — it means a hover is not achievable, but a landing may still be possible using a run-on or roll-on landing technique that does not require a hover. Ground effect (IGE hover) requires significantly less power than out-of-ground-effect (OGE) hover, and a run-on landing requires even less because translational lift is maintained through touchdown. The pilot must select a suitable landing surface that accommodates a rolling or sliding landing, plan an approach profile that transitions through translational lift as late as possible, and accept that a go-around below a certain altitude may not be feasible. This is precisely why route and destination planning for OEI operations must include performance evaluation at every phase — not just cruise — and why the decision to continue an approach or divert must be made before the aircraft is committed to a single possible outcome.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Glossary (translational lift); 14 CFR 91.9

questions.question: Why is it critical to maintain translational lift airspeed for as long as possible during an OEI approach and landing in a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: Translational lift significantly increases rotor system efficiency, reducing the power required to maintain flight. With one engine inoperative, available power is reduced. If the helicopter decelerates below translational lift speed prematurely during an OEI approach, the surviving engine may not be able to produce enough power to arrest the descent, potentially leading to a hard landing or crash. Maintaining translational lift airspeed delays the high-power demand phase of deceleration until the helicopter is in a position to safely land.

questions.question: Before beginning an OEI approach, what aircraft configuration items should a pilot typically accomplish per the helicopter's RFM/POH?
questions.answer: Typical OEI approach configuration items include: confirming the inoperative engine is identified and secured per the emergency checklist (fuel shutoff, fire suppression if applicable), verifying the operative engine is set to the appropriate OEI power rating (e.g., 2.5-minute or 30-minute OEI power as certified), setting landing gear if applicable, selecting the appropriate fuel tank, confirming hydraulic and electrical systems are configured, and briefing the intended landing profile and go-around options. Specific items vary by aircraft type and must be referenced in the RFM/POH.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 27.1585 / 29.1585 (flight manual requirements); Helicopter RFM/POH emergency checklist

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter on final approach when an engine fails at 300 feet AGL. You have confirmed OEI power is available on the remaining engine. Describe how you would modify your approach profile from this point to landing.
questions.answer: At 300 feet AGL with OEI power confirmed, the priority is to maintain a safe airspeed above effective translational lift and execute a continuous, committed approach. You should: (1) maintain an airspeed per the RFM/POH OEI approach speed — typically above ETL to minimize power required; (2) fly the approach angle recommended in the RFM/POH for OEI operations; avoid steeper-than-normal approaches as they increase power demand — instead manage power through appropriate airspeed and angle of attack; (3) minimize hover time at the bottom — plan to land with minimum deceleration rather than attempting a normal hover landing unless OEI hover is confirmed available; (4) commit to landing rather than attempting a go-around unless OEI go-around performance is explicitly confirmed available in the RFM for your current altitude, weight, and density altitude; (5) select a clear landing area early and aim for a running or roll-on landing if surface permits to reduce power demand at touchdown.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Helicopter RFM/POH OEI landing procedures

questions.question: Explain the difference between an OEI hover-capable landing and an OEI run-on or roll-on landing. When would you choose one over the other?
questions.answer: An OEI hover-capable landing means the performance charts show the surviving engine can sustain a stabilized hover at the existing density altitude, gross weight, and wind conditions — allowing a normal approach to hover and then a vertical touchdown. A run-on or roll-on landing is used when OEI hover is not achievable: the helicopter maintains forward airspeed through touchdown, using forward motion to reduce power required by preserving translational lift. You choose a hover landing when performance charts confirm OEI hover is available. When OEI hover is not available or marginal — due to high DA, heavy gross weight, or hot conditions — a run-on/roll-on landing is the correct technique, requiring a suitable surface (runway or flat terrain). The RFM/POH performance charts determine which technique is appropriate.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR Part 27/29 Rotorcraft flight manual performance data

questions.question: A student says during an OEI approach they plan to set up a standard 8-knot final approach speed to allow for a normal hover landing. What is the flaw in this plan and what would you correct?
questions.answer: The flaw is that 8 knots is at or below effective translational lift (ETL), which requires a significant increase in power to maintain flight. With one engine inoperative, the surviving engine may already be near or at its OEI power limit. Decelerating to 8 knots on final dramatically increases the power required, which could exceed OEI available power, causing an uncontrolled descent or hard landing. The correction: the student should fly the RFM/POH OEI final approach speed — typically well above ETL — and delay deceleration until committed over the landing zone. Whether to attempt a hover at all depends on whether the performance charts confirm OEI hover capability at current gross weight and density altitude.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Helicopter RFM/POH OEI approach speeds

questions.question: Many twin-engine helicopters have both a 2.5-minute OEI power rating and a continuous OEI power rating. How does the existence of these two ratings affect how you configure and manage an OEI approach and landing, and what is the risk of mismanaging the 2.5-minute power limit?
questions.answer: Twin-engine helicopters certified under FAR Part 29 (and some Part 27) typically have OEI power ratings including a 2.5-minute (or 30-second) emergency rating and a continuous OEI rating. The 2.5-minute rating is higher than continuous — it is available for the most critical phase (initial response to engine failure, establishing the approach) but must not be used beyond its time limit or engine damage/failure of the surviving engine can result. During an OEI approach, the pilot should configure to continuous OEI power for the sustained approach phase and reserve 2.5-minute power for the critical deceleration and landing phase if needed. If the pilot unknowingly or carelessly runs the 2.5-minute rating beyond its limit, the surviving engine may overstress or fail, converting a controllable OEI situation into a complete power loss requiring autorotation. Proper time monitoring, engine instruments, and adherence to RFM/POH power management procedures are essential.
questions.follow_up: If you consume the full 2.5-minute OEI power allotment during the approach and still need to go-around, what are your options and what does the go-around decision really depend on?
questions.follow_up_answer: Once the 2.5-minute OEI power limit is consumed, the pilot is limited to continuous OEI power for any go-around. The go-around viability depends entirely on whether continuous OEI power is sufficient to achieve a positive climb gradient at the current gross weight, density altitude, and airspeed — as shown in the RFM/POH OEI climb performance charts. If continuous OEI power cannot sustain a climb, a go-around is not a viable option and the pilot must commit to landing. This is exactly why the landing site selection and approach briefing must happen before entering the OEI approach — late go-around decisions when power-limited are one of the most dangerous situations in multiengine helicopter operations.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 29.1 (Part 29 certification standards); 14 CFR 29.45 (general performance requirements); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Helicopter RFM/POH OEI power ratings

questions.question: During an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, how does the failed engine's position — left versus right — affect the aircraft configuration, flight control inputs, and approach profile, particularly in helicopters with counter-rotating or side-by-side engine configurations?
questions.answer: In most twin-engine helicopters, both engines drive the same main rotor transmission, so the directional effect is not about asymmetric thrust the way it is in fixed-wing aircraft. However, the position of the failed engine can affect: (1) torque asymmetry in some configurations — if the engines contribute differentially to anti-torque via separate gearbox pathways, one engine failure may produce a slight yaw tendency; (2) systems affected — hydraulic pumps, generators, fuel boost pumps, and bleed air systems are often engine-specific, so identifying which engine failed determines what systems require backup; (3) fuel management — crossfeed or individual tank selection may depend on which engine is operative. On some tandem-rotor or coaxial helicopters with separate rotor systems per engine, the failed engine side can affect rotor balance and require specific control compensation. In all cases, the pilot must reference the RFM/POH for specific failed-engine-position procedures, as these are aircraft-type dependent and not generic.
questions.follow_up: In a side-by-side twin-engine helicopter where the left engine has failed, would you expect any persistent pedal input requirement during the approach compared to two-engine flight, and why or why not?
questions.follow_up_answer: In most conventional single-rotor helicopters — even twin-engine ones — the tail rotor is driven by the main rotor transmission regardless of which engine is running. So pedal inputs compensate for main rotor torque, which is now being produced solely by the remaining engine at a potentially higher power setting. If the surviving engine (right engine, in this example) is producing more power than the normal two-engine cruise setting, more left pedal (in a counterclockwise rotor system) may be required to counteract the increased torque. The pilot should expect a different pedal trim setting than normal two-engine flight, and should re-trim as appropriate during the approach. The specific pedal effect depends on the power state and rotor system design, not on which specific engine failed.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR 29.1 (Part 29); Helicopter RFM/POH system descriptions and OEI procedures

questions.question: When you lose an engine on a multiengine helicopter during an approach, why does your available altitude matter so much for your landing options?
questions.answer: Altitude is directly tied to your energy reserve and decision time. More altitude gives you more time to assess the situation, configure the helicopter, and select or reach a suitable landing area. At low altitude with one engine inoperative, your margin for error shrinks dramatically — you may not have enough altitude to arrest a descent or maneuver around obstacles. The remaining engine may not provide enough power to maintain altitude at all weights and conditions, so the altitude you have at the moment of engine failure largely determines what options are available to you.

questions.question: How does wind direction and speed affect your landing area selection during a one-engine-inoperative approach in a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: Wind directly affects performance and control during an OEI approach. A headwind reduces groundspeed and increases effective lift, which can assist in slowing down and reaching the landing area more safely. A tailwind or crosswind creates additional challenges — a tailwind increases groundspeed and reduces rotor system efficiency at low speeds, while a crosswind demands more anti-torque pedal input and careful directional control. Strong winds can also create turbulence or wind shear, especially near terrain or obstacles. You always want to land into the wind if at all possible to maximize aerodynamic efficiency on the remaining engine and reduce the energy required to decelerate to a landing.

questions.question: What characteristics make a landing area suitable versus unsuitable when you are conducting an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: A suitable landing area should be large enough to accommodate the helicopter with a margin for error, free of obstructions on the approach path and within the landing zone itself, and ideally level or slightly sloped toward you. The surface should be firm enough to support the aircraft and free of obstacles that could cause dynamic rollover or damage to the tail rotor. An unsuitable area would be one that is too small, has tall obstacles blocking the approach path, has an unfavorable slope that increases dynamic rollover risk, or has an unknown or soft surface. With one engine out, you have reduced performance and potentially limited go-around capability, so committing to a bad landing area carries extreme risk.

questions.question: You are flying a multiengine helicopter at 1,500 feet AGL when you lose an engine. To your left is a large open field about a mile away, and directly ahead is a highway with light traffic about a quarter mile away. The terrain between you and the field is rising and has scattered trees along a ridgeline. How do you evaluate these two options?
questions.answer: You must rapidly weigh altitude and energy against terrain, obstacles, and landing area quality. The open field to the left seems ideal in terms of surface quality, but you must assess whether you have enough altitude and single-engine performance to cross the rising terrain and trees along the ridgeline — if the terrain is rising and trees obstruct the approach path, you may not clear them with degraded performance. The highway ahead is closer and may require less altitude and power to reach, but introduces the risk of collision with vehicles, unpredictable surface conditions, and hazards like power lines, signs, and traffic. The most important factor is whether your current altitude and remaining engine performance actually give you a realistic chance of reaching each option. If the terrain and obstacles between you and the field make it marginal, the closer highway — despite its hazards — may be the survivable choice. The goal is to avoid the situation where you are 'probably' going to make the field, because 'probably' in an emergency is not good enough.

questions.question: You are established on a visual approach to a helipad on top of a hospital building in a multiengine helicopter when you lose one engine. The helipad is still ahead and within glide distance, but you notice the wind has shifted to a direct tailwind of about 12 knots. What risks does this change introduce, and how does it affect your decision to continue to the helipad versus diverting to a ground-level area?
questions.answer: A tailwind of 12 knots on an OEI approach to a rooftop helipad introduces several compounding risks. First, your groundspeed is higher, which means you arrive over the pad faster and with more energy to dissipate — this increases the chance of overshooting a confined area. Second, single-engine performance is already reduced, and a tailwind reduces the effective translational lift benefit you would normally get on approach, requiring more power to slow down. Third, rooftop helipads typically have obstacles or mechanical equipment nearby, limiting your maneuvering options if you need to go around. With one engine inoperative, a go-around from a rooftop pad in a tailwind may not be feasible. Diverting to a ground-level area may be safer if you have enough altitude and performance to reach it, because it offers more space, lower obstacle density, and more options to land into the wind. The combination of confined area, tailwind, and OEI creates a high-risk scenario that may exceed the helicopter's performance margins.

questions.question: During an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, you identify two possible landing areas. One is upslope and into the wind; the other is level but has a line of trees requiring you to fly a downwind leg before turning final. Walk me through how you weigh these options given your altitude and terrain.
questions.answer: This is a classic forced trade-off between slope and wind alignment. Landing upslope and into the wind provides the aerodynamic advantage of a headwind, which aids in energy management and deceleration, but an upslope landing surface increases the risk of dynamic rollover — the uphill skid touches first and can cause the helicopter to roll over the high side if lateral cyclic is not properly managed. The level but downwind option requires you to fly a downwind leg and turn final, which consumes altitude and time, uses more power, and may place you below a safe energy margin by the time you are on final. If you have sufficient altitude to execute the pattern to the level area safely with the available single-engine power and the tree obstruction is manageable, the level surface is generally preferable. If altitude is critically low, the upslope headwind option may be forced upon you — but you must be prepared to execute landing technique that accounts for the slope. The terrain between you and each area must be factored in as well — rising terrain or obstructions en route to either option may eliminate that choice entirely.

questions.question: A student tells you that during an OEI approach they planned to fly directly toward the best-looking landing area without considering what the terrain looked like between their current position and the field, because 'the landing area was clearly in sight.' What is the specific risk this mindset creates, and how would you correct it?
questions.answer: Fixating on the destination without evaluating the terrain in between is a classic tunnel-vision error that can lead to controlled flight into terrain (CFIT). Just because a landing area is visible does not mean you have the performance to reach it. With one engine inoperative, your climb capability may be zero or negative at gross weight — if rising terrain, a ridgeline, or a tree line lies between you and the field, you may be unable to clear it regardless of what the destination looks like. The error chain here involves target fixation, overconfidence in single-engine performance, and failure to conduct a comprehensive terrain scan. The correction is to teach the student to evaluate the entire approach path — not just the endpoint — by scanning from their current position to the landing area, identifying any terrain or obstruction that rises above their current altitude or projected flight path, and then honestly assessing whether single-engine performance supports that route. If it does not, an alternate area must be chosen even if it is less ideal as a surface.
questions.follow_up: How would you teach a student to quickly assess terrain clearance during an OEI scenario without getting distracted from flying the helicopter?
questions.follow_up_answer: The technique is to use a rapid scan sequence during the initial response: first stabilize the helicopter (maintain control, confirm engine failure, manage power on the operating engine), then quickly scan the horizon from current position to the intended landing area looking for anything that appears to rise toward or above your altitude. A practical memory aid is to imagine a straight line from your nose to the landing zone — anything that appears above that line is a potential obstruction. In training, you pre-brief the likely terrain features before the flight so the student already has a mental picture of the environment. During the scenario debrief, you review whether the student's chosen path was actually obstacle-clear based on the actual terrain, reinforcing that visual confirmation of the destination is not the same as clearing the path to get there.

questions.question: You are evaluating an applicant who, during a simulated OEI approach, correctly identified a suitable landing area but then began a very shallow, slow approach over a line of trees because they were trying to preserve options. By the time they cleared the trees, they were below effective translational lift, at a very slow airspeed, and the remaining engine was near its limit. What risk did this create, and what should the correct technique have been?
questions.answer: The applicant created a situation where they had simultaneously exhausted their airspeed energy, their altitude margin, and their power margin — a triple squeeze that left them with no recovery option if the approach path was wrong. By trying to preserve options through a shallow, slow approach over the obstacle, they actually reduced their options to near zero. Hovering or slow flight at low altitude on a single engine at high power is extremely demanding — if the remaining engine falters at that point, there is insufficient altitude to autorotate and insufficient airspeed to convert to translational lift. The correct technique in an OEI approach over an obstacle is to approach with enough airspeed to maintain translational lift efficiency, plan the obstacle clearance with an adequate margin (not a razor-thin crossing), and commit to the landing area on a stabilized approach angle that allows the helicopter to be managed to touchdown without prolonged hover in the OEI power regime. Slow flight over obstacles on one engine is not a conservative technique — it is a high-risk energy trap.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant's multiengine helicopter had a published OEI hover ceiling that was above their current density altitude, does that mean an OEI hover in ground effect was safe in this scenario?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not necessarily. OEI hover ceiling data from the flight manual assumes standard conditions and is typically calculated at a specific gross weight with optimal engine performance and no degradation. In a real emergency scenario, the remaining engine may have been at maximum continuous power for an extended period, oil temperatures and pressures must be monitored, and the published ceiling represents an absolute limit — not a comfortable operating margin. Additionally, a hover in ground effect requires precise collective control, and any slight increase in demand (gust, small altitude gain to clear the obstacle, weight shift) can push the engine beyond its limits or into compressor stall. The applicant should have used the published data only as a reference to assess whether a short-field or no-hover landing was feasible, not as a green light to hover at the limit. Operating at the ceiling is operating at the edge — that is never where you want to be in an emergency.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; ACS PH.X.C; Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) OEI performance charts

questions.question: When planning a flightpath to a landing area following an OEI situation in a multiengine helicopter, what is the primary reason you must commit to a landing area earlier than you would during a normal approach?
questions.answer: With one engine inoperative, the helicopter has significantly reduced power margin and climb capability. This limits the pilot's ability to go around or reposition if the initial flightpath judgment is poor. The reduced performance means any deviation from the planned flightpath may not be correctable, so early commitment to a suitable landing area and a stable, well-planned approach path is essential to ensure adequate energy management throughout the approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Helicopter Emergencies and Hazards

questions.question: What does the term 'flightpath discipline' mean when conducting an OEI approach to a selected landing area, and why does it matter more than in a normal approach?
questions.answer: Flightpath discipline means deliberately maintaining the planned angle, track, and energy profile all the way to the landing area without significant deviations. It matters more during an OEI approach because the helicopter is operating at or near its single-engine performance limit. Any deviation — going too high, too shallow, or off-track — may require power corrections or repositioning maneuvers that exceed the remaining engine's capability, potentially leading to loss of control or inability to reach the landing area.

questions.question: When selecting a landing area during an OEI emergency, what three physical characteristics of the area most directly affect whether your planned flightpath to it is viable?
questions.answer: The three primary physical characteristics are: (1) Size and surface condition — the area must be large enough for a safe landing with adequate margins for potential drift or rollout; (2) Obstacle clearance along the entire approach path — the flightpath must be free of wires, trees, structures, and terrain that could intercept the helicopter given its degraded climb performance; and (3) Wind alignment — landing into or near the wind reduces groundspeed at touchdown and improves single-engine performance during the approach, making the planned flightpath more manageable.

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter at 1,500 feet AGL in cruise when you experience an engine failure. There are two potential landing areas ahead: one is a large, paved parking lot 1.5 miles away directly into the wind, and the other is a grass field 0.5 miles away but requires a 90-degree crosswind approach. Your helicopter's single-engine performance charts show marginal OEI climb capability at current density altitude. Which area do you select, and how does that decision shape your flightpath planning?
questions.answer: In this scenario, the marginally capable OEI performance makes flightpath planning critical. The closer grass field reduces the distance and time the helicopter must sustain single-engine flight, lowering overall risk exposure. However, the 90-degree crosswind approach increases difficulty in tracking the intended flightpath and managing drift, particularly at reduced power margins. With only marginal OEI climb capability, any upwind correction or go-around attempt may not be achievable. The preferred choice is generally the closer landing area — the 0.5-mile grass field — because reaching it requires less sustained single-engine performance. The flightpath must be planned with a gradual, stable descent accounting for crosswind correction throughout, with no expectation of a go-around. If the distance to the parking lot can be covered with confidence given altitude and performance, and the pilot prefers the wind-aligned approach, that remains a valid choice — but the decision must be made early and committed to immediately.

questions.question: During an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, you realize at mid-approach that your glidepath is too high and you will overshoot the selected landing area. Describe the risk management considerations before deciding whether to steepen the approach or abandon the landing area for an alternate.
questions.answer: The pilot must assess several risk factors simultaneously: (1) Remaining altitude and energy — is there enough altitude to steepen the approach without creating an excessively steep, high-sink rate that exceeds the operating engine's ability to arrest? (2) Single-engine go-around capability — does the helicopter have sufficient OEI climb performance at this density altitude, weight, and configuration to safely execute a missed approach and reposition? If not, attempting a go-around may be more dangerous than continuing a steep approach. (3) Obstacle environment — does steepening the approach create an unacceptable obstacle clearance issue? (4) Alternate landing area availability — is there a closer, more accessible option that avoids the need for a go-around? The conservative risk management answer per FAA ADM principles is: avoid actions that will 'probably' work — if a go-around is marginal, the known option (continuing to the selected area with a corrected approach) is safer. However, if continuation creates an uncontrollable sink rate, the pilot must abort early enough to make a controlled repositioning possible.

questions.question: You are flying a multiengine helicopter over mountainous terrain when one engine fails. The only available landing area is a small meadow in a valley that requires a descending turn to align with the approach path. What specific flightpath planning risks does the descending turn introduce in an OEI situation?
questions.answer: A descending turn in an OEI situation introduces several compounding risks: (1) Increased load factor during the turn increases effective weight and power demand on the operating engine, potentially exceeding its OEI limits; (2) Bank angle must be controlled carefully — excessive bank in a descending turn can accelerate the descent rate beyond what the remaining engine can manage; (3) The inside of a descending turn toward terrain creates a CFIT risk if the flightpath is misjudged, since the helicopter's altitude advantage over terrain is being consumed simultaneously with the turn; (4) Rotor RPM management becomes more complex as both the turn and descent affect power requirements; (5) Workload is dramatically increased, raising the risk of target fixation on the meadow and neglecting aircraft control. The pilot should plan the shallowest bank angle possible, begin the turn early to allow gradual alignment, and verify throughout that the descent rate is controlled and obstacle clearance is maintained.

questions.question: A student pilot preparing for a multiengine helicopter checkride argues that in an OEI emergency, the priority should always be flying the helicopter first, and that detailed flightpath planning to a specific landing area is secondary — something you do only if time permits. How would you respond to this argument from a risk management perspective, and where does flightpath planning fit within the actual hierarchy of OEI actions?
questions.answer: The student is partially correct but dangerously incomplete. The immediate priority in any emergency is always aircraft control — maintaining rotor RPM, managing the failed engine, and preventing loss of control. However, 'flying the helicopter first' and 'planning the flightpath' are not sequential tasks in an OEI scenario — they are parallel workload items that must begin nearly simultaneously. Here's why flightpath planning cannot be deferred: in a multiengine helicopter, the power available from one engine is finite and decreasing in usefulness as altitude is consumed. Every second without a committed flightpath toward a landing area is wasted energy and altitude that cannot be recovered. If the pilot focuses exclusively on aircraft control and defers flightpath selection, they may find themselves too low, too slow, or in a position where all available landing areas require a go-around that the single engine cannot support. FAA ADM principles emphasize that the 'error chain' in accidents rarely involves a single failure — it is accumulated poor decisions. Delaying flightpath commitment is itself a risk-management failure. The correct hierarchy is: (1) Maintain aircraft control, (2) Execute emergency checklist items simultaneously or immediately after control is established, (3) Identify and commit to a landing area early, (4) Plan and follow the flightpath — these last two steps must happen before the helicopter's energy state narrows the options to zero.
questions.follow_up: If the student's argument were applied in practice and the pilot waited until they felt 'stabilized' before selecting a landing area, what specific performance threshold might already be lost by that point that makes flightpath planning much harder?
questions.follow_up_answer: By the time a pilot considers themselves 'stabilized' after an OEI failure — having run checklists, confirmed the failed engine, and adjusted power — the helicopter has likely descended several hundred feet and decelerated toward a lower airspeed. At this point, the single-engine service ceiling may already be below the current altitude, meaning the helicopter is in a continuous descent regardless of power input. This eliminates the option to climb over obstacles that might have been clearable had the flightpath been committed earlier at a higher energy state. Additionally, at reduced airspeed, the helicopter's ability to glide or maneuver to a more distant but better-aligned landing area is gone. The landing area selection is now dictated by geometry and physics rather than pilot preference — which is precisely the risk that early flightpath planning is designed to prevent.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, error chain)

questions.question: During an OEI approach checkride evaluation, a candidate selects a suitable landing area and establishes a reasonable flightpath, but then makes a series of small heading and altitude corrections throughout the approach that each seem individually justified. At what point do these incremental corrections become a risk management problem, and how would you evaluate whether the candidate's flightpath following was acceptable?
questions.answer: Individually justifiable corrections that accumulate throughout an OEI approach represent a risk management problem when they indicate the pilot is reacting to the flightpath rather than anticipating and controlling it. This is a manifestation of the 'error chain' concept — each small correction seems reasonable, but together they signal that the pilot never truly established and maintained a planned flightpath. The risk is twofold: (1) Each correction consumes power and workload that is already constrained in the OEI regime, and (2) Accumulated corrections can move the helicopter progressively further from the ideal energy state, potentially resulting in a high, fast approach or an undershoot that the remaining engine cannot correct. For checkride evaluation purposes, acceptable flightpath following means the candidate identified the landing area and approach path early, established a consistent angle and track within the first third of the approach, made at most minor trim adjustments (not large corrections), and arrived at the landing area with appropriate energy and alignment. A candidate who is constantly chasing the flightpath — even with technically correct individual inputs — demonstrates a risk management deficiency in planning, which is the core of PH.VIII.C.R2. I would note this as a weakness and probe further.
questions.follow_up: How would you distinguish between a candidate who made frequent corrections because of genuine turbulence or wind shear versus one who made them because of poor flightpath planning — and does that distinction change your evaluation?
questions.follow_up_answer: The distinction matters significantly for evaluation fairness but not for the underlying risk management lesson. A candidate dealing with genuine environmental factors should verbalize those factors — 'I'm getting wind shear on short final, correcting' — demonstrating situational awareness and intentional response rather than reactive chasing. The key evaluative indicators are: (1) Were the corrections proportional and prompt? Environmental corrections tend to be discrete and followed by re-establishment of the planned path. Poor-planning corrections tend to be continuous and slightly late. (2) Did the candidate's callouts and scan reflect awareness of the external factor? (3) Did the helicopter's energy state at landing still fall within acceptable parameters? If turbulence caused the corrections but the approach remained controlled and the landing was safe, the performance may still be acceptable. However, I would ask the candidate to debrief the approach — if they cannot identify the environmental factor as the cause, that itself reveals a situational awareness gap. Either way, the standard requires that the pilot plan and follow a flightpath; understanding why deviations occurred is part of demonstrating that competency.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, SRM, error chain); PH.X.C ACS standards

questions.question: During an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, what types of collision hazards should you be scanning for as you descend toward the landing area?
