questions.answer: During an OEI approach, you must scan for terrain and obstacles in the flight path (towers, trees, wires, buildings), other air traffic in the pattern or vicinity, ground personnel or vehicles near the intended landing area, and any structures along the extended approach path. Because your options for maneuvering are severely limited with one engine inoperative, identifying these hazards early is critical — you cannot execute aggressive avoidance maneuvers without risking loss of control.

questions.question: Why are power lines and wire strikes considered especially dangerous during a simulated OEI approach compared to a normal approach?
questions.answer: Wires are extremely difficult to see and are often strung between poles at irregular heights. During an OEI approach, your attention and workload are heavily concentrated on aircraft control, engine monitoring, and crew coordination, which reduces the time and capacity available for obstacle scanning. Additionally, with reduced power margin, you cannot perform a sudden steep climb or aggressive avoidance maneuver to clear an unexpected wire. This combination of high workload and limited performance margin makes wire strikes a leading collision hazard during OEI approaches.

questions.question: What is CFIT, and how does it relate to collision hazard risk during an OEI approach?
questions.answer: CFIT stands for Controlled Flight Into Terrain — an accident in which an airworthy aircraft under pilot control is unintentionally flown into terrain, an obstacle, or water. During an OEI approach, CFIT risk increases because high cockpit workload can cause the pilot to lose situational awareness of terrain and obstacle proximity, especially during low-altitude maneuvering. The pilot may be focused on maintaining aircraft control and monitoring the failed engine while inadvertently descending into terrain or an obstacle below the intended glide path.

questions.question: You are conducting a simulated OEI approach to a confined area landing zone at a hospital helipad. As you turn final, you notice a news helicopter orbiting in the vicinity and a medical transport vehicle parked at the edge of the pad. How do you manage these collision hazards while also managing the OEI emergency?
questions.answer: First, immediately broadcast your OEI status and intentions on the appropriate frequency (CTAF or ATC) to alert the orbiting news helicopter and request traffic separation. If ATC is available, declare the emergency and request priority handling. Assign collision hazard scanning to the co-pilot if available — this is a key SRM/CRM task-sharing moment. Assess whether the parked vehicle creates an unacceptable obstruction. If the landing zone is compromised, a go-around on one engine may not be a safe option depending on aircraft performance; you may need to select an alternate landing area. Do not fixate on the engine-out emergency at the expense of losing awareness of other traffic and ground hazards. Prioritize: Aviate, Navigate, Communicate.

questions.question: During a simulated OEI approach, your instructor fails an engine while you are on a 3-mile final over a congested suburban area. You identify your intended landing field ahead, but there are high-tension power lines crossing your final approach path at approximately mid-field. How do you assess and mitigate this collision hazard?
questions.answer: Immediately assess the wires as a go/no-go factor for that approach path. Determine the height of the wires relative to your glide path — if you cannot confirm adequate clearance, do not attempt to fly under or over them given reduced performance margins with one engine. Options include: (1) offset the approach to avoid the wires by choosing a clear corridor to the side, (2) select an alternate landing zone that does not have the obstruction on the approach path, or (3) if performance permits and the aircraft POH supports it, transition to an approach angle that clearly clears the wire hazard. Do not attempt to thread through wires under high workload and reduced power. Communicate your actions and intentions. The error chain must be broken — pressing ahead through a known obstruction hazard with degraded performance is a classic CFIT precursor.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; ACS PH.VIII.C.R3

questions.question: How does high pilot workload during an OEI approach directly increase the risk of a mid-air collision or ground collision, and what technique can help counteract this?
questions.answer: High workload during an OEI approach causes cognitive tunneling — the pilot's attention narrows to the immediate emergency task (managing the failed engine, maintaining performance, configuring the aircraft) while traffic scanning and obstacle awareness degrade. This is sometimes called 'get-there-itis' in the emergency context — the pilot becomes fixated on reaching the landing area and stops actively looking for conflicting traffic, rising terrain, or obstacles. The technique to counteract this is structured task-sharing and callouts in multi-crew operations, or a deliberate habit of brief, timed visual scans outside the cockpit even during high-workload phases. In single-pilot operations, SRM principles require the pilot to periodically force an outside scan and maintain positional awareness regardless of workload. Declaring an emergency early also alerts ATC to provide traffic separation, reducing mid-air risk.

questions.question: A pilot conducting a simulated OEI approach decides to continue the approach despite seeing a helicopter enter the traffic pattern ahead of them, reasoning that the other pilot 'probably' sees them and will stay clear. From a risk management standpoint, what is wrong with this reasoning, and what is the correct course of action?
questions.answer: The word 'probably' signals an unacceptable level of uncertainty in a life-safety situation. FAA ADM guidance specifically warns against 'probably' reasoning — if an action will only 'probably' work, you must choose an option known to work. The other pilot may not have established visual contact, may not be monitoring the same frequency, and may not be aware of the OEI status. The correct action is to actively communicate: broadcast position and OEI emergency status on the CTAF or with ATC, make your intentions explicit, and visually confirm separation before continuing. If separation cannot be confirmed, break off the approach or delay it until the traffic conflict is resolved. An OEI approach does not grant right-of-way over all other traffic — it does, however, justify declaring an emergency (14 CFR 91.3) which then gives ATC the authority to move other traffic for you.
questions.follow_up: If this OEI situation leads the pilot to declare an emergency under 14 CFR 91.3, what regulatory authority does that declaration grant, and is the pilot required to file a report afterward?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.3(b), the pilot in command of an aircraft in distress may deviate from any FAR to the extent necessary to meet that emergency. This means the PIC can deviate from traffic pattern procedures, altitude requirements, communication requirements, or other regulations as needed to safely handle the emergency. Regarding reporting: if the pilot deviates from an ATC clearance during the emergency, 14 CFR 91.123 requires the pilot to submit a written report to ATC upon request. Additionally, if ATC requests a deviation report under 91.3(c), the pilot must comply. There is no blanket automatic requirement to file a report simply for declaring an emergency, but the pilot should be prepared to explain actions taken if requested by ATC or the FAA.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.123; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; ACS PH.VIII.C.R3

questions.question: During an OEI approach to an uncontrolled airport at night, how does the collision hazard environment change compared to a daytime OEI approach, and what pre-approach actions should the pilot have taken to mitigate those hazards?
questions.answer: At night, visual detection of terrain, obstacles, wires, unmarked towers, and other aircraft is severely degraded. Traffic on CTAF may be sparse, and aircraft without lights (ultralights, gliders, drones) may not be visible at all. The reduced performance margin on one engine leaves little room for abrupt avoidance maneuvers if a hazard is detected late. Additionally, depth perception and spatial orientation are compromised at night, increasing CFIT risk during the final low-altitude maneuvering. Pre-approach mitigations should have included: (1) thorough review of the airport/area NOTAMs for obstacle, tower, and temporary flight restriction information; (2) identification of obstacle locations on sectional or terminal area charts before arrival; (3) briefing the approach path specifically for night hazards including any unlit towers or wire crossings; (4) confirming all aircraft lighting is operational; (5) making position broadcasts early and frequently to alert any traffic; and (6) ensuring familiarity with published visual approach paths or instrument approaches that provide obstacle clearance. The error chain for a night OEI collision often begins with inadequate pre-flight planning — this is where it must be broken.
questions.follow_up: If during this night OEI approach the crew identifies a previously unreported obstruction light outage on a tower that lies within their approach corridor, what is the correct immediate action and what reporting obligation follows the flight?
questions.follow_up_answer: The immediate action is to alter the approach to avoid the unlit tower — treat it as a known collision hazard and route around it or select an alternate approach path. If the hazard cannot be safely avoided given OEI performance constraints, divert to an alternate landing area. After the flight, the crew should report the obstruction light outage to the FAA via the standard reporting mechanism — pilots can report obstruction lighting outages to the FAA's Obstruction Evaluation / Airport Airspace Analysis (OE/AAA) office or through Flight Service (1-800-WX-BRIEF), and the information may also be submitted as a NOTAM request. Reporting the outage protects subsequent crews from the same hazard and is consistent with the safety culture expected of professional flight crews.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.159; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; AIM 7-5-2 (obstruction light reporting); ACS PH.VIII.C.R3

questions.question: During an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, what does 'task prioritization' mean, and why is it critical at this phase of flight?
questions.answer: Task prioritization means identifying and performing the most critical tasks first while deferring or delegating less urgent ones. During an OEI approach, the pilot must focus on flying the aircraft (aviate), then managing the failed engine and systems (navigate/communicate), then checklists. Failure to prioritize correctly can result in fixation on secondary tasks — such as troubleshooting or radio calls — while allowing airspeed, rotor RPM, or approach path to deteriorate. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that approximately 80% of aviation accidents are caused by pilot error, often involving fixation or improper task management rather than a single catastrophic failure.

questions.question: Define 'loss of situational awareness' as it applies to a multiengine helicopter pilot executing an OEI approach and landing.
questions.answer: Loss of situational awareness (SA) occurs when the pilot no longer has an accurate mental picture of the aircraft's position, state, and trajectory relative to the environment and threats. During an OEI approach, this can manifest as the pilot losing track of airspeed, altitude, descent rate, remaining power margin on the operating engine, or position relative to the landing area. It is often preceded by an unexpected event — such as an engine failure — that overloads the pilot's cognitive resources. The FAA defines SA as a key component of Single-Pilot Resource Management (SRM).

questions.question: What is the 'error chain' concept, and how does it relate to distractions during an OEI approach?
questions.answer: The error chain is the sequence of multiple contributing factors or poor decisions that, taken together, lead to an accident. No single mistake typically causes an accident; rather, a series of errors — each individually survivable — combine to create a catastrophic outcome. During an OEI approach, a distraction (e.g., a radio call, a cockpit warning light, or a passenger comment) can be one link in the error chain. If the pilot is already low on power margin, slightly off airspeed, and distracted simultaneously, the chain is nearly complete. The FAA notes that breaking any single link can change the outcome, so pilots must actively recognize accumulating errors.

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter and experience a simulated engine failure on short final at 200 feet AGL. Your copilot immediately begins running the OEI checklist aloud and asks you to confirm each item. How do you manage this without compromising the approach?
questions.answer: The pilot flying (PF) must maintain absolute focus on flying the aircraft — airspeed, rotor RPM, approach angle, and power management — and should verbally communicate to the copilot or examiner that checklist completion is deferred until after landing or a stabilized hover is established. The standard crew resource management (CRM) response is 'Aviate first — hold the checklist.' On single-pilot operations, the pilot should mentally prioritize: (1) maintain correct airspeed and rotor RPM, (2) manage the operating engine's power to avoid exceeding OEI limits, (3) land or go around as appropriate, and (4) run checklists after the immediate threat is resolved. Reading a checklist at 200 feet AGL while managing a degraded-power approach is a classic distraction-induced task saturation scenario. The FAA's ADM framework specifically warns against cognitive fixation on secondary tasks during high-workload phases.

questions.question: During a night OEI practice approach to a confined area, you notice the CAAS (or AFCS) annunciating a fault as you cross the threshold. You are single-pilot. Walk me through how you prioritize competing demands in this moment.
questions.answer: The priority order is: (1) Aviate — maintain aircraft control, correct airspeed, rotor RPM, and descent rate; do not divert visual attention from the landing area at this critical phase. (2) The AFCS/CAAS fault is a secondary distraction — acknowledge it visually but do not attempt to diagnose or reset it while on short final at night over a confined area. (3) Decide whether to land or execute a go-around based on aircraft control and power availability, not based on resolving the annunciator. (4) After landing and securing the aircraft, address the fault. Night operations in confined areas already degrade visual cues and increase disorientation risk; adding cognitive load from an avionics fault can quickly cause loss of situational awareness. The FAA's SRM model identifies workload management and CFIT awareness as specific components pilots must actively manage in exactly this type of compound-stressor scenario.

questions.question: A student pilot you are instructing is practicing OEI approaches. On the third repetition, you notice the student has become complacent — they are flying the approach mechanically without actively monitoring torque on the operating engine. What specific risk does this represent, and how would you address it during the debrief?
questions.answer: This represents a classic situational awareness degradation driven by task familiarity and complacency — a recognized human factors risk. When a pilot 'normalizes' a simulated emergency through repetition, they may stop actively cross-checking critical parameters such as operating engine torque, TGT/ITT limits, rotor RPM, and airspeed. In a real OEI event, exceeding the operating engine's OEI power limits due to inattention could result in a double-engine failure scenario. During the debrief, I would use the ADM framework to have the student identify: (a) what parameters they were monitoring versus ignoring, (b) what could have happened if the scenario were real and they exceeded OEI torque limits, and (c) how to build a consistent instrument scan habit even during repetitive training. The FAA notes that accidents decrease significantly after 100 hours in type precisely because instrument scan and task management become more automatic — but that same automaticity can breed complacency if not managed intentionally.

questions.question: You are single-pilot in a twin-engine helicopter on an instrument approach in IMC when the right engine fails at 500 feet AGL on final. ATC immediately calls traffic on the frequency for an unrelated aircraft and your TAWS gives a nuisance terrain alert simultaneously. Describe the cognitive and physiological risks in this moment and the specific strategies to prevent disorientation and loss of situational awareness.
questions.answer: This scenario creates classic cognitive overload through simultaneous, competing inputs: an actual emergency (engine failure), an external distraction (ATC traffic call), and a false/nuisance alert (TAWS). The cognitive risk is 'attention tunneling' — the pilot fixates on one input (e.g., the TAWS alert) while the primary threat (maintaining OEI performance and instrument scan) degrades. The physiological risk is spatial disorientation, which is elevated in IMC at low altitude with high workload, because the vestibular system provides false cues and the pilot may subconsciously respond to those cues instead of the instruments. Specific strategies: (1) Verbally reject the non-critical inputs — mentally or aloud say 'ignore TAWS, ignore ATC' and refocus on attitude and power. (2) Trust instruments completely — do not chase vestibular sensations. (3) Fly the OEI missed approach/go-around if altitude and performance permit; do not attempt to continue the approach while managing distractions. (4) Declare emergency when workload permits (squawk 7700, advise ATC) — this removes the ATC communication burden. The FAA ADM framework's guidance that 'if an action will only probably work out, choose an option known to work' directly applies: a go-around with OEI performance is a known-good option; continuing an unstabilized IMC approach while distracted is a 'probably' scenario.
questions.follow_up: If your multiengine helicopter's OEI performance charts show that you are at or near the limit of single-engine climb performance at your current weight and density altitude, and you are already at 500 feet AGL in IMC, how does that change your decision-making in this scenario?
questions.follow_up_answer: If OEI performance is marginal, the decision tree changes significantly. A go-around may not be viable if the aircraft cannot achieve a positive single-engine climb gradient to clear instrument approach obstacles or maintain minimum vectoring altitude. In this case, the pilot must immediately assess: (1) Can I complete this approach to landing safely with the runway or landing area in sight, or will I reach decision altitude/minimums without visual contact? (2) If the approach cannot be completed visually, and a go-around is not performance-viable, the pilot may face forced landing options. This is precisely why OEI performance planning must be completed before every instrument approach in IMC — not in the cockpit during the emergency. The FAA emphasizes pre-flight risk management as part of the ADM process; identifying that OEI climb performance is marginal at planned weight and density altitude should have been a go/no-go factor before the flight or before the approach was commenced. This is also why some multiengine helicopter operators establish company minimums higher than published approach minimums when operating near single-engine performance limits.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR Part 135 (if applicable to operations); Rotorcraft Flight Manual OEI performance charts

questions.question: During a checkride OEI approach, the applicant correctly establishes the approach but then becomes visibly fixated on verifying the simulated failed engine's indications on the instrument panel rather than monitoring the approach path. The aircraft begins to slow below best single-engine climb speed and the descent rate increases. As the examiner, what risk management failure is being demonstrated, and at what point do you intervene?
questions.answer: The applicant is demonstrating 'cognitive tunneling' — a specific form of task fixation where attention is locked onto a single, less-critical task (verifying engine indications) at the expense of the highest-priority task (aircraft control). This is a textbook task prioritization failure within the ADM/SRM framework. The risks compounding are: airspeed decaying below Vy-OEI, increased descent rate potentially exceeding OEI go-around capability, and loss of situational awareness regarding approach path and obstacles. As an examiner, my intervention threshold is governed by 14 CFR 61.43 — I must intervene whenever continuation of the maneuver presents an immediate safety-of-flight risk. If airspeed continues to decay toward minimum single-engine control speed (Vmca or helicopter equivalent) or rotor RPM begins to droop, I intervene immediately and take control or direct 'go-around, my aircraft.' I would not wait until the aircraft is in an unrecoverable state. The test failure is documented not just as a 'skills' deficiency but as a risk management failure — the applicant demonstrated inability to identify and manage the distraction/fixation risk, which is the explicit standard under PH.VIII.C.R4.
questions.follow_up: After the checkride, the applicant argues that they were 'just being thorough' by checking the engine gauges and didn't realize the airspeed was decaying. How does this response itself reveal a deeper ADM problem?
questions.follow_up_answer: The applicant's response reveals a fundamental lack of situational awareness about their own cognitive state — sometimes called 'meta-cognitive failure' or 'I'm not aware that I'm not aware.' A pilot who doesn't recognize in real time that their attention has tunneled onto a secondary task — and who doesn't notice airspeed decaying — has demonstrated exactly the hazardous attitude of 'invulnerability' combined with poor self-assessment. The FAA's ADM framework identifies self-awareness as a core component: pilots must continuously monitor not just the aircraft but their own cognitive performance. The correct action during the approach would have been to consciously defer engine gauge verification — a task that provides no actionable value at that moment — in favor of the primary instrument scan. The argument 'I was being thorough' also suggests the pilot does not have an internalized priority hierarchy for OEI operations, which is a training deficiency. This response would inform my recommendation on whether the applicant is ready to retest and what additional training should be prescribed.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; 14 CFR 61.43 (Practical tests: general procedures); ACS PH.VIII.C.R4

questions.question: When flying a multiengine helicopter with one engine inoperative, what does 'OEI limits' refer to, and where do you find those limits for your specific aircraft?
questions.answer: OEI limits are the power, torque, temperature, and RPM limits published for the operating engine when it is carrying the full load of both engines. These limits are found in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for the specific aircraft, typically in the Limitations section and the Performance section. OEI limits are usually higher than normal all-engine-operating (AEO) limits because the certificated OEI ratings allow the engine to produce more power for a limited time to compensate for the failed engine. Common OEI ratings include: OEI 2-minute (maximum emergency power for up to 2 minutes), OEI 30-minute (for continued flight after engine failure), and OEI continuous (maximum continuous power with one engine inoperative).
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 27/29 (airworthiness standards); aircraft-specific RFM Limitations section

questions.question: During an OEI approach, what are the three most common engine parameters you must monitor on the operating engine to ensure you stay within OEI limits?
questions.answer: The three most critical parameters to monitor on the operating engine during an OEI approach are: (1) Torque (Q) — the most direct indicator of power being demanded from the engine; exceeding the OEI torque limit can cause gearbox or drivetrain damage. (2) Turbine gas temperature (TGT) or inter-turbine temperature (ITT) / exhaust gas temperature (EGT) — temperature limits are often the most restrictive OEI limit and can be exceeded quickly when demanding high power. (3) Engine/rotor RPM (N1, N2, Nr) — must remain within the green arc; rotor RPM decay indicates the engine cannot meet the power demand. The specific parameters and their OEI limit values are published in the aircraft RFM.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; aircraft RFM Limitations section

questions.question: What is the difference between a 2-minute OEI power rating and a 30-minute OEI power rating, and why does it matter during an OEI approach and landing?
questions.answer: The 2-minute OEI rating is the maximum emergency power the operating engine can produce for a period not to exceed 2 continuous minutes. It is the highest OEI power setting and is typically used only during the critical phase immediately following an engine failure — such as to maintain altitude or arrest a descent while establishing a stabilized approach. The 30-minute OEI rating is a lower power setting that the engine can sustain for up to 30 minutes, and is used for the continued flight and approach to landing. During an OEI approach, the pilot must be aware of which rating is being used and for how long, because exceeding the time limit at the 2-minute rating can cause engine damage or failure. The goal is to transition to the 30-minute or continuous OEI rating as quickly as practical and complete the approach and landing before those time limits expire.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 27.1521, Part 29.1521; aircraft RFM Limitations section

questions.question: You are established on a normal OEI approach in a twin-engine helicopter and at 200 feet AGL you notice the torque on the operating engine is already at the 30-minute OEI limit. As you slow below translational lift airspeed and begin the flare, what happens to the power demand, and how do you manage the collective to avoid exceeding OEI limits while still completing the landing?
questions.answer: As the helicopter slows below translational lift airspeed (approximately 16–24 knots depending on the aircraft), the rotor loses the efficiency provided by translational lift and requires significantly more power to maintain altitude and rotor RPM. This means torque, TGT/ITT, and other engine parameters will all trend upward — possibly into the 2-minute OEI range or beyond the 30-minute limit. To manage this: (1) Anticipate the power demand increase early by adjusting the approach angle so you arrive at the 'cushion' phase with energy to spare. (2) Allow a controlled, positive rate of descent through the loss of translational lift rather than trying to arrest it completely — trading altitude for airspeed management reduces the power spike. (3) Use the ground effect cushion in the final feet to reduce the power required for touchdown. (4) If torque exceeds OEI limits even momentarily, note the exceedance time and report it — the engine must be inspected per the RFM before the next flight. Do not attempt to hold a hover at OEI limits longer than necessary; get on the ground.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; aircraft RFM Emergency Procedures and Limitations

questions.question: During a simulated OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, the instructor reduces one engine to idle and you notice TGT on the operating engine is creeping toward the OEI red line as you fly the approach. What corrective actions can you take to bring TGT back within limits without abandoning the approach?
questions.answer: If TGT is approaching the OEI red line during the approach, the primary corrective action is to reduce the power demand on the engine: (1) Lower the collective slightly to reduce the power requirement — this is the most direct way to reduce TGT. Even a small collective reduction can bring TGT back within limits. (2) Adjust airspeed to the OEI best rate or best angle speed (published in the RFM) to maximize rotor efficiency and reduce power needed. (3) Verify the approach angle — a shallower approach reduces the power required to maintain the glidepath. (4) If at altitude, consider a slight descent to convert potential energy to rotor energy rather than demanding more from the engine. If TGT cannot be controlled within limits on approach, the pilot must be prepared to go around using available power (if within limits) or, if limits are already exceeded, to execute an immediate landing to the nearest suitable area. Prolonged over-temperature operations require post-flight inspection per the RFM.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; aircraft RFM Emergency Procedures

questions.question: You are flying a simulated OEI approach to a confined area. The only available landing spot requires a steeper-than-normal approach and a near-vertical final descent. How does this affect the power demands on the operating engine, and what technique adjustments do you make to protect the engine from exceeding OEI limits?
questions.answer: A steep approach with a near-vertical final descent significantly increases the power demand on the operating engine in the final phase. As the helicopter transitions from forward flight to a steep descent, rotor disk angle changes create increased induced power requirements. The loss of translational lift is more abrupt in a steep approach, creating a spike in power demand right when you are closest to obstacles and have least margin for error. Technique adjustments include: (1) Fly the approach at the upper end of the recommended OEI airspeed range to maintain translational lift as long as possible before the final descent. (2) Use a shallower power-on approach to the obstruction clearance point, then transition to the steeper segment — spreading the power demand over time rather than concentrating it. (3) Monitor TGT and torque continuously and anticipate the 'power bucket' at translational lift loss — pre-position the collective conservatively so you have upward range remaining. (4) Plan a positive rate of descent onto the landing surface rather than attempting a hover — this reduces total power time at OEI limits. (5) Know the OEI ceiling/hover OGE capability at the existing density altitude before committing to the approach; if the aircraft cannot hover OGE OEI at that altitude and weight, a vertical descent to hover is not a viable option.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; aircraft RFM Performance charts (OEI hover ceiling)

questions.question: During an OEI approach to landing, you momentarily exceed the 2-minute OEI torque limit by 5% for approximately 30 seconds. You land uneventfully. As the pilot in command, what are your obligations regarding this exceedance, and what determines whether the aircraft is airworthy for the next flight?
questions.answer: As PIC, you have an obligation to document the exceedance in the aircraft maintenance logbook, noting the parameter exceeded, the magnitude of the exceedance, and the duration. Under 14 CFR 91.7, the PIC is responsible for determining airworthiness before flight — an undocumented or unresolved engine exceedance means the aircraft cannot be legally dispatched. Most turbine engine OEI exceedances trigger mandatory inspection requirements specified in the Engine Maintenance Manual (EMM) or the Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM), which are part of the Type Certificate data. In many aircraft, any torque or temperature exceedance above the 2-minute OEI limit — even briefly — requires an engine inspection (borescope, hot section inspection, or full teardown depending on severity) before the next flight. The specific inspection requirement is found in the aircraft RFM (pilot's responsibility to know) and the maintenance manuals (mechanic's responsibility to execute). The aircraft is not airworthy until a certificated A&P mechanic or IA inspects the engine per those requirements and makes the appropriate logbook entry. The PIC cannot self-certify airworthiness following an engine exceedance.
questions.follow_up: What if the OEI exceedance occurred during a simulated emergency — the instructor reduced one engine to idle but it was still operating, so no actual engine failure occurred? Does that change the maintenance obligation?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — the maintenance obligation is determined by what the operating engine actually experienced, not the cause of the condition. If the good engine exceeded its OEI torque or temperature limits, regardless of whether the other engine was truly failed or only at flight idle during training, the exceedance happened and the engine must be inspected per the EMM. The engine has no way to 'know' it was a training scenario — the thermal and mechanical stresses are real. The PIC must still log the exceedance and ground the aircraft until the required inspection is completed. This is a critical ADM point: training scenarios that push OEI limits to the edge of the envelope carry real maintenance consequences and must be planned accordingly. Instructors and operators should be aware of this when designing OEI training profiles.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7 (airworthiness); 14 CFR 91.409; aircraft RFM Limitations; Engine Maintenance Manual (EMM)

questions.question: On an OEI approach, you are maintaining 30-minute OEI power on the operating engine. As you cross the threshold and reduce collective to land, rotor RPM begins to decay below the normal operating range. Walk me through exactly what is happening aerodynamically and mechanically, and what immediate corrective actions you take — without exceeding OEI limits.
questions.answer: Rotor RPM decay on an OEI landing flare occurs because the collective reduction reduces the fuel flow signal to the FADEC/fuel control, but if the engine is already at or near its OEI power limit, the governor may not be able to recover RPM quickly enough — or the reduction in collective may cause the rotor to lose energy faster than the engine can replenish it at the current power setting. Aerodynamically, as collective is reduced and disk loading decreases, the rotor should actually unload and RPM should increase or hold — but if the pilot reduces collective too aggressively (over-shoots the reduction), or if the rotor was already at the low end of the green arc due to high power demand throughout the approach, the sudden reduction can cause an RPM transient below limits. Mechanically, rotor RPM is a function of the balance between engine torque input and rotor disk drag load. Corrective actions: (1) Immediately apply a small collective increase to re-engage the engine drive and arrest RPM decay — this is counterintuitive because it adds torque, but restoring Nr protects the entire drivetrain. (2) Monitor TGT and torque during this correction — if torque goes to the 2-minute OEI limit, accept it for the few seconds needed to arrest the RPM decay, then reduce to 30-minute power as quickly as possible. (3) Simultaneously, use aft cyclic to reduce forward speed (reducing rotor disk drag) and help RPM recover. (4) Complete the landing with a positive rate of descent to the surface — do not attempt to arrest the descent to zero in a hover. The key principle is: rotor RPM below limits is an immediate emergency — a momentary 2-minute OEI torque exceedance to recover Nr is the correct trade-off. Get on the ground.
questions.follow_up: At what point during this scenario would you decide to enter autorotation rather than attempt to maintain powered flight OEI, and what tells you that you've crossed that threshold?
questions.follow_up_answer: The threshold for transitioning to autorotation during an OEI low-RPM scenario is when the operating engine can no longer maintain rotor RPM within or recoverable to the operating range — meaning collective increases are not arresting the Nr decay and the engine is at or beyond its OEI limit with no response. Specific indicators: (1) Nr continues to decay below the minimum operating RPM (bottom of green arc) despite collective input. (2) Engine instruments show the engine is at or beyond 2-minute OEI limits and still cannot maintain Nr. (3) The FADEC or engine control system signals a fault or the engine begins to surge. At this point, continuing powered flight risks a complete drivetrain failure or blade stall — both unrecoverable. The correct action is to immediately lower collective to full down to convert the remaining disk inertia into lift energy for the autorotation landing. Because you are already in the final approach phase and near the ground, this autorotation will be short and immediate — height/velocity diagram compliance prior to the approach is what makes this survivable. This is precisely why OEI approaches should always be flown with an escape route and within the H/V curve for the OEI condition.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Autorotation, Multiengine Failures); aircraft RFM Emergency Procedures; H/V diagram in aircraft RFM

questions.question: What are the specific tolerances you must maintain for altitude, airspeed, and heading during the final approach setup segment of an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: Per ACS standard PH.VIII.C.S2, prior to beginning the final approach segment you must maintain altitude within ±200 feet of the recommended profile altitude, airspeed within ±20 knots of the recommended speed, heading within ±10° of the desired heading, and maintain the correct lateral track to the landing area.

questions.question: Why does the ACS specify a 'recommended flight profile' rather than a fixed airspeed for the OEI approach setup segment?
questions.answer: The recommended flight profile is aircraft-specific and defined by the RFM/POH for that particular multiengine helicopter model. Different helicopters have different OEI best-rate-of-descent speeds, best single-engine climb speeds, and approach profiles depending on remaining engine power available, gross weight, and density altitude. The ACS defers to the manufacturer's recommended profile because no single speed or altitude applies universally across all multiengine helicopter types.

questions.question: What is the significance of 'prior to beginning the final approach segment' in this ACS standard — when exactly does the final approach segment begin for an OEI approach?
questions.answer: The final approach segment begins at the point where the helicopter transitions from the approach setup or downwind/base segment into the final descent path aligned with the landing area. This is often called the final approach fix or, in visual approaches, the point at which a stabilized descent profile to the intended landing spot is established. Everything prior to that point — the pattern, downwind, base turn — is where PH.VIII.C.S2 tolerances apply, ensuring the helicopter arrives at the final approach entry point configured correctly with energy and position well managed.

questions.question: You are flying the downwind leg of an OEI approach pattern and you notice your airspeed is 25 knots above the RFM-recommended approach setup speed. You are 1.5 miles from the turn to final. What are the risks of carrying that excess airspeed into the final approach segment, and how do you correct it?
questions.answer: Carrying 25 knots excess airspeed — which exceeds the ±20-knot ACS tolerance — into the final approach segment creates several risks: (1) The helicopter will arrive at the approach gate too fast, requiring aggressive deceleration during final which increases workload and power demand at a critical phase; (2) With one engine inoperative, the remaining engine is already near peak output, so a botched approach requiring a go-around or balked landing may exceed OEI power limits or be impossible; (3) Excessive airspeed reduces the pilot's ability to manage a precise energy profile to landing. To correct: reduce collective slightly to reduce power and increase parasitic drag, apply aft cyclic to increase pitch attitude and bleed off airspeed, cross-check with VSI and altimeter to avoid excessive descent while decelerating. Extend the downwind if needed to allow stabilization before turning final. The goal is to be within tolerance before beginning the final approach segment.

questions.question: During an OEI approach setup, you are holding the recommended airspeed and altitude within tolerances, but you have drifted 300 feet left of the extended centerline to the landing pad. The examiner has not called out a deviation. What should you do, and why does lateral track matter at this stage?
questions.answer: You should immediately correct back onto the centerline track with a coordinated turn. Although the ACS tolerance for heading is ±10°, maintaining track is a separate explicit requirement in PH.VIII.C.S2. A 300-foot lateral offset at approach distances means: (1) You will enter the final approach segment off-axis, requiring an S-turn correction that introduces heading and airspeed deviations during the most critical phase; (2) Off-track final approaches in OEI conditions increase the risk of a confined area miss or overshoot; (3) In real-world OEI scenarios, a runway or pad missed due to track error may leave no OEI go-around option. The correction is a gentle coordinated turn back to centerline, re-establishing track before beginning the final approach segment. Do not wait for the examiner to call it — self-correction is expected.

questions.question: You are setting up for an OEI approach at a density altitude of 6,500 feet. The RFM lists an OEI approach speed of 70 KIAS at sea level standard conditions. Should you fly exactly 70 KIAS, and how does density altitude affect your approach profile management to stay within ACS tolerances?
questions.answer: At 6,500 feet density altitude, you must consult the RFM performance charts to determine any density altitude adjustments to approach speed and to confirm OEI power margins. Do not assume the sea-level published speed of 70 KIAS applies unchanged — most RFMs provide separate performance sections or altitude-corrected speed tables that must be verified before committing to the approach. Key considerations: (1) OEI power available from the remaining engine is reduced at high density altitude, making airspeed management critical — maintain the RFM-specified speed for your density altitude to minimize excessive power demand; (2) Increased density altitude reduces translational lift efficiency, affecting the final transition to landing; (3) Any go-around or balked landing at high density altitude with OEI may be marginal or impossible — confirm power margins against the performance charts before beginning the approach; (4) The approach setup tolerances in PH.VIII.C.S2 become less forgiving because there is little room to recover from a poorly configured approach. Always cross-check density altitude performance in the specific aircraft RFM before proceeding, and plan for a no-go-around commitment point.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS PH.VIII.C.S2; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft RFM performance charts

questions.question: A student pilot flying an OEI approach setup consistently maintains the correct altitude and track, but repeatedly allows the heading to wander ±15° during the base-to-final turn before correcting back. The student argues this is acceptable because they always return to within ±10° by the time they roll out on final. How do you evaluate this performance, and what does it reveal about the student's understanding of the ACS standard?
questions.answer: This performance is unsatisfactory. The ACS standard PH.VIII.C.S2 states heading must be maintained within ±10° prior to beginning the final approach segment — this means throughout the setup segment, including during the base-to-final turn, not merely at the roll-out. Transient exceedances of ±15° during the turn indicate the student is managing the deviation rather than preventing it. In an OEI context, a ±15° heading swing during the base-to-final turn can carry the helicopter significantly off track (especially at lower speeds near approach profile speeds), which then requires correction on final at precisely the moment workload is highest. Additionally, excessive heading variation during a turn suggests insufficient coordination of pedals with bank angle, which in a single-engine-marginal power condition could introduce unwanted yaw and airspeed decay. The student's rationalization reveals a misunderstanding of 'maintain' versus 'return to' — the standard requires sustained maintenance, not periodic correction.
questions.follow_up: If the student continues to show heading wandering during the base-to-final turn, what specific control coordination technique would you teach to address this, and why is it more pronounced in OEI conditions?
questions.follow_up_answer: The correction is to pre-plan the bank angle and roll-out point for the turn, using a lead of approximately 10° of heading before the desired roll-out heading. In a multiengine helicopter with asymmetric thrust from OEI, the torque effect from the single operating engine is unbalanced compared to normal dual-engine flight. The pilot must actively apply more antitorque pedal input on the side opposite the failed engine to maintain coordination and prevent yaw-induced heading excursions during the turn. The uncoordinated tendency is more pronounced in OEI because rotor torque is being generated by only one power source, and without proper pedal trim, the helicopter will yaw as power changes occur during the turn. Teaching the student to consciously re-trim pedals throughout the bank, maintain a consistent rate of turn with cyclic, and use a specific roll-out lead heading will address both the symptom (heading wandering) and its OEI-specific cause.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS PH.VIII.C.S2; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9

questions.question: You are administering a practical test and the applicant, during the OEI approach setup, is 180 feet below the recommended profile altitude — within the ±200-foot tolerance — but the descent rate is 800 FPM and the nose is pitched down. They are at the recommended airspeed and heading. Do you allow this approach to continue to the final approach segment, and what does this situation reveal about the limits of using tolerances as the sole evaluation criterion?
questions.answer: This is a critical judgment call, and the correct answer for an examiner is to evaluate the trend, not just the snapshot value. The applicant is 180 feet low — technically within the ±200-foot ACS tolerance — but the 800 FPM descent rate and nose-down attitude indicate the helicopter is continuing to descend rapidly. At that rate, within seconds the applicant will breach the lower tolerance limit, and they will enter the final approach segment low and fast in a nose-down attitude — a dangerous energy state in OEI conditions. The ACS standard requires the pilot to 'maintain' the profile, which implies a stable, controlled condition, not a momentary pass through a tolerance band while trending further out of limits. A responsible examiner recognizes this is an unstable approach setup and should either call for a go-around/re-entry or, if safety of flight is immediately threatened, take control. This situation reveals the fundamental limitation of tolerances as pass/fail gates: they measure point-in-time position, not trajectory or trend. Competent OEI approach management requires the pilot to fly a stable, controlled profile — not chase tolerance limits on the way through them.
questions.follow_up: If you allow the applicant to continue and they arrest the descent, return to profile altitude, and stabilize before the final approach gate — should this be marked as a fault on the practical test report?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, this should be documented as a deficiency even if the applicant recovered. The ACS requires the pilot to maintain the recommended profile throughout the segment, and a 180-foot-low, 800 FPM uncontrolled descent represents a loss of the required flight profile even if momentarily within the altitude tolerance. The recovery itself also needs to be evaluated: in OEI conditions, a rapid collective pull to arrest an 800 FPM descent at low altitude could spike engine torque beyond limits on the operating engine, or induce mast bumping on certain designs. A complete practical test evaluation considers whether the applicant recognized the problem proactively or reacted late, what control inputs were used to recover, and whether the recovery introduced any secondary deviations. If the applicant demonstrated awareness, smooth recovery, and remained safely within all tolerances throughout, an unsatisfactory finding may not be warranted — but the deficiency must still be noted and discussed during debrief.

questions.question: During an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, what is the first radio call you should make once you have the aircraft under control and have identified the failed engine?
questions.answer: The first priority is aircraft control. Once the aircraft is stabilized and you have determined the situation is a distress condition (immediate danger to aircraft or life), declare Mayday on the current ATC frequency or 121.5 MHz: 'Mayday, Mayday, Mayday' followed by aircraft identification, nature of emergency (engine failure), position, altitude, intentions, number of souls on board, and fuel remaining. If the OEI is controllable and landing is assured without immediate danger, PAN-PAN (urgency) may be appropriate. Reference: AIM 6-3-1; 14 CFR 91.183 (IFR); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11.

questions.question: What is the international distress frequency, and when should you use it during an OEI approach if you cannot reach ATC on your assigned frequency?
questions.answer: 121.5 MHz is the international aeronautical emergency frequency. It is monitored by most ATC facilities, military radar, and many aircraft. If you cannot reach ATC on your assigned frequency during an OEI approach, you should immediately switch to 121.5 MHz and transmit your Mayday call. Guard (121.5) should always be your fallback when normal ATC contact is lost during an emergency.

questions.question: What information should be included in a pilot's initial emergency radio call when declaring an OEI emergency in a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: Per the AIM, the initial emergency transmission should include: (1) the distress signal 'Mayday' spoken three times; (2) the aircraft identification (call sign); (3) nature of the emergency (one engine inoperative); (4) pilot's intentions (e.g., landing at nearest airport or suitable area); (5) present position and altitude; (6) airspeed and heading; (7) number of persons on board; (8) fuel remaining in time. Not all of these must be in strict order — the key is communicating enough information for controllers and rescue personnel to assist.

questions.question: You are flying a multiengine helicopter on a VFR cross-country at 2,500 feet MSL and one engine fails. You are not currently talking to ATC. Walk me through the sequence and content of your radio calls from the moment you identify the failure through landing.
questions.answer: After stabilizing the aircraft (aviate first): (1) On current or nearest ATC frequency, transmit 'Mayday, Mayday, Mayday, [call sign], one engine inoperative, [position], [altitude], [heading], [airspeed], [POB], [fuel remaining], intend to land at [location or nearest airport].' (2) Squawk 7700 on the transponder to alert ATC radar. (3) If no ATC response, switch to 121.5 MHz and repeat the Mayday call. (4) If landing at a towered airport, contact tower and advise OEI status and intentions so emergency equipment can be alerted. (5) If landing off-airport, provide the most accurate position possible to aid search and rescue. Throughout the approach, maintain concise communication — do not let radio calls distract from flying the aircraft.

questions.question: You are conducting an OEI approach to a towered airport. ATC asks you to confirm your intentions and requests the number of souls on board. At the same time, your aircraft is drifting off course and your airspeed is decaying. How do you prioritize this situation?
questions.answer: Aviate-navigate-communicate — in that order. Immediately correct the aircraft heading and airspeed first. A brief 'Stand by' transmission to ATC is appropriate if you cannot safely handle both tasks simultaneously. Once the aircraft is stabilized, respond to ATC's request. Controllers understand that a pilot declaring an emergency has flying as the top priority. Attempting to answer ATC while allowing the aircraft to drift or lose airspeed in an OEI configuration is a classic workload trap that can be fatal — the aircraft will not fly itself while you talk.

questions.question: During a simulated OEI approach training flight, your instructor asks whether you need to transmit a Mayday call during the practice. What is the correct answer, and what radio calls should you make instead?
questions.answer: No — you should NOT transmit a Mayday call during a simulated emergency training flight because it would trigger an actual emergency response from ATC and emergency services. Instead, if the training is conducted at a towered airport, advise the tower that you are conducting simulated OEI approaches and practicing emergency procedures. If operating in practice areas, no specific call is required unless entering controlled airspace. The Mayday call is reserved for actual emergencies only. Misusing emergency frequencies is a violation and wastes emergency resources.

questions.question: You declare a Mayday during an OEI approach and land safely at an uncontrolled airport. ATC never canceled the emergency. Are you required to file a report, and what are the potential consequences of not doing so?
questions.answer: If ATC is aware of an emergency situation, the pilot may be required to file a report. Per 14 CFR 91.3(c), a pilot exercising emergency authority is not required to file a report — however, if requested by ATC, the pilot must submit a written report within 48 hours to the chief of that ATC facility. More practically, if you declared Mayday and went off frequency without canceling the emergency, ATC may have initiated search and rescue (SAR) operations, which are expensive, dangerous, and waste emergency resources. Best practice: as soon as you are safely on the ground, call ATC on a landline or radio to cancel the emergency and confirm your status.
questions.follow_up: What if you decided not to cancel the emergency because you were unsure if the aircraft was airworthy after the OEI landing — do you have any reporting obligations under the NTSB regulations?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes. If the emergency involved an engine failure that resulted in aircraft damage or injury, it may qualify as an accident or incident under 49 CFR Part 830 (NTSB regulations). An accident requires immediate notification to the NTSB and preservation of the wreckage. An incident involving engine failure in flight may require a report within 10 days. The pilot must assess whether the event meets the definitions under 49 CFR 830.2. Additionally, under 14 CFR 91.3, emergency authority protects the decision-making during the emergency, but it does not exempt the pilot from post-event reporting obligations.

issues: 14 CFR 91.3(c) actually requires a written report to the FAA (not just ATC) if requested — the answer states 'chief of that ATC facility' which is incomplete
49 CFR Part 830 is NTSB authority, not a reporting requirement that flows from 14 CFR 91.3(c); the follow-up answer conflates emergency authority with NTSB reporting, which are separate regimes
The answer should clarify that canceling emergency with ATC is prudent but not a regulatory requirement; the real issue is SAR response prevention
verification.suggested_correction: Revise: '14 CFR 91.3(c) states the pilot is not required to file a report of emergency authority exercise, but if requested by ATC or the FAA, must submit a written report within 48 hours. More critically, if you declared Mayday, you must cancel the emergency with ATC as soon as safely able to prevent SAR activation. Best practice: land, secure the aircraft, then call ATC (landline preferred) to cancel emergency and confirm status. NTSB reporting under 49 CFR Part 830 is a separate obligation triggered by accident/incident criteria, not by 91.3(c).'
verification.triage_note: Answer conflates 14 CFR 91.3(c) emergency-authority reporting with NTSB Part 830 incident/accident reporting as separate but related obligations; the regulatory basis and thresholds for each differ significantly and require expert clarification to avoid misleading a pilot on actual reporting requirements.

questions.question: During an OEI approach in IMC, ATC issues you a heading change and altitude restriction that would conflict with your established emergency descent profile. You are single-pilot, high workload, and struggling to maintain OEI approach power. How do you handle the communication and authority conflict?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.3(b), when an in-flight emergency requires immediate action, the pilot in command may deviate from any rule to the extent necessary to meet that emergency. This includes ATC instructions. You are legally authorized to deviate from the ATC clearance to maintain a safe flight profile. Communicate your inability to comply as soon as workload permits: 'Unable [instruction], emergency descent in progress, OEI, advise.' ATC is trained to support declared emergencies and will provide vectors, airspace protection, and obstacle clearance. Do not sacrifice aircraft control to comply with ATC — you have the authority and obligation to prioritize aircraft safety. Document the deviation and report it to ATC afterward.
questions.follow_up: After landing, ATC files a pilot deviation report because you violated the clearance. What is your best course of action, and does the emergency authority of 91.3 protect you?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 91.3(b) explicitly states that the pilot may deviate from any rule to the extent necessary to meet the emergency, and is required to submit a written report only if requested by ATC. The FAA's enforcement policy generally protects pilots who exercise good judgment during genuine emergencies — the Aviation Safety Hotline and the NASA ASRS (Aviation Safety Reporting System) report (Form ARC-277) provide additional protection from certificate action if filed within 10 days of the violation. Filing the ASRS report does not prevent a violation letter but does prevent suspension or revocation as long as the pilot was not acting recklessly. The key defense is demonstrating that the deviation was necessary, reasonable, and that proper emergency communication was attempted.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3(b) and (c); FAA Order JO 7110.65 (ATC Emergency Procedures); NASA ASRS Advisory Circular AC 00-46

questions.question: When planning your flightpath to a landing area during an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, what are the four primary factors you must account for?
questions.answer: The four primary factors are altitude, wind, terrain, and obstructions. Altitude determines how much energy and time you have to maneuver. Wind affects glide distance, groundspeed on final, and drift correction. Terrain dictates routing to avoid high ground and influences your decision on which direction to maneuver. Obstructions such as trees, wires, and structures define your obstacle clearance margins and may force you to modify your approach path or landing point.

questions.question: Why is wind direction particularly important when selecting and flying your flightpath to a landing area during an OEI approach?
questions.answer: Wind direction is critical for several reasons. Landing into the wind reduces groundspeed, which shortens the landing roll and minimizes kinetic energy at touchdown — both important when one engine is inoperative and performance is degraded. A headwind also improves translational lift during the approach, helping the operating engine carry the load more efficiently. Crosswinds complicate directional control, especially with reduced power margins, and a tailwind significantly increases groundspeed and the risk of a hard or overrun landing.

questions.question: During an OEI approach, what does it mean to 'follow a flightpath' to the selected landing area, and why must the flightpath be planned before beginning the descent?
questions.answer: Following a flightpath means executing a deliberate, pre-planned route from your current position down to the landing area — maintaining the correct groundtrack, descent angle, and airspeed throughout. Planning must occur before the descent because an OEI helicopter has limited power reserves and reduced margins for error. If the pilot improvises en route, there may not be enough altitude or energy to correct a path error, avoid a newly noticed obstruction, or go around. Preplanning ensures obstacle clearance, an into-wind final, and arrival at the landing area with controllable energy.

questions.question: You're flying a twin-engine helicopter at 1,500 feet AGL when an engine fails over rolling, forested terrain. There's a highway to your left that runs crosswind and a farm field 3/4 mile ahead that's aligned into the wind but has power lines across the approach end. Walk me through how you plan your flightpath to the farm field.
questions.answer: First, I confirm the aircraft is stabilized on the operating engine and assess whether I can maintain altitude or must descend — that determines urgency. I select the farm field as the better landing area because an into-wind landing is safer than a crosswind highway landing with traffic hazards. To address the power lines, I plan my flightpath to approach from an offset angle that allows me to visually clear the lines before transitioning to final, or I plan to cross them at sufficient altitude and then steepen the approach angle to land beyond them. I consider whether I have enough altitude to maneuver around the obstacle rather than over it. Throughout, I keep the terrain below me in view, avoid crossing high ridgelines unnecessarily, and maintain best single-engine speed until I'm established on a stabilized final. I commit early — I don't want to be low and slow while still deciding.

questions.question: You initiate an OEI approach and realize partway down that your angle is too steep to land short of your intended spot, and you're now low enough that a go-around on one engine may be marginal. What flightpath adjustments do you make, and how does your altitude awareness affect your decision?
questions.answer: If I'm high and steep on the approach, I have options: I can extend my flightpath by flying past the landing area and circling back if altitude permits, or I can shallow the approach by reducing collective slightly and flying a longer, lower-angle path. However, if I'm already committed — meaning I'm below a safe go-around altitude and airspeed is decaying — my priority shifts entirely to executing the safest possible landing with what I have. I avoid fixating on the original touchdown point; I aim for the first suitable surface available. Altitude is my most critical asset in this scenario — once it's gone, options disappear. The key lesson is that the flightpath must be evaluated continuously, not just at the start, and I must recognize quickly when a situation has shifted from recoverable to committed.

questions.question: How does terrain elevation change along your flightpath affect your OEI approach planning, and what mistake do pilots commonly make when descending toward rising terrain?
questions.answer: When terrain rises along the flightpath, your actual clearance above the ground decreases faster than your altimeter indicates because the ground is coming up to meet you. Pilots commonly fixate on the altimeter and believe they have more clearance than they actually do — this is a classic setup for controlled flight into terrain (CFIT). During OEI approach planning, I must evaluate the flightpath in terms of height above the terrain at each point along the route, not just altitude MSL. I plan to route around or above high terrain early, before I've descended to an altitude where options close off. On approach to a landing area in a valley or on a hillside, I must also account for rising ground on the sides of my approach corridor, not just directly ahead.

questions.question: During a checkride OEI approach simulation, you observe a student who selects an appropriate landing area and flies a reasonable path, but consistently allows the aircraft to drift 20-30 feet off the planned groundtrack due to uncorrected crosswind. At what point does this tracking error become a genuine safety concern on an OEI approach, and how would you debrief it?
questions.answer: Groundtrack deviation becomes a direct safety concern the moment it places the aircraft closer to obstructions, changes the approach angle relative to the landing area surface, or positions the helicopter for a crosswind or downwind landing rather than the planned into-wind landing. A 20-30 foot drift may appear minor in open airspace but near trees, wires, or structures it can eliminate safe margins entirely. On the debrief, I'd point out that the student's failure to apply wind correction early in the approach compounded over time — a small early drift becomes a large late deviation. The practical lesson is that crosswind correction on an OEI approach must be established early and checked continuously using ground reference points along the planned groundtrack. Workload and stress during OEI operations tend to degrade scan quality, making deliberate groundtrack monitoring a conscious discipline, not an afterthought.
questions.follow_up: The student argues that the drift was small and they corrected it before final. Why is late correction on an OEI approach more dangerous than on a normal approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: On a normal approach, a late correction typically requires a brief power addition or an S-turn to realign — actions the aircraft can absorb with normal power margins. On an OEI approach, power is limited and the operating engine may already be near or at contingency power limits. A late aggressive correction requires either additional collective input — which may not be available — or a steeper bank angle at low altitude and low airspeed, which increases the risk of vortex ring state, blade stall, or loss of effective translational lift. Additionally, late corrections mean the pilot is making high-workload control inputs in the final phase of the approach when they should be stabilizing for landing. Any destabilization late in an OEI approach significantly raises the risk of a hard landing or terrain contact.

questions.question: A multiengine helicopter crew loses an engine at night over suburban terrain with limited lighting. The crew identifies what appears to be a dark open area one mile ahead and slightly left. How should they plan the flightpath, and what factors make nighttime OEI flightpath planning fundamentally different from the daytime scenario?
questions.answer: At night, the crew must immediately recognize that visual assessment of the landing area and obstacles is severely degraded. The 'dark open area' may be a parking lot, rooftop, water, or terrain with invisible obstructions. Flightpath planning must incorporate available lighting — streetlights, vehicle headlights, and if equipped, the helicopter's landing light and any NVG systems — to continuously evaluate what lies along the route. The crew should not commit to a final approach until the landing area is positively identified as a safe surface with a clear approach path. Altitude management is even more critical at night because low-altitude maneuvering with terrain and obstruction uncertainty dramatically compresses reaction time. Crew coordination becomes essential: one pilot flies and manages the operating engine; the other scans and verifies the landing zone and approach corridor. The fundamental difference from daytime is that spatial awareness of terrain, obstructions, and even the landing surface itself cannot be assumed — every element that daylight makes obvious must be actively confirmed with available tools.
questions.follow_up: The crew has NVGs. Does NVG use eliminate the hazards of nighttime OEI flightpath planning?
questions.follow_up_answer: NVGs significantly improve situational awareness at night — they allow the crew to detect terrain, obstructions, and surface textures not visible to the naked eye. However, they do not eliminate the hazards. NVGs have a limited field of view (typically around 40 degrees), which means peripheral threats can be missed if the crew does not actively scan. They do not perform well against backgrounds with similar thermal or light signatures — wires, for example, are notoriously difficult to see on NVGs. Depth perception is also degraded compared to daylight, making accurate assessment of glide angle and flare timing harder. NVG-equipped crews must still apply systematic flightpath planning discipline and cannot treat NVG use as equivalent to daylight visual conditions.

questions.question: During an OEI approach and landing in a multiengine helicopter, at what point in the procedure are you required to complete the appropriate checklist?
questions.answer: Checklists must be completed at the appropriate phase of flight as prescribed by the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for that specific helicopter. For OEI operations, this typically includes an immediate-action memory items checklist at engine failure recognition, a follow-up checklist after the aircraft is stabilized, and a landing/shutdown checklist after landing. The specific timing and content are always dictated by the manufacturer's RFM, not pilot preference.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM for the specific multiengine helicopter

questions.question: What is the difference between memory items and a printed checklist in the context of an OEI emergency, and why does that distinction matter during an approach and landing?
questions.answer: Memory items are critical immediate-action steps that must be performed from recall without referencing a checklist because the urgency of the emergency does not allow time to look at a printed list — for example, securing the failed engine before it causes further damage. A printed checklist is used after the immediate threat is controlled to verify all steps were completed correctly and to complete remaining non-time-critical items. During an OEI approach, the distinction matters because the pilot must stabilize the aircraft and manage the approach first, then use the checklist to confirm actions without fixating on the printed page at a critical flight phase.

questions.question: Who has final authority on which checklist is used during a simulated OEI approach — the examiner, the instructor's notes, or the Rotorcraft Flight Manual?
questions.answer: The Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) has final authority. The RFM is the FAA-approved document for that specific make, model, and serial number of helicopter. During a practical test, the examiner is evaluating whether the applicant uses the correct manufacturer-approved checklist in the correct sequence. An instructor's notes or a generic checklist are study aids only and do not supersede the RFM.

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter at 1,500 feet AGL on final approach when an engine fails. You complete your memory items and stabilize the aircraft on a single-engine approach. At what point would you physically reference the printed OEI checklist, and how do you manage that task without losing situational awareness on the approach?
questions.answer: After completing memory items and stabilizing the aircraft in a controlled single-engine approach profile, the pilot should reference the printed checklist during lower-workload moments on the approach — not during the most critical phase such as short final or flare. Effective workload management involves scanning the printed checklist briefly, then returning full attention to aircraft control. If workload is too high (e.g., gusty winds, tight pattern), delay the printed checklist until the aircraft is on the ground or at a safe hover, then complete it. The key principle is: fly the aircraft first, complete the checklist second. Never sacrifice aircraft control to complete a checklist.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); applicable RFM

questions.question: During a simulated OEI approach on your checkride, you complete the memory items correctly but then skip the follow-up checklist because you are focused on flying the approach. The landing is smooth and controlled. Is this an unsatisfactory performance item? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: Yes, this would likely result in an unsatisfactory performance determination. ACS element PH.VIII.C.S5 specifically requires the applicant to complete the appropriate checklist(s), not just the memory items. Skipping the follow-up checklist is a task omission. In a real OEI event, failing to complete the follow-up checklist could mean a fuel shutoff valve was not positioned correctly, a fire handle was not pulled, or the dead engine was not properly secured — any of which could lead to an engine fire or other secondary emergency. A smooth landing does not compensate for incomplete emergency procedures.
questions.regulatory_ref: PH.VIII.C.S5 ACS Standards; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM

questions.question: Your multiengine helicopter RFM has a 'Continued Flight After Engine Failure' checklist and a separate 'Landing with One Engine Inoperative' checklist. Walk me through how you would sequence those two checklists during an OEI approach scenario from cruise altitude down to landing.
questions.answer: After completing immediate-action memory items at engine failure recognition: (1) 'Continued Flight After Engine Failure' checklist is completed once the aircraft is stabilized in level flight or a controlled climb/descent on the surviving engine — this typically includes confirming the failed engine's fuel, fire handles, and electrical systems are secured appropriately per the RFM. (2) As the aircraft transitions to the approach phase, the 'Landing with OEI' checklist is completed — this may include setting the remaining engine's power limits, landing gear configuration, confirming hydraulic systems, and briefing the landing zone. The pilot must not rush either checklist, but must also prioritize aircraft control and must not initiate the landing checklist so late on approach that checklist referencing distracts from the critical flare and landing sequence.

questions.question: You are conducting a simulated OEI approach and landing. During the approach, you are completing the OEI checklist and you notice a checklist item that calls for a cockpit action that would normally be unsafe to perform during a simulated emergency on a checkride — for example, actually shutting off fuel to an engine. How do you handle this, and what does this reveal about the limits of simulation?
questions.answer: During a simulated OEI checkride, certain checklist items — particularly those involving actually securing an engine (fuel off, fire handle pulled, ignition off) — are simulated rather than executed, because performing them on the operating engine or the 'failed' engine in flight could compromise actual aircraft safety. The correct technique is to verbalize and point to (challenge-and-response or read-and-do, per RFM guidance and training norms) each checklist item, clearly calling out 'simulating' for items that cannot be safely executed in flight. This reveals an important limit of simulation: not every checklist step can be fully executed in a training environment. The examiner is evaluating that the pilot demonstrates knowledge of the full checklist and the judgment to identify which steps are simulated versus completed, not just whether buttons are pressed.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot on a checkride actually shut off fuel to a simulated failed engine and then could not restart it, what are the regulatory and safety implications?
questions.follow_up_answer: This would constitute a genuine emergency requiring immediate action to restore fuel flow and attempt an engine restart per the RFM, or to execute an actual emergency landing. From a regulatory standpoint, 14 CFR 91.3 makes the pilot in command responsible for the safety of the flight, and no examiner instruction or checklist simulation protocol overrides that responsibility. The examiner has authority to take control of the aircraft per 14 CFR 61.47. The incident could also trigger an FAA investigation if the aircraft was placed in an unsafe condition. This scenario illustrates why simulated checklist items must be carefully briefed and pre-agreed upon before the flight, and why the PIC must exercise judgment about what is safe to simulate versus verbalize.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 61.47; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; applicable RFM

questions.question: During an OEI approach, your workload is high and your crew coordination with the co-pilot results in a checklist item being called but not confirmed as complete before you land. After landing, the review reveals the remaining engine's power turbine temperature limiter was not properly set per the checklist. The landing was safe. As a solo applicant on a checkride or as PIC in a real operation, what is the significance of that missed confirmation step?
questions.answer: In a real operation, failing to confirm the power turbine temperature limiter was properly set means the operating engine could have been exposed to an over-temperature condition during the high-power demands of a single-engine approach and landing — potentially causing undiscovered damage that shortens engine life or creates a latent failure mode. The fact that the landing was safe does not validate the omission. For a checkride applicant, this is a skills deficiency under PH.VIII.C.S5 because the standard requires the checklist to be completed, not just initiated. In crew operations, this reflects a breakdown in challenge-and-response discipline, which is a known contributor to incidents and accidents.
