This is a significant discrepancy that must be documented immediately in the aircraft logbook or discrepancy form. The aircraft is grounded until a qualified A&P mechanic inspects the chip detector and the oil system. The nature and location of the chip light (engine, transmission, tail rotor gearbox, etc.) should be clearly noted in the write-up.

questions.question: You complete a postflight inspection and discover a small crack in the tail boom skin near a rivet line. The crack appears superficial. Can you defer this and fly the helicopter on the next flight? Walk me through your decision-making process.
questions.answer: No, you cannot simply defer this on your own authority. Structural damage such as a crack in the tail boom skin must be evaluated by a certificated A&P mechanic before the next flight. The pilot must document the discrepancy in the aircraft records, and a mechanic must determine whether the damage is within the manufacturer's allowable limits as specified in the Structural Repair Manual (SRM) or requires repair. Unless the aircraft has an approved MEL that specifically lists this type of damage as deferrable (which is extremely unlikely for structural items), the aircraft is grounded. The FAA-H-8083-21B notes that components not listed as deferrable in the MEL require repair before departure. The pilot's responsibility is to document and report — not to make the airworthiness determination on structural damage.

questions.question: You just completed a hard landing in the field — the skids flexed noticeably. The helicopter appears normal during your postflight visual inspection. Are you required to document this, and what should your next steps be?
questions.answer: Yes, a hard landing must be documented regardless of whether visible damage is apparent. Many helicopter manufacturers have specific hard landing or over-stress inspection requirements triggered by exceedance of defined touchdown sink rates or load limits. The pilot must document the hard landing in the aircraft logbook or discrepancy form, noting the date, location, and nature of the event. A certificated A&P mechanic familiar with that airframe must then conduct a hard landing inspection per the manufacturer's maintenance manual before the aircraft is returned to service. Invisible structural damage (e.g., cracked frame members, compressed skid gear attachment fittings) can exist despite a clean visual check.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.409; 14 CFR Part 43; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8; applicable Rotorcraft Maintenance Manual

questions.question: During your postflight inspection, you find the fuel quantity is below minimums for the next planned flight, and the oil level on the main transmission is at the low mark. Walk me through how you document and handle both servicing requirements.
questions.answer: Both items are servicing requirements and must be documented. For the fuel, you would note in the discrepancy log or servicing record that fuel was required, the quantity added, and the fuel grade used. For the transmission oil, you document the low oil level observed and the quantity and type of oil added to bring it to within the specified range per the RFM and maintenance manual. All servicing entries must include the date, the product used (confirming it meets the manufacturer's specification), quantity added, and the servicing person's signature. If the transmission oil is repeatedly low or trending low, this is a discrepancy requiring maintenance investigation — not just a routine top-off. The pilot is responsible for ensuring these servicing records are accurate and retained per 14 CFR 91.417.

questions.question: You are flying a part 91 helicopter with an approved MEL. During your postflight inspection, you find a discrepancy on a system that IS listed on the MEL as deferrable. The MEL specifies an (O) category operation with a required placard and crew operating procedure. As the pilot, what are your documentation obligations, and who has authority to formally defer the item under the MEL?
questions.answer: Under an approved MEL, an (O) category item means a specific crew operating procedure must be performed before or during operation. The pilot does NOT have unilateral authority to defer a MEL item — in most operations, deferral authority rests with a certificated A&P mechanic or the operator's authorized representative, depending on the operator's MEL procedures document (MPD). The steps are: (1) document the discrepancy in the aircraft logbook; (2) have an authorized mechanic or person per the MEL/MPD formally defer the item with a proper logbook entry referencing the MEL section; (3) apply the required placard in the aircraft; and (4) ensure the crew operating procedure is briefed and understood before the next flight. The FAA considers an approved MEL to be an STC for that specific aircraft, meaning deviations from MEL procedures are deviations from the aircraft's approved type design.
questions.follow_up: The A&P mechanic defers the item and places the placard. The next morning a different pilot is assigned to the aircraft. Who is responsible for ensuring that pilot knows about the deferral and the required crew operating procedure?
questions.follow_up_answer: Both the operator and the acting pilot-in-command share responsibility. The operator must have a system in place (e.g., pre-flight briefing, squawk sheet review, logbook review requirement) to communicate active MEL deferrals to all assigned crews. The PIC has an independent obligation under 14 CFR 91.7 to determine airworthiness before flight, which includes reviewing the aircraft records, noting the deferral and placard, and understanding the required operating procedure before accepting the aircraft. A pilot who fails to review active deferrals and does not perform the required (O) procedure is operating outside the approved MEL and thus outside the aircraft's airworthiness limits.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.213; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8; SFAR 73 (as applicable to Robinson aircraft); operator MEL/MPD

questions.question: During your postflight inspection at a remote off-airport site, you find fresh oil streaking along the tail rotor driveshaft fairing. You have no mechanic on site, no maintenance manual, and the next scheduled flight is in two hours to return to base. What factors govern your decision on whether to document and depart, and what are the risks of getting this wrong?
questions.answer: This is a safety-critical situation with no simple 'right answer' that permits automatic departure. The pilot must document the discrepancy immediately — the finding of oil streaking on the tail rotor driveshaft fairing. The relevant decision factors are: (1) 14 CFR 91.7 requires the PIC to determine the aircraft is airworthy before flight — that determination cannot be made without understanding the source and severity of the oil leak; (2) a tail rotor driveshaft bearing or gearbox leak could result in loss of tail rotor effectiveness or catastrophic gearbox failure in flight; (3) without a maintenance manual and qualified mechanic, the pilot cannot make an informed airworthiness determination. The appropriate course of action is to NOT depart until a qualified mechanic can assess the source of the leak. Resources to contact include: maintenance via phone with photos, the aircraft manufacturer's tech support line, and if needed, arranging for a mechanic to travel to the site. The pilot must resist the 'get-home-itis' pressure, which is a recognized ADM hazard. Departing with an unknown oil leak on a safety-critical system like the tail rotor drive would be an exercise of poor risk management. Approximately 80% of aviation accidents are caused by pilot error and human factors — this is exactly the scenario where sound ADM must override operational pressure.
questions.follow_up: Suppose you call the manufacturer's tech support line and they tell you 'a small amount of oil weeping from the tail rotor gearbox filler cap is normal.' Does that conversation legally satisfy your airworthiness determination obligation under 91.7?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. An informal phone call with a manufacturer's tech rep, while valuable for gathering information, does not constitute a formal airworthiness determination or a maintenance action. The PIC's obligation under 14 CFR 91.7 is a judgment call they must make, but any actual maintenance action — including a determination that the leak is within limits — must be performed and documented by a certificated mechanic under 14 CFR Part 43. The tech support guidance should be relayed to a mechanic who can physically inspect and make the call. If the pilot decides to depart based solely on the phone call without a mechanic's inspection and logbook entry, they are assuming full personal liability for that airworthiness determination, and if an incident occurs, they will face scrutiny from the NTSB and FAA for departing with a known undocumented discrepancy.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR Part 43; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8 and Chapter 13

questions.question: After shutting down the engine, what is the primary reason you need to secure the main rotor blades, and how is this typically accomplished?
questions.answer: Rotor blades must be secured to prevent them from flapping or rotating in wind, which can cause blade strikes against the tail boom or fuselage and result in structural damage. This is typically accomplished by using rotor blade tiedowns or a rotor brake (if equipped), tying the blades to dedicated securing points on the airframe per the manufacturer's procedures in the RFM. The specific method varies by helicopter model and must follow the AFM/RFM for that aircraft.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8; aircraft-specific RFM securing procedures

questions.question: What document is your primary authority for the correct sequence and items required to secure your specific helicopter after flight?
questions.answer: The Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for that specific aircraft is the primary authority. The RFM is specific to each individual helicopter by serial number and registration, and it contains the manufacturer-approved shutdown and securing checklists. Per 14 CFR Part 91, pilots must comply with operating limitations and procedures specified in the approved RFM.

questions.question: Name at least four items you would typically address when securing a helicopter after parking.
questions.answer: Typical securing items include: (1) applying rotor blade tiedowns to prevent blade movement in wind, (2) installing pitot tube covers to prevent insect or debris intrusion, (3) setting the parking brake or placing wheel chocks as applicable, (4) installing control locks or gust locks to prevent flight control movement, (5) covering engine air intakes and exhaust stacks to prevent animal or debris entry, (6) ensuring all switches and avionics are off and the master switch/battery is off, and (7) locking cockpit doors and any external access panels. The specific items required are listed in the aircraft's RFM shutdown/securing checklist.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8; aircraft RFM securing checklist

questions.question: You've just landed at a remote off-airport site with no tiedown rings available and winds are forecast to increase overnight. What improvised securing options might you consider, and what are the limitations of those choices?
questions.answer: Options could include: using natural anchoring points such as trees or fixed objects with ropes tied to the skids, placing heavy objects on the skids to increase resistance to wind movement, and if available using portable tiedown stakes driven into the ground. However, all improvised methods carry limitations — ropes tied to skids may shift load into airframe structures not designed for that stress; staking in soft ground may pull free; no improvised method replaces certified tiedown hardware. The pilot should also consult the RFM for any guidance on skid loading limits and acceptable tiedown attachment points. If conditions are severe enough, the pilot must weigh whether the helicopter can safely remain at that site at all versus repositioning before conditions deteriorate.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8; aircraft RFM; ADM principles Chapter 13

questions.question: You complete your shutdown checklist and begin applying rotor blade tiedowns, but you notice one rotor blade has drifted well aft of its normal rest position before you could secure it. What hazard does this create, and how do you safely manage this situation?
questions.answer: A rotor blade that has drifted aft — particularly in a two-bladed system — can droop low enough that it approaches the tail boom height, creating a blade strike hazard if the blade swings further or if wind gusts cause additional movement. To manage this safely: do not walk under or near the blade path; approach cautiously from the fuselage side while keeping clear of the arc of movement; carefully guide the blade back toward its normal rest position using the blade grip or a blade sock — never grab the trailing edge; and then apply the tiedown. Personnel awareness is critical — ensure any bystanders are clear of the rotor disk before attempting to reposition the blade.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8 (rotor hazard awareness, ground safety)

questions.question: It's the end of the day and you're in a hurry. You decide to skip installing the pitot cover and intake plugs because 'you'll be back in the morning.' What are the realistic risks of that decision, and how does it connect to ADM principles?
questions.answer: Skipping pitot covers risks insect nesting inside the pitot tube overnight, which can block the system and cause erroneous or zero airspeed indications on the next flight — a serious instrument failure. Skipping intake plugs risks insects, rodents, or debris entering engine air intakes or exhaust stacks, potentially causing FOD damage on engine start. From an ADM perspective, this is a classic example of hazardous attitudes — specifically 'anti-authority' (dismissing checklist steps) and 'invulnerability' ('it won't happen to me'). Per Chapter 13 of the HFH, approximately 80% of aviation accidents are caused by human factors, and the error chain often begins with seemingly minor shortcuts. A single blocked pitot tube has caused fatal accidents. The correct action is to follow the full securing checklist every time regardless of schedule pressure.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8 and Chapter 13; ADM/SRM principles

questions.question: You're securing a turbine helicopter in high winds and notice that despite the rotor blade tiedowns being applied, the blades are still oscillating vertically. Walk me through your decision-making process — what are you looking for, and at what point does this become a maintenance issue rather than a securing technique issue?
questions.answer: First, verify the tiedowns are attached to the correct manufacturer-specified attachment points and are tensioned appropriately per the RFM — an incorrectly routed or slack tiedown will allow blade movement even when installed. Check that the tiedown hardware itself (straps, ratchets, rings) is serviceable and not worn. If tiedowns are correctly applied and the blade continues to oscillate excessively, this shifts from a securing technique issue to a potential maintenance concern. Possible causes include worn or failed blade dampers, loose hub components, or a teetering head with excessive play — none of which can be corrected by tightening a tiedown strap. At that point, the pilot must ground the aircraft, document the discrepancy in the maintenance logbook, and have a certificated A&P or IA inspect the rotor head before the next flight. Attempting to over-tension tiedowns to compensate for mechanical slop risks damaging blade roots or airframe attach points.
questions.follow_up: If you document this discrepancy and hand the aircraft off, but the next pilot looks at it and says 'it's been doing that for months, it's fine' — how do you respond and what are your options?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot-in-command of each flight bears independent responsibility for airworthiness under 14 CFR 91.7. The fact that a defect has been present previously does not make it airworthy. If the discrepancy has not been evaluated and signed off by an A&P, the aircraft remains unairworthy for that item. The responding pilot should not authorize the next pilot to fly the aircraft with an undocumented, uninspected mechanical issue. The correct action is to ensure the write-up is in the maintenance logbook (14 CFR 91.417 requires maintenance records be kept), contact maintenance for an inspection, and if operating under a Part 135 certificate, notify the Director of Maintenance. 'It's always been like that' is not an FAA-approved return to service.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7 (airworthiness responsibility); 14 CFR 91.417 (maintenance records); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8

questions.question: You land at an unfamiliar FBO and a line service technician immediately begins applying rotor tiedowns before you've finished your shutdown checklist. The tiedown points they're using don't match what you see in your RFM. What do you do, and who bears responsibility if the improper securing causes airframe damage?
questions.answer: Immediately stop the line technician before they apply tension to incorrect attachment points. The pilot in command retains responsibility for the aircraft until it is properly turned over to maintenance or a designated responsible party. Incorrect tiedown attachment points can transfer loads into the blade root, hub, or airframe structures not designed to accept those forces, potentially causing hidden structural damage not visible during preflight. Politely but firmly redirect the technician to the correct attachment points as specified in the RFM, or personally apply the tiedowns yourself. Regarding responsibility: the pilot in command has a duty of care for the aircraft under 14 CFR 91.7, and allowing an improper securing procedure to continue without objection creates shared liability. If damage results from improperly applied tiedowns the pilot permitted, the PIC could be held responsible for operating an unairworthy aircraft if they then flew it, and potentially face certificate action. Always document any concerns about ground handling in a written squawk or verbal notification to maintenance.
questions.follow_up: Suppose you allowed it to happen because you were fatigued and didn't notice until you came back the next morning. You see the tiedowns on incorrect points but no visible damage. Can you legally preflight and fly the aircraft?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not without a maintenance inspection. The fact that no visible damage is present does not mean structural damage didn't occur — composite blade roots and metal fittings can sustain hidden damage from improper load paths. Under 14 CFR 91.7, the PIC must determine the aircraft is in airworthy condition before flight. An improper tiedown application that may have imposed abnormal structural loads is a known discrepancy requiring an A&P to inspect and sign off the affected components before flight. Flying without that inspection would mean knowingly operating a potentially unairworthy aircraft, which is a violation of 14 CFR 91.7 and could constitute reckless operation under 14 CFR 91.13.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 91.13; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8; aircraft RFM tiedown attachment specifications

questions.question: When conducting parallel slope operations, what is the primary regulatory requirement regarding how the maneuver must be performed?
questions.answer: Parallel slope operations must be conducted in accordance with the helicopter manufacturer's limitations, if published. This means the pilot is required to consult the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) or Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) for that specific helicopter and comply with any stated restrictions, such as maximum slope angle, rotor RPM tolerances, or prohibited configurations during slope operations.

questions.question: What does 'parallel slope operation' mean, and how does it differ from a standard upslope or downslope landing approach?
questions.answer: A parallel slope operation means the helicopter is maneuvered so that its longitudinal axis runs parallel to the slope contour, rather than pointing directly up or down the slope. This exposes the helicopter to lateral slope angles instead of fore-and-aft ones, which changes how the skids or landing gear contact the terrain and how dynamic rollover risk presents itself. Standard upslope/downslope operations involve the nose or tail being higher or lower, while parallel operations place the high side and low side along the fuselage laterally.

questions.question: What happens if your specific helicopter's RFM does not publish any limitations for parallel slope operations? Are you free to perform the maneuver without restriction?
questions.answer: The ACS standard states manufacturer's limitations apply 'if published.' If no specific limitations are published in the RFM, the pilot is not automatically free to perform the maneuver without restriction. The pilot must still operate within safe aerodynamic limits, comply with 14 CFR 91.9 (never exceeding VNE or structural limits), apply sound aeronautical decision-making, and consider the helicopter's design characteristics such as tail rotor clearance, mast bumping susceptibility, and dynamic rollover thresholds. Absence of published limits does not equal unlimited authority.

questions.question: You are preparing to demonstrate a parallel slope operation on a 10-degree side slope. Before beginning, how would you determine whether this operation is within your helicopter's published limitations, and what specific items would you look for in the RFM?
questions.answer: Before the maneuver, I would open the RFM to the Limitations section and the Normal Procedures section. I would look for: (1) any published maximum slope angle for lateral or parallel operations; (2) restrictions on slope landing with certain fuel or weight configurations that could affect the center of gravity laterally; (3) tail rotor clearance warnings on sloped terrain; (4) any prohibition on lowering collective below a certain position during sloped landings to prevent blade-to-ground contact; and (5) any note about dynamic rollover critical angle for that specific model. If the RFM lists a maximum lateral slope of, say, 8 degrees, then a 10-degree slope would be a no-go and I would select a less severe site.

questions.question: During a parallel slope operation, you notice that as the uphill skid touches down, the helicopter begins to roll toward the slope more rapidly than expected. What risk does this represent, and how does compliance with manufacturer limitations reduce this risk?
questions.answer: This describes the onset of dynamic rollover. During parallel slope operations, if the uphill skid catches or if the pilot allows the helicopter to roll past the critical rollover angle — which varies by helicopter type and is typically published in the RFM — the rotor thrust vector begins to contribute to the rolling moment rather than opposing it, and recovery becomes impossible. Manufacturer limitations define the maximum allowable slope angle and may specify the correct cyclic position and rate of collective reduction during touchdown. Following these limits ensures the pilot keeps the rotor disk tilted uphill and maintains control authority throughout the landing sequence, preventing the rollover threshold from being exceeded.

questions.question: You are flying a Robinson R44, and your student asks whether they can skip reading the slope operations section of the RFM because 'helicopters land on slopes all the time.' How do you respond, and what specific risk does ignoring manufacturer limitations create on a parallel slope?
questions.answer: I would explain that skipping the RFM limitations section is never acceptable and creates direct legal and safety risk. Under 14 CFR 91.9, no person may operate an aircraft above its limitations, and the RFM is the authoritative source for those limits. On a parallel slope specifically, ignoring limits risks: (1) exceeding the dynamic rollover critical angle unique to that model; (2) allowing a main rotor blade to strike the uphill terrain if slope angle exceeds blade clearance limits; (3) imposing an asymmetric load on the skid gear beyond its structural design; and (4) tail rotor ground strike risk on steep lateral slopes. Each of these risks is model-specific and only quantified in the RFM.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.9; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; Robinson R44 RFM (model-specific)

questions.question: A pilot argues that because the ACS says manufacturer limitations apply 'if published,' and his helicopter's RFM is silent on lateral slope limits, he is legally permitted to perform parallel slope operations on any slope angle he can physically land on. Evaluate this argument from both a regulatory and risk management standpoint.
questions.answer: The argument is flawed on both levels. Legally, 14 CFR 91.9 prohibits operating beyond any limitation established for that aircraft, and while the RFM may not specify a slope angle, it still contains structural limitations, CG limits, and operating procedures that could be violated on extreme slopes. Additionally, 14 CFR 91.13 prohibits careless or reckless operation, which would apply if a pilot chose a slope clearly beyond safe limits. From a risk management standpoint, absence of a published limit does not mean unlimited capability — it means the manufacturer did not test or certify that specific parameter. The pilot assumes full liability for operating in an envelope the manufacturer has not validated. Aeronautical decision-making (ADM) principles require the pilot to assess the risk of the specific site, not default to 'if it's not forbidden, it's allowed.'
questions.follow_up: If during a post-incident investigation, it was found the pilot exceeded the helicopter's lateral CG limit because of uneven cargo loading on a parallel slope, which regulation would most directly apply beyond 91.9?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 91.9(a) directly covers operating above a maximum weight or outside the CG envelope. Additionally, if the imbalance resulted from improper weight and balance calculation, 14 CFR 91.9(b) applies, which states that no person may operate a civil aircraft unless it is within the weight and balance limitations in the flight manual. Both sections work together: 91.9(a) addresses the operating limitation, and 91.9(b) specifically addresses weight and balance compliance, which is directly implicated when lateral cargo loading shifts CG beyond RFM limits during a sloped landing.

questions.question: During a checkride, you ask the applicant to demonstrate a parallel slope operation. Before executing, the applicant states the RFM has a published maximum lateral slope limitation of 8 degrees, but visually estimates the site at approximately 7 degrees. What risk management issues do you want the applicant to address, and what is the consequence of proceeding if the estimate is wrong?
questions.answer: The applicant should address: (1) the reliability of a visual slope estimate — without a clinometer or slope measurement tool, a 1-degree margin is not a meaningful safety buffer; (2) variable terrain within the landing zone that may present localized steeper angles than the average slope; (3) the consequence of being wrong is operating outside manufacturer limitations, which means the helicopter is being operated outside its tested and certified envelope; (4) the dynamic rollover risk is non-linear — exceeding the critical angle even slightly can result in an unrecoverable rollover; (5) proper ADM requires either measuring the slope more precisely, selecting a site that is clearly within limits with a comfortable margin, or declining to conduct the operation. Proceeding on a 1-degree estimated margin when the stakes are rollover and structural damage reflects inadequate risk management and is a potential PTS/ACS failure point.
questions.follow_up: What practical technique can a pilot use in the field to more accurately assess slope angle before committing to a parallel slope landing?
questions.follow_up_answer: Several practical techniques exist: (1) Use a dedicated slope measurement app on an EFB or smartphone with a built-in inclinometer to measure actual terrain angle before landing; (2) carry a physical bubble inclinometer in the flight bag; (3) perform a low hover recon pass and observe how the helicopter must be banked to maintain a level attitude parallel to the slope — the required bank angle approximates the slope angle; (4) assess ground references such as water runoff lines and vegetation patterns which give visual cues to steeper-than-expected terrain; (5) consider that if you are uncertain whether the slope is within limits, it is always safer to select a different, more clearly acceptable site rather than proceed on a marginal estimate.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Slope Operations); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM); 14 CFR 91.9

questions.question: When no slope limitations are published in a helicopter's RFM, what is the generally accepted maximum slope angle for demonstrating slope operations?
questions.answer: When no slope limitations are published in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual, the FAA accepts slope operations in the range of approximately 5 to 10 degrees as a safe demonstration range. Pilots should treat this as a conservative operational limit, not a challenge to exceed. The specific angle within that range should be chosen based on terrain, conditions, and aircraft performance on the day of the operation.

questions.question: Where is the primary place a pilot should look to find published slope limitations for a specific helicopter model before attempting slope operations?
questions.answer: The primary source for slope limitations is the helicopter's Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) or Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH), specifically in the Limitations section. If that section contains no slope limitation data, only then does the 5–10 degree guideline apply. Never assume limitations are absent without actually checking the RFM.

questions.question: What are the key mechanical risks that make slope angle a critical safety concern during slope landing or takeoff operations in a helicopter?
questions.answer: The primary mechanical risks during slope operations are (1) main rotor blade contact with terrain as the helicopter tilts on the slope—the downhill rotor blade sweeps closer to the ground as cyclic is applied toward the uphill side—and (2) dynamic rollover, which occurs when the uphill skid becomes a pivot point and the aircraft's rolling moment exceeds rotor control authority. Dynamic rollover is particularly dangerous because it can develop in less than a second and lead to catastrophic structural failure. Both risks increase with slope angle and underscore the importance of slope angle limits and precise cyclic control during touchdown and liftoff.

questions.question: You are flying an older turbine helicopter for which the RFM contains no slope limitation. The landing zone coordinator tells you the slope is 'about 12 degrees' and asks you to land. How do you evaluate and respond to this request?
questions.answer: Since no RFM limitation is published, the FAA guideline of 5–10 degrees applies as the safe operational range. A 12-degree slope exceeds that range and should be treated as a significant risk factor. Before refusing outright, I would conduct a low reconnaissance to visually assess the actual slope angle, soil stability, rotor clearance, and any dynamic rollover potential. If the slope genuinely appears to exceed 10 degrees, I would decline the landing and communicate to the coordinator that the slope exceeds safe operating parameters for this aircraft without published approval for steeper angles. Mission urgency does not override mechanical limits—rotor blade strike or dynamic rollover could result in a fatal accident.

questions.question: A student pilot asks why the 5–10 degree range is described as 'approximately' in the ACS rather than a hard limit. How do you explain this from a risk management perspective?
questions.answer: The word 'approximately' reflects the reality that slope risk is multifactorial — the exact safe limit varies with rotor diameter, skid width, aircraft weight, slope surface conditions, wind direction relative to the slope, and pilot proficiency. A larger-diameter rotor has less clearance margin on a given slope than a smaller one. A soft or uneven surface adds dynamic rollover risk. The 5–10 degree range is a conservative general guideline in the absence of manufacturer data, not a tested and certified approval. Treating it as a hard limit at 10 degrees would be a false sense of precision. Risk management requires pilots to assess all factors and remain well within the margin, not push to the edge of any guideline.

questions.question: During slope operations on a 7-degree slope, wind is blowing directly up the slope at 15 knots. How does this wind direction affect your risk assessment, and what approach technique should you use?
questions.answer: Wind direction relative to slope orientation affects aircraft handling during slope approaches. An upslope wind can complicate control inputs and approach stability because it affects the relative wind angle to the rotor disk and may require increased anti-torque pedal inputs. Best practice is to approach perpendicular to the slope (across the fall line) whenever possible, which naturally tends to align the approach into the wind on sloped terrain. A 15-knot upslope wind on a 7-degree slope is manageable but requires heightened attention to approach stability and dynamic rollover risk during touchdown. Always execute a go-around if the approach becomes unstable.

questions.question: An operator verbally tells you that their company uses 15 degrees as the standard for slope operations in your helicopter model, claiming their chief pilot approved it. No RFM limitation or FAA-approved supplement exists. What is your legal and professional obligation, and what risk does exceeding the 5–10 degree guideline introduce?
questions.answer: Verbal operator guidance does not override FAA standards or the absence of RFM-published limits. In the absence of a manufacturer-published limitation or an FAA-approved operational specification authorizing steeper slopes, the 5–10 degree guideline from FAA-H-8083-21B is the applicable reference. Operating at 15 degrees without RFM backing puts the pilot at risk of blade strike, dynamic rollover, and a finding of reckless operation under 14 CFR 91.13 if an accident occurs. The pilot in command bears ultimate responsibility under 14 CFR 91.3 and cannot delegate that responsibility to a chief pilot's verbal approval. The correct course of action is to decline operations beyond the 5–10 degree guideline until the manufacturer provides a flight-tested approval or the operator obtains a formal deviation authority. Pressure from operators to exceed safety guidelines is an ADM red flag.
questions.follow_up: If the operator provides a written SOP authorizing 15 degrees and tells you it's been 'approved by the FAA,' what document would you need to actually see to confirm that approval is legitimate?
questions.follow_up_answer: A legitimate FAA approval for operations exceeding the published or guideline slope limits would appear as an Operations Specification (OpSpec) issued under 14 CFR Part 135 or Part 91 Subpart K if the operator is certificated, or as an FAA-approved amendment to the RFM (Rotorcraft Flight Manual Supplement). A company SOP, even if labeled as FAA-approved, has no regulatory authority on its own. The pilot should ask to see the actual OpSpec document or the FAA-approved RFM supplement, not just take the operator's word for it. If those documents do not exist, the 5–10 degree guideline remains the operative limit.

questions.question: You successfully complete a slope landing at approximately 8 degrees. While the uphill skid is on the ground and the downhill skid is still airborne, you notice the helicopter beginning to roll toward the uphill side faster than expected. What is happening, and what is your immediate corrective action and abort threshold?
questions.answer: What you are experiencing is the onset of dynamic rollover. As the uphill skid contacts the ground and becomes a pivot point, lateral cyclic toward the uphill side combined with collective application can create a rolling moment that exceeds the rotor's ability to counteract. The critical rollover angle varies by helicopter but can be reached in less than a second once rolling momentum builds. Immediate corrective action: reduce collective aggressively to decrease total rotor thrust and the rolling moment, while simultaneously applying cyclic away from the direction of roll (toward the downhill side). If the roll rate is not arrested immediately, execute a go-around by increasing collective and lifting off entirely — do not attempt to hold the ground contact while the roll is progressing. The abort threshold is any moment when roll rate toward the uphill side is increasing rather than stopping. There is no value in maintaining ground contact while dynamic rollover is developing — the consequence is a catastrophic rollover and blade strike.
questions.follow_up: After safely going around, what reconnaissance steps would you take before attempting the slope landing again, and would you change anything about your approach technique?
questions.follow_up_answer: After a go-around due to dynamic rollover onset, the pilot should conduct a low slow reconnaissance of the slope to assess whether the surface condition changed (soft spot, unexpected depression, or loose material under the skid caused the sudden roll). Reassess the actual slope angle — it may be steeper than initially estimated. Check wind for any crosswind component that may have contributed to the lateral rolling moment. For the next attempt, land with a shallower approach angle, touch the uphill skid with more deliberate control, and apply collective reduction more smoothly and earlier. Consider whether the slope is within the 5–10 degree guideline — if the rollover onset occurred at what appeared to be 8 degrees, the actual slope or a terrain irregularity may have placed the effective contact angle higher than safe. If conditions cannot be confirmed as safe, select an alternate landing site.

questions.question: The ACS specifically states that landings with the helicopter facing downhill or uphill will not be tested during certification. Why does the FAA exclude these orientations from the practical test?
questions.answer: Landings facing directly uphill or downhill are excluded because they represent the highest-risk slope orientations. When facing uphill, the upslope skid touches first and the pilot must apply significant aft cyclic to keep the rotor disk level, which risks the downhill rotor blade striking the terrain. When facing downhill, forward cyclic is required, which raises the tail and risks tail rotor/empennage contact with the slope. Both orientations dramatically reduce the margin for error and are considered too hazardous to standardize as a certification maneuver. The FAA limits slope landing testing to approaches made across the slope (perpendicular to the fall line), which is the safest technique.

questions.question: What is the primary hazard associated with landing a helicopter on a slope when the helicopter is oriented facing directly downhill?
questions.answer: When facing downhill, the pilot must apply forward cyclic to maintain a level rotor disk relative to the slope. This forward cyclic input tilts the nose down and raises the tail, increasing the risk of the tail rotor or tail boom striking the uphill slope surface. Additionally, if the helicopter begins to slide, it will slide forward in the direction of the downhill slope, which can accelerate the aircraft uncontrollably. This combination of tail strike risk and loss of directional control on a downhill slope makes this orientation extremely dangerous.

questions.question: When conducting a slope landing across the slope — the method that IS tested — which skid contacts the ground first, and why is that sequence important?
questions.answer: The uphill skid contacts the ground first. This is important because it allows the pilot to use lateral cyclic toward the uphill side to keep the rotor disk level as collective is reduced. If the downhill skid touched first, the helicopter would roll sharply toward the uphill side as weight settled onto the skids, dramatically increasing the risk of the rotor blade striking the uphill terrain. Landing uphill-skid-first gives the pilot control over the settling process and minimizes dynamic rollover risk.

questions.question: You are on a mountain rescue mission and the only available landing zone requires you to land facing uphill due to terrain and wind constraints. As pilot-in-command, how do you assess whether to attempt this landing, and what does the ACS exclusion of this maneuver from testing tell you about the risk level involved?
questions.answer: The ACS exclusion signals that facing uphill on landing is considered too hazardous to standardize for certification — meaning even trained, certificated pilots are not expected to demonstrate it as a routine skill. As PIC, this should trigger a full risk assessment: (1) Evaluate slope angle — even a few degrees uphill can require significant aft cyclic that brings the rear rotor close to terrain; (2) Assess whether tail rotor/empennage clearance from the uphill slope is sufficient; (3) Consider all alternatives including a running-on or hovering load set; (4) Apply PAVE/IMSAFE and accept that mission urgency can create get-there-itis. The real-world nature of a rescue does not eliminate the physics — if the slope is too steep or the LZ too confined, attempting an uphill-facing landing risks the aircraft and crew, potentially worsening the rescue situation. The ADM principle from FAA-H-8083-21B applies: if an action will only 'probably' work, choose a known-safe alternative.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 13; ACS PH.XIV.A

questions.question: During a slope landing approach across the slope, you realize at the last moment that your intended touchdown spot is actually steeper than it appeared during reconnaissance. At what point in the maneuver does it become most hazardous to continue, and what are your options?
questions.answer: The most hazardous point is once the uphill skid has made contact and weight has begun transferring to the skids — at that point you are committed to that specific spot and slope angle. The risk of dynamic rollover increases rapidly as collective is reduced because the uphill skid becomes a pivot point. If you recognize the slope is steeper than expected before the skid touches, the safest option is to abort — apply collective to re-establish a hover and reposition. During reconnaissance, the FAA recommends a low hover reconnaissance pass to accurately assess slope angle before committing. Once partial contact is made, removing the downhill skid from the slope while maintaining heading requires careful lateral cyclic; if the slope exceeds the aircraft's lateral cyclic authority limits, continuation is not safe and power must be applied immediately to depart.

questions.question: Wind direction can force you into an uphill or downhill landing orientation on some slopes. How does wind interact with slope orientation risk, and what tradeoffs must a pilot weigh when wind favors an orientation that is excluded from testing?
questions.answer: Landing into the wind is normally preferred to reduce groundspeed and improve translational lift/controllability. However, on a slope, if the wind is blowing directly up the slope, landing into the wind means landing uphill-facing — one of the excluded orientations. The tradeoff is: a crosswind slope landing (across the slope) is safer structurally and for dynamic rollover prevention, even with a slight tailwind component, rather than landing uphill. The pilot must assess wind velocity — a light tailwind component during an across-slope landing is generally far safer than the cyclic limit and tail-strike risk of an uphill-facing landing. At higher wind speeds the calculus changes, but the FAA's exclusion of uphill/downhill landings from testing reflects that the mechanical hazards of those orientations typically outweigh tailwind penalties in a certification context. The PIC must apply sound ADM and not allow wind preference to override structural safety limits.

questions.question: A student preparing for a checkride asks you: 'If facing uphill and downhill are excluded from testing because they're too dangerous, why do we even train for them at all?' How do you answer that, and what does this exclusion reveal about the relationship between training standards and operational risk tolerance?
questions.answer: The ACS represents minimum certification standards, not the full scope of what a pilot may encounter operationally. Excluding these orientations from testing acknowledges that demonstrating them in a standardized test environment — where conditions may not be ideal and an examiner is aboard — carries unacceptable risk for a certification event. However, a mountain rescue pilot, utility operator, or fire suppression pilot may routinely face these situations. Training for uphill/downhill landings should occur progressively, in controlled environments, with an experienced instructor, on known gentle slopes, building up the pilot's understanding of cyclic authority limits and dynamic rollover risk. The exclusion actually reinforces the principle that additional training beyond minimum standards is the pilot's responsibility. FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 notes that accidents decrease significantly after 100 hours in type — meaning experience beyond certification minimums is where real risk reduction occurs.
questions.follow_up: You said cyclic authority limits matter for uphill landings. How does a pilot determine, before landing, whether the slope angle exceeds their specific helicopter's lateral cyclic authority?
questions.follow_up_answer: The helicopter's Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) specifies the maximum slope angle the aircraft is certified to land on — typically expressed in degrees. For most light helicopters this is in the range of 8–10 degrees, though it varies by type. Before landing, the pilot should perform a low reconnaissance hover directly over the intended spot and compare the apparent slope angle to the known limits in the RFM. Some operators use a simple visual check: with the helicopter in a level hover just above the slope, observe how much lateral cyclic displacement would be needed to place the rotor disk parallel to the slope — if you're approaching the cyclic stops, the slope is too steep. In mountainous operations, an inclinometer or slope meter is sometimes used during the recon. The pilot must never commit to a slope landing without first confirming the angle is within the RFM-specified limit.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 13; ACS PH.XIV.A; Aircraft RFM (manufacturer-specific)

questions.question: Dynamic rollover is the primary structural hazard during slope landings. Explain the mechanism by which a slope landing — even one performed correctly across the slope — can initiate a dynamic rollover, and what specific pilot input errors accelerate it.
questions.answer: Dynamic rollover occurs when the helicopter rotates about a fixed pivot point — in a slope landing, the uphill skid — faster than the pilot can counteract with cyclic. The mechanism begins when the uphill skid contacts the slope and the pilot reduces collective. As lift decreases, more weight transfers to the uphill skid. If the pilot then allows the downhill skid to settle without maintaining uphill lateral cyclic, or if the helicopter begins to slide uphill, the center of gravity shifts beyond the pivot point and the rotor's natural tendency is to continue rolling uphill. Once the roll rate exceeds approximately the critical rollover rate (which varies by type but occurs rapidly), cyclic input alone cannot arrest it. Specific input errors that accelerate the process: (1) Reducing collective too quickly, transferring weight to the pivot point before the pilot is ready; (2) Allowing the downhill skid to catch on the terrain or vegetation, fixing it as a second pivot; (3) Applying downhill lateral cyclic inadvertently, which adds angular momentum in the rollover direction; (4) Using excessive left pedal (on counterclockwise rotor systems) which increases tail rotor thrust and can contribute to lateral rolling moment. The correct technique is to maintain uphill cyclic pressure throughout the landing and be prepared to immediately add collective and abort if any lateral rolling tendency develops.
questions.follow_up: At what point during a slope landing is it too late to abort if dynamic rollover begins, and what is the last effective recovery input available to the pilot?
questions.follow_up_answer: Once the roll attitude reaches approximately 5–8 degrees past the critical angle — which varies by helicopter type — collective reduction actually accelerates the rollover because it removes the gyroscopic rigidity of the rotor system and reduces the effectiveness of lateral cyclic. The last effective input is a rapid, simultaneous application of full collective and lateral cyclic away from the slope (downhill cyclic) to attempt to become airborne before the roll attitude becomes unrecoverable. However, this window is extremely narrow — dynamic rollover can progress from onset to unrecoverable in under one second. This is why prevention through proper technique and immediate abort at the first sign of uncommanded lateral movement is far more effective than any recovery attempt. The FAA and manufacturers emphasize that dynamic rollover is almost always fatal once it progresses past a certain threshold, reinforcing why the ACS excludes the highest-risk slope orientations from certification testing entirely.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; Aircraft RFM (manufacturer-specific dynamic rollover limitations)

questions.question: Before conducting slope operations, what specific types of hazards should you be looking for during your area reconnaissance?
questions.answer: During a slope reconnaissance you must identify: (1) obstacles that could strike the rotor system — trees, rocks, brush, or terrain features near the intended landing spot; (2) surface conditions — loose rock, soft soil, or unstable ground that could shift under skid weight; (3) slope angle relative to your helicopter's maximum allowable slope landing limit (typically 8–10° depending on the aircraft); (4) wind direction and potential rotor-to-terrain clearance on the upslope side; and (5) escape route availability if the landing must be aborted. The goal is to confirm the area is clear of anything that could contact any part of the helicopter during approach, landing, or departure.

questions.question: Why is rotor clearance from the upslope terrain considered the most critical hazard during slope landing operations?
questions.answer: When a helicopter lands on a slope, the cyclic must be tilted into the slope to keep the rotor disc level and prevent the helicopter from sliding. This positions the upslope rotor blade much closer to the terrain than on flat ground. If the slope is too steep, or if the pilot allows the aircraft to drift toward the slope, the rotor blade can strike the terrain, resulting in a catastrophic accident. This is why the upslope rotor-to-terrain clearance must be visually confirmed before committing to landing, and why the slope must be within the helicopter's approved limitations.

questions.question: What is the purpose of conducting a low reconnaissance pass before landing on a slope, and how should it be flown?
questions.answer: A low reconnaissance pass allows the pilot to closely inspect the intended landing area for obstacles, surface conditions, slope angle, and escape route viability that may not be visible from altitude. It should be flown at a safe altitude and airspeed that keeps the helicopter within the height-velocity (H-V) diagram safe zone while still providing an adequate view of the slope. The pass should cover all four sides of the intended landing spot to evaluate upslope rotor clearance, approach and departure paths, and any hazards hidden by terrain features or vegetation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Advanced Flight Maneuvers — Reconnaissance Procedures

questions.question: You are on final approach to a sloped hillside when you notice the intended landing spot has loose shale and scattered boulders partially obscured by tall grass. How do you manage this risk and what is your decision process?
questions.answer: This scenario demands an abort or relocation decision before committing to landing. The risks are: (1) loose shale can shift under skid weight causing rollover; (2) boulders obscured by vegetation could contact the belly, skids, or tail rotor; (3) grass can hide the true slope angle. The appropriate risk management process is: recognize the hazard early enough to maintain a safe go-around option (do not allow yourself to get low and slow into a bad spot), execute a go-around, conduct another reconnaissance pass at a lower altitude to reassess, and either select an alternate landing site that meets safety criteria or abort the operation entirely. Continuing into a known hazard violates basic risk management principles — if the area cannot be confirmed clear of hazards, do not land.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations; Chapter 13, ADM and Risk Management

questions.question: During your slope operations area review, you note that the slope faces into the wind, which would give you a nice headwind on approach. However, the upslope terrain rises sharply just 50 feet behind the intended spot. How does this terrain feature affect your risk assessment?
questions.answer: While a headwind is favorable for approach performance, the rising terrain 50 feet upslope creates two significant risks: (1) Rotor blade clearance — during landing with cyclic tilted into the slope, the upslope rotor blade arc extends toward that rising terrain; 50 feet may be insufficient clearance depending on rotor diameter. (2) Escape route restriction — if a go-around or abort becomes necessary after touchdown (e.g., unexpected slope shift or rollover tendency), the rising terrain behind you blocks a rearward exit and limits your forward climbout corridor. The favorable headwind does not offset these hazards. The upslope terrain must be assessed for rotor clearance using the specific helicopter's rotor diameter, and an alternative escape route must exist before this site can be considered acceptable.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations — Rotor Clearance and Escape Routes

questions.question: You are planning a slope landing in a mountainous area at 7,500 feet MSL on a warm afternoon. How does density altitude factor into your area review and hazard assessment for slope operations specifically?
questions.answer: High density altitude directly degrades power available, which creates slope-specific hazards: (1) Hover power margin is reduced — you may not be able to hover OGE or even IGE to reposition if the landing spot is unsuitable; this means your go-around option is degraded. (2) If you encounter a dynamic rollover tendency or need to lift off abruptly, the helicopter may not have sufficient power to respond quickly. (3) The effective translational lift (ETL) speed on approach occurs at the same airspeed but provides less actual lift benefit at altitude, requiring more precise power management. For area review purposes, this means you must pre-confirm adequate power margins during planning (performance chart check), avoid committing to a spot where a hover-repositioning abort may be impossible, and ensure the selected slope is within limits because corrective control inputs will be more sluggish with reduced power available.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations; Chapter 11, High Altitude Operations

questions.question: A pilot conducts what appears to be a thorough visual reconnaissance of a slope site from 200 feet AGL at 40 knots and decides the area is clear. He lands, and the upslope skid settles into soft soil hidden beneath ground cover, beginning a slow rollover. What systematic failures in the area review contributed to this outcome, and how should the reconnaissance have been conducted to reveal this hazard?
questions.answer: The systematic failures include: (1) Insufficient altitude-to-detail tradeoff — at 200 feet AGL and 40 knots, ground cover texture, soil moisture, and surface stability cannot be reliably assessed; a slower, lower pass (within safety limits) over the specific landing spot is necessary. (2) Failure to evaluate surface composition — soft or waterlogged soil beneath vegetation is a known hazard in slope operations; the pilot should have looked for indicators like saturated color, depression marks from prior rain, or vegetation types associated with wet soil. (3) Single-pass reconnaissance — one pass from one direction cannot reveal all surface characteristics; multiple passes at different angles expose different hazards. (4) No ground truth — if operationally feasible, a hover-taxi to test the surface before full weight transfer (letting one skid touch lightly while maintaining collective) provides tactile feedback before committing full weight. (5) Cognitive bias — having committed to a slope landing, the pilot may have seen what confirmed his plan rather than actively seeking disqualifying hazards. The reconnaissance should include a slow low pass specifically over the intended skid contact points to evaluate surface color, texture, and vegetation indicators of soil stability.
questions.follow_up: Once the rollover begins with the upslope skid sinking, what immediate corrective action should the pilot take, and at what point does that action become no longer viable?
questions.follow_up_answer: The immediate corrective action is to apply downslope cyclic and increase collective simultaneously to lift the helicopter off the slope and fly away before the rotor strikes the terrain. This must be initiated the instant any unexpected movement or sinking is felt — before the rotor disc tilts to the point where blade-ground contact becomes geometrically inevitable. The action becomes non-viable when the rotor disc has tilted enough that blade strike is imminent (typically when the helicopter has rolled beyond approximately 5–8 degrees of unexpected tilt, depending on aircraft type and rotor clearance), because applying collective at that point accelerates blade strike rather than preventing it. Dynamic rollover progresses very rapidly — corrective action is measured in fractions of a second, which is why prevention through proper area assessment is the only reliable safeguard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations; Chapter 13, ADM — Error Chain and Decision-Making

questions.question: You are conducting a slope area review and the site looks acceptable, but you notice the grass on the slope is all bending in a consistent direction that does not match the reported surface wind. What risk does this create for your slope operation, and how does it change your reconnaissance requirements?
questions.answer: Grass bent in a direction inconsistent with the reported wind indicates a localized wind condition — most likely mechanical turbulence or a channeled valley wind caused by the terrain features of the slope itself. This creates the following risks for slope operations: (1) The actual wind direction at the landing spot may differ significantly from what you are experiencing at reconnaissance altitude, meaning your planned upwind approach heading may actually result in a crosswind or tailwind at the surface — altering the required cyclic tilt and skid geometry relative to the slope. (2) Rotor clearance calculations based on your approach wind assumption may be incorrect; a crosswind from the upslope direction is particularly dangerous because it pushes the rotor disc toward the terrain. (3) Localized turbulence can cause abrupt uncommanded movement during the low hover and landing sequence when power margin and control authority are most critical. Modified reconnaissance requirements: conduct the low pass directly over the grass-covered area while closely observing how your aircraft responds to wind shifts; assess the grass bend direction relative to escape routes and intended approach path; consider a different landing site if the wind at the surface cannot be reliably determined and planned for. The principle is that slope terrain creates its own micro-meteorological environment that surface visual cues can reveal — the pilot must interpret those cues rather than relying solely on reported or sensed winds at altitude.
questions.follow_up: If you confirm through low reconnaissance that the surface wind is indeed 30 degrees different from what you planned, how does that change the specific mechanics of how you will execute the slope landing itself?
questions.follow_up_answer: A 30-degree wind shift requires the pilot to reassess the optimal landing heading to achieve the best compromise between headwind component, upslope rotor clearance, and skid geometry. If the actual wind makes the planned approach a crosswind or quartering tailwind, the pilot must either select a revised approach heading that accepts more crosswind on the slope but maintains a headwind component, or identify a different slope face that aligns better with the actual surface wind. For the landing execution itself: cyclic tilt into the slope remains the same technique, but the pilot must be prepared for the rotor disc to weathervane with the crosswind component, requiring additional anti-torque pedal inputs to hold heading on the slope. Additionally, the crosswind from the upslope side increases the risk of rotor blade contact with terrain, so the pilot must maintain even more conservative clearance margins and be prepared to abort at the first indication that rotor clearance is insufficient for the actual wind conditions encountered.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations; Chapter 12, Mountain Flying and Terrain Effects

tasks.title: Task B. Straight-In Autorotation in a Single-Engine Helicopter

questions.question: The ACS requires a minimum entry altitude of 500 feet AGL for a straight-in autorotation. What is the primary reason this minimum altitude exists?
questions.answer: The 500-foot AGL minimum entry altitude exists to ensure the pilot has sufficient time and altitude to establish a stabilized autorotative glide, manage rotor RPM, select and align with a suitable landing area, and execute the flare and collective cushion before touchdown. Below this altitude, there may be insufficient time and rotor energy to safely complete the maneuver. It directly relates to the height-velocity (H/V) diagram, where low-altitude/low-airspeed combinations place the helicopter in a zone with inadequate recovery capability.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; ACS PH.XV.B Risk Management

questions.question: What does 'AGL' mean in the context of the 500-foot minimum entry altitude, and why is AGL used instead of MSL for this requirement?
questions.answer: AGL stands for Above Ground Level. It is used instead of MSL (Mean Sea Level) because autorotation performance and survivability are determined by the actual height above the terrain or landing surface — not above sea level. The critical factors during autorotation, such as time to complete the flare, distance to the ground, and rotor energy management, are all functions of true height above the surface. Using MSL could create a dangerously misleading reference if terrain elevation is significant.

questions.question: You are flying a practice autorotation at 600 feet AGL when your instructor calls a simulated engine failure. The wind is reported as 25 knots gusting to 40 knots. You are currently at the ACS minimum of 500 feet. Should you continue or abort? Explain your risk management reasoning.
questions.answer: You should abort or delay initiating the autorotation to a higher altitude. The ACS explicitly states that in strong wind conditions, a 'suitable higher entry altitude' above 500 feet AGL is required. At 600 feet AGL with gusts to 40 knots, the risks are compounded: gusty winds will cause rotor RPM fluctuations and airspeed instability, the flare timing will be harder to judge due to rapidly changing relative winds, and effective glide range will be unpredictable. A prudent decision would be to climb to a higher entry altitude — such as 800 to 1,000 feet AGL — before initiating the maneuver. This aligns with ADM principles: when conditions introduce elevated risk, adjust the plan rather than accept unnecessary hazard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; ACS PH.XV.B

questions.question: A student pilot wants to practice straight-in autorotations to a runway. The airport is at 4,500 feet MSL and the terrain around it is relatively flat. The student plans to begin the autorotation at 5,000 feet MSL, saying 'that gives me 500 feet above the airport.' What risk has the student potentially overlooked in this altitude calculation?
questions.answer: The student must measure the 500-foot minimum from the intended landing surface (AGL), not from an arbitrary reference. If the runway elevation is 4,500 feet MSL, then 5,000 feet MSL gives exactly 500 feet AGL above the runway — which meets the bare minimum. However, the risk overlooked is that 500 feet AGL is the absolute floor, and the student should also consider that obstacles, displaced thresholds, approach path hazards, or any terrain features between the entry point and the runway may be higher than runway elevation. Additionally, density altitude at 4,500 feet MSL will degrade rotor performance, meaning more altitude may be needed to safely complete the maneuver than at sea level. The student should apply conservative judgment and likely begin at a higher altitude.

questions.question: During preflight planning for autorotation practice, what factors related to the helicopter itself — not the environment — should influence your decision to use an entry altitude higher than the 500-foot AGL minimum?
questions.answer: Several helicopter-specific factors warrant a higher entry altitude: 1. Rotor inertia — helicopters with low-inertia rotor systems (lighter blades, smaller diameter) lose RPM faster after engine failure, requiring more altitude and time to stabilize the autorotation. 2. Aircraft weight — a heavier loaded helicopter has a faster rate of descent and requires more altitude to execute a controlled flare and cushion. 3. Autorotative glide ratio — some helicopters have a steeper descent profile, requiring more entry altitude to glide to a suitable landing area. 4. Pilot/aircraft currency — if the pilot is not recently current in the specific make and model, additional altitude provides a safety buffer. 5. Any abnormal rotor system condition or known high-drag configuration that increases descent rate.

questions.question: A pilot argues that because they have hundreds of hours of autorotation experience, 400 feet AGL is perfectly safe for entry, and the 500-foot AGL standard is just an arbitrary number. As an examiner, how do you respond, and what is the regulatory and safety basis for maintaining this minimum even for experienced pilots?
questions.answer: The 500-foot AGL minimum is not arbitrary — it is an established safety standard derived from the ACS that accounts for the worst-reasonable-case scenario, not average-case performance. Even for an experienced pilot, there are factors beyond skill that can make a sub-500-foot entry dangerous: rotor RPM may already be degraded before entry is initiated, wind shear near the surface can disrupt the flare, and mechanical anomalies (sticky collective, delayed recognition) compress reaction time further. The ACS minimum represents the boundary below which the margin for error becomes unacceptably thin even with good execution. More critically, checkride standards exist to evaluate pilots performing to a defined standard — the examiner's role is not to adjust minimums based on self-reported experience. The standard is the standard, and ADM principles require recognizing personal minimums versus regulatory minimums. An experienced pilot should have the judgment to know that 'I can probably do it' is not the correct risk management framework.
questions.follow_up: What specific rotor RPM-related hazard becomes most acute when an autorotation is initiated below 500 feet AGL at low airspeed, and why is it unrecoverable?
questions.follow_up_answer: The hazard is main rotor RPM decay to the point of rotor stall. When a helicopter is at low altitude and low airspeed, there is insufficient time and altitude to lower the collective, establish the autorotative descent angle, and allow upward airflow through the rotor disk to restore RPM before ground contact. Low-inertia rotor systems are especially vulnerable because blade RPM decays within seconds of collective being applied or engine failure occurring. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states explicitly that rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable — once RPM decays below the stall threshold, there is no corrective action that will restore lift before impact. This is the fundamental aerodynamic reason the minimum entry altitude standard exists.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (rotor stall discussion); ACS PH.XV.B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM)

questions.question: You are conducting a checkride and the applicant initiates a straight-in autorotation at exactly 500 feet AGL on a day with a direct 15-knot headwind. Midway through the maneuver, the wind suddenly shifts to a direct tailwind. Walk me through every risk that has now materialized and what the applicant's correct response should be.
questions.answer: A sudden wind reversal from headwind to tailwind during autorotation creates multiple simultaneous risks: 1. Airspeed — the helicopter's indicated airspeed will drop suddenly, which increases the AOA and can cause blade stall tendency; rotor RPM may decay if the pilot does not compensate. 2. Glide range — a tailwind dramatically increases groundspeed and ground track distance, likely overshooting the intended landing zone; the glide path becomes flatter relative to the ground but the touchdown point moves further away. 3. Flare effectiveness — the flare is designed to convert forward speed into rotor RPM and reduce groundspeed; with a tailwind, groundspeed is higher at flare initiation, meaning the flare must be initiated earlier and more aggressively, or the pilot risks a high-speed ground run or hard landing. 4. Energy management — the overall energy state has changed mid-maneuver, and the pilot may not have sufficient altitude remaining (starting from only 500 feet AGL) to fully adapt. Correct response: immediately assess whether the planned landing zone is still reachable; if not, select an alternate landing area; adjust airspeed to best glide for the new wind condition; anticipate a higher groundspeed at flare; be prepared for a running landing or wave-off if altitude permits. If altitude does not permit a go-around, commit to the adjusted landing with modified flare timing.
questions.follow_up: At what point in a straight-in autorotation does a tailwind present the greatest single hazard, and what specific control input error is most likely to occur as a result?
questions.follow_up_answer: The greatest hazard from a tailwind occurs during the flare phase. With a tailwind, groundspeed is substantially higher than in a headwind scenario. The most likely control error is a late or insufficient flare — the pilot may misjudge the flare initiation point because the visual approach cues (ground rush) are distorted by the higher groundspeed, leading to under-flaring. This results in insufficient rotor RPM recovery from the flare, excessive groundspeed at touchdown, and potential for the helicopter to touch down in a nose-low attitude with high forward momentum — creating risk of dynamic rollover, ground contact with tail boom or rotor blades, or loss of directional control on the ground.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; ACS PH.XV.B Risk Management

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation checkride task, when does an examiner-initiated go-around result in unsatisfactory performance?
questions.answer: An examiner-initiated go-around results in an unsatisfactory grade on the autorotation task only if the examiner called it specifically because the applicant cannot complete the maneuver within ACS tolerances. A go-around initiated by the examiner for other safety reasons (e.g., traffic, wind shear, surface hazard, or loss of landing area) does not automatically constitute unsatisfactory performance on that task; in such cases, the examiner may allow the applicant to re-attempt the maneuver.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-14 Helicopter ACS, Area XV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: Who has the authority to initiate a go-around during a practical test, and under what specific circumstance does doing so result in an unsatisfactory grade?
questions.answer: Either the examiner or the applicant may call for a go-around during a practical test. However, when the examiner initiates the go-around specifically because the applicant cannot complete the straight-in autorotation within the ACS-required skill tolerances — such as being unable to reach the intended touchdown point or maintain proper rotor RPM — that task is graded unsatisfactory. A go-around initiated for safety reasons unrelated to pilot error does not automatically fail the task.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-14 Helicopter ACS, Area XV, Task B; 14 CFR 61.43

questions.question: Name at least three skill element tolerances specified in the ACS for the straight-in autorotation that, if not met, could lead to an examiner-initiated go-around.
questions.answer: The ACS specifies the following skill tolerances for straight-in autorotation: (1) Maintain rotor RPM within the normal operating range throughout the maneuver; (2) Touch down within 100 feet of the designated landing spot; (3) Maintain a stabilized approach at the recommended autorotation airspeed ±10 knots; (4) Avoid dragging the tail rotor or main rotor blades; and (5) Perform a controlled touchdown with minimal lateral movement. Consistent failure to stay within any of these tolerances justifies an examiner-initiated go-around and an unsatisfactory grade.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-14 Helicopter ACS, Area XV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: You are on final approach in a straight-in autorotation during your checkride. You recognize early that your glide angle is too steep and you are going to overshoot the designated landing spot by a significant margin. What is your best risk management decision, and how does it affect your grade?
questions.answer: The best risk management decision is to verbalize the problem and initiate a go-around before the situation becomes a safety issue. If you initiate the go-around yourself because you recognize you cannot complete the maneuver within tolerances, the examiner will still likely grade the task unsatisfactory — because the go-around was a result of your inability to complete the task within specified tolerances. However, self-initiating the go-around demonstrates situational awareness and sound ADM, which the examiner should note. More importantly, attempting to salvage an overshooting autorotation by flaring aggressively or pulling collective prematurely risks rotor RPM decay, a hard landing, or exceeding aircraft limits — outcomes far worse than a re-fly. Safety always supersedes checkride performance.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-14 Helicopter ACS, Area XV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Chapter 13

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, an applicant consistently allows rotor RPM to decay below the normal operating range on approach. The examiner calls for a go-around each time. From an ADM standpoint, what is the root cause of this error chain, and how should the applicant break it?
questions.answer: Low rotor RPM during autorotation is typically caused by delayed collective reduction at entry, failure to maintain proper autorotation airspeed, or excessive use of collective during the flare and cushion phases. The error chain often starts at entry — if the pilot hesitates to lower collective aggressively upon simulated engine failure, RPM begins decaying and the deficit compounds throughout the approach. To break the error chain, the applicant must: (1) immediately lower collective to the full-down position at autorotation entry to allow upward airflow through the rotor disk; (2) maintain the POH-recommended autorotation airspeed, which optimizes rotor RPM and glide ratio; and (3) manage collective carefully during the flare and cushion to avoid over-pulling. The FAA notes that rotor stall in helicopters is unrecoverable, making early recognition and correction of low RPM critical.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-S-ACS-14 Helicopter ACS, Area XV, Task B

questions.question: A student tells you they plan to push through an autorotation that is clearly going to land short of the designated spot because they don't want to fail the checkride. How do you respond as their instructor, and what risk does this decision introduce?
questions.answer: This is a classic example of 'get-there-itis' or 'press-on-itis' applied to a checkride environment — allowing the desire to pass to override sound judgment. As an instructor, I would explain that attempting to stretch a short autorotation by pulling collective early sacrifices rotor RPM, potentially creating a low-RPM hard landing or rotor stall condition — neither of which is survivable at low altitude. The ACS task will already be unsatisfactory if tolerances are not met; the only question is whether the unsatisfactory outcome comes with property damage or injury. The correct risk management decision is to go around early, accept the unsatisfactory, and demonstrate to the examiner that you recognize when to abandon a deteriorating approach. Examiners value safety judgment; a student who pushes an unsafe approach to avoid a grade has demonstrated exactly the kind of poor ADM that warrants a failed checkride regardless.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-S-ACS-14 Helicopter ACS, Area XV, Task B
